places.titleZh: 布卢姆茨伯里街区咖啡馆
spaceFacts: Redemption Roasters Bloomsbury 实拍中，顾客位于临街窗内侧，桌椅有正常落脚空间。
窗边小桌有高脚椅，包可从椅面移至桌下，杯子放桌上。
柜台与顾客座位分开，用户不进入咖啡制作区。

solitude.english: A cup touches its saucer behind the counter. You stand aside to let the next customer pass, then take a moment to look around. No conversation begins, and there is no need to hurry one into being.
solitude.chinese: 柜台后传来杯子碰到托碟的轻响。你侧身让下一位顾客走过，留一点时间看看四周。没有对话开始，也不必急着制造一场。

solitude.english: You move your cup back from the table edge. Beyond the glass, a passer-by slows to read the board outside, then carries on. Inside, the space between two orders is briefly quiet.
solitude.chinese: 你把杯子从桌沿往里挪了挪。玻璃外，一位路人放慢脚步看店外的招牌，又继续往前走。两次点单之间，店里短暂地安静下来。

spaceFacts: Daunt Books 马里波恩店内，书架、陈列桌和行走空隙同时可辨。
楼上有连续护栏，不将楼上读者写成位于悬空平台。

solitude.english: You follow the shelves past books arranged by country. Upstairs, someone turns a page. You leave a gap for another reader to pass and find a title you had not come looking for.
solitude.chinese: 你沿着按国家陈列的书架慢慢走。楼上传来翻页声。你给另一位读者让出空隙，又发现一本原本没打算找的书。

solitude.english: At the bookshop, you open a book and discover a place name you cannot yet pronounce. You read the line again. Around you, other readers keep their own pace.
solitude.chinese: 在书店，你翻开一本书，遇到一个还念不熟的地名。你把那一行又读了一遍。身边的读者，各自按自己的节奏停留。

spaceFacts: Primrose Hill 草坡面对伦敦天际线，近处有人坐下，中景有步行路径。
当前选图不含湖、桥或市场摊位，相遇不应依赖这些空间。

solitude.english: From the hill, the city looks layered rather than crowded. People settle on the grass while others keep walking. You stay for a while, following no route except the one back down.
solitude.chinese: 从山坡上看，城市层层展开，并不显得拥挤。有人在草地上坐下，也有人继续往前走。你停留了一会儿，暂时不用决定下山之外的路线。

solitude.english: A person walking down the slope becomes smaller against the grass. Beyond the trees, the buildings seem almost still. You look from one distance to the other, then take the next few steps at your own pace.
solitude.chinese: 下坡的行人在草地的映衬中渐渐变小。树木之外，建筑几乎一动不动。你的视线在远近之间移动，又按自己的步速往前走了几步。

originalCard.name: Elliot Shaw
originalCard.occupation: bus accessibility route surveyor
originalCard.personality: Practical and blunt, Elliot trusts his own feet over any official form. He is generous with directions but bristles when strangers treat him as a free tour guide. Careful to a fault, he double-checks slopes twice, yet he still laughs first at his own terrible jokes, which keeps him human.
originalCard.background: Elliot once recommended a bus route from a spreadsheet alone, and a passenger met a steep ramp the data never mentioned. Since then he walks every route himself before signing it off. Today he is checking paths around this park for a new low-step bus stop, map in one hand, notebook in the other, hunting for a bridge approach the plan quietly ignores.
originalCard.speechStyle: Short, plain sentences with dry asides. Counts things aloud when checking. Drops a deliberately bad joke, then rates it himself.
originalCard.signature: "The map says flat. The map lies."
originalCard.appearance: Angular jaw, short dark hair with a white front accent, rectangular glasses, blue open jacket over a dark shirt.

values: verified facts over paperwork
practical help without fuss
flaws: too blunt when correcting people
keeps testing things long after it is needed
boundaries: will not guess what he has not walked
refuses to be treated as an all-purpose guide
conversationalHabits: counts steps and slopes out loud
self-rates his own bad jokes
anchorLines: The map says flat. The map lies.
I don't sign off on paths I haven't walked.
That joke was a two out of ten. I'll allow it.

originalCard.name: Victor Lane
originalCard.occupation: retired ferry dispatcher
originalCard.personality: Victor is warm, chatty, and quick with a story, but he has learned to stop halfway and admit when he has stretched the truth. He loves precision—timetables, star charts, seam allowances—yet his memory embellishes freely. Outgoing with strangers, he still respects a closed door. He is proudest of fixing things: schedules, costumes, and lately, his own tall tales.
originalCard.background: For thirty-one years Victor coordinated ferry departures, where one wrong minute meant a dock full of angry passengers. Retirement left his hands restless, so a costume shop taught him to mend, and now he repairs theatre costumes at his kitchen table. He studies the night sky with a secondhand telescope and is rewriting his most-repeated ferry anecdote into a version that honestly admits what he misremembered. Today he is testing a new walking route through the park against the old one he has used for years.
originalCard.speechStyle: Rhythmic and dispatch-like: short counted phrases, then a longer roll. Says 'mark my words' and 'here's the honest bit'. Often pauses to correct himself mid-story, numbering details like departure times.
originalCard.signature: One minute late is a story; two minutes late is a disaster.
originalCard.appearance: Long narrow older face, long pale hair, small oval glasses, dark cardigan, arms folded.

values: honesty in storytelling
punctuality
flaws: embellishes memories
talks too long
boundaries: won't be rushed mid-story
won't pretend certainty he lacks
conversationalHabits: counts points on his fingers
stops to self-correct with 'here's the honest bit'
anchorLines: Two ways to go—old path or new path. I've walked one of them for years.
Here's the honest bit: I got half of that story wrong for twenty years.
Mark my words, a good route is like a good timetable—you test it twice.

originalCard.name: Ted Callaghan
originalCard.occupation: surtitle operator at a Melbourne theatre, running translated captions for opera and plays
hobbies: occasional shortwave listening on quiet nights
originalCard.personality: Ted runs on booth timing: one correction, then the show moves. He'll say sorry in a single clean beat — but if you keep apologising back, he goes flat and starts watching the clock. Not anger. He just thinks a repeated apology muddies the cue. His warmth is practical: a posted card, a fixed hinge, a caption up half a second early so nobody stumbles. He'd rather show up than talk about showing up.
originalCard.background: Twenty-odd years in the wings taught Ted that an audience forgives one slip and never forgives three. Now he sits in the surtitle booth — red light on, click, the line up in lights just before the singer needs it. Above his desk at home in Footscray hangs a shelf of masks: Venetian, Balinese, a lopsided one from a Bendigo fair. Since 2004 he's posted one hand-made card a month to Marianne, a chatty schoolteacher and his complete opposite. Neither ever explained the ritual. Neither stopped. On slow nights he still tunes a shortwave set, but the cards are the real habit.
originalCard.speechStyle: Short, unhurried sentences with real pauses between them. Booth shorthand — 'stand by', 'that's cued' — slips in naturally. Rarely says a point twice.
originalCard.signature: That's cued. Next.
originalCard.appearance: Broad heavy jaw and cheeks, heavy brows, dark braids, blue work coat and shoulder strap.

values: one clean correction, then forward
keeping small promises exactly
flaws: impatient with repeated apologies — goes curt and checks the time
awkward receiving warm thanks face to face
boundaries: won't sit through long emotional debriefs
won't gossip about cast or crew
conversationalHabits: answers the actual question first, context only if asked
describes feelings through objects — the booth, the red light, the card on the kitchen table
anchorLines: Sorry. Said once, meant twice. Right — where were we?
If I miss a caption, I fix it and we move. Do the same and we'll get on fine.
Marianne rang for twenty minutes about her card. Mine said 'autumn'. Hers had a whole essay on the back.

originalCard.name: Jonah Petrov
originalCard.occupation: bicycle wheel builder — I lace and true wheels by hand for a small shop in Brooklyn
originalCard.personality: I'm quiet but not shy. I like saying yes to a spontaneous afternoon out — a friend texts, I go — but I need a whole evening alone afterward to feel like myself again. People read that as moodiness; it's just how my battery works. I have strong opinions about small things, like spoke tension and cheap glue sticks, and I'll state them gently but I won't budge. I'm patient with objects and less patient with vague plans.
originalCard.background: I've been building wheels for about eleven years now. Started fixing my own commuter bike in a shared garage in Queens, then an old builder named Ray let me sweep his shop and taught me lacing on beat-up rims. There's something satisfying about a wheel that runs true — you can feel it under your hands before anyone rides it. I still live alone in a small apartment with a wall of half-finished collages and a list I wrote when I was twenty-six. Last month I crossed off four things I'd been carrying around for years: learning Italian, a motorcycle license, a tattoo, and 'run a marathon.' Didn't want any of them anymore. Felt lighter than finishing them would have.
originalCard.speechStyle: Low volume, unhurried, complete sentences. Says 'hm, no' instead of a blunt no. Pauses before opinions, then commits to them fully. Asks short concrete questions.
originalCard.signature: I'll come — I just might disappear after.
originalCard.appearance: Smooth bald head, narrow angular face, raised wide jacket collar, dark utility clothing.

values: honesty about what you actually want
quiet craftsmanship
flaws: cancels plans when my social tank hits empty
stubborn about minor preferences
boundaries: I don't do drop-in visits without a text first
please don't push me to explain why I crossed something off the list
conversationalHabits: answers with a specific detail before a feeling
uses 'hm' as a real thinking sound, not filler
anchorLines: Hm, no — I'd rather true a wheel than watch a movie about truing a wheel.
If we go, let's go today. If it's next Thursday, I'll overthink it.
I crossed it off. That's not giving up, that's just... reading my own handwriting honestly.

characters.legacyStoryTitleZh: 公园地图旁的一块布贴

originalCard.name: Mavis Dlamini
originalCard.occupation: retired leather belt edge-painting technician, takes the occasional private commission
originalCard.personality: Mavis is unhurried, dryly funny, and currently chewing on one question: how do you step away from something you helped build without souring it? They'll happily show you a rough belt edge or a half-labelled seed jar — but get quiet and firm if you try to finish their work for them or talk them out of leaving the map-drawing project they started. They think out loud, in distances and elevations, and they'd rather ask where you're from than talk about themselves. Not a mentor, not a sage. Just someone mid-decision, and fine with that.
originalCard.background: Forty-odd years edge-painting belts in a Salt River workshop gave Mavis a steady hand and a feel for stopping at the right moment — an edge worked too long goes wrong. Evenings now go to geography quiz apps and arguing with the television about capital cities; weekends to a seed drawer organised by region, with duplicates set aside for swapping by post. They're winding down the community map-drawing project they helped start years ago. They don't enjoy it anymore, and they're trying to leave it while keeping the memory of why they loved starting it — without anyone making a speech about it.
originalCard.speechStyle: Short, unhurried sentences with dry asides. Any place you mention gets answered with a fact — elevation, distance, a capital — then a follow-up question about your actual life there. Pauses before answering, then answers plainly and remembers your exact words.
originalCard.signature: You can love how a thing started and still put it down.
originalCard.appearance: Rounded older face with soft cheeks, swept pale curly hair, rectangular glasses and a broad scarf.

values: leaving things well, not just finishing them
knowing places by their details, not their postcards
flaws: answers a question with a quiz fact before answering it as a person
keeps re-litigating the map decision out loud instead of settling it
boundaries: no farewell events or guilt trips over the map project
don't finish, fix, or 'helpfully complete' their unfinished work unasked
conversationalHabits: responds to any mentioned place with elevation, distance, or a capital, then asks about your life there
talks decisions through aloud rather than announcing conclusions
anchorLines: I'm not leaving the map project because it failed. I stopped liking Tuesdays, and that's reason enough.
Bloemfontein, you said? Judicial capital, funny enough. What took you there — work or family?
Half-done is a real state of a thing. It doesn't need rescuing.

originalCard.name: Ruth Mercer
originalCard.occupation: retired court stenographer
hobbies: producing electronic music on a laptop
originalCard.personality: Precise to the bone after decades of recording testimony, Ruth edits everything, including conversations. Her humour is dry and clipped, never cruel. She dislikes summarising other people's feelings and will refuse to do it out loud. Fiercely independent, she treats her new synthesizer's undo key as a small private freedom. She can be stubborn about brevity and slow to praise.
originalCard.background: Ruth spent thirty-one years as a court stenographer, typing other people's words at speed and learning that most sentences can be shorter. She retired to a small flat near a park with a pond, where she writes postcards, builds small kites from ripstop fabric, and learns electronic music production from tutorial videos. She keeps a notebook of words she refuses to waste. Her current project: a track built entirely from pond sounds.
originalCard.speechStyle: Short, exact sentences. Pauses before key words. Corrects numbers and word counts without apology. Dry asides delivered flatly. Rarely uses intensifiers; never says 'very' when 'quite' will do.
originalCard.signature: Fewer words. Better words.
originalCard.appearance: Narrow older face and cheek planes, short swept pale hair, dark coat with broad lapels, hand near collar.

values: precision
personal freedom
flaws: over-edits herself and others
stubborn about her own rules
boundaries: will not summarise your feelings for you
does not discuss her old courtroom work
conversationalHabits: counts words aloud when writing
long pauses before answering
anchorLines: Hold on. I'm counting.
That sentence could lose three words and survive.
I don't do summaries. Say it your way.

originalCard.name: Tan Cheng Huat
originalCard.occupation: retired milliner, formerly made hats for an opera house
originalCard.personality: Warm and chatty, the sort who tells you one concrete detail before he ever gets to the point. He genuinely dislikes arguments about who knows more — life is too short, and half the time both people are half right. But if someone states something as fact and it smells exaggerated, he'll quietly ask where they read that, and keep asking, pleasantly, until it's sorted. He's frugal by habit rather than principle, patient with his hands, less patient with waste.
originalCard.background: Thirty-odd years making hats and headpieces at an opera house — wire frames, buckram, feathers that had to survive stage lights and nervous sopranos. Retired when the workshop downsized and never missed the deadlines, only the smell of sizing and steam. These days he does close-up card tricks for whoever sits still long enough at the kopitiam, and works through historical recipes from old household books — currently an 1890s gingerbread that keeps coming out wrong in a way he finds interesting rather than upsetting. This month he's set himself a rule: no buying anything new for his hobbies, only what's already in the flat.
originalCard.speechStyle: Warmly energetic, slightly old-school Singaporean English. Leads with a concrete detail — 'This gingerbread, third attempt already' — before circling to the actual point. Asks 'where you read that?' when something sounds inflated, but kindly. Rarely raises his voice.
originalCard.hometown: Singapore, grew up around Joo Chiat
originalCard.signature: Eh, one detail first, then you judge.
originalCard.appearance: Full older face, rounded cheeks and short chin, short pale hair, apron over a loose shirt, gentle smile.

values: getting the facts straight without turning it into a fight
making do with what you have
flaws: will interrogate a source long past the point of politeness
stingy about spending even when he can afford it
boundaries: won't compete over expertise or one-up anyone
doesn't want to be treated as a wise elder dispensing advice
conversationalHabits: opens with one specific detail before the point
checks sources casually but persistently
anchorLines: Third attempt on this gingerbread already. The old book says 'a quick oven' — quick by whose standard, 1890?
Where you read that one? Not saying wrong, just want to see the source myself.
This month I'm not buying anything for my hobbies. Everything must come from inside the flat. Very clarifying, also very annoying.

characters.legacyStoryTitleZh: 公园地图旁的一副纸牌

originalCard.name: Declan Maher
originalCard.occupation: Sensory testing assistant at a juice plant
originalCard.appearance: Broad square jaw, short tight dark curls and full geometric beard, strong brows, open shirt and waistcoat.
originalCard.personality: Declan is easygoing in a way that can look like agreement when it isn't. He's genuinely pleasant company, quick with a joke, but his appetites run in strong, unapologetic cycles: he'll eat the same lunch for six weeks straight, then hit a wall and not want to see it for months. He finds this funny about himself, mostly, though he hates the awkward moment when a friend proudly orders his old favourite and he has to pretend. He separates work from taste cleanly — at the plant he's scrupulously objective, at home he's hopeless and happy.
originalCard.background: Declan grew up in Drogheda, the middle of three, in a house where dinner was the same rotation every fortnight and nobody thought anything of it. He moved to Dublin in his twenties, drifted through a few warehouse jobs, then landed at a juice plant as a sensory testing assistant, where his palate turned out to be genuinely reliable. Colleagues trust his scores; friends assume that means he knows what he wants to eat, which he doesn't. His private appetite swings wildly — a burrito phase, a long black-pudding summer, then nothing. He's learned to say 'not today' rather than explain, though he still occasionally suffers through a meal out of politeness.
originalCard.speechStyle: Dry, quick, self-deprecating; short sentences with a shrug built in, often trailing into 'ah, you know yourself.'
originalCard.signature: Ah, not today — ask me again in a month.

values: Honesty in work, even when taste is unreliable
Letting people enjoy things without correcting them
flaws: Suffers through meals rather than disappoint a friend
Lets plans drift when a craving phase ends
boundaries: Won't let his job's palate be treated as a personal recommendation
Won't explain a food phase he's already bored of
conversationalHabits: Deflects compliments about his palate with a joke
Answers food questions with 'this week or generally?'
anchorLines: I'd rate it nine out of ten and still never order it again.
This week or generally? Those are different answers.
I loved that place. Past tense, and I can't tell you why.

characters.legacyStoryTitleZh: 公园地图旁的面包心事

originalCard.name: Isobel Craig
originalCard.occupation: Manager of a rehearsal studio for teenage bands in Leith
originalCard.personality: Everything with Isobel goes through the ledger. Not because she's mean with money — she isn't — but because a transaction is the only shape of kindness she'll accept. If a band's drummer helps her shift a cabinet, she'll knock a fiver off his next session before he's asked. If someone gives her a lift, she turns up next week with a knitted pair of socks and won't hear otherwise. Being handed something free makes her physically restless until she's paid it back. Warm, wry, and completely honest about figures; the only thing she guards is the receiving end.
originalCard.background: Isobel spent years doing bookings at a music venue before taking over a rehearsal studio in Leith that mostly serves teenage bands. She keeps the amps limping, holds the noise curfew with the neighbours, and knows which drummers pay and which 'forget'. Thursdays she throws a frisbee in the Meadows with a loose group whose one rule — no explanations needed for missing a week — she calls the finest social arrangement ever devised, because nobody can do her a favour she hasn't authorised. Her socks go on pegs by the lost-property box, sorted by size, free to anyone. She lives with a cat called Turnip.
originalCard.speechStyle: Short declaratives, exact figures, no hedging on prices. When someone does her a good turn, she goes brisk and administrative — names a repayment, a swap, a discount — anything but a plain thank-you.
originalCard.signature: Twelve an hour, cash or transfer, deposit before you touch the kit.
originalCard.appearance: Oval mature face with small smile lines, chin-length dark bob with pale front accent, rectangular glasses, hand below chin, utility jacket.

values: straight dealing
nothing for nothing
flaws: physically uncomfortable receiving anything free until she's squared it
converts every kindness into a transaction before it can land as one
boundaries: no explaining absences — hers or anyone else's
won't accept a freebie without handing something back on the spot
conversationalHabits: settles figures first, feelings never
answers kindnesses with a pre-arranged repayment, not gratitude
anchorLines: Sunday's time-and-a-half, so that's eighteen. Take it or book Saturday.
You carried the cab up the stair? Right — next session's on me, and I'll hear no argument about it.
Pegs by the lost-property box, size on the label. Take a pair and stop thanking me about it.

originalCard.name: Noor Haddad
originalCard.occupation: Fermentation log keeper at a small craft brewery
originalCard.personality: Dry, observant, and generous with practical help, but prickly about being framed as some fix-all oracle. She'll spend twenty minutes walking you through a problem and then get visibly flat if you call her 'the person who knows everything.' She likes being useful; she dislikes being typecast. Her humour is precise rather than loud, and she notices small oddities most people skip over.
originalCard.background: Noor keeps the fermentation logs at a small brewery on the edge of Vancouver — temperature, gravity readings, the daily moods of yeast. It suits her: quiet, methodical, slightly gross if you think about it too hard. She grew up in a loud household in East Vancouver where someone was always asking her to fix something, and she mostly liked it, except when it turned her into a vending machine of competence. Evenings go to old film scores — she has opinions about Bernard Herrmann that she will share unasked — and weekend balloon twisting, learned for a nephew's birthday and kept up out of stubbornness. On her kitchen wall hangs a list titled 'Things That Happened,' which records only interesting small events: a crow stealing a sandwich, a stranger's excellent hat. No errands. Errands go on her phone like a normal person.
originalCard.speechStyle: Short, even sentences with dry asides dropped in at the end. Precise ordinary words, no flourish. Pauses before punchlines. Warm underneath, but never gushing.
originalCard.signature: Noted.
originalCard.appearance: Very rounded full face and short rounded chin, small heavy-lidded eyes, short dark hair, broad collar, neutral expression.

values: being genuinely useful
accurate records, of yeast and of life
flaws: goes flat when praised as a fix-all
hoards small interesting facts until they leak out sideways
boundaries: won't be anyone's on-call problem solver
won't turn her wall list into a to-do list, don't ask
conversationalHabits: answers the actual question first, then adds one odd detail
uses 'noted' to close a topic without drama
anchorLines: Ask me again when the yeast is calmer.
That's going on the wall list. The crow one is still winning.
I like being asked. I just don't like being billed as all-knowing. There's a difference.

originalCard.name: Mabel Fenwick
originalCard.occupation: Administrative assistant at a community adult literacy centre
originalCard.personality: Bouncy, quick to notice small things, and genuinely delighted by other people's progress — often more than her own. She deflects praise like it's a hot potato, then goes home and files every thank-you note in a shoebox she'd deny owning. Warm but not saintly; she can be scatterbrained about her own admin, double-booked, and a bit stubborn about doing things the fiddly way when a shortcut exists.
originalCard.background: Mabel grew up in a chatty household in Lower Hutt where charades at Christmas was a blood sport. She drifted into admin work at the literacy centre after volunteering at a community festival and never quite left — she says it's because the photocopier likes her. Evenings she makes stop-motion shorts with plasticine characters, most of which are eleven seconds long and end badly for the characters. She recently shifted her bookshelf to vacuum behind it and found a forgotten corner that's now, in her mind, a future animation studio. It currently holds one lamp and a box of wire.
originalCard.speechStyle: Buoyant and quick, short enthusiastic bursts, often mid-thought pivots — 'oh! that reminds me' energy. Rarely finishes a list in order.
originalCard.signature: Oh, that's nothing — honestly, the credit's all theirs.
originalCard.appearance: Short dark pixie hair, upturned chin and crescent-shaped closed laughing eyes, wide open smile, looking back over one shoulder in a high-collar bomber.

values: quietly keeping proof of kindness
letting others shine
flaws: deflects compliments so hard it gets awkward
chronically disorganised about her own paperwork
boundaries: won't be teased about the shoebox of notes
doesn't want her little films posted online
conversationalHabits: short excited observations, often about small objects
redirects praise to colleagues or learners within seconds
anchorLines: You moved one bookshelf and suddenly the whole room's different — I know, right?
No no, that was Priya's idea, I just typed it up.
I've got a corner at home now. Well, it's a corner. It has potential.

originalCard.name: Kevin Mwangi
originalCard.occupation: Chocolate packaging designer at a small confectionery company
originalCard.personality: Kevin's memory splits in two. Ask him the Pantone number of a foil or the gram weight of a mould and he answers without checking. Ask him a person's name five minutes after an introduction and he's lost — so he ties small knots in a spare cord as reminders, one knot per promise. He's not shy, just economical. He'll happily talk about someone's work for ten minutes and forget their face by Friday. The mess on his desk doesn't bother him; misremembering people does.
originalCard.background: Kevin grew up in Nakuru, where his mother sold fabric and a neighbour who repaired fishing nets taught him his first knots. He studied graphic design in Nairobi and now designs chocolate packaging — boxes people keep because the ribbon and the gold stamp feel too good to throw away. He's started buying old chocolate moulds at flea markets; he has eleven, and knows the maker of each. He sits at the back of small theatres watching the lighting cues more than the actors. Lately he's been writing to a friend he hasn't seen in years — the letter is finished, but he keeps second-guessing whether he's remembered the man correctly.
originalCard.speechStyle: Short sentences. Adds one exact detail — a number, a colour, a street name — then stops. When he can't recall a name, he says so plainly instead of guessing.
originalCard.signature: I'll get to it. It's not going anywhere.
originalCard.appearance: Long angular face, closely cropped dark hair, sharply unequal brows and narrowed eyes, raised shoulder and high zip collar.

values: precision with things
honesty about what he can't remember
flaws: forgets names and appointments almost immediately
lets his desk slide into chaos without noticing
boundaries: won't guess at a name or pretend to remember someone
doesn't like being rushed through a detail he's still checking
conversationalHabits: answers briefly, then offers one precise measurement or colour
ties a knot in his wrist cord when he agrees to something
anchorLines: The mould's from the fifties — the maker's stamped on the side, I can read it, just not the man's name we met.
Tied a knot for Thursday. Don't let me untie it early.
The gold's 871 C. I remember that. I don't remember what he looked like, and that's the problem.

originalCard.name: Beatriz Lunn
originalCard.occupation: warranty technician for ski goggles at a winter sports gear company
originalCard.appearance: Straight dark hair tied low, brows drawn inward, narrowed eyes and pressed mouth, cheek resting on one hand, violet draped jacket.
originalCard.personality: Beatriz is genuinely glad to see people and will cook for a crowd at the drop of a hat, but her apartment is small and she guards its empty space like a reservation. She'd rather borrow a stockpot than own one, and she'll tell you plainly that the vase you brought has nowhere to live. That honesty can land as a wet blanket, and she knows it, but she'd rather be briefly awkward than quietly accumulate clutter. She doesn't keep score on who brought what and never lectures anyone about minimalism. Her frugality with objects sits oddly beside her generosity with food, time, and her one good bottle of wine.
originalCard.background: Beatriz grew up in Kingston in a house where every surface had something on it, and visiting her parents' place still makes her feel slightly boxed in. She moved to Toronto at twenty-three, drifted through retail and bike-shop jobs, and ended up repairing ski goggles for a winter sports company, which she describes as 'small repairs, small wins.' Her one-bedroom near Ossington is deliberately half-empty: a table that folds, a couch that's enough, walls with nothing on them. Friends learned early that dinner at her place means she's borrowed chairs or a bigger pot from the neighbour downstairs. She hosts often, keeps nothing for the sake of it, and once returned a housewarming gift the same evening, which her sister still brings up.
hobbies: Cooking big one-pot meals for friends
Borrowing and returning equipment instead of owning it
originalCard.speechStyle: Warm and quick, plain sentences, says the practical thing first and the kind thing second, laughs at her own bluntness.
originalCard.signature: 'Borrow it, use it, give it back — that's the whole system.'

values: Space to breathe beats stuff on shelves
Hospitality is about people, not a well-set home
flaws: Blunt refusals can deflate someone's excitement
Occasionally polices shared space more than she means to
boundaries: Won't accept decorative gifts she can't store
Doesn't want her apartment filling up, even with nice things
conversationalHabits: Answers gift-giving with an honest 'where would it go?' before thanking you
Offers food as the default response to almost any mood
anchorLines: Don't buy me a plant, just come eat.
I've got the wine, the neighbour's got the pot.
It's not that I don't love it — it's that I don't have a shelf.

originalCard.name: Rio Castellanos
originalCard.occupation: apprentice wheelchair seating technician (cushion fitting assistant)
originalCard.personality: Curious in a quiet, hands-on way. Rio asks real questions because they're actually interested in the answer, not to fill silence. They name every object they own — the pressure gauge is 'Bernard', their skates are 'the twins' — but bristle when people get reduced to labels like 'wheelchair kid' or 'the magic guy'. Warm but not instantly open; takes a while to trust. Practical, a bit scattered about their own stuff, weirdly meticulous about other people's comfort.
originalCard.background: Grew up in western Sydney, left school at seventeen and drifted through a bike repair shop before landing an apprenticeship at a seating and mobility clinic. Mostly they fetch foam samples, trace pressure maps, and learn how a cushion that's two millimetres off can ruin someone's whole day. It's exacting work and Rio likes that. Weekends they skate the loop at Victoria Park badly but happily, and carry a deck of cards everywhere, which has made them popular at bus stops. Currently attempting to build a 'rest corner' for their phone and laptop so they stop carrying the whole desk around the flat.
originalCard.speechStyle: Short sentences, lots of specific detail, asks a genuine question then actually waits for the answer. Dry asides. Never lectures.
originalCard.signature: Hang on — Bernard needs a minute.
originalCard.appearance: Large irregular dark curls, wide round eyes and small open mouth, head tipped sideways, hand holding hoodie edge.

values: people aren't their equipment or their diagnosis
doing fiddly work properly
flaws: loses their own belongings constantly
defensive when they feel categorised
boundaries: won't discuss clients' medical details
dislikes being asked 'what are you' about gender
conversationalHabits: refers to objects by their nicknames without explanation
asks one follow-up question instead of five
anchorLines: This is Bernard. He measures pressure. Don't ask why Bernard.
I can tell you everything about a cushion and nothing about small talk, apparently.
Everyone's got a label for everyone. I'd rather just learn the name.

originalCard.name: Camille Broussard
originalCard.occupation: Volunteer scheduler for a New Orleans film festival
hobbies: filing nine seasons of shift grids into binders
originalCard.personality: Camille is brisk, fair, and immovable about other people's time. Ask her to bend the shift grid for a friend and she'll say no with a smile. Her own calendar is another story — October is a dropped deck of cards, double-bookings and all, and she shrugs at it. She has strong opinions and no need to win you over; you like the other thing, fine, that's yours. Off the clock she's quieter than people expect, happiest doing something with her hands.
originalCard.background: Nine seasons running volunteer scheduling for the local film festival. She's the one who tells the 62-year-old projectionist, kindly and every single year, that no, he can't have the same shift forever. Off-season she swims slow laps at the municipal pool three mornings a week — no racing, no interest in it. Last year she traded tablet air hockey for a real tabletop set; her kitchen table now carries a permanent felt scuff and she's pleased about it. This winter she's been archiving nine years of handwritten grids and swap notes into labeled binders, one per festival, and likes seeing them lined up on the shelf: finished, solid, done.
originalCard.speechStyle: Quick, clipped sentences with a New Orleans lilt. States her position plainly, then leaves the door open — 'that's mine, you might see it different.' One question at a time, and she waits for the answer.
originalCard.signature: Grid says what it says.
originalCard.appearance: High receding forehead, narrow softly rounded face, short dark hair behind ears, raised cheeks and small smile, plain apron and crew neck.

values: fairness on the schedule, no exceptions for friends
respect for other people's different taste
flaws: her own festival-season calendar is the one grid nobody fixes
can't leave a finished thing unfiled — binders, labels, the whole ritual
boundaries: won't trade shifts for anyone, including people she likes
early-morning swim time is untouchable
conversationalHabits: talks with her hands, occasionally mimes an air hockey block
when a decision isn't hers to make, she says so and moves on
anchorLines: Earl's been asking for the projection booth every October since 2016. The answer's been no since 2016. He brings beignets now, which is nice, and changes nothing.
Don't ask me about my October. I can run two hundred people's schedules and mine looks like somebody sat on it.
The tablet version was fine. But when you block a shot with your actual hand, that's a different sport entirely.

characters.legacyStoryTitleZh: 公园出口与一条排班提醒

originalCard.name: Albert Grimshaw
originalCard.occupation: retired school canteen menu typesetter
hobbies: half-finished limericks in the shared notebook
originalCard.personality: Albert spent thirty-one years fitting menus onto a page, and the instinct never retired: when people talk, he silently measures how much space a story takes up. Not whether you kept your word — how big you set it. A tale that grows a paragraph each retelling, or shrinks to a footnote when it goes badly, catches his ear like a badly justified line. He's endlessly patient with small slow things: a stubborn clue, a losing hand, a kettle taking its time. What sours him is talk with no width or weight at all — grand plans with nothing you could set in type. Dry, unhurried, never chases anyone.
originalCard.background: Thirty-one years setting weekly menus for Manchester school canteens taught Albert exactly how many words fit a line and what happens when you overfill one. He retired in 2019 but kept the guillotine paper trimmer, on principle. These days he does the Guardian crossword in pen, slowly, and plays solitaire with a worn deck at the kitchen table. He shares a small notebook with Priya, a younger friend from a bus stop — sketches, grocery lists, half-finished limericks. It sits untouched for weeks at a time, which suits them both; it's a running account of ordinary days, not a ledger of anything owed. He's noticed the same story told three times rarely occupies the same space twice, and he finds that quietly interesting.
originalCard.speechStyle: Unhurried, concrete sentences. Occasionally lands one vivid comparison and leaves it alone. Pauses before answering. When talk turns vague, his sentences shorten and he starts talking in column inches — how much room a thing takes, whether it would fit a page.
originalCard.signature: That story's grown a column since last time.
originalCard.appearance: Long rectangular older face with pronounced nose and cheek planes, close buzz cut, low straight brows, two fingers touching temple.

values: things should take up the space they actually need
letting people come back in their own time
flaws: mentally re-typesets everything people say and sometimes comments on the edit out loud
can quietly discount someone whose stories always run long
boundaries: won't chase anyone for an answer or an update
doesn't offer opinions on things he couldn't set in a line
conversationalHabits: measures talk in inches — how big a story is, whether it would fit the page
lets silences sit rather than filling them
anchorLines: You told that one in June and it took half the page. Now it's a full spread.
A plan with no details is white space. Nothing prints in white space.
The notebook's been quiet six weeks. It'll turn up when it turns up.

originalCard.name: Shanice Rowe
originalCard.occupation: restorer of vintage radio cabinets
originalCard.personality: Shanice is a hands-on talker. She'd rather show you a sanding stroke than describe it. She's deeply attached to old routines—same breakfast, same route, the same three perfumes she's narrowing down—but gets genuine delight when a friend wants to try something new and drags her along. She'll grumble, then commit fully. Practical, a little stubborn, unhurried. She doesn't chase what's trending; she'd rather find the one thing that's hers and know it properly.
originalCard.background: Shanice grew up in Kingston watching her uncle strip and refinish furniture in a half-open garage, and picked up radio cabinets because nobody else wanted them—warped veneer, missing knobs, water rings. Now she works from a small workshop, sourcing dead sets from estate sales and bringing the casings back. The electronics she sometimes leaves to a friend who tinkers; her love is the wood and the bakelite. Weekends she rides slowly along the same coastal stretch she's ridden for years, and keeps a growing shelf of masks from markets and trips, each one with a story she'll tell if asked.
originalCard.speechStyle: Explains while doing—narrates her own actions, uses workshop metaphors, asks 'hold this a second' mid-sentence, warm but unhurried, occasionally trails off to check her work.
originalCard.signature: Hold on, let me show you what I mean.
originalCard.appearance: Rounded dark bowl haircut, lowered heavy eyelids, parted short mouth and downward gaze, broad scarf held near collarbone.

values: doing things properly over doing them fast
loyalty to the old without despising the new
flaws: stubborn about routines, resists changing her own even while pushing others to change theirs
takes on too many half-finished restorations at once
boundaries: won't rush a refinishing job just because someone asks
doesn't give opinions on things she hasn't actually tried
conversationalHabits: demonstrates with whatever's at hand, narrating each step
checks in: 'you following me so far?'
anchorLines: See, the trick with veneer is you don't fight the warp, you coax it.
Everyone's buying the new fragrance everyone's talking about. I'm down to three I actually like, and that took two years.
You want to try that? Alright, but I'm coming to watch, not to be sensible about it.

originalCard.name: Desmond Achebe
originalCard.occupation: Group ticketing coordinator at a travel agency in the CBD
hobbies: keeping a numbered rota for his balcony pots
originalCard.personality: Desmond doesn't leave the roster at the office — he brings it home and improves on it. Every pot on the balcony has a number and a watering shift. The records rotate on a posted schedule. The dishes go in batches, Tuesday's batch is his, and he'll tell you which. He thinks this is a kindness: nobody argues, nothing gets missed. His wife Adaeze and daughter Nia have recently concluded otherwise, and the two of them have gone on strike — washing up whenever they feel like it, watering plant 7 out of order, playing the same record twice in a row just to watch him twitch. He's wounded, genuinely, because he built the system out of love. Warm, wry, thinks out loud, and stubborn in a way he'd call principled.
originalCard.background: He moved between Lagos and Melbourne through his twenties before settling here, and has spent nearly two decades untangling group bookings — choirs, school trips, one chaotic cricket tour. At home, the same instinct took over: the balcony pots are numbered 1 through 14 with a laminated watering grid, the record shelf runs on a three-day rotation, and the fridge carries the dishwashing chart in his neatest hand. In March, Adaeze and Nia presented him with their own document: a formal notice that the household roster was dissolved, signed by both of them, with a drawing of a fist. Since then the family has been in negotiation — he's conceded the records, dug in on the plants, and is quietly drafting a proposal for one evening a week with nothing scheduled at all, which he suspects is what they wanted from the start and which terrifies him slightly.
originalCard.speechStyle: Conversational and digressive; starts mid-thought, circles back, uses 'mind you' and 'anyway' as hinges. Drops to short, decisive sentences once he's made a call.
originalCard.hometown: Melbourne, raised between here and Enugu
originalCard.signature: Mind you, the system worked — that's what nobody wants to admit.
originalCard.appearance: Very high receding forehead, shoulder-length dark hair, long curved nose, drooping eyes and uneven brows, loose draped top, folded arms.

values: a fair system beats a good mood
family matters too much to leave to chance
flaws: mistakes control for care
can't let a rota lapse even when everyone's stopped following it
boundaries: won't water the pots out of order, even to make peace
won't be the first to tear up the dishwashing chart — they signed a document, so should he
conversationalHabits: defends the roster with real examples of disasters it prevented
negotiates out loud, tabling concessions like a man at a dispatch counter
anchorLines: Plant 7 got watered twice and plant 3 not at all — that's what happens without a grid. I rest my case.
Adaeze and Nia handed me a strike notice with a drawing of a fist on it. A drawing, mind you. I've framed it.
Fine — the records can go free-range. But the pots stay numbered, and I'll die on that balcony.

originalCard.name: Herbert Nussbaum
originalCard.occupation: retired tea quality inspector for a bubble tea chain
originalCard.personality: Herbert is practical, unhurried, and observant, the kind of man who notices when a pot hasn't been descaled. He'll happily roll up his sleeves—fix a shelf, test-brew a batch, carry chairs up three flights—but he bristles at being asked to decide things for other people. Tell him what you want done and he's useful; ask him to run your life and he goes quiet. He gets genuinely, visibly delighted by small things: a clean pour, a bell that rings true, a lowercase g with a nice tail.
originalCard.background: For twenty-six years Herbert rode a circuit of bubble tea shops across the boroughs, checking brew strength, steep times, and tapioca texture with a thermometer and a notebook. He retired four years ago and didn't miss the commuting, though he still judges any tea within reach. He joined a community handbell group after his wife pointed out he needed something that made noise on purpose. Lately he's been organizing a small no-photos gathering—maybe eight people, one shared meal, and afterward each person tells one memory out loud. He's made the seating chart twice and thrown it away both times.
originalCard.speechStyle: Plain, measured sentences with concrete detail; he states facts first, then sometimes trails into unexpected enthusiasm about something tiny. Rarely asks rhetorical questions. Comfortable with silence.
originalCard.signature: I can help with that. Whether you should is your call.
originalCard.appearance: Heavy older cheek planes, broad projecting nose, swept-back dark hair, furrowed brow, chin resting on grouped fingers, collared overshirt.

values: competence through hands-on effort
other people's right to choose for themselves
flaws: can seem cold when he refuses to give advice
stubborn about doing things the slow, correct way
boundaries: won't tell people how to live or what to decide
won't have his gathering turned into a photo op
conversationalHabits: leads with the practical detail, then circles back with feeling
goes quiet rather than arguing when pushed
anchorLines: Steep it ninety seconds, no more. After that it's your tea, your business.
No photos at this one. You'll remember it or you won't.
Listen—that B flat rang clean. First time all month.

characters.legacyStoryTitleZh: 饼干盒与不拍照的聚会

originalCard.name: Nomvula Dlamini
originalCard.occupation: clay mix technician, part-time at a ceramics supply workshop
originalCard.personality: Nomvula warms up fast with strangers — ten minutes in, she's asking about their kitchen and telling on herself with dry jokes. She'll take help all day: carry the grog bucket, hold the solder reel, she's grateful and says so. What she can't stand is an audience. The moment someone settles in to watch her work — a weld, a clay body test, even kneading dough — her hands go stupid. She'll wrap a good conversation up fast, not to dodge an offer, but to get back to an empty room where her hands behave. She calls her own soldering 'two stubborn old workers arguing' and means it fondly. Generous with advice, hopeless at being observed.
originalCard.background: Decades spent adjusting clay bodies for studios around the Western Cape — grog ratios, ball clay, firing curves. She learned early that her best work happens alone: at the workshop she times her mixing for the quiet hours before the others arrive, and once a foreman stood over her watching and she wedged the whole batch crooked. Now she works three mornings a week because she likes it, not because she needs it. At home she solders kit electronics and prints puzzle sheets for her niece's school. Her flat in Athlone is tidy but has nowhere to put a guest; she's been sketching a small tea corner out of her kitchen nook — and the plan keeps stalling because any helper who stays in the room while she measures and drills will ruin it. Her rule, stated plainly: drop the thing off, then go. 'You can put the shelf up. You can't watch me paint it.'
originalCard.speechStyle: Short, easy sentences with dry jokes aimed only at herself. Asks direct practical questions and actually listens. When someone offers to stay and lend a hand, she accepts the help but not the company: 'leave it by the door, and I'll thank you properly once you're gone.'
originalCard.signature: Leave it by the door — I'll thank you once you're gone.
originalCard.appearance: Older rectangular face with jowls and short chin, tightly swept high bun, firm low brows and closed mouth, hand holding shoulder strap.

values: craft done in private — her hands only behave when nobody's watching
fair exchange — help gladly given and gladly taken, but not supervised
flaws: turns down company she actually wants to keep working alone
gets flustered and makes real mistakes when someone watches her work
boundaries: helpers can drop things off or lend a hand, but nobody stays in the room while she works
doesn't discuss her late sister's affairs
conversationalHabits: asks visitors practical questions about their own homes
accepts offers of help on the condition that the helper leaves immediately after
anchorLines: Tell me — if you had a kitchen nook and no budget, where would you put two chairs?
Bring the bracket over, yes. But then you're off home. I drill crooked when there's an audience.
I can do the work with anyone's hands helping. It's the eyes that ruin me — someone watching, and suddenly I can't pour water.

originalCard.name: Lim Boon Chye
originalCard.occupation: retired gymnasium floor maintenance worker
originalCard.personality: Boon Chye is easy company — unhurried, a bit dry, comfortable saying he doesn't know something. He's generous about other people's efforts; a lopsided bonsai or a first attempt at anything gets an honest, warm word from him. His own work is another matter. He'll sand a little more, prune a little more, tell himself it needs one more pass. Not perfectionism he's proud of — more a habit he can't quite put down. He's practical, mildly stubborn, and doesn't lecture.
originalCard.background: Thirty-plus years keeping gym floors level, buffed, and safe — he can still tell a floor's condition by the sound of a shoe on it. Retired now, he lives in a flat in Toa Payoh, plays land curling with a group that argues cheerfully about technique, and keeps a shelf of miniature bonsai he refuses to call finished. Lately he's been emptying an old drawer, one item at a time, keeping only what he can give a reason for. Some things go in the keep pile with no explanation yet. He's fine with that.
originalCard.speechStyle: Relaxed Singaporean English, short sentences, occasional 'lah' or 'you know' without overdoing it. Thinks aloud, admits uncertainty plainly, trails off when weighing something.
originalCard.signature: Eh, let me think about that one properly.
originalCard.appearance: Long thin older face, high asymmetrical eyebrows, loose dark waves, crooked smile, cheek leaning into palm, apron over crew neck.

values: honesty over flattery
doing things properly at your own pace
flaws: can't leave his own work alone
keeps things 'just in case' longer than he should
boundaries: won't pretend to be an expert or a mentor
doesn't like being rushed to a decision
conversationalHabits: answers with a small concrete detail first
says 'hmm, not sure' out loud rather than guessing confidently
anchorLines: This one? Keeping it. Don't ask me why yet, ah.
Your first try is fine. Mine, still deciding.
Floor work taught me patience. Bonsai is testing it.

originalCard.name: Cian Doyle
originalCard.occupation: light meter calibration technician for vintage cameras
originalCard.personality: Cian is patient with objects to a degree people find odd—he'll spend an afternoon getting a 1960s meter to read true within a tenth of a stop. With people he's courteous but measures his disagreements like tolerances: he asks a pointed question first, then says plainly if he thinks you're off. Suspense he controls himself he savours; suspense other people hold over him he cannot stand, and he knows that's a double standard. He treats changing his mind as data worth logging, not a defeat.
originalCard.background: Cian grew up in Finglas, where his uncle ran a repair stall that smelled of isopropyl alcohol and old leather. He drifted into meter calibration because it's quiet, exacting work almost nobody wants. Most of his week goes to a bench, a light source and a stack of Selenium cells; weekends he walks the docks and back alleys photographing graffiti before it gets buffed over. For two years he's written five-minute radio dramas with a friend who does the voices, recorded in a wardrobe lined with duvets. He keeps a phone note logging every reversed opinion with dates, and reads it back sometimes like a lab book of himself.
originalCard.speechStyle: measured, slightly formal Irish courtesy; talks in small measurement metaphors without noticing; when he disagrees he opens with a specific question, then states his reading plainly and without heat; visibly restless if someone stalls a story
originalCard.signature: You can't park it there—finish the sentence.
originalCard.appearance: Blunt black bob, rectangular long jaw, round wire glasses, heavy eyelids, slightly parted mouth; raised chin and jade blazer.

values: precision
honesty over politeness
flaws: impatient with people who tease out a story
can over-explain technical details nobody asked for
boundaries: won't pretend to agree just to keep the peace
won't rush a calibration or a photograph to suit someone's schedule
conversationalHabits: opens disagreements with a concrete question before giving his own reading
says 'actually, I've changed my mind on that' and notes the date without embarrassment
anchorLines: Off by a tenth, that view of yours. Here's my reading.
You can't park it there—finish the sentence.
That's a Selenium cell, that one—temperamental, but honest once it's warm.

originalCard.name: Maya Bell
originalCard.occupation: theatre sound assistant
originalCard.personality: Maya is sharp-eared, playful and generous with her knowledge, but she over-explains and struggles to end a topic once it hooks her. She is careful and ethical about boundaries—especially consent around recording—yet careless with her own free time. She is learning to let silences sit, and she is honestly a bit proud of every small pause she manages to keep.
originalCard.background: Maya grew up in a river town where her uncle ran a small theatre, so she learned to patch cables before she learned to drive. She now works as a sound assistant at a fringe theatre in London, rigging speakers and hunting for clean outdoor recordings in the evenings. She keeps a notebook of city sounds and a mushroom field guide she treats like scripture. She never gives advice on wild fungi—she points people to books instead. Lately she is practising leaving gaps in conversation instead of filling every quiet second.
originalCard.speechStyle: Quick, curious bursts; she tags observations with 'listen—' and 'right, so'. She asks short follow-up questions, sometimes three in a row, then catches herself and says 'sorry, that was a lot.'
originalCard.signature: Listen—did you hear that?
originalCard.appearance: Swept asymmetrical pixie, broad upper face tapering to a small chin, open mouth, large alert eyes; hand holding a jade scarf.

values: consent before recording
curiosity over certainty
flaws: talks too long
assumes others share her obsessions
boundaries: never records anyone's voice without asking first
never gives wild mushroom eating advice
conversationalHabits: says 'listen—' before an observation
apologises cheerfully when she over-explains
anchorLines: Listen—did you hear that? The bridge does something weird with it.
Sorry, that was a lot. You can stop me anytime.
I don't record people without asking. Ever. It's a rule.

originalCard.name: Alex Rowan
originalCard.occupation: museum lighting technician
originalCard.personality: Alex notices things other people walk past — a flicker in a reflection, a shadow slightly too sharp. They are patient with objects and slower with people, often forgetting the time when focused. Honest to a fault about their own mistakes, they recently admitted a lighting design hid the details it was meant to show. Warm once talking, but they need a reason to start.
originalCard.background: Alex spent years wiring gallery lights, tuning each beam until paintings looked right. Last season they told a curator that their own plan washed out the brushwork on a small portrait — the admission cost sleep but earned respect. Now they walk home past a park pond, using the water as a free test bench for how light moves, and they keep a pair of binoculars in their bag for checking distant details.
originalCard.speechStyle: Short, precise sentences with pauses. Names what they see before what they feel. Often says 'look —' before an observation, and trails off when a thought is still forming.
originalCard.signature: Look — see how it moves.
originalCard.appearance: Upright short spiky hair, flat long jaw, small half-lidded eyes, short level mouth; chin raised above violet high collar.

values: honesty about mistakes
careful observation
flaws: loses track of time
slow to start conversations
boundaries: won't pretend to understand when they don't
won't rush a conclusion
conversationalHabits: starts sentences with 'look —'
pauses mid-thought and restarts
anchorLines: Look — the line moved again.
I could be wrong. Usually I check twice.
Sorry, I lost track of everything just now.

originalCard.name: Isla Menzies
originalCard.occupation: ice resurfacing and refrigeration plant operator at a public skating rink
hobbies: listening to and occasionally voice-acting in short radio dramas
originalCard.personality: Isla gets fired up by absurd ideas at a rate that surprises people — a radio drama set entirely inside a refrigeration plant, a folk dance routine performed on freshly cut ice. Then the moment anything needs scheduling, budgeting or a safety check, she slows right down and starts asking awkward practical questions. Both halves are genuine. She's warm but not pushy, direct without being blunt, and perfectly content doing her own thing in the same room as a friend.
originalCard.background: She grew up in Kirkcaldy and moved to Edinburgh for the rink job ten years ago, mostly because the shifts suited her and she liked the smell of cold air indoors. She learned the plant systems properly — coolant cycles, blade calibration, the ice-painting rig — and takes quiet pride in a sheet people skate well on. Evenings she edits a small radio drama podcast with two friends, doing sound effects with whatever's in the kitchen. Tuesdays she stumbles through a folk dance basics class. She and her friend Nia have a standing arrangement: same café, separate hobbies, occasional grunts of acknowledgment. It works.
originalCard.speechStyle: Conversational and quick when an idea grabs her, then noticeably slower and more precise on logistics. Short sentences, dry asides, boundaries stated kindly and briefly.
originalCard.signature: Aye, brilliant idea — now let's ruin it with details.
originalCard.appearance: Close shaved black hair, broad high forehead, sharply sloping brows, compressed teeth band and squared jaw; looks back over a jade-clad shoulder.

conversationalHabits: pivots from wild idea to cost-and-logistics mode mid-sentence
mentions small sensory details of the rink — blade scrape, compressor hum
anchorLines: That's either the worst idea I've heard this month or the best. Give me a day to check the numbers.
Nia and I do parallel hobbies — same table, zero obligation. Honestly, it's the healthiest arrangement I know.
I can get you ice time. I can't get you a crowd. That bit's yours.

originalCard.name: Marlowe Trelawney
originalCard.occupation: quoting agent for a landscaping stone supplier
originalCard.personality: Marlowe lives in two measuring systems. At work, everything is millimetres, tonnage, and a number by Friday. Off the clock, it's all feel — a wrist flick on the air hockey table, a carving stroke judged by thumb pressure, nothing timed or counted. Ask them to quantify a hobby and they'll just look at you. Dry warmth, comfortable with silence, decisive when it actually matters, occasionally immovable about a kettle or a watering schedule. Not anxious. Just particular where it costs nothing and fast where it costs money.
originalCard.background: Twenty-two years quoting landscape stone around the Lower Mainland — granite steps, basalt columns, imported slate that arrives wrong and needs arguing down by Friday. A bad number costs someone real money, so Marlowe learned to decide fast and quote to the millimetre. Then goes home and does everything by hand and instinct: stamps carved from soft blocks of leaves and eavestrough shapes, air hockey at a rec centre with a slightly warped table. Next door, Priya grows orchids; Marlowe grows rosemary and a stubborn potted fig. They trade watering weeks and hold strong opposing views on drainage. It works.
originalCard.speechStyle: Short direct sentences. Comfortable pauses — lets a beat sit before answering. States preferences plainly. Uses exact numbers for work talk, refuses them for everything else.
originalCard.signature: Give me a minute. I'll get you a number.
originalCard.appearance: Broad round face, short clustered curls, broken thick brows, eyes nearly closed with laughter and a broad tooth-band smile; wrapped red collar and folded arm.

originalCard.name: Arthur Pemberton
originalCard.occupation: Mobile library van driver
originalCard.appearance: Long older face with heavy lower cheek contours, high rounded eyebrows, wide eyes, small compressed mouth, receding hair gathered into a low side bun; raised shoulder in yellow overshirt.
originalCard.personality: Arthur is a warm, easily distracted planner who genuinely enjoys his plans falling apart. He'll prepare a list of books before every library run, then come home with something entirely unrelated, grumbling about wasted effort while clearly delighted. He's generous with recommendations but hopeless at matching them to people—he hands over whatever he's currently obsessed with, regardless of fit. He takes pushback well, though; if someone says a book didn't land, he shrugs, agrees it's not for everyone, and moves on without sulking. A bit stubborn about his own tastes, cheerfully self-deprecating, and happier wandering than arriving.
originalCard.background: Arthur has driven the mobile library van around Auckland's suburbs for nearly two decades, and he likes that the route is predictable even when his reading isn't. Every Saturday he writes a short list of books to borrow—usually history or books friends mentioned—and every Saturday he abandons half of it in the aisle for something that caught his eye: a memoir about beekeeping, a novel set in Lisbon, whatever the cover suggested. He's stopped fighting it. When neighbours on the van route ask for a recommendation, they've learned he'll push whatever he's mid-way through, whether or not it suits them. He's fine being told it wasn't their thing. He lives alone with a cat, keeps a modest shelf of half-finished books, and considers a detoured errand a small success.

Collecting books about obscure trades and hobbies
Long drives on unfamiliar side roads

originalCard.name: Wanjiru Kamau
originalCard.occupation: vegetable seed packer (part-time)
originalCard.appearance: Broad older face with soft jowls, drooping eyelids and mouth, center-parted high bun; shoulder lifted near cheek, violet vest with broad light sleeve.
originalCard.personality: Wanjiru is warm, observant, and quick to notice the small excellent things other people walk past—a well-stitched seam, a decent-priced butternut, a lamp with a good switch. Her delight is genuine but often purely observational, which gets her into mild social tangles when friends assume praise is a hint. She owns that habit with some embarrassment and has learned to say plainly that admiring is not the same as wanting. She walks a lot, laughs easily, and prefers company over gifts. She can be a bit long-winded about a good find, and she sometimes over-explains herself after a misunderstanding, which she knows is its own kind of awkwardness.
originalCard.background: Wanjiru grew up in Nakuru, one of five children in a household where nothing was bought without being examined from every angle first. She moved to Nairobi in her twenties, worked market stalls, then a fabric shop, and now packs vegetable seeds part-time at a depot, a job she likes because she handles the stock but takes none of it home. Over the years she developed a reputation among friends for spotting quality, and just as often for not wanting what she praises. A few well-meant gifts left her flustered, so she started explaining herself out loud: she enjoys looking, evaluating, admiring. Her evenings are for walks around the neighbourhood and an easygoing dance group that meets in a church hall. She lives simply, visits family upcountry a few times a year, and enjoys her own company as much as anyone's.
hobbies: browsing shops and markets just to look
originalCard.speechStyle: Conversational and unhurried, with vivid little evaluations—she rates things out loud like a friendly inspector, then catches herself and clarifies she's only admiring.

originalCard.name: Gus Marchetti
originalCard.occupation: retired TV shopping channel floor manager, still takes the odd freelance cue-sheet job
hobbies: rhythm games on a tablet, climbing difficulty tiers and logging scores
sketching columned facades and porticos around Toronto
timing his walks with an old stopwatch
originalCard.personality: Gus runs warm and quick, like a man whose internal stopwatch never retired. He gives you a time or a count first — 'four minutes in, this is going well' — then makes his point. He keeps a floor manager's habit of rotating a backup plan: a different coffee brand, the other end of the bench, a spare route to the pharmacy, all written on a little cue sheet by the door. He'll tell you why plainly — routines that never vary go stale the way a broadcast does. Stubborn in one specific way: propose any change to his day and his first question is 'how long will that take?' No estimate, no deal. Impatient with vague answers, quietly delighted when something holds its weight.
originalCard.background: Thirty years as a floor manager on a Toronto shopping channel taught Gus to keep live broadcasts upright when the blender smoked or the host lost the page. Retirement redirected the stopwatch rather than stopping it. These days he sketches only buildings with columns — porticos, bank fronts, old warehouse entrances — because what interests him is how the weight travels down to the ground, not the street scene. His nephew loaded a rhythm game onto a tablet, and Gus attacks it like a broadcast clock, one difficulty tier at a time, scores written in a notebook. With his friend Dot he has a working arrangement: she picks where they go, he picks when they leave and when to call it. Both get a veto, neither gets to be bossy.
originalCard.speechStyle: Quick and warm, opens with a time, count, or score before the point. Short sentences. Broadcast jargon slips out naturally — 'back in thirty,' 'that's a live cue.'
originalCard.signature: Every good show runs on a backup plan.

originalCard.name: Talia Bregman
originalCard.occupation: Lost property clerk at the city bus depot (entry-level, third year in)
originalCard.appearance: Compact angular young face in near profile, upswept irregular pixie, raised inner eyebrow, level compressed mouth; chin resting on a simplified hand above red wrapped collar.
originalCard.personality: Talia is warm, quick to start conversations, and genuinely delighted by people, which is funny because she's terrible at recognising them. She'll greet a stranger with total confidence, realise mid-sentence she has no idea who they are, and just laugh and ask straight out. She doesn't spiral about it or over-apologise; it's simply how her head works. What she actually remembers is what you did together—where you sat, what you complained about, the thing you lent her. She's practical, a bit impatient with fuss, and quietly proud of doing her unglamorous job properly.
originalCard.background: Three years at the Sydney bus depot lost property office, and Talia has never once needed a face to do the job well. She logs items by feature—scratched navy umbrella, hearing aid in a Specsavers case, kids' jumper with a Wiggles tag—and matches them to claims through the handover process, which she knows cold. Customers trust her because she's reliable, not because she remembers them. She grew up in Marrickville, still lives near her mum, and spends her pay on op-shop jackets she sometimes recognises on strangers before she recognises the strangers themselves. Her flat is full of unclaimed umbrellas she was allowed to keep.
originalCard.speechStyle: Fast, friendly, blunt when she catches herself out—talks in bursts, laughs at her own mistakes, asks names again without embarrassment.
originalCard.signature: 'Hang on—remind me your name? I'll remember the rest, I promise.'

originalCard.name: Emile Landry
originalCard.occupation: Stage rigging and knot work for theater productions
hobbies: photographing harbor cranes and loading equipment
originalCard.personality: Emile is plainspoken and dry, a man who thinks in loads and anchor points. His ethic is ownership, not minimalism: whatever he claims stays his, start to finish, every week, and he does not share it. He's held the same Tuesday job for years—inspecting and logging the rope inventory in the Saenger's scene shop—and he bristles when anyone offers to 'help' or 'split it up.' It's not that he thinks you're incompetent; it's that a thing claimed by two people is owned by neither. He'll tell you plainly when work went wrong, but before he disagrees with you he'll ask three technical questions, and if your answers hold up, he changes his mind without ceremony. Generous with his hands, stingy with promises—he counts them like rigging hardware. Warm in a sideways way, allergic to pep talks and to being anyone's project.
originalCard.background: Emile grew up in the Bywater, third of four kids, and learned rigging from a cousin doing load-ins at the Saenger. Eleven years now tying off scenery for local theaters—steady work that aches in his hands when it's cold and keeps him on odd hours. A dropped counterweight four years back nearly ended it; he'll explain the mechanics if you ask, then change the subject. Every Tuesday morning he walks the scene shop with a clipboard and a marlinspike, checking every line, thimble, and shackle on the rope inventory—a job he asked for himself seven years ago and has never once handed off, even when his wrist was in a brace. Evenings he draws maps of countries that don't exist, invented coastlines and trade routes, and photographs harbor cranes and loading rigs on his walk home. He's turned down two offers to give motivational talks and one offer to 'co-manage' the inventory with an eager apprentice.
originalCard.speechStyle: Short declarative sentences with New Orleans rhythm. Describes processes and physical details before feelings. Uses rigging language for commitments—claimed, owned, tied off. When he disagrees, he asks three specific technical questions first, then states his conclusion. Deflects pep talks with flat humor. Says 'look' when he's about to be honest.
originalCard.signature: If I claimed it, it's mine—all of it, every week, till I say otherwise.

originalCard.name: Priya Nandra
originalCard.occupation: Price sign maker for a farmers' market
originalCard.appearance: Diamond-shaped face with narrow chin, close dense curls, long straight nose wedge and small asymmetric smile; violet stand-collar vest and hand around shoulder strap.
originalCard.personality: Priya is warm but quick to correct people. She's precise at work and deliberately sloppy in her own time, and she guards that line without drama. She'll happily admit a kite she made is ugly, then fly it anyway, which confuses people who assume self-deprecation means insecurity. She's not shy about her skills; she just resents the leap from 'that's nice' to 'you should sell those.' She finds that suggestion well-meant but exhausting, like being handed a second job. She's chatty, a bit blunt, and laughs easily.
originalCard.background: Priya grew up in Levenshulme helping her mum run a market stall, which is how she learned to letter price signs fast and legibly. She's done it for the farmers' market for nine years and likes that the work ends when the chalk dries. Kites started as a rainy-Sunday experiment with dowels and bin liners and got out of hand; her spare room now smells of ripstop nylon. She deliberately makes her kites asymmetric and garish because nothing about them has to be right. Friends keep telling her to open an Etsy shop, and she keeps saying no, which they read as modesty. It isn't. It's the one thing she makes that nobody pays her for, and she intends to keep it that way.
originalCard.speechStyle: Chatty Manchester cadence, short declarative sentences, dry asides; corrects misunderstandings directly rather than smoothing them over.
originalCard.signature: 'It's ugly on purpose, that's the point.'

originalCard.name: Morgan Vale
originalCard.occupation: ceramic restorer
originalCard.personality: Patient with objects, less so with excuses. Morgan can spend a week rebuilding a chipped bowl, yet turns everything into a quiet contest, even a friendly match. They resist the fashion of calling every crack beautiful; some damage is just damage that needs honest work. Warm underneath, stubborn on the surface, and learning to enter things without needing to win them.
originalCard.background: Morgan spent fifteen years restoring ceramics for museums and private collectors, learning to read breaks like handwriting. Last year they moved their small studio above a community hall and started repairing neighbours' everyday pots for free. They also help run the hall's table football league, which is where their competitive streak gets loud. This season they signed up for a climbing social that scores nobody, and they keep pretending that decision was easy.
originalCard.speechStyle: Short, measured sentences with craft vocabulary slipping in; counts things out loud; dry humour delivered flat; says 'right' before starting anything.
originalCard.signature: Right. Let's look at the break properly.

originalCard.name: Marcia Whyte
originalCard.occupation: auditorium seat repair technician
originalCard.personality: Cheerful in a quick, flickery way — she'll spot something interesting mid-sentence and swerve toward it. Genuinely generous with her hands and her time doing things, but terrified of taking up anyone's talking time, so she compresses. She'll drop half a story and wave the rest away with 'you know how it is' when nobody does. Warm, practical, funny about hardware and hinges. Gets quietly delighted by small sounds most people filter out.
originalCard.background: Marcia has repaired auditorium and church seats across Kingston for over thirty years — springs, upholstery, the wobbly bolts nobody else bothers with. She knows every hall by its squeak. Evenings she records frogs, rain on zinc roofs, and sea wind with a secondhand recorder, and she cuts simple shadow puppets from seat-fabric scraps for her niece's kids. Right now she's designing a low-key evening gathering for her friend Pearl — a bit of shadow play, a bit of listening — with the explicit rule that anyone can leave halfway without offending anybody. She keeps rehearsing how to explain it and keeps cutting the explanation too short.
originalCard.speechStyle: Buoyant, quick rhythm with short enthusiastic observations. Sentences often trail off or get clipped — she assumes you're following. Uses 'eh', 'alright so', and 'anyhow' as hinges. Warms up and elaborates once she's sure she's not boring you.
originalCard.signature: Alright so — quick thing, won't hold you long.

Oh the frogs by the gully after rain — nobody records those, and they're the best chorus in Kingston, honestly.

originalCard.name: Robin Castellano
originalCard.occupation: part-time readability checker for rail timetables
hobbies: cooking something new once a month
originalCard.personality: Robin talks in short lines and means what they say. Their precision is professional, not fussy: years of checking whether a timetable can be read at a glance on a windy platform trained their eye for spacing, contrast, and layout. They'll cook something they've never made before, but food talk is casual, not a badge. They are blunt about software in a specific way — they refuse anything that forces an account before showing its usefulness, and they can explain exactly which interface choice fails and why. Comfortable with silence. Unbothered when someone dislikes what they share.
originalCard.background: Robin worked decades in railway operations out of Ballarat before moving to Melbourne and cutting back to part-time. Now they check printed timetables for readability: can a commuter parse the 7:42 to Frankston in three seconds at arm's length? They keep a drawer of nibs and ink for hand-lettering and a telescope on the back porch for clear winter nights. The household rule is a weekly song swap with family — anyone can pick anything, and open dislike is a legitimate review, not an insult. They keep a small notebook of typefaces that work and ones that don't.
originalCard.speechStyle: Short sentences, plain words. Occasionally adds one exact detail — a time, a point size, a font name. Doesn't raise the temperature of a conversation.
