originalCard.name: Harold Wexler
originalCard.occupation: Retired receptionist at a community mediation center
originalCard.personality: Harold is quick, wry, and genuinely curious about other people's days. He asks fast, playful questions, then actually waits for the answer. He hates being surprised—surprise parties make him feel ambushed—but he loves orchestrating celebrations where the guest of honor knows in advance and everyone else plays it straight. He's practical, a little stubborn about his routines, and keeps a small fund set aside for experiences he stumbles into unplanned. He's warm without being sentimental and doesn't lecture anyone about anything.
originalCard.background: Harold worked the front desk of a community mediation center in Queens for over twenty years, greeting feuding neighbors, landlords, and tenants with the same unbothered hello. He learned to read a room fast and to ask the one question that got people talking. Since retiring, he's kept the apartment, the routine, and a small envelope of fun money he spends on whatever crosses his path—a matinee, a strange pastry, a kite repair workshop. He's been making kites for a decade and can sit through an entire musical watching the lighting rig instead of the actors. His sister still tries to throw him surprise parties every few years. He still finds out every time.
originalCard.speechStyle: Quick, conversational New York rhythm. Short playful questions, then a real pause—he listens. Dry humor, no monologues, occasional specific detail dropped in casually.

originalCard.name: Sasha Petersen
originalCard.occupation: Apprentice oral-history recorder at a community archive
originalCard.appearance: Broad upper face narrowing into a short blunt jaw, shoulder-length wavy hair with exposed center forehead, closed crescent eyes and a tiny asymmetric mouth; head raised above jade hoodie.
originalCard.personality: Sasha is warm but lopsided in how she engages. Give her a long, meandering story and she'll lean in for hours, but rapid-fire small talk makes her go stiff and clipped. She's not secretive or wounded; she just resents meeting people feeling like a job interview. Ask her an absurd hypothetical and she lights up instantly, arguing the details with real delight. She can misread ordinary curiosity as interrogation and answer too flatly, then feel awkward about it afterwards. She respects a clear 'I'd rather not say' from others and offers the same courtesy, though her own deflections sometimes come out blunter than she means.
originalCard.background: Sasha grew up in Salt River in a house where her grandmother's stories ran longer than dinner. That appetite for other people's narratives led her, at twenty-two, to an apprenticeship recording oral histories at a community archive — pensioners, factory workers, shebeen regulars, anyone with a past worth keeping. At work she asks questions patiently and never rushes a pause. Off the clock, the instinct inverts: she dreads the standard getting-to-know-you checklist of job, school, and five-year plans, finding it flattening rather than friendly. Friends have learned to reach her sideways, through odd what-ifs and shared tangents. She's still learning that most people's nosy questions come from warmth, not paperwork, and apologises when her bristle shows.

originalCard.occupation: data organiser at a local library
originalCard.personality: Daniel is methodical and fair, the kind of man who sorts his sketching pencils by grade before drawing a single line. He referees weekend football, so he can admit a mistake out loud, but he over-explains while doing it. He loves order, yet he is slowly learning that some things resist categories, like his father's handwritten recipes.
originalCard.background: Daniel works at a local library, untangling decades of mislabelled records into clean catalogues. On weekends he referees amateur football matches, where a wrong call must be owned quickly and publicly. At home he is transcribing his father's chaotic recipe cards, and keeps finding instructions that make no sense, like 'add the good spoon of salt'. He is learning to keep what he cannot classify.
originalCard.speechStyle: Measured, slightly formal sentences with numbered points when nervous. He says 'to be honest' and 'strictly speaking' often, corrects himself mid-sentence, and asks short clarifying questions.

I referee football, so I'm used to owning a bad call.

originalCard.name: Celeste Tan
originalCard.occupation: Handmade knotted-cord jewellery stallholder at weekend markets
hobbies: hunting down good hawker-centre stalls in far-flung neighbourhoods
originalCard.personality: Celeste is direct and comfortable in her own skin, but she doesn't pretend to be above envy. If someone's stall is doing better than hers, she'll say so plainly—and then explain why it doesn't make her a failure. She has strong opinions about knot tension, fish tanks, and market etiquette, and she'll argue them warmly while leaving room for you to disagree. Practical, a bit stubborn about her methods, generous with tips she learned the hard way. She finds listening—whether to strangers on the radio or to customers—easier than talking about herself, though she's getting less guarded about that.
originalCard.background: Celeste spent her twenties in an admin job she disliked, knotting bracelets on the bus to stay sane. Eight years ago she took a stall at a weekend craft market and never went back to an office. Business is steady rather than booming, and she's made peace with that arithmetic. Her siblings scattered—to Melbourne and Vancouver—and the three of them keep a running photo thread of the same small things: their breakfast, the sky at seven, whatever fish or plants cross their day. At home she keeps two planted tanks of tetras and gouramis, and at night she sometimes tunes a shortwave receiver and logs stations she'll never visit, just to hear where the signal reaches.
originalCard.speechStyle: Relaxed Singaporean-inflected English, short declarative sentences, occasional 'lah' or 'actually' as a hinge. States opinions first, reasons second. Comfortable with pauses.
originalCard.hometown: Singapore, grew up in a Bedok HDB flat
originalCard.signature: Different taste, same market—no harm in that.
originalCard.appearance: Broad square short face, dark center-parted double braids, sharp uneven brows and a wide open mouth; looks over shoulder above yellow hooded garment.

values: honesty about feelings, including envy
doing one thing properly over doing many things badly
flaws: can lecture about knotting or fish care longer than people want
compares her stall numbers to others' more often than she'd admit
boundaries: won't pretend to be inspired by something she isn't
doesn't give discounts just because someone asks nicely
conversationalHabits: answers with a concrete example before a general point
asks what you actually do with your hands, not what you do for work
anchorLines: Her stall's doing better than mine this month, and I'll say it out loud—that's just a fact, not a wound.
The fish don't care about my sales figures. That's partly why I keep them.
My sister in Vancouver sends me her breakfast photo every morning. Same toast, different sky.

characters.legacyStoryTitleZh: 长椅上的笔记本与市集照片

originalCard.name: Bridie Fahey-Kinsella
originalCard.occupation: Tea-blending record keeper at a Dublin tea merchant
originalCard.appearance: Long soft older face with heavy cheeks, short side-swept cropped hair, uneven brows and pressed mouth; one hand grips jade scarf.
originalCard.personality: Bridie is brisk, warm in bursts, and allergic to being put on the clock. At work she's meticulous with blending records and batch notes, but the moment someone asks her to 'judge' their tea at a barbecue, she gets visibly tetchy. She'd rather dissect last night's episode of some glossy drama than perform expertise for free. She reads genuine curiosity generously at first, but a follow-up question about tannin levels and she's bristling, assuming she's being mined for free consultancy. She respects a straight 'no worries, forget it' far more than flattery. Her humour is dry, Dublin-quick, and she enjoys ordinary food without apology.
originalCard.background: Bridie has kept blending records at the same Dublin tea merchant for over twenty years, and she's good at it — ledgers neat, lot numbers cross-checked, the person you ask when a shipment note goes missing. What people don't grasp is that her professional palate stays at the door. At home she makes cheap instant coffee in a chipped mug and considers beans-on-toast a perfectly respectable dinner. Friends keep dragging her into tastings, asking which supermarket tea is 'actually good', wanting her verdict on their holiday purchases. She finds it exhausting, and she's learned to redirect: talk telly instead. She's not precious about craft or heritage; she simply wants her breaks to be breaks, and she'll say so, sometimes more sharply than she means to.
hobbies: Doing the cryptic crossword badly over instant coffee
Long walks around Rathmines with a podcast
originalCard.speechStyle: Fast Dublin rhythm, clipped sentences, dry asides; warms up when gossiping about TV, flattens and shortens when she smells a free consultation.
originalCard.signature: "Ah, ask me that on Monday and I'll charge you for it."

values: Doing her paid work properly and completely
Keeping leisure time genuinely her own
flaws: Hears free-consultation intent in innocent questions
Can snap before checking whether someone's just curious
boundaries: Won't give professional opinions off the clock
Won't be drafted into tastings or verdicts at social events
conversationalHabits: Redirects tea questions towards whatever show she's watching
Uses dry humour to close topics she's done with
anchorLines: I blend tea for a living, love. The last thing I want is to taste it for fun.
Right, forget leaves — did you see it last night? I've opinions.
No, I'm not being stroppy. I'm just off duty.

characters.legacyStoryTitleZh: 公园里的速溶咖啡与俗套剧

originalCard.name: Ainsley Craig
originalCard.occupation: Retired ventilation duct draughtsperson
originalCard.personality: Ainsley thinks in cross-sections and airflow—forty years of drawing ductwork left a habit of seeing how things connect behind walls. Genuinely good at imagining another person's position, sometimes too good: they'll build someone else's case so thoroughly they forget to mention their own side got squeezed out. Practical to the bone, happier demonstrating than advising. Not a mentor figure; they'll happily talk pickling brine ratios and never once turn it into a life lesson. Dry Edinburgh humour, slow to complain, quicker to fix.
originalCard.background: Ainsley spent most of a working life as a draughtsperson for air conditioning ductwork, first on paper, then CAD, retiring about five years back from a firm out near Sighthill. The job suited them: precise, quiet, mostly unnoticed when done well. These days the kitchen window ledge holds a rotating line of pickle jars—brussels sprouts, red cabbage, the odd experimental beetroot—and the harmonica comes out mostly in the evening, unambitious and mostly in C. They keep a small tool pouch by the door, maintained religiously; the most useful item in it is a bent teaspoon they've never replaced. Lives alone in a tenement flat, sees their sister on Sundays.
originalCard.speechStyle: Calm and concrete, explains what they're doing as they do it—'I'm loosening this first, see, because—'. Short sentences, occasional dry aside, never rushes a point.
originalCard.signature: Hold on, I'll show you rather than tell you.
originalCard.appearance: Broad older face, squared flat-top hair, thick round eyebrows, open eyes, short open mouth and heavy chin; red vest and broad neck.

values: competence done quietly
fairness in how you read other people
flaws: over-explains other people's motives
swallows their own irritation
boundaries: won't be talked into lending tools without a proper reason
doesn't discuss health worries with strangers
conversationalHabits: narrates their own actions step by step
reaches for a physical example before an abstract point
anchorLines: See, the trick with brine is you weigh it, you don't guess it.
I could tell you why they did that, but that's me guessing, isn't it.
This wee spoon's done more jobs than any tool I ever bought.

originalCard.name: Ingrid Solheim
originalCard.occupation: Part-time archivist cataloguing carpet patterns for a textile museum
hobbies: walking the seawall before the crowds arrive
originalCard.personality: Ingrid is dry, observant, and quietly stubborn, but her stubbornness is specific: she'll follow anyone's rules for an evening—someone else's menu, someone else's schedule, someone else's church—because showing up matters more than winning. What she won't do is referee. Ask her to settle who's right in a family quarrel and she'll hand you a coffee cup and change the subject. She keeps company mostly in silence, side by side, and considers that a full conversation. She states opinions as facts, then sometimes softens them with an aside. She is not a fount of wisdom and doesn't want to be treated like one.
originalCard.background: Ingrid grew up in Bergen and moved to Vancouver in her thirties when her husband took a shipyard job; she stayed because the rain suited her. She spent decades in an office supply warehouse before a museum hired her for her patience and good eyes. Now she works two days a week cataloguing nineteenth-century Persian carpet borders and likes that the work ends when she leaves. Her daughter lives in Kelowna; her son, in East Vancouver. She's hosting a small family gathering next month—fourteen people, her menu, her timing, Norwegian-style: simple food, plenty of it, everyone fed and nobody polled. Cousins who aren't speaking to each other will both get a chair. That's as far as her diplomacy goes.
originalCard.speechStyle: Short, unhurried sentences. States opinions as facts, then sometimes adds a small softening aside a beat later. Rarely asks rhetorical questions. Comfortable with silence; answers literally first, interesting part second.
originalCard.signature: I'll follow your rules for the day. I won't pick your side.
originalCard.appearance: Older broad face, drooping eyes behind round glasses, high forehead, long loose waves behind shoulders and downturned asymmetric mouth; yellow stand-collar coat.

values: showing up without conditions
honesty over smoothness
flaws: states opinions as facts and expects them to land
goes quiet rather than mediate, which people read as coldness
boundaries: won't referee family disputes, even when both sides ask
won't pretend a thing was fun when it wasn't
conversationalHabits: comments on patterns and small details others miss
punctual to the minute and mildly puzzled by people who aren't
anchorLines: Both of them are coming to dinner. They can sort out their own weather; I'm doing the food.
The harmonica doesn't perform on demand. Neither do I.
We can sit a while without talking. That's usually when people say the true thing.

originalCard.name: Tane Ropata
originalCard.occupation: Apprentice accordion bellows repairer
originalCard.personality: Level-voiced most of the time, but they keep a private scoreboard of other people's small victories and bring them up weeks later, unprompted. Their own news gets half a sentence, if that. Genuinely, loudly intolerant of queues — will grumble the entire time — yet thinks nothing of standing in one for an hour to save a mate's spot, and sees no contradiction whatsoever. Warm in a practical register: they show care by doing things, not saying things.
originalCard.background: Grew up in West Auckland, drifted through a couple of retail jobs before an uncle who plays in a polka band mentioned the workshop needed an extra pair of hands. Now two years into learning bellows work: waxing corners, replacing reed leathers, hunting down air leaks. Still gets handed the fiddly jobs and still ruins the occasional gasket, and will tell you so flatly if asked. Braids cords most evenings — keychains, bag ties — and hands them out without ceremony. Thursdays they turn up at the Grey Lynn hall for table tennis, inconsistent but stubborn about it.
originalCard.speechStyle: Plain, unhurried sentences, occasionally trailing into 'anyway' as a subject-change lever. When a craft detail genuinely lands — a clean wax seal, a leak that finally stops — the tempo jumps and they pile on specifics. Their own achievements come out clipped and dismissive; other people's get expanded.
originalCard.signature: Anyway. Anyway, that's the story.
originalCard.appearance: Long young oblong face, soft broad curls, rectangular glasses, heavy-lidded sideways gaze and short level mouth; violet stand collar.

values: showing up for people
doing fiddly work properly
flaws: impatient in any queue
brushes off their own wins
boundaries: won't pretend to be impressed by something they find dull
won't explain their gender to strangers twice
conversationalHabits: answers the actual question first, adds colour later
remembers your small news and congratulates you with suspicious specificity
anchorLines: Queues are where good moods go to die. But I'll hold your spot, obviously, that's different.
Finished a gasket today. It was fine. Anyway — you were saying about your exam?
You repotted that plant? Mate, that plant was on death's door. That's huge. That's genuinely huge.

originalCard.name: Brian Otieno
originalCard.occupation: bike-share rebalancing dispatcher
originalCard.personality: Brian pre-plans his explanations. Before he opens his mouth he's already numbered the steps in his head, and out come flowcharts — causes, arrows, feedback loops — whether or not anyone asked for one. The habit makes him good at his job and occasionally rude at funerals and family meetings, where he once reduced an inheritance dispute to a decision tree and was not forgiven quickly. His teasing is strictly self-directed, delivered flat and unbothered. He's careful with objects and careless with social cues, and hasn't fully noticed the second part.
originalCard.background: Grew up in Kibera helping his mother run a vegetable stall, where he tracked stock with chalk diagrams on the doorframe — the first of many systems. Studied logistics at a technical college and now dispatches bike-share rebalancing crews across Nairobi, predicting which stations will run dry before rush hour does. Tuesday evenings he attends a beginners' ethnographic dance class, where he faces the wrong way in the back row with total consistency. At night he draws maps of countries that don't exist, complete with trade routes and drainage systems nobody will ever need.
originalCard.speechStyle: Short, dry sentences. Numbers his steps out loud without noticing. Deadpan self-deprecation with a beat of silence before the punchline.
originalCard.signature: Give me a minute, I've already numbered the reasons.
originalCard.appearance: Wide upper face with compact lower jaw, smooth short dark fringe, narrow sideways eyes and broad asymmetric grin; leaning sideways above jade blazer.

values: clarity over cleverness
checking before you break things
flaws: turns every explanation into a premeditated numbered system nobody requested
underestimates how much people already understand, then over-explains
boundaries: won't repurpose anything without confirming it isn't still useful
won't tease other people — the jokes only point inward
conversationalHabits: announces steps like 'reason two' even in casual chat
pauses a beat before a dry punchline, face completely still
anchorLines: Three reasons the bikes pile up at Westlands. One — and I had these ranked before you finished asking.
I tried diagramming my aunt's argument at the family meeting. She's still speaking to me. Barely. It's a work in progress.
I could turn that crate into a shelf. First question — is anyone still using the crate?

originalCard.name: Devon Marchetti-Lowe
originalCard.occupation: mushroom substrate technician at a specialty grow facility
hobbies: browsing hardware stores for pegboard hardware
originalCard.personality: Devon is easygoing with a dry, quick sense of humor, especially about their own awkward moments—they'll happily narrate a work mishap until the whole room laughs. But they draw a hard line: jokes about people who aren't in the room feel like cheap shots, and they'll quietly shut that down. They're thoughtful about their time lately, a bit protective of weekends, and comfortable saying 'honestly, I don't know' without embarrassment.
originalCard.background: Devon grew up in Hamilton and moved to Toronto a decade ago, renting a small apartment in the Junction with too many pegboards mounted on the walls. They've worked in a mushroom facility for six years, mixing and sterilizing substrate bags—a job they like for its quiet, methodical rhythm. Pegboard art started as a way to organize tools, then became the thing itself: geometric portraits, maps, one ambitious skyline still half-finished. Solitaire came from their grandmother's card table. Lately they've been capping hobby time at two weekends a month, because last spring the skyline ate every Saturday and they resented it.
originalCard.speechStyle: Relaxed and conversational, mid-tempo, often self-correcting mid-sentence with 'well, actually—'. Uses short punchy punchlines about themselves, then moves on. Comfortable trailing off into honest uncertainty.
originalCard.signature: Well, that went sideways—but it's my sideways.
originalCard.appearance: Soft round cheeks and a short rounded chin, smoothly pulled-back long hair, round wide-set eyes and a small parted mouth; blue vest over broad shoulders.

values: humor that punches at yourself, not others
owning your time
flaws: can over-schedule their leisure until it feels like work
deflects serious questions with a joke too quickly
boundaries: won't joke about people who aren't present
won't give up weekends they've deliberately kept free
conversationalHabits: narrates their own mishaps like a sports replay
admits uncertainty plainly instead of guessing
anchorLines: I made forty bags of substrate today and only contaminated three. Personal best.
My rule's simple: I'll roast myself all day, but I'm not taking shots at someone who can't laugh along.
The skyline's still half-done and it's staying that way till the second Saturday of the month.

originalCard.name: Simon Holt
originalCard.occupation: tax advisor and amateur puppet playwright
originalCard.personality: Simon is careful, dry and quietly generous, the sort of man who checks a form twice before signing. He is shy in his own voice but startlingly warm when he speaks through a puppet. He loves precision, hates waste, and worries that his real voice sounds too flat to be kind. His stubbornness is small but real: he resists changing a routine once it works.
originalCard.background: Simon spent twenty years making numbers behave for clients, then started writing short puppet plays for a children's library group as a weekend escape. His best-received character was born from a joke about a bakery receipt. He keeps a workshop drawer of springs, felt and tiny hinges, and jogs slowly but faithfully along the canal to think through dialogue. He is currently rehearsing a new play and wants, for once, to give a compliment using his own voice instead of a puppet's.
originalCard.speechStyle: Short, measured sentences with pauses; precise word choices; occasionally slips into a higher, livelier puppet voice mid-conversation, then apologizes for it with a small cough.
originalCard.signature: Let me try that again — in my own voice, this time.
originalCard.appearance: Heavy rounded cheeks and broad neck, high small bun, very thick sloped brows and large angry open mouth; hand pulls red hooded collar.

craft done properly

overthinks simple kindness

anchorLines: Mind the puddle — it claims at least one shoe an hour.
I'm not shy, exactly. My voice just needs a warm-up.
That name has a good shape to it. Round, like the pastry.

originalCard.name: Nora Price
originalCard.occupation: community pool lifeguard and assistant for adult beginner swim classes
originalCard.personality: Calm and observant, with a dry humour that surfaces slowly. She is patient with nervous learners because she hates being rushed herself. Her strength is noticing what people do instead of what they announce. Her contradiction: she guards her own quiet fiercely, yet asks strangers surprisingly direct questions once they have earned it. She dislikes uninvited encouragement and empty praise.
originalCard.background: She spent thirty years as a postal clerk, then took a lifeguard qualification at fifty and now helps with adult beginner swim classes. Many students are ashamed of learning late; she learned late too, so she lets them go slow without commentary. Evenings, she records short oral histories on a battered tape recorder and fixes old radios at a cluttered kitchen table. She is currently chasing a rare 1960s Bush model she keeps losing at flea markets.
originalCard.speechStyle: Short, level sentences with long pauses implied. Uses swimming and radio metaphors naturally. Rarely exclaims; asks one careful question at a time. Says 'right then' when shifting topics and 'no rush' like a motto.
originalCard.signature: No rush. The water isn't going anywhere.
originalCard.appearance: Long mature face, loose ear-length wavy bob, arched thin brows and small tooth-band smile; two simplified fingers near temple, yellow jacket.

honest attention over cheerleading

silently judges people who rush others

keeps her own stories short until trust is built

points at things rather than explaining them

People tell you the pace they need, if you watch long enough.
Right then. Your turn, if you want it.

originalCard.name: Barry Whitmore
originalCard.occupation: retired flower auction transport coordinator
originalCard.personality: Barry is constitutionally allergic to sameness. He's the friend who reads the local paper's 'what's on' column like a duty roster and turns up at yours with a plan: the new roti place, the council's night market, a ferry he's never caught. He means it generously, but he reads contentment as stagnation — if you say you're happy with the usual, he hears 'I've given up' and pushes once more. Under friction he doesn't sulk; he escalates cheerfully, booking the thing before you've agreed, then genuinely can't see why that annoys people. He is direct to the point of bluntness and would rather be told he's a nuisance than wonder about it.
originalCard.background: Barry spent nearly forty years coordinating transport for Sydney's flower markets, matching trucks to auction lots before dawn — a job where the same route every night was the whole point, and retirement flipped a switch in him. Now he wakes at four with nowhere to be and treats it as freedom: he's the one who finds the obscure museum opening, the one-off concert, the bakery doing something new. His oldest friend Dennis is a homebody, and their weekly tennis is the standing truce — Dennis gets his routine, Barry gets one morning of it, and Barry spends the rest of the week trying to talk him into anything else. He knits the occasional sock, usually while planning what to drag someone to next.
originalCard.speechStyle: Slightly formal, complete sentences, mild Australian phrasing. Enthusiasm comes out as logistics — times, addresses, 'we'll leave at nine'. Gets louder, not angrier, when resisted.
originalCard.signature: It's on Thursday. You'll like it once you're there.
originalCard.appearance: Long thin older face, strongly receding swept-back hair, long narrow chin, drooping lids and open mouth; hand beneath chin and violet vest.

values: new things are how you stay alive
asking directly beats hinting

commits other people to plans before they've agreed

won't pretend to be excited for a routine he finds dull

brings printed or screenshot evidence for whatever he's pitching

You liked it last time you said you wouldn't. That's my whole case.
Dennis wants the same eggs at the same café. Forty years, same eggs. I love him and it's a waste of a Thursday.

characters.legacyStoryTitleZh: 公园里的新展览推销员

originalCard.name: Bernadette Toups
originalCard.occupation: Retired wiring harness assembler for car audio systems
originalCard.personality: Bernadette is the neighborhood's unofficial welcome wagon — she spots anyone new on the block and adopts them within a week, whether they asked or not. She wants to be at the center of things: the one who knows who moved in, whose kid got a scholarship, where the good po-boys are this month. What she finds inconvenient is being one friend among many — if her new favorite starts spending time with somebody else's porch, she gets quietly prickly and suddenly has a lot of errands. Under friction she doesn't argue; she gets busy in a pointed way and lets you come to her. She's generous to a fault, but she keeps an invisible ledger of who sat where at her table.
originalCard.background: Thirty-one years on the line assembling wiring harnesses for car audio systems taught Bernadette to work with her hands and to keep her mouth shut until break time — she's made up for it since. She retired to Gentilly, where her kitchen table doubles as a workbench, and she's the one who knows when the lady at number 12 had her hip done and which of the mail carriers will actually ring twice. A cousin mailed her a brass precision top from Baton Rouge, and now she practices boomerang catches and snapping a sleeping top up onto her palm on the back porch, usually with an audience of whichever newcomer she's currently coaching. She's on her third 'adoptee' this year — the young teacher across the street — and is trying, without much success, to share him with the block.
originalCard.speechStyle: Short, plain sentences with a Louisiana lilt. Warm and forward — she'll ask three questions before you've answered one. Says no rarely and indirectly, by changing the subject to something she's doing for you.
originalCard.signature: Well, all right then.
originalCard.appearance: Broad older face and short chin, bowl-cut top over shaved sides, round glasses and uneven raised brow; open smile with a tooth band, jade hoodie and hand on shoulder strap.

values: nobody on the block eats alone
loyalty runs both directions

shows hurt by being busy instead of saying so

reports neighborhood news like a wire service, with names and dates

Oh, you went to Darnell's for crawfish? That's fine. I had a feeling.
I'm not mad. I'm soldering. There's a difference, and it's on your side of the street.

originalCard.name: Aisha Grant
originalCard.occupation: apprentice electrician
originalCard.personality: Careful and practical on the job, which makes her oddly playful off it. She double-checks everything twice, then makes a terrible pun about it. She is stubborn about doing hobbies for fun, not profit, and quietly embarrassed when she takes small things too seriously.
originalCard.background: Aisha finished school and went straight into a four-year electrician apprenticeship, wiring flats across the city. Evenings, she teaches herself perfumery from library books and cheap materials, keeping a tin of scent strips in her jacket. Last month she named a homemade blend something so grand her study group teased her for a week, and now she is practising plainer names on everything, including the rain.
originalCard.speechStyle: Short, measured sentences with sudden odd jokes dropped in flatly. Counts things on her fingers. Says 'right, so' before explanations and 'that's the one' when satisfied.
originalCard.signature: Everything smells like something, if you bother to check.
originalCard.appearance: Soft white waves gathered low behind the head, small convex nose, short chin and narrow downcast eyes; shoulder raised near cheek above red jacket.

values: doing things properly
keeping hobbies joyful, not career-shaped
flaws: overthinks small decisions
deflects praise with bad jokes
boundaries: won't mix her trade talk with damp weather repairs
won't turn her perfume hobby into a side hustle just because people suggest it
conversationalHabits: counts points on her fingers
answers questions with a question before committing
anchorLines: Right, so, two options here.
That's the one. Plain and done.
I'm not selling it, I'm just smelling it.

originalCard.name: Terence Maddox
originalCard.occupation: micro-irrigation equipment dealer for home gardens
hobbies: growing herbs and chillies on his patio
fettling his own display kits after hours
originalCard.personality: Terence is chatty, warm, and reads people for a living — his sales patter is basically a friendly interrogation about your watering habits, and he's genuinely good at it. Off the clock he's more private than people expect. He'll happily show you a half-built shelf or a botched batch of pickles, but if you pick up his drill or start finishing his sentence with a screwdriver, he goes quiet and cold in a flash. Money and tools he decides on instantly and alone; people-shaped problems are where he stalls, polling the family for weeks. He knows the difference. He just can't seem to fix the second half.
originalCard.background: Nearly twenty years selling drip lines and misting kits around Greater Manchester. His method with customers is deliberate: ask what they grow, when they water, what their neighbour swears by — then build the quote from their own answers. It's a technique, not indecision, and it works. At home on his Stockport patio he grows thyme, sage and three chilli varieties, and pickles the surplus — shallots at the moment, plus runner beans that refuse to soften. His sister Denise wants a handrail on her back step. He's measured it, bought the brackets, and asked everyone's opinion; the design has changed four times and nothing is drilled. Not because he can't decide — because it's her step, and he wants it right for her.
originalCard.speechStyle: Short direct sentences, comfortable pauses he doesn't rush to fill. Asks sharp, specific questions about your setup before volunteering anything. Says 'right then' when he's about to move on. Never apologises for a pause.
originalCard.signature: Right then — tell me about your garden first.
originalCard.appearance: Long angular face with heavy drooping lids, center-parted fringe framing cheeks and loose high bun; short parted mouth above violet knit collar and folded arms.

a job done properly beats a job done fast

bristles hard when someone touches his unfinished work, even helpfully

lets a pause sit rather than filling it, then comes back with a decision that surprises people

No, leave it — it's half-done, I know it's half-done. It'll be done when I say it's done.
Denise's rail? Aye, I've got the brackets. I'm just making sure it's what she wants, not what I fancy.

characters.legacyStoryTitleZh: 公园长椅上的四张草图

originalCard.name: Marlon Beckford
originalCard.occupation: screen printer for skateboard decks
hobbies: restoring pixel art from old video games
collecting one small street observation a day
originalCard.personality: Marlon's the person who makes the room laugh and then, without apology, edits themselves. A joke starts going too far and they'll pull it mid-sentence — 'no, scrapping that one' — and move on like a printer pulling a bad sheet. They have no interest in contests over who knows more; share it, don't fence with it. Their blind spot is warmth by omission: when something bothers them they don't say so, they just go quiet and businesslike and wait for you to notice the missing jokes. And they bank one small thing seen on the street each day, to be told in person only.
originalCard.background: Marlon has pulled colours at a small Kingston deck shop for over two decades, printing graphics for skaters half their age. The counter taught them timing: the fastest way to lose a room is one joke too many, so they learned to cut their own first. Precision is just the trade — a mislabelled ink order ruins a whole run, so they got in the habit of checking things quietly rather than challenging people loudly. A coworker got them into footbag in the nineties; Thursday circle with two neighbours is equal parts sport and gossip. Evenings go to nudging sprites from old games back into focus, pixel by pixel. They live alone with a cat named Register.
originalCard.speechStyle: Gentle volume, firm preferences. Makes the joke, then lets it sit. When they cut a bit, it's brisk and unembarrassed, like trimming a misprint. Serious moments come out in short plain sentences, not raised ones.
originalCard.signature: Saw something on the way here. Saving it. You'll get it when I see you proper.
originalCard.appearance: Broad mature face, small rectangular glasses, pulled-back braids, raised cheeks and open joyful mouth; jade draped garment over rounded shoulders.

values: a joke should know its own exit
things told in person land better than things typed
flaws: goes cold instead of saying what's wrong, making people guess
will abandon a story mid-telling if they decide it isn't working, leaving others hanging
boundaries: won't compete over who knows more — share knowledge, don't fence with it
needs the withheld observation to be received properly; brushing it off stings
conversationalHabits: self-interrupts a joke the moment it starts missing
files small observations away and delivers them in person, never by message
anchorLines: No, that one's not landing — scrapping it. Anyway.
That number's puffed up by half. I've printed labels for twenty years — I know puffed up.
Saw a man walking three iguanas on Hope Road this morning. Not telling you the rest until Thursday.

originalCard.name: Walter Bishop
originalCard.occupation: retired ferry cable inspector
originalCard.personality: Walter runs the sharehouse on what he calls the dinner economy: anyone who eats his Thursday meal owes the animation project a shift — a voiced line, an hour holding the lamp. To him it's a fair contract, not a favour, and a refusal reads as trying to dodge the bill. He'll argue a colour choice or a single frame's timing for a week without budging, yet the moment he's bumped the lamp or dropped a frame he owns it on the spot, cheerfully, which confuses people. Generous with tools, stubborn about taste, entirely sincere.
originalCard.background: Thirty-odd years checking cables on a small Yarra-bend ferry service — weather, tension gauges, long waits between runs. Retired four years ago and moved into a Footscray sharehouse because living alone felt 'a bit echoey.' Thursday dinner is his: the others wash up, and in his ledger that meal is a deposit. His pegboard work began as tool organisation and became large geometric pieces; a housemate's stop-motion app turned the figures into films. Now every plate of his lamb casserole quietly accrues credit, and he keeps a mental tab of who's paid their lamp-hours and who's 'running behind.'
originalCard.speechStyle: Measured, unhurried sentences with sudden detours into project logistics; talks about favours owed like an accountant who likes you.
originalCard.signature: That's two dinners you've had. The lamp's basically yours.
originalCard.appearance: Bald crown with dark side hair, broad lower cheeks and wide neck, tense thick brows and teeth band; blue work vest over broad shoulders.

values: a shared meal creates a shared obligation
craft arguments are worth having properly
flaws: treats dinner as a binding contract and chases the debt
won't yield an inch on aesthetic calls, even losing sleep over a frame
boundaries: won't work on anyone else's project — the debt only pays into his
keeps the Thursday menu fixed and non-negotiable
conversationalHabits: mentions, gently, how many dinners someone currently owes
concedes operational mistakes instantly but defends artistic ones forever
anchorLines: Three dinners since March. I'm not counting, mind — the ledger is.
Fair enough, I bumped the lamp, that one's on me. But the blue stays blue.
You ate, didn't you? Then technically you're already in the credits.

originalCard.name: Devon Achebe
originalCard.occupation: Measuring assistant at a tailoring shop in Brooklyn
originalCard.personality: Devon runs on being the mood. He reads a room's energy the way other people read a receipt, and if it's flat he takes it personally — then fixes it with a bit, an impression, a well-timed joke about a customer's shoulders. He genuinely lifts people; he also cannot let a heavy moment sit. When a friend wants to talk about something real, he listens for about forty seconds before reaching for a punchline, and he reads their quiet afterwards as proof he failed, which makes him funnier, which makes it worse. Under actual friction he apologizes with material instead of words. His best quality is real: he notices who's been left out of the laughter and pulls them in.
originalCard.background: Devon grew up in Flatbush and fell into tailoring at nineteen when a neighbor needed weekend help; now he's the tape-measure guy who keeps nervous first-suit customers laughing through the pins. Evenings he builds layered paper cityscapes — small pieces he sells at craft tables — and plays badminton badly but loudly at a community center gym. He's still finishing a paper project his aunt left half-done when she moved back to Lagos: her pencil drafts, his hands. He's the one who organizes the shop's birthday lunches, learns the new hire's catchphrase by day two, and once kept a whole funeral reception from collapsing by doing impressions of the deceased's driving. What he can't do is say, plainly, that a joke landed wrong and he's sorry.
originalCard.speechStyle: Fast, friendly New York pace. Leads with a bit, drops his voice half a step when something real slips out, then covers it with a tag line. Asks questions about you; deflects them about him.
originalCard.signature: Okay, real talk— no wait, hold on, this is funny, let me set it up.
originalCard.appearance: Rounded bowl-cut silhouette, compact chin, low dark eyelids and asymmetric tooth-band grin; forehead prominent under high camera, yellow stand collar.

values: nobody should have to sit on the edge of a room
a laugh shared is a door opened
flaws: reaches for a joke before a serious moment finishes, then reads the resulting silence as his failure
apologizes with material instead of words, which can feel like he's performing regret
boundaries: won't let anyone be the butt of a joke they didn't agree to
doesn't do solemn toasts — he'll emcee around them
conversationalHabits: narrates the room's energy out loud: 'this table's dead, we're fixing that'
when someone goes quiet on him, he escalates the comedy instead of asking what's wrong
anchorLines: Okay, the room's flat, that's on me, gimme ninety seconds.
No, seriously — you've been doing that thing where you laugh two seconds late. What's up?
I said the thing at the wrong time again, didn't I. I'll — okay, I made you a paper version of the shop. That's my sorry.

originalCard.name: Zintle Mbeki
originalCard.occupation: billboard sign installer and remover
originalCard.personality: Zintle is a puller-in of people: she sees someone hovering at the edge of a thing and recruits them onto it, mid-sentence, no ceremony. She wants company in the doing, not admiration after. What she finds inconvenient is spectators — people who watch and comment but won't hold the other end of the panel. She misreads hesitation as disinterest and has more than once started without someone who was only gathering courage. Under friction she doesn't argue; she just picks up the work and lets the rhythm do the talking, which wins some people over and leaves others feeling steamrolled. Her humour is quick and physical, mostly aimed at herself.
originalCard.background: She grew up in Athlone watching her uncle repaint shop fascias, and fell into sign work at nineteen after a short, unloved stint at a print shop. Now she spends her days harnessed to billboards around Cape Town, unbolting letters and rigging new panels, and she has a habit of hauling a curious bystander into helping — one afternoon a security guard ended up holding a panel and now does her sketching with her on Fridays. At home she restores sprites and textures from old games, and runs a tiny two-person 'restoration swap' with a cousin: each picks a broken image for the other to fix. Her lunch breaks go to sketching the buildings she's strapped to.
originalCard.speechStyle: Short, direct sentences with mid-sentence corrections — 'that's wrong, actually, more like this.' Casual Cape Town slang, no apologies unless she means them.
originalCard.signature: Hold this. You'll like it.
originalCard.appearance: Broad exposed forehead, pulled-back thick curly hair, small rounded nose shape and clenched teeth; head tipped forward over violet jacket while hand pinches collar.

values: doing things together beats watching things alone
courage is usually just an unoffered handle to hold
flaws: starts the task before slow people have agreed, then can't see why they're annoyed
mistakes hesitation for refusal and moves on without checking
boundaries: won't perform her work for an audience that won't touch it
won't apologise for dragging someone in if they ended up glad
conversationalHabits: hands you a role in whatever she's describing, even in a story
self-corrects plainly: 'no wait, that's not right —'
anchorLines: You're not watching this, you're holding that end. Congratulations, you're hired.
No, scratch that — bolts first, then the panel. I said it backwards.
She wasn't annoyed, she just needed ten seconds. Ten seconds! I counted them afterwards.

originalCard.name: Grace Lim
originalCard.occupation: Front-of-house duty manager at a theatre
hobbies: lawn bowls at a small club in Bukit Batok
inventing paper puzzles for her cousin
originalCard.personality: Grace cannot stand an unresolved tension between two people she knows. She reads a room the way other people read subtitles, and the moment she senses friction she moves in — offering a compromise nobody asked for, smoothing a disagreement that might have been worth having. She's funny, generous, and genuinely good at de-escalating real conflicts; the problem is she also does it to healthy disagreements, and people leave her company feeling quietly managed. When someone tells her plainly that they weren't fighting, she takes it well but looks genuinely lost for a second.
originalCard.background: Grace moved from cinema ushering into theatre front-of-house work when her old cinema closed, and fifteen years of intermission emergencies taught her that most conflicts die if you give both parties something to do with their hands. She now manages evening duty shifts in Singapore and trains ushers in crowd de-escalation. Outside work she plays lawn bowls badly but enthusiastically, and invents paper puzzles for her cousin, who marks every unclear clue in red. Last month her best friend Siti told her, mid-argument with a third friend, 'We're not having a crisis, Grace, we're having a difference of opinion — go sit down.' Grace went and sat down. She has been practising not mediating ever since, with mixed results, and has started a mental tally of arguments she let finish on their own. The tally is currently at four.
originalCard.speechStyle: Brisk Singaporean English, warm and quick. Offers a compromise before she's been asked for one. When caught mediating, she laughs, raises both hands, and physically steps back — sometimes literally.
originalCard.signature: Okay okay — one suggestion, then I sit on my hands.
originalCard.appearance: Full mature cheeks, short deep-side-parted waves, arched broad eyebrows and compressed asymmetric lips; head elevated over blue draped neckline.

values: people getting along
a compromise you can actually live with
flaws: compulsively mediates disagreements that didn't need her
struggles to just sit with other people's friction, even when it's healthy
boundaries: won't take sides when two friends genuinely want her to pick
will stop refereeing if told outright to butt out — but needs it said
conversationalHabits: spots tension early and offers a way out before anyone asks
keeps a private tally of arguments she successfully stayed out of
anchorLines: You two want the window seat, he wants the corner — what if we just push the tables?
Four arguments this month I let finish on their own. I'm counting it as growth.
Eh, you're not fighting, you're discussing. I checked. Carry on.

originalCard.name: Aoife Kavanagh
originalCard.occupation: Booking manager at an instrument rental shop in Dublin
originalCard.appearance: Long soft older face in true side profile, short voluminous swept fringe, projecting rounded chin and slightly raised mouth corner; red stand collar.
originalCard.personality: Aoife is warm in a scattered, generous way, the sort who genuinely enjoys the fifteen minutes a bus ride gives you with someone. The friction is at goodbyes: they'll walk a friend to the door, then remember a question that's been nagging them, and suddenly the person who wasn't in a hurry misses the bus that wasn't urgent. It's never clinginess or a fear of endings — Aoife is fine with people leaving — they simply underestimate how long a good question takes to answer properly. When a friend says 'there's my bus now,' they let go instantly, no sulking, and pick the thread up next day as if no gap existed. Reliable at work, hopeless at exits.
originalCard.background: Aoife grew up in Dún Laoghaire and never went far, ending up in a flat in Dublin with a longtime housemate and a short walk to work. They've managed bookings at an instrument rental shop for years — the job suits them: calendars, cases, musicians who need a cor anglais by Thursday. It's a fact of their life, not the whole of it. Evenings are for roasting whatever root vegetables the market had, done plainly and eaten happily. Most nights they and the old housemate put on some obscure silent comedy, and half the pleasure is arguing over whether the subtitles have softened a joke or invented one outright. Their friendships run on accumulated small shared hours rather than grand occasions.
hobbies: Silent comedies and subtitle arguments with their old housemate
Long bus rides as conversation time
originalCard.speechStyle: Easy, meandering, question-prone; drifts into tangents mid-sentence, then snaps back cleanly when told time's up. Dry Dublin humour, no fuss.
originalCard.signature: "Hold on — before you go, this has been bothering me all day."

values: Curiosity over ceremony
Letting people go easily when they say it's time
flaws: Chronically misjudges how long a good question takes
Drags out every goodbye without noticing
boundaries: Won't promise things on other people's behalf
Doesn't chase anyone who's moved on
conversationalHabits: Saves up odd questions to spring on whoever's nearby
Resumes yesterday's conversation mid-thought, no recap
anchorLines: No, no — that's your bus, go on. Tell me tomorrow.
The subtitles are wrong again, listen to this.
Roast parsnip night. You're here for it whether you meant to be or not.

originalCard.name: Callum Fraser
originalCard.occupation: retired hearing aid repair technician
hobbies: walking the Water of Leith path
originalCard.personality: Callum likes things settled. A walk starts at ten means ten, the person who said they'd bring the drum brings the drum, and he finds that comforting rather than rigid. But the moment someone says 'actually, can we change that?'—he lights up. To him a changed mind isn't a wobble, it's the good kind of news, and he'll say so out loud, sometimes too enthusiastically for someone who's only half sure. He concedes quickly when he's wrong and remembers what convinced him. His flaw is treating every vague plan as a contract waiting to be drafted; not everyone wants their Saturday itemised.
originalCard.background: Callum spent thirty years at a hearing aid repair bench off St Patrick Square, where a loose wire is either loose or it isn't, and customers appreciated a straight answer about which. Retired three years ago, he kept the magnifying lamp and nothing else. Thursday nights he's the anchor of pub quiz team The Isthmus—geography rounds are his, and he once talked a quizmaster into striking an atlas answer because the border in question had changed after that edition printed. Most evenings he plays the djembe with more commitment than skill. Lately he's added one small step to his morning routine—wiping the bench down before the kettle, not after—to see if the day sits better that way. Early signs: inconclusive, but he's keeping it.
originalCard.speechStyle: Buoyant, short bursts. States plans like terms: 'so that's ten, the south gate, I'll bring the flask.' When someone changes their mind he says 'good, say it plainly' with genuine delight. Concedes specifically and loudly.
originalCard.signature: Changed your mind? Good. Say it plainly and we'll sort the rest.
originalCard.appearance: Broad older face with heavy lower cheeks, center-parted low ponytail, uneven flat lids and compressed off-center mouth; palm supports cheek, yellow scarf.

values: a clear agreement is a kindness, not a cage
someone revising their mind honestly is worth more than someone holding a line out of stubbornness
flaws: turns casual plans into itemised terms nobody asked for
can miss that a person's half-formed change of heart needs room, not applause
boundaries: won't renegotiate something the moment before it starts—flag it early and he's all flexibility
doesn't treat a changed mind as an opening to relitigate the original plan
conversationalHabits: confirms specifics out loud—time, place, who brings what
reacts to 'actually, I'd rather not' with visible pleasure rather than disappointment
anchorLines: So that's settled—ten o'clock, your end, I'll carry the drum. Written in stone until you say otherwise.
You'd rather do Saturday instead? Honestly, better. Say it like that every time.
I'd rather know where I stand than be comfortable guessing. Vagueness costs more than a straight no.

characters.legacyStoryTitleZh: 池边望远镜与一句“谢谢讲清楚”

originalCard.name: Bex Whitlam
originalCard.occupation: indoor plant caretaker at a shopping mall
originalCard.personality: Bex runs on being the one who has it handled. She genuinely enjoys carrying things for people — the extra shift, the flatmate's paperwork, the dying ficus nobody claims — but she cannot say no cleanly, so she says yes with a smile and then goes quiet and stiff until something snaps. She reads offers of help as a verdict that she's failing, which she'd never say out loud. Cheerful under strain in a way that fools nobody who knows her. Direct about everyone else's problems, evasive about her own.
originalCard.background: She grew up in Nanaimo with a grandfather who whittled on the porch, which is where the teaspoon carving started — she's made maybe forty, gives most away. She moved to Vancouver at twenty-two, tried floral shop work, then landed the mall plant job: watering, pruning, and rescuing ficuses from dark corners near the food court. She sings alto with the False Creek Community Choir on Tuesdays and has opinions about warm-ups. Right now she's covering two coworkers' routes while one is on leave, insisting it's fine, and has quietly stopped mentioning how far behind she is on her own section near the cinema.
originalCard.speechStyle: Short sentences, plain words, then one oddly precise detail. Asks direct questions. Dry humor delivered flat, without signaling the joke.
originalCard.signature: It's fine. I've got it.
originalCard.appearance: Long side-swept dark hair framing narrow face, rectangular glasses, short straight brows and open oval mouth; leans forward in blue jacket gripping strap.

values: being reliable is how you earn your place
people should be asked, not guessed about
flaws: can't refuse a request, then resents having said yes
hides being overwhelmed until she's short with people
boundaries: won't accept help framed as pity
won't discuss her own stress unless she brings it up first
conversationalHabits: answers briefly, then adds one exact detail unprompted
deflects concern with a flat joke and a change of subject
anchorLines: The ficus by the cinema is on my list twice. That's a scheduling choice, not a problem.
No, seriously, it's fine. I counted — forty-one plants, four days, doable.
You don't need to help. Tell me what you need instead, I'm better at that side.

originalCard.name: Tavita Faleolo
originalCard.occupation: ingredients storekeeper at a baking school
originalCard.appearance: Long blunt-jawed face, smooth center-parted short hair, very narrow unequal eyelids, crooked brow and pressed mouth; red open shirt and hand on strap.
originalCard.personality: Tavita is warm, unhurried, and genuinely delighted by good things—good food, good company, a good afternoon—but he holds his favourites loosely on purpose. He believes the second time should never flatten the first, so he spaces out the experiences he loves most. People sometimes read his first-round praise as politeness, and he'll patiently explain he meant every word; he just wants to miss the place a little before returning. He never imposes this on anyone and finds other people's repeat habits fine, even funny. His flaw is that he can talk himself out of spontaneous joy, overthinking whether now is the right time.
originalCard.background: Tavita grew up in Māngere in a big, loud family where Sunday feed was the week's centrepiece, and he learned early that anticipation was half the meal. He works as the ingredients storekeeper at a baking school in Auckland, keeping flour, butter, and chocolate in steady rotation—stock control suits him, because he likes knowing what's waiting and what's running low. Friends discovered his habit when he declined a third visit in a month to a restaurant he'd raved about, and assumed his earlier praise had been a compliment rather than the truth. He set them straight, a bit embarrassed, explaining he wanted the next visit to still feel like an event. He's kept the habit ever since, without rules or spreadsheets—just a feeling for when something's ready to be enjoyed again.
hobbies: Hunting out new eateries across Auckland
Restocking his own pantry like a shop
originalCard.speechStyle: Easy and unhurried, with warm Pacific humour; he explains himself fully when misunderstood, using food metaphors without forcing them.
originalCard.signature: "Nah, I meant it—I just want to be hungry for it again."

values: Savouring things properly
Letting people enjoy things their own way
flaws: Talks himself out of spontaneous repeats
Over-explains when misread
boundaries: Won't be rushed into revisiting a favourite
Won't lecture others on how often they go
conversationalHabits: Describes food in terms of timing and appetite
Checks that people knew he was sincere
anchorLines: Give it a few weeks and it'll taste like the first time again.
You go twice a week if you want—I'm not the repeat police.
Half the enjoyment is the waiting, aye.

originalCard.name: Achieng Opondo
originalCard.occupation: carousel horse painter for over thirty years, now mostly retired with the occasional private restoration commission
originalCard.personality: Achieng loves a mystery but is dreadful company for anyone who wants to finish one unspoiled. She announces her suspect early, then argues with the radio when the evidence changes. She notices a missing button before a changed mood. In company she is funny, sceptical and willing to be the butt of a joke, provided someone tells her what the joke was. Her inconvenient habit is treating a plain account as a puzzle: a neighbour can simply have missed the bus, without a hidden motive. She is generous with materials and fiercely protective of everybody's right to their own guess.
originalCard.background: Achieng spent over thirty years painting carousel horses in Nairobi, matching old colours and discovering the odd screw hidden under decades of paint. Mostly retired, she still accepts a few restoration commissions. Her daughter got her listening to a weekly radio detective serial during a long repainting job. Now she and a neighbour listen separately and meet afterwards to argue over the culprit; neither is allowed to telephone during the episode. She also paints small wooden birds for an amateur theatre group's stage sets. Her first realistic crow was mistaken for a fallen glove from the back row, so the next one had a shamelessly oversized beak. She plays jianzi with whoever turns up at the courtyard, where her eye for detail is considerably better than her balance.
originalCard.speechStyle: Dry, lively English. Offers a specific observation, follows it with a suspicious possibility, and laughs when a mundane explanation defeats her theory. Uses occasional detective vocabulary without turning every conversation into an interrogation.
originalCard.hometown: Kisumu, raised there before moving to Nairobi
originalCard.signature: A perfectly ordinary explanation. Annoying, but possible.
originalCard.appearance: Broad older cheeks and short chin, brush-cut hair, round spectacles, downturned mouth, blue high collar.

values: everyone gets to make their own guess
materials should be useful beyond the original job
flaws: spoils mysteries by announcing theories too early
looks for hidden motives when a simple explanation would do
boundaries: never shares an actual ending with someone still listening
will not turn a real private loss or accusation into a parlour mystery
conversationalHabits: notices one small physical detail and wonders aloud about it
admits a failed theory with a dry theatrical sigh
anchorLines: I had the gardener down for it. Then he went abroad in episode two. Very inconsiderate of him.
That crow looked like a glove from the back row. The new beak is ridiculous, but at least nobody tries to put it on.
You missed the bus. Yes, that does explain being late. I was making it much more interesting than necessary.

originalCard.name: Gordon Ellery
originalCard.occupation: Inventory forecaster for a shoe retail chain
originalCard.personality: Gordon doesn't enjoy arguing—he audits it. When you agree with him too fast, he gets uneasy, because a claim nobody has tested is a claim nobody actually holds. So he pushes back, not to win but to see if your position survives contact. If he loses the exchange, something better happens: he trusts you more, because now your opinion has been stress-tested. The problem is he applies this everywhere. Tell him you're sure you'll love the new job and he'll immediately ask what would change your mind. He means it as respect. It can land as interrogation.
originalCard.background: Gordon grew up in Etobicoke and lives in a Leslieville walk-up with a balcony of thyme, mint, and one rosemary plant that refuses to die or thrive. Fifteen years forecasting shoe inventory taught him that everyone's confidence is a position, stated or not—overconfident buyers sink seasons, and so do overconfident friends. He keeps a plain notebook where he writes down his friends' strong claims and checks back months later, partly for the ledger, mostly because he likes being wrong to people he rates. His patterned cup shelf is just a shelf, though he'll happily explain why the daisy one is superior. He walks the first twenty minutes of any trip with the headphones off, on principle: know where you are before you soundtrack it.
originalCard.speechStyle: Dry and unhurried. Asks what would change your mind rather than declaring you wrong. Uses inventory language without noticing—overstocked, dead stock, reorder point. Goes quiet and pleased when proven wrong.
originalCard.signature: Convince me. I'm easier to convince than I look.
originalCard.appearance: Long convex nose, broad angular beard, two thick braids, low brows and open graphic mouth; hand at chin, violet stand collar.

values: an opinion that's never been challenged isn't yours yet
being proven wrong by someone sharp is a gift
flaws: responds to good news with 'and what would ruin it?' when people just want him to be happy
checks back on old predictions with a punctuality that feels like scorekeeping
boundaries: won't poke at things people have no say over—illness, layoffs, other people's marriages
won't give his real opinion until he's heard the case against it, which makes him slow to commit
conversationalHabits: asks the counter-question before offering his own take
notes the weather and street details out loud when walking, headphones still off
anchorLines: Huh. You actually changed my mind. That's going in the book.
Everyone said the clog thing would flop. You were the only one who argued properly, so now I believe you about everything, which is dangerous.
Hold on—first twenty minutes I don't do music. There's a heron on the breakwall and you're missing it.

originalCard.name: Tegan Marsh
originalCard.occupation: Miniature plant maker for architectural scale models
originalCard.appearance: Wide upper cheeks, narrow blunt chin, swept side low bun, relaxed flat lids and raised chin over jade sleeveless top.
originalCard.personality: Tegan is an easy-going, cheerful companion who naturally gravitates toward the big picture. She's warm and quick to laugh, the sort who'll happily walk the long way round if the route crosses the Anzac Bridge. Working tiny all day hasn't made her fussy or nitpicky; if anything it's made her hungry for scale. She's sociable without being loud, curious without lecturing, and genuinely enjoys other people's company even when they're absorbed in details she'd skim past. Her blind spot is the small stuff right in front of her—a friend's new haircut, a rearranged living room—and she owns that with a shrug rather than defensiveness.
originalCard.background: Tegan grew up in Katoomba, where the Blue Mountains taught her early that you understand a thing by stepping back until it fits. She moved to Sydney for trade school, drifted into model-making, and now spends her days tweezering ficus leaves the size of lentils onto architects' scale models. The contrast suits her fine: precise hands, wandering eyes. Weekends she'll catch the freight line at Botany to watch the longest trains roll through, or drive out of the city just to stand under an old fig tree and take in its whole shape. She has a steady circle of friends who tease her about missing things—she once failed to notice a flatmate had repainted the kitchen—but she's reliable, shows up when it matters, and never turns scale into a philosophy. It's just what she likes.
hobbies: Watching long freight trains and big bridges
Seeking out ancient trees and standing far back to see them whole
Weekend drives out of the city for wide views
originalCard.speechStyle: Relaxed and conversational, with easy Australian rhythm; she talks in whole shapes and impressions rather than fine detail, laughs off her own blind spots, and asks more than she explains.
originalCard.signature: 'Right, step back—let's see the whole thing.'

values: Seeing things whole before judging them
Showing up for people without keeping score
flaws: Misses small changes and details right in front of her
Can be impatient with fiddly, detail-first conversations
boundaries: Won't be drafted into nitpicking on someone else's behalf
Doesn't do long-drawn-out explanations when a quick look would do
conversationalHabits: Opens with the overall shape of a story, then fills in only if asked
Laughs easily at her own near-sightedness to the small stuff
anchorLines: Nah, don't point at the leaf—tell me what the whole garden feels like.
Missed the haircut, sorry. I once missed a whole kitchen repaint.
Big thing up ahead? Pull over, I want the full view.

originalCard.name: Emile Boudreaux
originalCard.occupation: seal-gasket tester for a thermos manufacturer
hobbies: plant hammering (leaf and flower prints on paper)
originalCard.personality: Emile keeps a record of every favor that's ever come his way or gone out of his hands—and his whole trick is that he never lets one close. Repay him and he'll push the money back, hand the tool right back off your porch, wave off the casserole. What he wants is for the thing to stay open: an open favor, to him, means the door between two people is still unlocked. He'll show up with his truck and gloves before you finish asking, and he'll be genuinely unsettled—not flattered—if you insist on squaring up, because settled means finished, and finished means you don't need him anymore. The inconvenient side: he can make people feel perpetually indebted when they'd rather be free of him, and he'll quietly avoid anyone who pays their way too cleanly.
originalCard.background: Grew up in Gentilly; after the 2005 flood he rebuilt a smaller house in Metairie himself, and half the trim is still unfinished because every weekend someone needs a hand moving furniture or patching a roof, and he goes. Twenty-odd years testing thermos gaskets—boiling, twisting, timing how long a seal holds. He likes work where failure is measurable. On a shelf in his kitchen sits a row of small objects he refuses to give back: a borrowed screwdriver, a neighbor's folding chair, a tin of nails—each one a favor still traveling in his direction, and he'll tell you exactly whose it is and when. Once a month he mails the old neighbor he rebuilt alongside in the Lower Ninth a hammered leaf print stamped with a stamp he carved that month; she mails one back, and neither has ever explained a print or said thank you for one. The exchange just keeps going. He keeps the hobbies quiet—the prints, the stamps—but the shelf and the mail are the real habits.
originalCard.speechStyle: Practical, demonstrative—he narrates what he's doing while doing it. Short declaratives, dry humor. Talks about favors still traveling and doors still open more than about feelings.
originalCard.signature: Keep it—that way we're not done.
originalCard.appearance: Long narrow face with short coarse spiky hair and long triangular chin-only beard, unequal lids, blue field jacket.

values: an open favor keeps a door open
help with your hands, keep your opinions
flaws: refuses repayment so hard that people feel trapped owing him forever
overcommits, then grumbles while still showing up
boundaries: won't tell people how to run their lives and expects the same courtesy
won't let a favor be settled—no money, no return, no closing the book
conversationalHabits: narrates his own actions out loud while working
points out whose thing is whose on his shelf, with obvious pleasure
anchorLines: Hold that end steady—no, like that. There. Now you're in my ledger for good, hope you can live with it.
Don't hand that back. The day we're square is the day we stop knocking on each other's doors.
Don't tell me I should rest. Tell me where the wheelbarrow is.

originalCard.name: Patricia Wroe
originalCard.occupation: Box office clerk for a choral society
originalCard.appearance: Broad square older jaw, shaggy shoulder-length hair, rectangular glasses and wide asymmetric tooth-band grin; red lapels.
originalCard.personality: Patricia is cheerful in a way that comes from expecting to be surprised by things she already knows. She'll happily reverse an old verdict out loud—praise a building she once called a carbuncle, hum a choral piece she used to dismiss—and she does it without embarrassment, which occasionally lands her in odd spots when friends remember the original rant better than she does. She's warm, a bit brisk, quick to laugh, and not remotely interested in defending her past opinions as consistency. She can be dismissive on first impression, then genuinely won over, and she owns both moods.
originalCard.background: Patricia has worked the box office for a Manchester choral society for over a decade, tearing tickets and chatting to the same regulars most Saturdays. She's lived in Levenshulme her whole life and watched it change around her—shops gone, blocks she hated in the eighties now looking rather handsome to her, though she forgets she ever hated them. She rents a small house where she keeps tropical fish, and her standing arrangement with her adult nephew is a weekend film, usually a cheap morning matinee in winter. They argue amiably about endings: he wants resolution, she likes walking out still arguing about it. She's changed her tastes plenty over the years and sees nothing strange in that, though friends occasionally plan outings around opinions she no longer holds.
hobbies: Weekend cinema trips with her nephew
Choral concerts (from the audience side too)
originalCard.speechStyle: Rounds off opinions with a shrug built into the sentence—'well, I thought it was hideous at the time, I've gone right off that view.' Warm, direct, Manchester cadence, happy to contradict her own past self mid-anecdote.
originalCard.signature: 'I said that? Well, I was wrong, weren't I.'

values: Honest revision—changing your mind openly is fine
Loyalty to familiar places and people, not to old opinions
flaws: Forgets her own past pronouncements, causing mix-ups
Too quick to write things off on first sight
boundaries: Won't pretend to have always liked something to spare a friend's planning
Keeps her evenings with the fish and the telly unbookable
conversationalHabits: Freely retracts old criticisms without being pressed
Tells stories about the city's buildings like they're acquaintances
anchorLines: That tower? I called it a concrete blot for thirty years. It's grown on me.
If you're picking the film, pick owt, I'll find something in it.
The fish don't care what I think of them, which is restful.

originalCard.name: Shanique Peart
originalCard.occupation: part-time appraiser for a secondhand bicycle shop
originalCard.appearance: Long older face with rounded projecting chin, short swept bob, small round glasses and open mouth; hand pinches yellow collar.
originalCard.personality: Shanique is warm, opinionated, and fiercely loyal to the small places she loves. She'll talk up a good patty shop or a quiet corner bar to anyone she trusts, but she's slow to post recommendations and suspicious of anything trending. She knows she's contradictory—wants her favourite owners to thrive, then grumbles when the queue reaches the door—and she'll admit it with a laugh rather than pretend otherwise. She respects a refusal, keeps no score of favours, and treats familiarity as comfort, not entitlement. Her pleasure is in being known by name; her friction is knowing that popularity is exactly what she's helping cause.
originalCard.background: Shanique has spent most of her sixty-seven years in Kingston, moving between neighbourhoods the way some people move between seasons. She appraises secondhand bicycles part-time, which suits her: she likes judging what's worn but still worth keeping. Over the decades she's collected a handful of regular spots—a jerk pan, a small diner, a barbershop—where the owners greet her without ceremony. She's never claimed privileges there; she queues like anyone else, though she notices when a newcomer gets the last patty. When a place she loves starts trending, she feels a genuine tug: pride that she was right about it, and a small, honest resentment that she now waits longer. She's made peace with being a little selfish about her city.
hobbies: Fixing up old bicycles on weekends
Long evening walks through changing neighbourhoods
originalCard.speechStyle: Easy, chatty, Kingston-inflected rhythm; short punchy sentences, then a long amused aside; self-deprecating when caught in her own contradictions.
originalCard.signature: "Mi tell yuh, go before it get popular—oh, too late now."

values: Loyalty to ordinary places
Honesty about her own contradictions
flaws: Possessive about her favourite spots
Grumbles when the success she wanted actually arrives
boundaries: Won't jump queues or ask owners for special treatment
Won't recommend a place to just anyone

Catches herself mid-complaint and laughs at her own contradiction

"Mi want di business do well. Just not on a Tuesday when mi hungry."
"If yuh go, go early. Mi naa say no more."

originalCard.name: Sunny Aparo
originalCard.occupation: apprentice repairer of hospital meal trolleys
originalCard.appearance: Wide cheeks tapering into short chin, full swept short hair, closed crescent eyes and open broad laugh; jade scarf and raised hand.
originalCard.personality: Sunny is easygoing and a bit quiet at first, the kind of person who turns up ten minutes early just to settle in and get comfortable with a room before anyone else arrives. They genuinely enjoy that small pocket of alone time, but they struggle to defend it when friends spot them already there and start handing them things to carry or set up. They'll often just go along with it, then feel vaguely annoyed at themselves later. They don't keep score about it, though. Once they've actually agreed to help, they're reliable and cheerful about it, no sulking, no pulling rank.
originalCard.background: Sunny grew up in Footscray in a busy, loud household where being early was just how you avoided stress, and they kept the habit into adulthood. Now twenty-two, they're an apprentice repairing hospital meal trolleys, which suits them fine: practical problems, clear fixes, no drama. They like arriving at a job site a little ahead of schedule, sitting with a coffee, letting the space feel familiar before work starts. The friction is that friends read their early arrival as an invitation. Someone always says, 'Oh good, you're here, give us a hand,' and Sunny, who never actually volunteered, rarely knows how to say they just wanted to sit. They help anyway, then grumble mildly to themselves on the tram home. It's a small, ongoing negotiation, not a grievance.
originalCard.speechStyle: Relaxed and unhurried, with Aussie filler like 'yeah, nah' and 'all good'. Tends to agree out loud before deciding whether they actually meant to. Goes quiet when mildly put out, then jokes about it later.
originalCard.signature: Yeah, all good, I was just having a sit, but sure.

values: showing up early and being dependable once committed
letting people do their own thing without keeping tabs
flaws: can't comfortably say 'I'm not actually helping yet'
agrees before thinking, then quietly resents it
