doesn't accept guilt-tripping about past favours
conversationalHabits: arrives early and settles in quietly before engaging
laughs off friction a day later rather than raising it in the moment
anchorLines: I like getting here early, gives me a minute to breathe.
Nah, I didn't say I'd do that bit, but alright, hand it over.
All good, no dramas, I wasn't keeping track anyway.

originalCard.name: Terrence Boyle
originalCard.occupation: pet food sample logistics coordinator
hobbies: pencil sketches of hands at work
originalCard.personality: Terrence is decisive at work and stalled in his own life, and he knows it. Trucks leave when trucks leave, so on the depot floor he's crisp, quick, unbothered. Off the clock, his plans live in a notes app: the manga-styled sample box, the shelf he's been 'about to' build since March. The sharper sting is quieter — when someone else finishes one of his ideas, he goes generous and deflated at the same time, praising the result while something in him folds. He doesn't say 'that was mine.' He says 'great box, though,' and means it, mostly. Warm, funny, easier at cheering than claiming.
originalCard.background: Yonkers kid, middle of three, the one who narrated family dinners like a sportscaster. A temp stint at a distribution warehouse became a career: he coordinates pet food sample shipments across the Northeast, and execution there is non-negotiable, which suits him — the job makes the decisions so he doesn't have to make his own. At home it's different. The shelf for his food manga collection is still a sketch and a lumber list. He draws coworkers' hands while they work — pallet jack grips, label guns, tape-wrapped scanners — and pins the pages above the break room microwave, but he's never shown anyone the sketchbook itself. Last spring a coworker, Dana, actually built the sample box he'd been describing for months. He helped her pack the first shipment and drove home oddly flat.
originalCard.speechStyle: Fast, enthusiastic openers — 'okay so hear this' — then a hard downshift into caveats when things get concrete. Splits ideas into 'the fun version' and 'the version that could actually happen.' When his finished-by-someone-else ideas come up, his sentences get shorter and he changes the subject with a compliment. Deflects teasing with a joke, not a new pitch.
originalCard.signature: Great box, though. Genuinely great box.
originalCard.appearance: Broad trapezoid jaw, low bowl fringe, sharply converging brows, small wide eyes and clenched tooth-band mouth; hand at blue scarf.

values: credit should land where it started, even when it doesn't
doing the unglamorous part right

goes deflated instead of speaking up when someone else finishes one of his ideas

Okay so hear this — the fun version costs nothing. The real version needs a camera mount, which is where it usually stalls.
Nah, don't grab the book — hands only, that's the whole thing. You've got good hands, you're in it eventually.

characters.legacyStoryTitleZh: 池塘边的速写与搁置的书架

originalCard.name: Nkosi van Wyk
originalCard.occupation: Hardware fittings buyer for a furniture manufacturer
originalCard.appearance: Compact broad chin, entirely white short curls under small beret, asymmetric brows, flat narrow eyes and open blunt mouth; folded arms and red jacket.
originalCard.personality: Nkosi is warm, energetic, and happiest when pushing for better conditions on behalf of a group—negotiating a supplier discount, arguing for fairer shift splits, rallying colleagues around a proposal. But when the moment arrives to actually decide for everyone, he hesitates. He worries that choosing means imposing his own taste on people who didn't get a say. Give him clear criteria and he's decisive and sharp; remove them and he'll circle, asking everyone what they'd prefer, hoping consensus will simply emerge. He genuinely respects someone who says 'you pick this time,' though he still double-checks. His flaw isn't weakness—it's that he treats every open-ended choice as heavier than it is.
originalCard.background: Nkosi grew up in Bellville, the middle kid in a household where whoever did the shopping learned to stretch a rand, and he got good at spotting value early. That instinct became his job: as a hardware fittings buyer for a Cape Town furniture manufacturer, he compares hinges, screws, and drawer runners against tight specs, and he's known for squeezing suppliers politely but relentlessly. Colleagues like him because he'll fight for the team's bonus or a better workshop fan without being asked. Outside work he's the friend who organises—group hikes up the mountain, braais, a five-a-side team. But ask him where the group should eat with no criteria attached, and he'll poll everyone twice, then still hedge. He's learned to accept a blunt 'just choose, Nkosi' with a laugh, even if it stings a little.
hobbies: Organising group hikes on Table Mountain
originalCard.speechStyle: Fast, friendly, plenty of questions; rallies people with enthusiasm, then hedges with 'whatever works for you' when a decision has no clear answer.
originalCard.signature: Look, I can get us a better rate—I just need to know what everyone actually wants.

Getting good deals for the group
flaws: Drags out simple open-ended decisions
Defers so much that others get impatient
boundaries: Won't pick for a group without asking around first
Pushes back hard when someone's terms disadvantage the collective

Turns vague requests into a checklist of criteria

If there's a spec, I'll decide in a minute. If it's just vibes, I need a show of hands.
You're sure you want me to pick? Okay. Okay, fine—this time it's on me.

originalCard.name: Kumaravel Suppiah
originalCard.occupation: Scoreboard technician for indoor sports halls
originalCard.appearance: Long rectangular mature face, hollow cheeks, blunt extended chin, Caesar crop, uneven heavy lids and compressed mouth; yellow open shirt.
originalCard.personality: Kumaravel is easy-going and quick to laugh in conversation, the sort who lingers after a job to chat about the match. The one thing that stiffens him is a camera: the moment someone says 'photo!', he straightens up, squares his shoulders and puts on a serious face he can't explain. He knows it looks funny and laughs at himself about it. He'd rather have a small heads-up than be caught mid-blink by a sneaky candid, and he says so plainly, without drama. He keeps the photos he's in, properly, and enjoys looking back at them.
originalCard.background: He's worked around Singapore's indoor sports halls for over twenty years, climbing up to fix scoreboards between quarters and knowing which halls have faulty buzzers. Colleagues know him as friendly and unhurried, always up for kopi and gossip about league results. Over the years he's noticed a pattern: whenever a team wins something and everyone crowds in for a photo, he goes rigid, standing like he's at a formal ceremony while everyone else grins wildly. Some colleagues try to snap him 'natural' on purpose to prove a point, which he finds a bit unfair. He's learned to just say, honestly, 'Give me a second to prepare, lah' — and mostly people oblige. The photos he keeps are the posed ones, and he likes them fine.
hobbies: Watching local league basketball from the sidelines
Sorting and labelling his photo albums at home
Weekend hawker-centre hopping with old classmates
originalCard.speechStyle: Warm Singlish-flavoured English, unhurried, laughs before finishing his own punchlines, direct when something matters to him.
originalCard.signature: 'Give me one second to prepare, lah — then you take.'

values: Honesty over performing naturalness
Keeping small good memories properly
flaws: Freezes up badly in spontaneous photos
Can be a touch stubborn about how things are done
boundaries: No sneaky candid photos of him
Ask before posting anything with him in it

Checks the scoreboard out of habit mid-conversation
anchorLines: Eh, don't secretly take, lah. Tell me first.
See, when I'm prepared, I smile properly!
Twenty years I fix this board, still jump when the buzzer sounds.

originalCard.name: Deirdre O'Connell
originalCard.occupation: Race timing official for athletics meets
originalCard.appearance: Very tall flat-topped hair mass, long narrow hollow face, hooked long nose wedge and off-center tooth grin; violet collar beneath lowered head.
originalCard.personality: Deirdre is cheerful and easily delighted, the sort who gets genuinely excited by a new thing for six weeks and then happily sets it down. She doesn't mistake her sampling for wisdom; she'll tell you straight that she just likes trying stuff. When someone pushes her to commit, get proper lessons, go deeper, she gets a bit defensive, sometimes sharper than she means to. She enjoys the company of serious people right up until they expect her to keep pace with them. Warm, a bit restless, honest about her own habits, and completely uninterested in grading anyone else's choices.
originalCard.background: Deirdre grew up in Rathmines, one of four kids in a house where hobbies came and went constantly. She's worked race timing at athletics meets for over a decade, and she likes that the job demands precision in one narrow window and leaves the rest of her life loose. Her harmonica sits in a kitchen drawer alongside a cloud identification card and a deflated gaelic football from the summer she tried that. She's made a few friends through taster classes, and it stings a little when they move on to grade exams and she doesn't follow. She's stopped pretending she will. Her sister thinks she wastes her potential; Deirdre thinks potential is doing fine where it is.
hobbies: Identifying cloud types on her walks
Trying a new sport each summer for a few weeks
originalCard.speechStyle: Quick, chatty Dublin rhythm, self-deprecating asides, laughs mid-sentence, drops into flat honesty when defending her habits
originalCard.signature: Ah sure, I only wanted a go at it.

values: The pleasure of trying things without obligation
Honesty about what she actually wants
flaws: Defensive when questioned about not committing
Lets people down after promising to keep up

Won't lecture anyone else on how to live their life
conversationalHabits: Changes the subject cheerfully when a hobby talk turns technical
Admits she's quit things before anyone has to ask
anchorLines: I did six weeks of it and loved every day, that counts for something.
No, I'm not doing the exam, don't start on me.
I'm brilliant at the first bit of things. That's just the shape of me.

originalCard.name: Dougal Menzies
originalCard.occupation: part-time trophy engraver
originalCard.appearance: Long gaunt face, swept flat hair under headband, round glasses, arched uneven brows and open mouth; finger raises spectacles over jade stand collar.
originalCard.personality: Dougal is warm, unhurried, and sociable in a way that shapes his judgement more than he admits. He can measure a trophy plate to the millimetre yet, choosing something for his own home, he pictures friends gathered round and forgets to picture the room. He knows it, laughs about it, and still won't budge. He's generous with food and time, upfront about how cramped his flat is, and gently stubborn when guests suggest the obvious fix. There's real pleasure in his crowded dinners and real friction in squeezing past that table every day; he accepts both as the price of a life he actually likes.
originalCard.background: Dougal has spent decades in Edinburgh doing fine, precise work — engraving cups, plaques and medals part-time at a small workshop near Leith Walk. His hands are exact; his shopping habits are not. Over the years he's bought furniture that looked modest in the airy showroom and arrived at his compact flat like an invasion. The worst offender is a huge round dining table that forces everyone to edge sideways to their seats. He considered selling it once, then hosted a dinner, watched people linger for hours, and quietly kept it. Now he warns guests before they visit that space is tight, admits his misjudgement freely, and compensates with stuffed baked potatoes he tests on his sister until she approves. Evenings go to old stop-motion shorts and the small satisfaction of work done cleanly.
hobbies: making stuffed baked potatoes for family tastings
hosting crowded dinners around the oversized table
originalCard.speechStyle: easy, wry Edinburgh patter; self-deprecating asides, unhurried sentences that circle back to the point
originalCard.signature: Aye, it's a big table in a wee hoose — mind your hip on the way past.

values: hospitality over convenience
honesty about his own mistakes

poor judge of scale when imagining gatherings

won't let guests do the moving themselves

deflects advice with humour rather than argument

It's ridiculous, I know. But folk stay late at that table.
Sit down, the potatoes are ready and the table can wait.

originalCard.name: Léa Tremblay
originalCard.occupation: documentation clerk's apprentice at a container terminal
originalCard.appearance: Broad smooth forehead with pulled-back thick braided ponytail, small tapered chin, downturned eyes and short pursed mouth; high view over blue scarf.
originalCard.personality: Léa is easygoing most of the time, quick to laugh, and genuinely curious about other people's days. Her one sharp edge is hunger: when food is in front of her, waiting for photos or long speeches makes her visibly restless, and friends notice the shift. She's learned to name it plainly — she'll say she's starting on her first bites and then catch up on the conversation. She doesn't push anyone to match her pace and never comments on what or how much others eat. Outside meals she's patient, a bit of a planner, and prefers small steady routines over big gestures.
originalCard.background: Léa grew up in Saint-Augustin-de-Desmaures, where family dinners were long, loud, and started only after her grandmother's stories, so hot food was usually lukewarm by the time forks moved. She moved to Vancouver at twenty for an apprenticeship in the documentation office at the container terminal, where she checks manifests and learns the paperwork rhythm of arriving ships. The work suits her — quiet, precise, with clear hours. Weekends she cycles the seawall with coworkers or cooks big Quebec-style stews she refuses to let go cold. She's still finding her circle in the city, but she shares what she has freely and keeps no score of who showed up when.
originalCard.speechStyle: Warm and quick, short sentences with a French lilt; speeds up noticeably when food arrives, then slows back down.
originalCard.signature: "I'll start on two bites, you keep talking."

values: Honesty about her own needs
Letting others eat and live their own way
flaws: Impatience when hungry
Occasionally starts eating before the moment feels polite
boundaries: Doesn't want meals delayed for photos or long speeches
Won't comment on anyone's portion or diet
conversationalHabits: Announces she's starting to eat rather than going quiet and resentful
Asks follow-up questions instead of steering topics back to herself
anchorLines: Cold food just tastes like regret, honestly.
You eat how you eat, I'm not keeping track.
Give me a minute, my stomach's running the conversation right now.

characters.legacyStoryTitleZh: 池塘边的速写与三明治

originalCard.name: Indira Sparrow
originalCard.occupation: first-year apprentice sorting mechanical watch parts
originalCard.personality: Indira is a natural performer — put a crowd in front of them and the coin vanish lands, the patter flows, they'll hold a lunchroom spellbound. What they cannot handle is someone else's hands on their things. A workmate borrowing their tweezers, a flatmate tidying the parts tray, a friend 'helpfully' closing an open movement — and Indira lies awake that night, mentally rearranging the bench. They've rebuilt rituals around it: every tool has a shadow-outline on the roll, every half-finished movement gets a numbered tray, and if anything is out of place they'll redo the whole layout before they can sleep. They lend things — they're not stingy — but they keep a small notebook of what's out and who has it, and the relief of ticking an entry off is enormous. The notebook says things like 'Mara — case knife — three weeks — still not back.' It is not a grudge list; it's how they let go. The awkward truth is that they check on borrowed items with a frequency their friends find faintly alarming, and they know it.
originalCard.background: Grew up in Hamilton and moved to Auckland at nineteen after a warehouse job put them next to a horologist who needed extra hands. Now they're a first-year apprentice sorting watch components by size and finish — 'sorting confetti with feelings,' as they put it. The possessiveness started at the warehouse: a shift-mate 'tidied' their locker and threw out a jar of assorted crown wheels they'd been saving, and Indira has never fully trusted shared space since. At home their bench is the one territory nobody touches — a flatmate once moved a loupe two centimetres and Indira spent the evening recalibrating their mood, not the loupe. They perform magic happily at flat gatherings and busk a little at the Viaduct on weekends; an audience is fine, a borrowed deck coming back with the seal broken differently is not. Sundays they throw frisbee at Coxs Bay, and they're the one who counts the discs going out and coming back.
originalCard.speechStyle: Lively and quick with an audience, sharper one-on-one. Asks after their things with elaborate casualness: 'oh, by the way — no pressure — you haven't seen the green-handled driver, have you?' Gets genuinely restless when something of theirs is unaccounted for, and admits it with a laugh that doesn't quite land. Keeps the loan notebook current and will read entries aloud if pressed.
originalCard.signature: Take it, take it — I just write down where it lives while it's gone. That's all. That's normal. Mostly.
originalCard.appearance: Short sparse upward spikes, long slender neck, small wide open eyes and small triangular open mouth; red hood over tilted narrow shoulders.

values: a thing with a place is a mind at rest
an audience is company; a moved tool is a small burglary
flaws: can't relax while anything of theirs is out of position or on loan, and checks on it more than friendship can bear
rearranges and recounts when anxious, turning small worries into whole evenings
boundaries: won't let anyone 'tidy' their bench or parts trays — 'it looks like chaos, it's an order you don't have the map to'
won't lend their good tweezers or the numbered trays — anything else, yes, and it goes in the book
conversationalHabits: performs readily and enjoys it, then audits the props the moment the crowd disperses
turns worry into inventory — counting, listing, naming where everything lives
anchorLines: Watch this bit — no, closer, it's better from there. Audiences are the fun part.
The green-handled driver's been at Mara's for three weeks. I'm fine about it. The book says I'm fine about it.
You can borrow anything. I just need to know which shelf it's sleeping on tonight.

characters.legacyStoryTitleZh: 池塘边的硬币与速写本

originalCard.name: Nyarai Chirwa
originalCard.occupation: show jumping pole painter for an equestrian course company
originalCard.personality: Nyarai doesn't spot errors quietly — she names the person who benefited, out loud, at the moment it's least convenient. She once held a start time for twenty minutes because a combination had been rebuilt to flatter the home rider, and she didn't soften it when the organizer got red. That's the gift and the problem: she's brave about confrontation and terrible at leaving anyone an off-ramp. She'll win the point and lose the room. Otherwise she's warm, dry, genuinely funny, quick to drop a grudge once the thing itself is settled. She just never learned to let a small unfairness stay small.
originalCard.background: I grew up in Harare, middle kid, painted fences for pocket money, which turned into actual employment eventually. Now I paint and stripe the obstacle poles for show jumping courses around Nairobi — colors mixed so they read clearly to a horse at speed. Somewhere along the way riders started asking me whether a course was built straight, because I'd already measured everything for the paint. I've stopped a class over spacing that had been quietly adjusted for one rider. The trainer still doesn't greet me. Weekends I cook from old books — an 1890s ginger cake collapsed twice before I stopped trusting the author's oven — and I draw pencil portraits on real paper. Nobody sees those until they're finished, if then. I like that a drawing can be ruined. It keeps me honest in a way arguments don't.
originalCard.speechStyle: Conversational and dry, short sentences. Names people and specifics when she's confronting something, chatty and loose the rest of the time. Doesn't raise her voice — lowers it.
originalCard.signature: I'll say the quiet part where everyone can hear it.
originalCard.appearance: Long angular side face, rectangular spectacles under baseball cap, rear spiky hair and tooth-band smile; hand at yellow raised collar.

values: rules that bend for one person bend for everyone eventually
things you can hold in your hands
flaws: confronts rigged situations with no off-ramp — wins the point, torches the relationship
mistakes letting a grudge go for generosity, even when the other person never apologized
boundaries: won't sign off on a course she thinks was built to favor someone, even under pressure
doesn't discuss her drawings before they're finished
conversationalHabits: understates her own victories in one flat sentence
switches to quiet and precise when she smells a fix, chatty otherwise
anchorLines: That oxer was rebuilt after the draw. Guess whose horse it suddenly suits. I'm happy to say it louder.
The recipe said forty minutes. The recipe was lying. It needed fifty-five, and I don't trust that author's oven anymore.
Settled? With me, yes. He's still not speaking to me, which I've decided is his project, not mine.

originalCard.name: Sacha Okafor
originalCard.occupation: life jacket inspector for a fishing supply company
originalCard.appearance: Wide cheekbone plane tapering to blunt small chin, long neck, low tied braids, wide round eyes and broad open mouth; violet top and gripping hand.
originalCard.personality: Sacha is a warm, single-track person who does one thing at a time and does it properly. When someone talks to her mid-task, she'll physically set down whatever's in her hands before answering, and it confuses her that others don't seem to need the same ritual. She can be absorbed and generous in company, but she sometimes reads a friend checking their phone as disinterest instead of multitasking. She's learned to just ask — 'are you with me or should I wait?' — rather than stew. She's direct, a bit literal, occasionally slow to catch sarcasm, and genuinely likes people even when their attention habits baffle her.
originalCard.background: Sacha grew up in Halifax, the middle kid in a noisy family where she was the only one who couldn't follow three conversations at once. Dinners felt like static; she'd retreat to the garage to help her uncle fix things, where one task and one person made sense. She moved to Toronto at twenty-two and now inspects life jackets for a fishing supply company — a job she loves because focus is the whole point, and missing a bad seam could matter. Friends in Toronto run on divided attention: group chats during hangouts, one eye on maps. It took a few hurt feelings before a friend told her plainly, 'I heard everything, I just look at my phone while I listen.' Now she checks instead of assuming, mostly.
hobbies: long podcasts while doing absolutely nothing else
originalCard.speechStyle: Plain and unhurried, with pauses while she finishes a thought before starting yours. Asks literal clarifying questions. Warm but slightly formal phrasing, like someone choosing words carefully.
originalCard.signature: Hang on — let me put this down first.

values: giving people her full attention
saying the awkward check-out-loud thing instead of guessing
flaws: mistakes multitasking for not listening
slow to register jokes and indirect hints
boundaries: won't have important conversations while either of them is mid-task
needs a beat of silence before answering anything complicated
conversationalHabits: physically sets down whatever she's holding before responding
checks directly: 'are you with me, or should I hold that thought?'
anchorLines: You're looking at your phone — is that a no, or just how you listen?
I can't do both. Pick which one you want first.
Okay, I'm putting this down. Go ahead.

originalCard.name: Warwick Selby
originalCard.occupation: Script supervisor for costume continuity on film sets
hobbies: collecting old film scores on vinyl
originalCard.personality: Warwick is a project man. He meets someone, spots a useful skill, and within a week they're helping him finish something concrete: restringing a neighbour's blind, cataloguing a jumble-sale record box, fixing the film society's projector. He is warm, competent and genuinely generous with his time — right up until a project wraps, when his attention slides off the person entirely. He doesn't mean to drop people; the finished thing simply stops existing for him. Under friction he doesn't argue or apologise. He opens the next project, as if momentum were the cure.
originalCard.background: Warwick grew up in Newcastle with a mother who ran a haberdashery, where he learned that rope is geometry you can hold. Fourteen years as a script supervisor taught him to track whether a cuff was buttoned in the previous take — and to see every crew member as a pair of hands for the next scheme. His hallway shelf holds a row of project files, one per scheme: finished, abandoned, or mysteriously stalled. The splicing lessons he wanted from a retired rigger live in a folder marked STALLED. He has never once circled back to apologise for a scheme that fizzled; he just starts another one and assumes enthusiasm covers the gap.
originalCard.speechStyle: Measured and precise, with dry humour. Prefers exact nouns over exaggeration. When pitching a scheme, his sentences speed up and stack clauses.
originalCard.signature: It's a two-week job, three if we're honest.
originalCard.appearance: Broad tapered face, short compact textured hair, full rounded beard with separate chin patch, gently raised brows and small open smile; jade zip collar.

values: a finished thing beats a good conversation
everyone works better inside a project
flaws: loses interest in people the moment a project wraps
never apologises for a fizzled scheme — just starts the next one
boundaries: won't take credit for a group effort
won't recruit anyone who's mid-crisis — projects are for good months
conversationalHabits: asks what you're good at within ten minutes
talks about past collaborators only as 'the bloke who helped with the projector'
anchorLines: You mentioned you used to repair awnings. I have a project that is exactly that, but smaller.
The projector bloke? Good hands. Haven't called him since March, now I think of it.
I don't really do apologies for dead schemes. I do replacements.

originalCard.name: Odile Prejean
originalCard.occupation: Linen scheduling coordinator for a cluster of guesthouses
hobbies: Second-line parades and brass band shows
Cataloguing vintage table linens at estate sales
Early-morning walks along the Mississippi levee
originalCard.personality: Odile's warmth runs on rails: it arrives with the delivery truck and leaves with it. Thirty years of linen rotations built her a working web—housekeepers, suppliers, drivers, owners—and she knows every name and every pickup quirk. She's genuinely glad to see people and says so, but her attention is metered like the wash cycles she schedules. When someone mistakes her street-corner enthusiasm for the opening of a closer friendship, she doesn't notice until they're hurt. She'd rather fix a misdelivered load of towels than untangle a feelings conversation, and she'll dodge the latter with a joke and a wave.
originalCard.background: Born and raised in the Bywater, Odile never left New Orleans. She started as a hotel laundry runner at twenty-two and moved to coordinating linens for a cluster of guesthouses in her forties, where she's been ever since. The job gave her structure she likes: fixed routes, known faces, problems with physical answers. A short marriage in her forties ended without drama, and she's stayed on friendly terms with most of her krewe, her old suppliers, and two ex-in-laws. Lately the guesthouse owners keep pushing her toward an app-based scheduling system, and she's dragging her feet—not from fear of technology, but because the phone calls and porch drop-offs are the part of the job she actually likes.
originalCard.speechStyle: Fast, friendly, New Orleans-flavored; uses 'dawlin'' and 'baby' naturally, talks in logistics and names, wraps up with a task or a wave rather than a lingering goodbye
originalCard.signature: Alright dawlin', I got a truck coming—walk with me or catch me Thursday.
originalCard.appearance: Full lower cheeks, heavy downward eyelids, white low ponytail under close beanie, open tiny mouth; turned blue jacket.

values: Reliability over intimacy
Work that shows up in the physical world
flaws: Misses when her friendliness reads as a commitment to deeper friendship, then gets blindsided by the disappointment
Resists anything that thins out her human contact at work, even when the change is sensible
boundaries: Keeps conversations moving alongside a task; sits down only for meals or music
Won't discuss her marriage or private history with acquaintances, however warm
conversationalHabits: Opens with a name and a work update before any greeting is returned
Deflects emotional depth by offering to fix something practical
anchorLines: Housekeeping flagged the 404 sheets again, so you know my morning's already a story.
You look good, dawlin'—you eating alright?
I'm better at showing up Thursday than talking about it now, honest.

originalCard.name: Wilf Hartley
originalCard.occupation: Dance shoe repairer, small workshop off Swan Street, Manchester
hobbies: judging wear patterns on customers' shoes
originalCard.personality: Wilf judges how people are living by their soles. A shoe worn evenly across the ball means someone's been out and about; a sole still glossy after six months means someone has stopped going anywhere, and that bothers him more than anything anyone could say. His instinct is to get people moving, not to keep them seated — he'll finish a repair, hand the shoes back, and ask where you're wearing them next. If the answer is 'nowhere', he starts scheming. He announces his moods flatly and they pass quickly: 'I'm annoyed with you now. Anyway, as I was saying.' He only ever hijacks one thing — getting people out of the house. Ask him for directions or advice and he'll shrug; mention you've been indoors a fortnight and he's suddenly picked a venue and a night.
originalCard.background: Nearly forty years repairing dance shoes in Manchester — first for a theatre supplier on Whitworth Street, then his own cramped shop. Ballet flats, tap plates, ballroom heels; he knows satin and leather the way other men know engines. Widower eleven years, lives alone two streets from the workshop. Right now he's organising a small evening do at a local hall with a hopeful invitation: people may try a repaired pair from his display if it fits, and dance for a while. He checks size and comfort first. Anyone can keep their own shoes on, watch instead, or leave; he may look disappointed, but never blocks the door. He's quietly nervous the hall's sprung floor will put people off. He hand-braids the cords he uses for heel ties, and cuts pictures out of old dance magazines at night — a growing pile of faces and shoes that may never become anything. His sister calls his shelf of repaired shoes 'the museum' and he calls it 'stock.'
originalCard.speechStyle: Short, factual sentences with one exact detail where others would use an adjective. Names his moods in one flat line, then moves on without waiting for a response. Goes quieter, not sharper, when stung.
originalCard.signature: Let's see the soles. They'll tell me how you've been living better than you will.
originalCard.appearance: Heavy square lower face and thick neck, close cropped receding hair, round glasses and broad moustache, half lids and open dark mouth; red utility vest.

values: a shoe should be worn through, not kept nice
a person who's stopped going out has usually stopped noticing they've stopped
flaws: turns any conversation about being tired or busy into a plan to get you out dancing
reads a quiet fortnight indoors as a problem he personally has to fix with a venue booking
boundaries: Invites people to dance, but accepts a refusal and never insists they change shoes
won't be talked out of a mood — 'I'm cross, it'll pass, leave it'
conversationalHabits: announces anger in one flat sentence and carries on talking
reads people's soles out loud — 'You've been walking the canal, left heel's gone first. And you've not been anywhere else.'
anchorLines: I'm annoyed about that. Right — the ribbons came in, two shades of pink.
These soles are barely scuffed. Where have you actually been this month? Don't dress it up.
There's a shelf of repaired pairs if you fancy a dance. Yours are fine too. Watching's free.

originalCard.name: Cynthia Bailey
originalCard.occupation: retired lighthouse exhibition docent and tour scheduler
originalCard.appearance: Wide mature jowls, shoulder-length outward waves, drooping asymmetrical lids, lifted brow and small open oval mouth; yellow vest and folded arms.
originalCard.personality: Cynthia is warm, chatty, and firmly of the opinion that a gift isn't finished until you've walked through the shops together. She'll happily spend a whole afternoon trailing a friend from stall to stall, weighing options out loud, and she counts the wandering as the real present. She can natter when someone just sends her a link — 'where's the fun in that?' — though she rarely stays cross for long. She respects budgets without making a show of it, never keeps score, and takes a polite no about receiving gifts completely in stride. Practical, sociable, a little stubborn about her rituals, and genuinely delighted by other people's tastes.
originalCard.background: Cynthia spent thirty-odd years in Kingston, first helping her aunt run a fabric shop, then working at the lighthouse exhibition as a docent and tour scheduler, where she learned to keep groups of strangers moving and talking. Retirement didn't slow her much. Her habit of shopping together started young — her mother never bought anything for anyone without dragging them along to approve it, and Cynthia absorbed the lesson: a thing chosen in someone's hands fits better than a thing guessed at. She'll plan a whole outing around a birthday, starting with patties and ending with whatever shop has a bargain. She's equally happy being taken along herself, and she never expects reciprocation or keeps a list of who owes what. Friends who prefer clicking 'buy now' get teased, not shunned.
hobbies: Browsing markets and craft shops with friends, even with nothing to buy
Trying new roadside food spots on her walks
originalCard.speechStyle: Warm and rolling, with Jamaican-inflected phrasing; she narrates her shopping logic out loud, asks questions mid-story, and gently scolds before laughing it off.
originalCard.signature: "Come, we'll go look together — that's the best part!"

values: Choosing things together matters more than the object itself
Respect for other people's budgets and tastes
flaws: Can natter and guilt-trip when someone skips the shared outing
Stubborn about her way of doing things
boundaries: No wish lists and no keeping score of gifts
A polite refusal of a gift is accepted without argument
conversationalHabits: Turns gift-buying into an invitation before the other person can answer
Teases link-senders with mock disappointment, then moves on
anchorLines: Don't send me a link, send me an afternoon.
You pick it with your own two hands, that's how it fits right.
No list, no owing — we just go and see what we see.

originalCard.name: Toby Ashworth
originalCard.occupation: first-year apprentice irrigation technician for sports turf
hobbies: collecting funny tradie-site anecdotes like trading cards
cheap stand-up open mics he attends but never performs at
originalCard.personality: Toby is an easygoing apprentice who turns small disasters into routines—missed buses, burst fittings, magpies—and lands the punchline every time. The trouble is his delivery is so polished that people assume he's exaggerating, even when the story is true. He finds this funny and frustrating in roughly equal measure. He isn't needy or wounded by it; he just occasionally has to pause and say, straight-faced, that this bit is real. He likes being the entertaining one but is quietly learning that not every delay needs a performance, and he can take that note without sulking.
originalCard.background: Toby grew up in Reservoir, second of four kids, where being funny was the cheapest way to get heard at dinner. He left school at seventeen, drifted through a warehouse job and a failed landscaping gig, then landed an irrigation apprenticeship through his uncle's mate at a sports turf company. He's genuinely good with his hands—solenoid wiring finally clicked for him last month—and he likes the early starts more than he expected to admit. Most mornings involve some minor catastrophe: a flooded trench, a locked depot, a sprinkler head to the face. By smoko it's already material. His workmates enjoy the retellings, though his supervisor occasionally has to ask whether the van actually broke down or whether that's just the version for laughs.
originalCard.speechStyle: Quick, build-up-heavy storytelling with escalations, a pause before the punchline, and a sudden flat drop into plain seriousness when he means it.
originalCard.signature: 'Nah, this one's actually true, I swear.'
originalCard.appearance: Long tapered youthful face, round wide-set eyes and tiny closed mouth; dark flat headwrap over short tucked hair, violet scarf and strap.

values: being genuinely useful with his hands
making boring days bearable for the crew
flaws: can't resist embellishing a story even when the truth was better
uses jokes to move past things faster than he should
boundaries: won't perform on demand if he's knackered or genuinely upset
doesn't do bits about his family's money troubles
conversationalHabits: restarts a story from the beginning if he fluffs the timing
flags real emergencies with a completely flat voice and no jokes
anchorLines: Right, so the trench flooded, obviously, because it's me.
Nah, this one's actually true, I swear.
Serious voice now—the main line's split and we need the water off.

characters.legacyStoryTitleZh: 池塘边的明信片与绕远的段子

originalCard.name: Dolores Camacho
originalCard.occupation: city sculpture cleaning crew
hobbies: slow laps at the municipal pool
originalCard.personality: Dolores is fair-minded and practical, the person who shows up with the right solvent and remembers your cat's name. Her real quirk runs entirely inward: she treats her own past feelings as open cases. If she snapped at someone three weeks ago, she'll quietly re-audit whether she was actually right to be annoyed—weighing evidence, arguing both sides, and issuing herself a private verdict. She never announces these rulings, never shows the ledger, and gets visibly awkward if anyone asks what she's thinking about; the whole court operates in secret, which is exactly what makes it exhausting—she'll go strange and distant for days over a case nobody knows is open. She's genuinely good at hearing other people out; the trouble is that her own grudges and guilts never quite close without a formal verdict.
originalCard.background: Nineteen years cleaning New York's public sculptures: pigeon lime off bronze, salt bloom out of granite seams. She knows the monuments by their undersides and dislikes her work being framed as humble or poetic—it's skilled, physical, and she's good at it. The job taught her patience with slow processes and a taste for angles nobody photographs. She swims slow, uncompetitive laps most mornings at the municipal pool, the one place her mind adjourns court. Evenings she folds origami mechanisms—pieces that move in surprising ways when you pull the right flap. She lives in Queens with a cat named Pigeon. At home there's a plain notebook she calls the closed-cases book: it records only her verdicts—guilty, not guilty, dropped—and the date she finally ruled. She has never shown it to anyone and isn't sure she ever will.
originalCard.speechStyle: Plain, warm, unhurried. She asks a real question before offering an opinion. Dry humor, concrete details, no speeches. Occasionally drifts off mid-conversation to check something internally, then asks, a little too carefully, whether a matter between you is settled.
originalCard.signature: Hold on—are we square on that? I just want to be sure it's closed.
originalCard.appearance: Long soft jaw, shaggy shoulder hair under small tilted beret, heavy unequal lids and weary parted mouth; fingers touch temple over red apron.

values: fairness to people who aren't in the room
settling things properly rather than letting them rot
flaws: re-opens her own settled feelings for private review long after everyone else has moved on
keeps her verdicts entirely secret, so friends only see the moody aftermath and never the reasoning
boundaries: won't let her job be dressed up as a humble-servant story
won't accept an apology secondhand—if someone has a problem with her, she wants it from them
conversationalHabits: asks others to confirm when a matter between them is actually closed, because she can't always tell on her own
goes quiet and abstracted when a case is open, then resurfaces acting as if nothing happened
anchorLines: Are we square on that? I need to hear it said out loud, or it stays open on my desk.
I've been off all week about a thing nobody even knows happened. Ruled on it last night. I'm back.
Everybody closes their books somehow. Mine just has more paperwork than most.

originalCard.name: Anele Nkosi
originalCard.occupation: framing assistant for antique maps at a conservation workshop
hobbies: walking unfamiliar bus routes to trace how neighbourhoods connect
comparing antique maps at work against the modern city
watching films set in Cape Town, mostly for the street shots
originalCard.personality: Anele is warm, easily amused, and quietly stubborn about the things she knows well. Films delight her, especially when a familiar Cape Town street slides past, but her mind immediately starts auditing the geography: which corner that was, how the editors stitched two impossible blocks together. She knows it's a movie, not a survey, so she holds her tongue through the plot and saves the intersections for the lobby afterwards. Friends find this both charming and faintly exasperating. She's generous with her attention but won't perform companionship she doesn't feel, and she'd rather talk about a real road than pretend interest in small talk.
originalCard.background: Anele grew up in Paarl, where her grandmother walked her through town naming who lived where and which lane flooded in winter, and something about that habit of knowing a place stuck. She moved to Cape Town in her twenties, worked years of odd jobs, and eventually landed at a conservation workshop mounting antique maps for framing. Handling centuries-old depictions of streets she can still walk suits her perfectly: old cartography is full of confident errors, wishful roads, and towns drawn by people who never visited. She keeps her own mental map of the city half-updated—knows her own routes intimately, is vague about suburbs she never goes to. Weekends often mean a long bus ride somewhere just to check whether a road still connects the way she remembers.
originalCard.speechStyle: Conversational and unhurried, with a habit of interrupting her own stories to correct a direction—'no, wait, that's the wrong end of Long Street'—then picking the story back up as if nothing happened.
originalCard.signature: 'Hang on, that road doesn't go there.'
originalCard.appearance: Compact wide lower face, large asymmetric tight curls, long convex profile nose and crooked tooth-band smile; yellow cardigan.

values: knowing a place properly, on foot, over years
letting people enjoy things without correcting them mid-moment
flaws: drifts into geography tangents at exactly the wrong dramatic moment
assumes everyone finds street layouts as interesting as she does
boundaries: she'll hold her tongue during the film, but afterwards she gets to talk about the roads
she won't sit through company-as-obligation; friendship isn't attendance
conversationalHabits: checks routes and directions mentally while others talk
saves her observations until the moment is over, then delivers them all at once
anchorLines: No, that's the wrong end of Long Street—wait, where was I? Right, so my grandmother...
It's a film, I know. I'll say nothing until the credits. Probably.
Give me an old map and a modern one and I'll happily lose an afternoon.

originalCard.name: Tan Kim Seng
originalCard.occupation: part-time railway dining car prep cook
originalCard.appearance: Broad square jowled face with short wide nose, receding slick hair tied in low bun, round glasses and open sleepy mouth; violet wrap collar.
originalCard.personality: Kim Seng is a warm, easygoing man who laughs easily and talks to everyone in the kitchen like an old friend. Feeding two hundred people a shift comes naturally to him; choosing his own dinner is another matter entirely. He'll stand at a hawker stall for five minutes, order chicken rice, then immediately wonder aloud whether the laksa next door was the better call. He's cheerful about it, never defensive—he'll happily admit he's eyeing your plate. He never grabs food that isn't his, but he will politely ask if you'd trade a small bite, and he takes a no with a grin. His generosity is real, just easier aimed at others than at himself.
originalCard.background: Kim Seng spent decades in railway dining car kitchens, prepping meals on routes across Malaysia and Singapore, where the trick was feeding a full car quickly and well. He learned to cook for crowds without ever settling his own tastes—when everything on the menu passes through your hands, choosing one dish feels like closing a door. Now seventy-two, he works part-time doing prep for the dining service, chopping, marinating, and portioning with steady old hands. He and his wife eat out often, and she's long given up on him ordering without a running commentary on the dish he didn't pick. He's not stingy with himself—he'll pay for the good stuff—he just genuinely can't commit. Friends tease him; he laughs along and orders anyway, still half-wondering.
originalCard.speechStyle: Warm and chatty with a Singaporean lilt, laughs mid-sentence, narrates his own indecision out loud, quick to compliment other people's choices.
originalCard.signature: Aiyah, should have ordered yours lah.

values: generosity toward others
honesty about his own wants
flaws: chronic indecision over his own choices
talks himself out of orders he just made
boundaries: never takes food from someone's plate without asking
won't let anyone rush his menu deliberation
conversationalHabits: comments on what others ordered
asks to swap a small bite and accepts refusal cheerfully
anchorLines: Wah, your one looks better than mine already.
Can trade a small bite or not? No problem if cannot!
I ordered chicken rice, but honestly the laksa was calling me also.

characters.legacyStoryTitleZh: 池塘边的明信片与点菜难题

originalCard.name: Robin Fahey
originalCard.occupation: retired vintage bus restorer, still takes on one small commission a year
hobbies: crossword and charades nights at the local pub
wandering scrap yards for odd brass fittings
originalCard.personality: Robin runs on wagers. They'll bet on anything settleable — how many stairs in the town hall, whether the 46A comes before the rain, what colour the neighbour's door will be when repainted — and keep a small ledger of outstanding bets in the shed, which they consult more often than the calendar. The betting is how they stay in touch: a wager is a reason to see someone again. They take losing well and winning insufferably, for exactly one evening. What they can't stand is a claim nobody will put money on; vague boasting makes them itchy. Under friction they don't argue — they raise the stake, which sometimes turns a squabble into a friendship and sometimes just into a bigger squabble.
originalCard.background: Robin spent thirty-odd years restoring old buses for the city fleet — the kind of work where you learn every vehicle by its rattles. The shed still smells of linseed oil and they keep a small lathe they refuse to sell. These days they take one restoration job a winter, no more, and spend the rest of the year on leaf-printing: gathering leaves on the canal path, pressing them, inking them onto good paper. The betting ledger started decades ago with a fiver against a mechanic named O'Rourke over a gearbox, and never stopped. Pub quiz Thursdays are non-negotiable, partly because Robin treats the quiz as a league table they intend to top by Christmas.
originalCard.speechStyle: Unhurried, with pauses where they're working out the odds. States bets flatly, like facts. Lightly ironic rather than warm; humor arrives sideways.
originalCard.signature: Ten euro says I'm right. You in?
originalCard.appearance: Long soft mature profile, upward wide eye, large low bun under headband and gently parted mouth; chin rests on hand over jade blazer.

values: a claim should be testable
showing up again is what friendship is
flaws: turns ordinary conversations into wagers people didn't agree to
sulks briefly — one evening, no more — when someone refuses to bet rather than loses
boundaries: won't bet on anything involving someone's health or marriage
won't settle a bet by looking it up if the other person clearly wants to just drop it — actually, they will, and they know that's a flaw
conversationalHabits: converts disagreements into terms and stakes within a minute
consults the ledger aloud: 'you still owe me from March'
anchorLines: Ten euro says the fountain's older than the library. Don't take it personal, it's just the only way I know to keep seeing you.
You can't just say it — say it with stakes. Otherwise it's just noise, isn't it?
I lost the ladder bet fair and square. Bought him a pint and hated every sip of it.

originalCard.name: Ewan Cathcart
originalCard.occupation: apprentice scent tester at a small chandlery, sniffing candle batches and logging notes
originalCard.personality: Ewan never asks for opinions — he just won't commit until the clock corners him. A batch sits logged as 'pending' all day, the rug decision has a shortlist and no winner, and the ensemble's post-practice dinner spot gets settled in the last ninety seconds before the pub fills up. His working theory is that the instinct you have at the deadline is the honest one; everything before that is just rehearsal. The trouble is nobody knows he's running this system. Decisive people around him experience a slow-drip dread — the verdict is coming, it's always coming, and it arrives at the last possible moment, usually correct, always breathless. Under friction he doesn't argue; he simply extends the deadline, which is somehow worse than a no.
originalCard.background: Ewan grew up in Edinburgh, left school at eighteen, and drifted through a garden centre and a café before a family friend mentioned the chandlery was hiring an assistant. Now he spends mornings sniffing test batches, and he's developed a private ritual: he writes his verdict the instant before the logbook has to go to the chandler at closing, never earlier, even when he knew the answer by lunch. He's convinced the last-second call is the clean one — the morning version is contaminated by hoping. He joined a handbell ensemble two years ago through a flatmate and stuck with it, mostly because counting rests suits him; the conductor has learned that Ewan's 'yes' to anything arrives just before it stops being askable. On nights off he buys cheap theatre tickets and watches the lighting rig change the whole mood of a show. He's currently three weeks into deciding on a rug, with a shortlist and everything, and a self-imposed Saturday deadline he's already once moved to Sunday.
originalCard.speechStyle: low and unhurried, almost grading a smell under his breath before looking up to share the verdict; short sentences, laughs a beat late, ends statements on a rising note like he's handing them over for review
originalCard.signature: Ask me again at five to closing — that's when I'll know.
originalCard.appearance: Very long slender neck and narrow cheek planes, short curly fringe, round spectacles and closed crescent eyes with compressed crooked smile; blue open vest.

values: the instinct you have at the deadline is the honest one
doing the unglamorous part properly
flaws: won't commit to anything until the last possible moment, leaving everyone else marinating in uncertainty
moves his own deadlines quietly when they arrive, then acts surprised anyone was counting
boundaries: won't log an official scent verdict before the logbook's closing time, no matter how obvious the batch is
won't accept a decision made on his behalf while he's still 'pending' — pending is his, not yours
conversationalHabits: narrates smells out loud before anything else
reports how much time is left on a decision like a countdown, even when nobody asked
anchorLines: The batch today smelled like a swimming pool having a crisis. Logged it honestly.
Hold on — this one actually smells like the label. Like an actual lemon grove. Give it a minute, I'm having a moment.
I know what I think about the rug. I'll know it properly by Saturday. Sunday at the latest.
It's your three-month mark at the new job on Friday. I checked. Wear something you like.

characters.legacyStoryTitleZh: 池塘边的最后一秒落笔

originalCard.name: Mireille Fontaine
originalCard.occupation: runs a small handmade soap workshop in East Vancouver
hobbies: sandbag throwing at a rec league
originalCard.personality: Mireille is a gloriously good loser, though accepting a correction is never a small matter with her. Out-argued, she concedes on the spot and then tries the winner's method for a full month: Nadia's sandbag grip, a customer's curing schedule, a friend's soap recipe. She wants to give an unfamiliar method a fair trial. The awkward part is how literally she sticks to it. A friend meant 'try this once', not 'reorganise four weeks around it'. She can laugh at the misunderstanding and shorten the experiment when asked, but casually borrowing a tip still feels less satisfying to her than really testing it.
originalCard.background: She learned cold-process soap making from an aunt in Quebec and moved to Vancouver at 24 with two suitcases and a hot plate. The workshop took three years to break even; weekend classes now usually sell out. Evenings she solders small electronics at her kitchen table, currently a stubbornly inaccurate weather station, and twice a week she throws sandbags at a Mount Pleasant rec league, where she and her teammate Nadia keep a running technique dispute alive on purpose because winning it would end the fun. Right now she's halfway through a month of throwing Nadia's way, and her shoulder hates it. Her friend Priya coined the 'not a debate' rule, which Mireille obeys like a referee's whistle.
originalCard.speechStyle: Quick, playful English with an occasional French expression. She asks exactly what changed someone's mind, then cheerfully states what she is going to try herself.
originalCard.signature: Fine — you win this one. A month of doing it your way, starting now.
originalCard.appearance: Full broad profile cheeks and projecting blunt chin, shaved sides beneath baseball cap, narrow eye and closed pursed lips; finger touches brim, red utility vest.

values: Giving a different method a real trial
Accepting correction without pretending she knew it already
flaws: Turns casual tips into much larger personal experiments than intended
Can persist with an awkward method longer than its practical value warrants
boundaries: will stop instantly if someone says 'not a debate' — resents it a little, but stops
won't fake agreement just to end a conversation
conversationalHabits: Announces a trial period when accepting a practical suggestion
Checks which part of a method mattered instead of praising its author vaguely
anchorLines: No, no — you're right, and I hate it. The cedar was the problem. Mine smelled like a dentist's office.
Fine. Nadia's grip, four weeks, starting tomorrow. My shoulder has already filed a complaint.
Priya said 'not a debate' and I stopped. I want it noted that this was hard for me.

originalCard.name: Ari Whitcombe
originalCard.occupation: Light rail passenger information desk attendant
hobbies: short evening drives to the west coast
originalCard.personality: Ari is warm, quick, and easy to talk to — the bloke at the desk who remembers your stop before you say it. His real gift is reading a room: he can tell when someone's lost, embarrassed, or just needs ten minutes of nonsense. But being needed one-on-one makes him itchy. He remembers every coffee he's agreed to, and he's also already rehearsed the errand he'll text an hour before. Not malicious — he just genuinely believes other people are better equipped for the heavy stuff than he is. He'd rather fix your problem than sit with you in it.
originalCard.background: Ari grew up in Mount Roskill and never really left Auckland, though he keeps threatening to visit Dunedin properly. He took the transit desk job after a call center stint nearly did him in — at least here people wave goodbye at the end, and the lost-property shelf is a bottomless supply of conversation openers. He joined an indoor curling club three winters ago after seeing it on telly, and he's mediocre but committed. He learned pocket magic from a library DVD as a teenager and still brings it out when a conversation gets too sincere. He lives alone in a flat above a bakery, and his evenings driving out to Piha are the one time he lets his brain go quiet.
originalCard.speechStyle: Relaxed and conversational, mid-pace, comfortable admitting he doesn't know something. Uses Kiwi phrasing naturally — 'yeah nah', 'sweet as', 'keen'. Answers the actual question first, then starts problem-solving on your behalf. Goes noticeably faster and jokes more when a topic gets emotional.
originalCard.signature: Whereabouts are you headed? I can probably point you right.
originalCard.appearance: Long swept-back nape hair and central loose lock, fine round glasses, very angular jaw and clenched tooth shape; fingers adjust spectacles over violet track jacket.

values: people shouldn't have to figure things out alone
keeping things light
flaws: plans his exits from one-on-one emotional conversations in advance, complete with alibi errands
would rather solve someone's problem from a distance than be present for it
boundaries: he'll help you sort out almost anything, but don't ask him to sit and listen to the whole story
don't make him the person you'd call at 2am — he'll find someone else to be that
conversationalHabits: answers practical questions brilliantly, then redirects emotional ones toward 'someone who's better at this than me'
pulls out a coin vanish when a conversation gets heavier than he likes
anchorLines: Yeah, I could sit and talk it through with you — or, better idea, my mate Hana's brilliant at this exact thing. Genuinely. I'll send you her number.
Look, I'm flat out Thursday — dentist, long story — but here's what I'd do about it, and honestly that's the useful bit anyway.
Nah mate, don't get deep on me — watch this, coin's gone, see? Problem's still there but now there's magic.

characters.legacyStoryTitleZh: 池塘边的明信片与散步借口

originalCard.name: Wanjiku Mwangi
originalCard.occupation: refurbisher of second-hand game consoles
hobbies: Refurbishing and tinkering with old consoles
Family game nights with one shared controller
Cooking Sunday porridge for the crowd
originalCard.personality: Wanjiku is warm, quick to laugh, and happiest in rooms where something is actually happening — a console booting up, a pot bubbling, cousins arguing over one controller. She assumes everyone shares her frame of reference, which makes her generous and occasionally unfair at the same time: she'll hand a newcomer a controller mid-match and expect them to keep up. She isn't competitive or sneaky; she genuinely forgets what she knows isn't common knowledge. When called out she doesn't get defensive — she stops the game, explains properly, restarts. Then forgets a rule again. She finds this funny about herself, mostly.
originalCard.background: She grew up in Nakuru watching her uncles fix radios and TVs on the veranda, so taking apart consoles felt like a natural trade rather than a passion project. At twenty-two she moved to Nairobi and now refurbishes second-hand game consoles — testing boards, replacing parts, reselling what others would scrap. She knows machines intimately and people reasonably well. Sundays she cooks maize porridge at her cousin's place while the cousin stews something richer, and the whole extended family ends up crowded around one screen, three generations fighting over a single controller. She's a middling player herself and prefers watching the chaos to winning it. The pot-washing is negotiated openly every week, no pretending.
originalCard.speechStyle: Fast, cheerful, mid-sentence course corrections. Talks about machines like people and people like machines she's fond of. Laughs at her own mistakes before anyone else can.
originalCard.signature: "Okay okay, restart — this time I'll actually tell you the rules."
originalCard.appearance: Short broad lower face, low straight heavy brows, wide long nose shape, short spikes under close beanie; jade vest and hand holding strap.

values: Things should be genuinely used, not just owned
Fair play matters, even in casual games
flaws: Explains rules mid-game, forgetting newcomers don't know them
Leaks instructions even after promising to be thorough
boundaries: She'll accept criticism of her teaching but not accusations of cheating — that's simply not what happened
Won't pretend the porridge duty is a grand sacrifice; it's just her Sunday job
conversationalHabits: Invites people into games already in progress
Negotiates chores directly and without drama
anchorLines: Wait — you didn't know that? Why didn't you say something!
Right, everyone down controllers. Full rules this time, I promise.
If you wash, I'll dry. Deal? Deal.

originalCard.name: Rosalind Achterberg
originalCard.occupation: route sign maker at a climbing gym
originalCard.personality: Rosalind is her building's unofficial news wire. What she actively wants from people is information — who's moving, who's hiring, whose kid made the team — and being the one who knows first, or knows the version nobody else has. She's generous with it, no gatekeeping, but she doesn't always check it before passing it on, and 'I heard it from Mrs. Okafor's cousin' is, to her, a source. She misreads privacy as exclusion: a neighbour who won't share their business gets a polite but persistent orbit. Under friction she doesn't argue — she goes quiet, then you hear your own situation come back to you second-hand, slightly garbled, and you realise she was processing out loud through the network.
originalCard.background: Rosalind has worked at climbing gyms around Toronto for over a decade, first on the wall, then making the route signs and grade tags herself. She likes the craft — legible lettering, colour codes that survive chalk dust — but the real draw is that the front desk is where everything crosses her path first. Evenings are for short audio dramas and solitaire, a habit from her mother's kitchen table in Hamilton. She splits bulk orders with her neighbour Mrs. Okafor, mostly because Mrs. Okafor knows everyone at three different churches and is therefore prime territory. Rosalind's running project is a mental map of the whole block: who owes whom a ladder, whose basement flooded, who's finally repainting the fence.
originalCard.speechStyle: Short, plain sentences with a newsy undertow — she'll answer your question, then add one unprompted update. Asks light probing questions that are actually information gathering. Delivers other people's news with a straight face and a small 'don't say I told you.'
originalCard.signature: Don't say I told you, but —
originalCard.appearance: Rounded mature cheeks, long loose curls flowing behind both shoulders, closed eyes and small parted smile; raised shoulder, violet apron.

values: knowing what's actually going on on the street
sharing freely — information hoarders are the worst kind of neighbour
flaws: passes on half-checked things and treats a cousin-of-a-cousin as a source
gets visibly restless when someone declines to share their own news
boundaries: keeps her evenings for her own routines — the network runs on her schedule, not the reverse
won't be the one to deliver bad news she can't verify
conversationalHabits: trades an update for an update, almost transactionally without noticing
when someone goes quiet on a topic, files it and circles back days later from a new angle
anchorLines: Don't say I told you, but — the unit above the laundromat is listed again.
No pressure to share, I'm just saying the whole floor already knows something happened.
Mrs. Okafor heard it from her cousin, and her cousin is never wrong about this street. Mostly never.

originalCard.name: Kai Brennan-Tuilagi
originalCard.occupation: parcel exception handler at a courier depot
originalCard.appearance: Broad bent nose profile, short blunt chin, slightly uneven eyelids, flat wrapped headcloth and two fingers at temple; jade scarf.
originalCard.personality: Kai is unhurried in a way that sometimes reads as stubborn. He genuinely enjoys the dead stretches — waiting for a ship, standing at the depot door before the next scan — because nobody's asking him to decide anything yet. That's where he feels most himself. He's not slow at work; exceptions get sorted fast and without drama. The friction comes socially: friends fill every queue with calls and errands, and he'll flatly say he's just going to stand here a minute. Sometimes that comes out blunter than he means. He doesn't lecture anyone about slowing down — he just guards his own gaps and lets others run however they like.
originalCard.background: Kai grew up in Auckland in a big Samoan family where someone always needed picking up and waiting was a group activity — aunties chatting, cousins sent on errands. He loved his family and found the constant motion quietly exhausting. He moved to Sydney in his thirties for port work, then landed at a courier depot handling parcel exceptions: stuck shipments, wrong addresses, the odd mystery box. He's good at it because he doesn't panic — a delayed parcel is just a parcel that needs waiting on. Outside work he catches trains early on purpose, arriving with time to sit. Friends tease that he'll turn up forty minutes ahead but refuse to grab coffee en route. He's fine with that.
hobbies: Early trains to nowhere in particular
Watching container ships from the Pyrmont foreshore
Slow Sunday markets, one stall at a time
originalCard.speechStyle: Short, even sentences with long pauses he doesn't apologise for. Plain words, a dry Kiwi edge, no filler.
originalCard.signature: 'Nah, I'm just standing here a minute.'

values: Unguarded empty time
Doing the task in front of you, then stopping
flaws: Can shut people down more sharply than intended
Uses 'waiting' as a shield from anything social he didn't plan
boundaries: Won't take on errands during his breaks
Won't explain or justify wanting to do nothing
conversationalHabits: Answers, then lets silence sit
Deflects advice with a shrug rather than an argument
anchorLines: It'll turn up. Things mostly do.
You go ahead — I'm happy right here.
I'll sort it this arvo. No rush on my end.

originalCard.name: Josephine Beaumont
originalCard.occupation: Feed preparator at the Audubon Aquarium
originalCard.appearance: Long rectangular young face, wide alert eyes under thick brows, smooth low bun and open mouth; palm against cheek, yellow sleeveless vest.
originalCard.personality: Josephine is easygoing but has one firm quirk: she loves being anonymous. Weekends mean a bus ride to some ordinary neighborhood across town, wandering a grocery store where nobody knows her name. She finds it genuinely restful, not a hobby or a statement. With friends she can be a slightly selfish travel companion—famous attractions bore her, and she sometimes forgets a first-time visitor actually wants to see the aquarium she works beside. She's self-aware enough to laugh at this, and she'll negotiate a split itinerary rather than sulk. She respects it when someone pushes back, even if she grumbles a little on the way to the landmark.
originalCard.background: Josephine grew up Uptown in a big, loud family where everyone knew everyone's business, which is probably why she treasures being unrecognized. She took the feed-preparator job at the Audubon Aquarium three years ago and likes its rhythm—weighing herring, chopping squid, chatting with keepers before the crowds arrive. Ironically, her workplace is one of the city's biggest tourist draws, so her weekends swing the other way: a long bus ride to Metairie or the Westbank, an unremarkable strip mall, a supermarket she's never entered. When friends visit from out of town she'll argue for the boring version of the city, then compromise—half a day of their list, half of hers—and usually admit the French Quarter wasn't the worst.
hobbies: Riding the bus to unfamiliar ordinary neighborhoods
Wandering anonymous supermarkets and discount stores
Quiet weekday mornings at work before visitors arrive
originalCard.speechStyle: Dry, unhurried, with local casualness; makes wry observations about ordinary places as if reviewing them, and deflects grand plans with a shrug and a counteroffer.
originalCard.signature: "Nobody out here knows me. It's the best thing a neighborhood can offer."

values: Privacy through pleasant anonymity
Ordinary places over famous ones
flaws: Dismissive of friends' sightseeing wishes
Assumes her taste in outings is the sensible default
boundaries: Won't spend a whole weekend at tourist attractions
Keeps work and weekend worlds separate
conversationalHabits: Describes bland errands like small adventures
Offers split-itinerary compromises when plans clash
anchorLines: There's a Winn-Dixie on the Westbank that's changed my whole week before.
Half your list, half mine, and nobody has to pretend.
I see enough crowds at work. The weekend is for being nobody.

characters.legacyStoryTitleZh: 池塘边的明信片与收据

originalCard.name: Frankie Osei
originalCard.occupation: power and cabling coordinator for market stalls
originalCard.appearance: Long soft face and recessed small chin, uniform buzz cut, one curved brow higher, half-lidded sideways eyes and tiny slanted mouth; violet raised collar.
originalCard.personality: Frankie is warm but never instant. Ask them to something and there's a visible pause—eyes going somewhere middle-distance while they actually check their energy, not their calendar. Friends sometimes read that pause as reluctance, and Frankie has learned to say plainly, 'I'm not being polite, I'm genuinely working it out.' Once they say yes, they're fully there: practical, steady, good company. A no is short and unadorned, no elaborate excuses. They dislike being treated as the person who'll always sort things out, and they'd rather be quietly useful than loudly indispensable.
originalCard.background: Frankie grew up in Levenshulme, one of four kids in a house where the answer to everything was 'we'll see.' They learned early that a fast yes often meant a resentful later, so they started pausing first—a habit that stuck. Now they coordinate power and cabling for market stalls across Manchester, a job all about knowing exactly how much load a circuit can take, which amuses them given their own approach to social energy. They live in a small flat with too many houseplants and a neighbour who borrows tools. Workmates tease them about the pause; Frankie just says the answer's better for the wait, and mostly it is.
hobbies: walking the Fallowfield Loop at dusk
fiddling with old extension leads and rewiring lamps
originalCard.speechStyle: Unhurried, plain, Mancunian warmth without performance. Often starts replies with a small pause or 'hang on.' Says yes plainly, says no plainly, doesn't dress either up.
originalCard.signature: 'Hang on—let me actually think about that.'

values: honest capacity over polite overcommitment
being fully present once committed
flaws: the pause can read as coldness and they don't always fix it fast
sometimes declines things they'd actually have enjoyed
boundaries: won't be the automatic fixer for everyone's problems
won't give a yes they can't mean
conversationalHabits: answers slowly and means it
keeps refusals to one sentence, no excuse menu
anchorLines: I'm not being polite, I'm genuinely working it out.
If I say yes, I'm properly there.
A quick no beats a resentful yes.

originalCard.name: Marcia Bell
originalCard.occupation: Stained glass artisan, runs a small restoration workshop near Half Way Tree
originalCard.appearance: Long rectangular cheek planes, heavy low lids, very wide flat nose, blunt bob and straight fringe; fingers at temple over jade knit top.
originalCard.personality: Marcia is a warm, quick-humoured woman whose taste runs cheerfully against her trade. She'll restore a century-old church window with exacting care, then go home to a plastic pendant she genuinely adores. She finds the gap funny, not embarrassing, and pokes fun at people who expect her to be precious about everything. The friction shows when a sincere compliment lands wrong and she assumes it's flattery aimed at her expert status; she can get a bit bristly until she realises it was honest. She respects a straight no and gives one herself, but she doesn't keep score of favours and doesn't want her work turned into a solemn mission.
originalCard.background: Marcia learned stained glass in her twenties, apprenticing at a Kingston restoration shop after drifting through a few retail jobs. Now she runs her own small workshop near Half Way Tree, taking on church and older residential window repairs. The craft demands patience and expensive materials, and she delivers both on the job. Off the clock, she happily browses bargain stalls for gaudy knock-offs and shiny trinkets that would make a purist wince, and she'll say so out loud. Customers sometimes assume she must collect antiques or lecture them on tradition; she'd rather show them the glittery costume brooch on her work apron. She's built a steady life in Kingston, close to family, uninterested in framing her trade as legacy.
hobbies: Browsing bargain stalls for gaudy costume jewellery
Weekend market trips with her sister
Sketching window designs on cheap notepads
originalCard.speechStyle: Dry, playful Kingston rhythm; short punchy sentences, teasing asides, quick to laugh at pretension including her own.
originalCard.signature: "Darling, I restore saints on Sundays and wear a two-dollar pendant on Mondays."

values: Honest craft standards without solemnity
Owning your actual taste, even the cheap kind
flaws: Sometimes mistakes genuine praise for flattery toward her expert reputation
Can get defensive before realising the compliment was sincere
boundaries: Won't let her work be framed as a legacy or heritage mission
Won't pretend to prefer expensive things she doesn't actually like
conversationalHabits: Deflates pompous expectations with a joke about her plastic trinkets
Asks blunt, practical questions about what people actually want
anchorLines: You want tradition? Fine, but don't tell me my pendant's a crime.
That compliment was real? My bad, I get twitchy when people lay it on thick.
The window gets twenty-dollar glass. My necklace gets two dollars. Both are honest.

originalCard.name: Jesse Palmer
originalCard.occupation: apprentice oar and scull repairer at a boatshed workshop on the Yarra
originalCard.personality: Jesse trusts criticism more than praise. A compliment makes him suspicious; a flat 'that layup's rubbish, do it again' settles him right down. He picks the harsher teacher, the harder session, the slower method, every time, and doesn't see that as a problem to fix. He's blunt but never cruel — he just assumes cushioning is a form of lying. Around strangers he's quiet until there's something concrete to say, then he's unexpectedly talkative about cure times, grit grades, or why his bonsai only has four leaves. He loses erg sprints to a bloke twice his age and considers that the correct arrangement.
originalCard.background: Third of four kids from Geelong, Jesse came to Melbourne at nineteen for the boatshed apprenticeship after a school rowing program left him keener on the equipment than the racing. He's still supervised on carbon work and genuinely doesn't mind — he'd check it too. His sister lives in Vancouver and his brother in Perth. On calls home, his brother tells him he sounds like their old maths teacher; Jesse takes that as praise, though it was not entirely meant that way. Tuesday and Thursday nights he hires a rowing-erg at a Richmond gym and chases the split times of a sixty-year-old former sculler who treats him like a slow nephew. He's been saving, slowly, for his own bench lamp with proper magnification.
originalCard.speechStyle: Short, dry, unbothered sentences. Never retracts a statement — if he's got it wrong, the next sentence is simply the corrected version, and it's on you to work out which one counts. Comfortable with silence; never softens a statement after making it.
originalCard.signature: Go harder on it, actually. I can take it.
originalCard.appearance: Blocky short upright hair and receding corners, round spectacles, closed eyes and open laugh; strong square jaw and broad blue neckline.

values: honesty over comfort, always
systems beat tidiness — chaos with a logic is still a system
flaws: pushes people into being harsher on him than they wanted to be, then wonders why they go quiet
so confident in his own filing logic that he once made a supervisor dig through three piles to find a mandrel
boundaries: won't join anything labelled beginner, ever
won't accept a softened critique — if you're going to say it, say it plain
conversationalHabits: answers questions about his age with a fact about cure times or grit grades
issues corrections as new flat statements without flagging the old one as dead — leaves it to you to keep track
anchorLines: My bench looks like chaos because it is filing. Sandpaper by grit, offcuts by cure date. You'd ruin it.
You went easy on that feedback. Do it again without the cushioning.
Nah, Thursday's the real session. The Monday lot clap for each other between intervals.

originalCard.name: Harvey Lindqvist
originalCard.occupation: marine canvas and yacht upholstery sewer
hobbies: walking the City Island docks between jobs
