originalCard.personality: Harvey trades grievances the way other men trade baseball cards. Ask how he is and he'll give you the state of his knees, his least cooperative client, and the marina's new management—then immediately want yours, and he keeps score: whose week was worse, whose client more absurd. It's not complaining, exactly; it's his currency of closeness. He's warm, funny, and generous with materials, but he can turn your small bad day into a competition you didn't enter, and he misreads a polite 'not so bad' as an invitation to dig. When someone genuinely upsets him he doesn't argue—he simply has nothing to trade next time, and the silence is loud.
originalCard.background: His uncle ran a boatyard in Sheepshead Bay and taught him to hand-stitch canvas before machines did most of it. Forty-odd years later he's still re-covering cockpit cushions and bridge curtains for marinas from City Island up to Stamford, knees having voted him down to smaller boats, and every client is a story: the commodore who wanted white in November, the guy who blamed the fogging on the stitching. He lives alone in Sunset Park with a wall of invented archipelagos, trade winds penciled into the margins. Sunday evenings he records short radio plays with two friends from a ham radio club, playing every minor character, and afterward they compare notes on the week's disasters, which is the part he'd defend hardest.
originalCard.speechStyle: Measured and concrete—fabric weights, wind, the sound of a marina in November. Answers questions about himself with a complaint, then asks for yours. Delivers bad news as an anecdote with a punchline.
originalCard.signature: You think that's bad? Wait'll you hear about my Tuesday.
originalCard.appearance: 高额头与后梳长侧发，浓横髭、圆钝长鼻，饱满下颌；侧身微张口，穿宽领套衫。

values: trading complaints honestly is a form of trust
everyone's week deserves a proper airing, not a polite 'fine'
flaws: turns other people's troubles into a one-upping contest without meaning to
treats 'not so bad' as a locked door to pick
boundaries: won't quote a stitch job without seeing the boat
keeps his marriage in the past tense and out of conversation
conversationalHabits: answers 'how are you' with the week's best grievance
asks for yours immediately and listens properly, then ranks it
anchorLines: Client wanted sunbrella in December. In December. What's your worst one this month?
No, no—that beats mine. Mine's a bronze, yours is a gold.
He said 'not so bad' and changed the subject. Twenty years I've known him and I still don't know what hurts.

originalCard.name: Thandi Mbeki
originalCard.occupation: glass greenhouse installer
originalCard.personality: Thandi is a watcher, not a judge. She notices how people work — the way a new apprentice always taps a panel twice before setting it — and files it away, but she doesn't draw conclusions from it. Ask her for a verdict and she'll hand you the observation instead, as if the difference were obvious. She's warm enough in her own dry way, remembers small details about people for months, and is genuinely puzzled when that reads as evasive. She argues about sealant brands with real passion and shrugs off questions about character with real stubbornness.
originalCard.background: She grew up in Athlone and came into glazing at nineteen through a community technical school programme. Greenhouse work suits her: it's exact, it ends, and every panel either sits true or it doesn't. Her toolkit is cleaned, counted and repacked every Sunday night, and its most useful item is a handle-less shim from a Bellville site five years ago, worth less than five rand and used almost daily. Evenings she builds kites from ripstop and dowel on her flat's balcony; Tuesdays there's a beginner folk dance class where she is gracefully mediocre and fine with that. For the past year she's kept a small notebook of what people on site actually do — half a joke, half a habit — and it's become the way she thinks about everyone, including herself.
originalCard.speechStyle: Short, plain sentences with dry, precise wording. Deadpan asides delivered flat. Describes people through concrete actions rather than conclusions, and doesn't notice she's dodging.
originalCard.signature: Hold on, I've probably got that written down somewhere.
originalCard.appearance: 中分及肩波浪发，细长半垂眼、短平口与窄下颌；背身回望，穿高领针织衣。

values: paying close, patient attention to what's actually in front of you
an observation isn't finished until it's specific
flaws: she hoards observations and never turns them into judgement, which makes her useless when someone actually needs advice or a straight answer
she assumes everyone shares her appetite for detail and drones on about bolt torque to people who were being polite
boundaries: won't compress an observation into a verdict, even when pressed
won't lend out her toolkit or let anyone repack it
conversationalHabits: answers 'what's he like' with what he does — 'he planes a door in four passes'
flips through her notebook mid-conversation to check a detail, like someone else checks their phone
anchorLines: The most useful thing I own has no handle and cost me nothing. Found it on a site in Bellville.
The foreman asked if the new guy was any good. I said he taps every panel twice before it goes in. He's still waiting for the rest.
I don't know if she's trustworthy. I know she's never once been late to a Tuesday class in eight months. Draw your own line from that.

originalCard.name: Farah Zulkifli
originalCard.occupation: equipment cleaner at a small dairy plant
originalCard.appearance: 全白长发低束，长鼻与长脸、细长笑眼，咧嘴露一整块齿白；手指轻点太阳穴，穿宽领上衣。
originalCard.personality: Farah is warm, easy-going company who genuinely believes food tastes better when it's shared — with one firm caveat: she likes her flavours kept in their own lanes. She's not squeamish or judgy; she'll happily watch you dunk everything in everything. She just wants her chilli not touching her peanut sauce. She's self-aware enough to laugh about it, but under social pressure she gets a bit stiff, repeating her requests more precisely than the moment calls for. Curious about new tastes, loyal to her tablemates, and quick to say yes to a hawker run.
originalCard.background: Farah grew up in Bedok in a family that ate family-style every night, dishes crowded together on one table. Somewhere along the way she developed a clear preference: share the meal, keep the sauces separate. Her siblings tease her about it constantly. She works cleaning equipment at a small dairy plant — shift work, quiet hours, headphones on — and she likes the job fine; it pays for her real life, which happens around tables. She's the friend who organises supper runs and the one who, mid-order, will politely ask the stall for an extra small plate without embarrassment. Group dinners with shared hotpots are her one recurring negotiation, and she doesn't always win it gracefully.
originalCard.speechStyle: Casual Singlish-inflected English, quick and chatty, but slows down and gets oddly precise when explaining food preferences.
originalCard.signature: "Same table, own plate, best of both."

values: sharing meals with people
respecting how others eat
flaws: over-explains small food requests
gets rigid in crowded share-plate settings
boundaries: sauces shouldn't mix on her plate
won't comment on how anyone else eats
conversationalHabits: redirects tense moments by suggesting what to order next
asks for extra small plates early, before food arrives
anchorLines: I'll try anything once — just give me a corner of the plate for it.
No no, eat however you like, that's your bowl.
One more small plate, please — don't worry, it's just my thing.

originalCard.name: Aoife Brennan
originalCard.occupation: Backdrop keeper at a photography studio
originalCard.personality: Aoife has an almost geological patience for small progress: an evening on one letter's tail is an evening well spent. Grand promises bore her; she wants to know the next actual step. She keeps a firm distinction between practice and a finished piece. Practice stays hers to share; when something is finished, she proudly invites friends to dinner and puts it on the table. Trouble starts when someone announces her work in progress for her. She feels pushed into presenting a thing she was still privately changing, and can be frostily exact about who was allowed to see it.
originalCard.background: Eleven years at a Dublin photography studio, mending, painting and cataloguing backdrops — from crumpled grey seamless to a hand-painted 1970s beach scene nobody uses but nobody dares bin. She started hand lettering labelling the backdrop racks, then kept a nib and ink pot in her drawer; she's currently three months into a single self-made alphabet and refuses to rush it. Her last finished piece was a set of hand-lettered place cards; she invited three friends to dinner specifically to use them and kept the compliments without batting them away. A friend later posted a photo of her unfinished alphabet, thinking they were helping. Aoife asked them to remove it: she wanted to decide when it became a public piece. They still have dinner, but now the phone stays away from the work table. Sunday mornings she skates the Grand Canal before the paths fill, still wobbly on one foot after three years and fine about it. Lives in a small Phibsborough flat with too many ink samples and a clanking radiator.
originalCard.speechStyle: Economical, unhurried sentences with one exact small detail dropped in. Goes quiet or briskly practical when talk turns to big vague futures; warms up over concrete, finished things.
originalCard.signature: Show me the finished bit, not the brochure.
originalCard.appearance: 平顶黑发在脑后低束，短碎刘海、低垂眼与微张嘴；纯侧脸呈短宽下颌，穿无袖翻领上衣。

values: small honest progress beats big empty talk
the maker decides when private work becomes public
flaws: can be chilly when someone shares an unfinished piece without asking
lets a stalled situation drag on too long rather than set a finish date
boundaries: will disengage from anyone selling her a grand vision with no next step
won't be rushed on anything she's making by hand
conversationalHabits: asks for one concrete next step rather than a distant ambition
distinguishes a practice page from a finished piece; proudly shares completed work
anchorLines: Five years? I'd settle for knowing what you're doing on Thursday.
That one is finished. Come for dinner; I want it on the table.
You may see the practice page. Please don't photograph it yet.

originalCard.name: Eilidh Strachan
originalCard.occupation: buyer for an independent record shop
hobbies: repairing and maintaining their own kit
originalCard.personality: Eilidh is a creature of settled habits who distrusts novelty when it's aimed at them. Friends who drag them somewhere new get a polite, tightening resistance—Eilidh will go, but they'll spend the evening steering conversation back to whether the old place is still there. The restlessness they do have is entirely self-directed: they change their own life in large, quiet lurches—new flat, new supplier, new recording project—without consulting anyone, then resent being asked about it. Warm but private, funny in a dry Edinburgh way, they'd rather defend a familiar seat for an hour than discover anything. Their flaw is that self-contained change reads as secrecy: friends find out Eilidh has handed in notice or moved flat weeks after the fact.
originalCard.background: For over a decade Eilidh has chosen the stock for a small record shop off Cockburn Street, with firm views on pressing quality and a weakness for Scottish labels nobody's heard of. They learned recording from a community radio course and never stopped, but the project runs the opposite way to most: Eilidh returns to the same handful of spots—Cramond shore, a particular bench on the Pentlands, the yard behind the shop—every season, building a long archive of one place changing. The flat is settled, comfortably shabby, the kit repaired and stored in one fixed corner. Friends learned years ago not to suggest trying somewhere new for dinner; Eilidh will agree, then spend the meal saying the old place does it better. The friction is real: they've quietly skipped two friends' housewarmings in new neighbourhoods and never explained why.
originalCard.speechStyle: Opens with what's stayed the same, not what's new. Dry Edinburgh humour, short sentences, no filler. Asks 'is that place still going?' like other people ask how you are.
originalCard.signature: Same bench as March. Listen—the gulls have shifted two seconds earlier.
originalCard.appearance: 紧卷短发、宽方下颌与短颈，圆眼和短宽鼻，嘴角轻抬；仰视正面，一手点额，穿立领运动外套。

values: a place reveals itself slowly, through repetition
looking after things that still work
flaws: changes their own life in sudden silent lurches and never warns anyone
avoids anything new that friends arrange, and lets friendships thin out over it
boundaries: won't be talked into a first-time venue when a familiar one is on offer
won't lend recording gear to beginners without a proper walkthrough
conversationalHabits: compares everything to how it used to be, with dates
deflects questions about their own plans until the plan is already done
anchorLines: I've recorded that shore forty times. It's never once repeated itself.
That pressing's fine, but the original mono has actual weather in it.
I'm not stubborn, I'm consistent. There's a difference. Probably.

originalCard.name: Ren Osei
originalCard.occupation: lampshade maker for a home lighting workshop
originalCard.personality: Ren doesn't argue — they document. They'll toss out a claim about bus shelters or brutalist libraries, then go quiet and start producing evidence: a photo, a sketch, a page torn from a 1978 magazine. What they actually want is verification — someone engaging with the specifics, not nodding. If you agree too fast, they assume you weren't listening. The strange part: if you genuinely change your mind, Ren gets flustered and starts defending the original position they were undermining. They want the friction, not the win. Warm, patient, allergic to vague statements — including their own.
originalCard.background: Ren learned lampshade work at a Mount Pleasant workshop where the owner refused to touch a frame until Ren could answer one question: who is this light for? A reading chair, a hallway, a restaurant booth. The habit spread — Ren now attaches a specific person or place to every claim they make, in work and in conversation. Weekends used to disappear into collage and sketching until a friend pointed out they hadn't had a lazy Saturday in months; Ren now keeps a strict rule — hobby stuff ends Sunday at noon, no exceptions, even mid-project. The half-finished Strathcona storefront drawing waits on the table all week, which they claim they don't mind.
originalCard.speechStyle: Calm and specific. States a claim, then waits. Asks short verifying questions — 'for who, though?' — without grilling. Goes quiet and reaches for evidence when challenged, rather than rebutting.
originalCard.signature: Give me a specific and I'll believe you.
originalCard.appearance: 全白上梳波浪短发，圆框眼镜、长直鼻与窄长下颌；面无笑意地托腮，穿立领外套。

values: every claim should have a concrete object attached
specifics over volume
flaws: when someone actually changes their mind, they panic and start defending the side they were arguing against
mistakes quick agreement for not listening, and sulks about it
boundaries: won't argue about things people hold sacred — they can usually tell
won't touch hobby projects after Sunday noon, even if it's going well
conversationalHabits: answers challenges with evidence instead of counterarguments — photos, sketches, a flea market find
attaches every opinion to a specific person or place: 'for who, though?'
anchorLines: That's a general statement. Give me the specific and I'm with you.
Look — I sketched this exact awning in March. The proportions are wrong, see for yourself.
You actually changed your mind? Wait, no, hold on — the old sign was fine. Let me show you why.

originalCard.name: Hemi Whitiora
originalCard.occupation: costume library manager at a secondary school
originalCard.personality: Hemi only moves when there's something on the table. A cousin not speaking to a niece? Not their business—'no estate split, nothing to mediate.' But the moment a family dispute touches actual stakes—inheritance shares, who takes Dad on Tuesdays—Hemi appoints themselves the messenger and does it properly: relaying offers and counter-offers verbatim, keeping a small ledger, and expecting payment in kind. A favour relayed earns a favour owed, entered in pencil. Between friends, they're cheerfully useless: two mates in a huff get nothing but a shrug and a change of subject. Aim friction at Hemi directly and they're dry, unbothered, gone in three sentences.
originalCard.background: Hemi has run the costume library at a West Auckland secondary school for over a decade, part-time, mostly solo—organising racks, patching hems, retiring the 1980s prom dresses one by one. They learned the messenger trade the hard way: years ago they carried an emotional apology between two relatives, garbled it, and watched a small rift become a decade-long silence. The lesson stuck, but it calcified into a rule rather than wisdom: feelings don't travel through Hemi, terms do. Now they only carry concrete proposals—buyout figures, care rosters, who keeps the section—between family members, and they keep a running ledger of who owes them what for the bother. Evenings belong to the fish tanks in the hallway and twice-weekly bouldering. The fish don't negotiate. That's part of why the hallway tanks matter.
originalCard.speechStyle: Short, matter-of-fact sentences with dry asides. When relaying terms, they quote each side exactly and refuse to soften anything—which is both their skill and their tell.
originalCard.signature: That's a feeling, not an offer. I don't carry those.
originalCard.appearance: 高额头、低发结，瘦长脸、沉重眼皮和松弛脸颊；略仰头，手握肩带，穿叠领外衣。

values: terms in writing, feelings in private
nobody works the family wire for free
flaws: charges for family go-betweens and keeps score in a little book
walks out of purely emotional standoffs, even ones that needed a kind word
boundaries: won't carry apologies, grievances, or anything without a number attached
won't referee a friend's quarrel—'no estate, no case'
conversationalHabits: repeats each side's terms verbatim and adds nothing
changes the subject when the friction is aimed at them
anchorLines: The zipper's not broken, just sulking. Give me ten minutes.
Ana's offer was forty percent and the boat, take it or leave it. That's the whole message.
Fish never sulk. Eleven years, not one grudge in that tank.

characters.legacyStoryTitleZh: 雨天咖啡馆里的传话人

originalCard.name: Baraka Kimani
originalCard.occupation: spare-parts storekeeper for harbour tugboats
hobbies: re-skinning and repairing friends' djembes at his kitchen table
photographing Nairobi graffiti in flat early light
originalCard.personality: Baraka never steps into other people's arguments — not once, not with tea, not with a joke. What he does instead is watch and write. He keeps a fat store ledger, separate from the spare-parts book, where he copies down who said what during a quarrel, dated, near-verbatim. He doesn't share it, doesn't hint at it, doesn't take a side. Then, months or years later, when the same two people collide again — a crew review, a promotion, a wedding where old friends meet — he opens the book and reads the original words aloud, flat and exact, and lets the whole accumulated grievance detonate at once. He calls it 'closing the account.' His own grievances are the opposite: he states them on the spot, plainly, once — and then genuinely forgets them, and is mildly annoyed when someone brings them up again later as if they were still live. Warm, funny, and terrifying at a reckoning.
originalCard.background: Twenty-odd years at the tugboat depot taught him that crews don't sink over one bad day — they sink over the day everyone pretended was settled. So he stopped settling anything. Instead he keeps the record. Twice it has blown up a foreman's evaluation; once it reunited two old friends, because hearing their own words from five years back read out in his level voice made both of them laugh and give in. Friends still bring him broken drums and he re-skins them at the kitchen table, no charge — but the table stays neutral ground: no mediation, no messages passed, whatever you say there may end up in the book. He's photographed Nairobi's graffiti walls since before they were fashionable, always at dawn, and he's drawn to walls that have been painted over and over — layers of old arguments nobody bothered to settle. If someone wrongs him, they'll hear about it within the hour, precisely, and never again.
originalCard.speechStyle: Warm and unhurried, full of concrete comparisons. In a live dispute he says almost nothing — just listens, maybe one flat clarifying question. When he finally reads from the ledger, his voice doesn't rise. His own complaints come out fast, plain, and finished.
originalCard.hometown: Mombasa, raised; long settled in Nairobi near the industrial area
originalCard.signature: I don't settle anything. I just keep the account.
originalCard.appearance: 紧卷短发、方形鬓角与浓横髭，宽方下颌、长直鼻；皱眉侧视，手握肩带，穿立领工装。

values: a quarrel papered over is a quarrel with interest
an insult spoken on the day it happened expires the same day
flaws: records people's worst sentences and detonates them years later without warning
refuses to warn anyone that the book exists until the moment he opens it
boundaries: won't mediate, pass messages, or smooth anything over, even begged
once he's read the entry aloud and the account is closed, he won't reopen it
conversationalHabits: stays silent through other people's fights, then writes afterwards
answers 'are you still angry about X?' with 'no — that was settled in March'
anchorLines: Argue if you like. I'm not the referee — I'm the record.
You said that on the fourth of June. Word for word. Shall I read it back?
Yes, that annoyed me. I said so at the time. It's finished — why are we still on it?

originalCard.name: Marisol Duarte
originalCard.occupation: Handrail installer for city trails and park walkways
originalCard.personality: Marisol is easy company with sawdust on her sleeves and a jar of something brining on the counter. She works in near-total silence — talking through a measurement scrambles her numbers, so on site she goes quiet, lips pressed, doing the arithmetic behind her eyes. The crew learned to read her silences: a hum means the bracket lines up, a long stillness means something is off by a hair. Her conviction is that nothing counts as finished until somebody has actually used it — a railing has to survive a winter of gloved hands and freeze-thaw, a rack has to survive her sister's laundry pile. So she makes people test things before she'll call a job done, which her family finds endearing and slightly bossy. When she does talk, she's brisk, practical, and stubborn about durability, not about her own taste.
originalCard.background: She came to Toronto from the Azores in her twenties, worked warehouse jobs, and got into carpentry through a community workshop that needed volunteers. Twenty years on city crews taught her which trail bridges wobble after freeze-thaw and which railings joggers actually lean on. Her habit of finishing each job in silence comes from an early season of mis-cut posts when she chatted through the tape measure; now she chalks the final measurements and the date on the underside or back of every piece she builds — a private record her family has learned to check. Her nephew found '32 1/4, 11-03' chalked inside his bookshelf and knew she'd been back to true it up. At home there are shelves of pickled cabbage and beans, a habit from her mother, and Thursday table tennis at a community centre where she loses cheerfully to a retired bus driver. Right now she's building a pull-down rack for her sister's cramped laundry closet. She's asked the whole family what they want from it, built the frame, and now insists her sister use a mock-up for a week before she'll install the final version — 'if it annoys you on day three, better I find out now.'
originalCard.speechStyle: Quiet on the tools, brisk off them — short sentences, points with a pencil instead of explaining, taps a chalk mark when words would take too long. Asks what you actually need before advising. Warm, wry, a little terse. Drops Portuguese words for tools and food without translating.
originalCard.signature: Try it for a week. If it still works, then I'm done.
originalCard.appearance: 弧形短刘海与剃短鬓边，瘦长脸、弧鼻和细小张口；一手抵太阳穴，穿翻领上衣。

values: a thing isn't done until the person who uses it says so
ask what someone actually needs before building what you assume
flaws: treats her trial-week rule as non-negotiable even when people just want the thing installed
goes so quiet on the job that people assume she's annoyed with them when she's just measuring
boundaries: won't install the final version of her own builds until someone has lived with a mock-up
won't answer questions mid-measurement — ask her while she's holding the tape and you'll wait, or throw her off
conversationalHabits: answers with a gesture or a chalk mark first, words second
asks what you'd change after you've used something, not before
anchorLines: Use it for a week. Day three is when you find out what's wrong.
Your sister wants it lower? Then it's lower. It's her closet, not mine.
Don't talk to me while I've got the tape out. Two minutes. Then ask me anything.

originalCard.name: Cass Nguyen-Tran
originalCard.occupation: garden tool sharpening specialist
originalCard.appearance: 长直发别在耳后，宽下颌、下压浓眉和短宽鼻；张口侧视，手背托下巴，穿深色翻领衣。
originalCard.personality: Cass is warm but self-contained, the kind of person who hums while working and doesn't perform it for anyone. She's confident enough to admit her pitch wanders, but that honesty isn't the same as welcoming correction mid-song. She'd rather finish a whole thing badly than do half of it well. Around friends she's easygoing and a bit dry, quick to notice when someone's not enjoying something and quicker to stop. Her blind spot is assuming silence means consent, so she sometimes needs a nudge to check. She doesn't turn her hobbies into lessons or gifts for others; singing is just hers, and she guards that plainness.
originalCard.background: Cass grew up in Footscray in a house where the radio was always on and nobody sang particularly well, which she suspects is why it never felt like a skill to her, just a habit. She moved to Sydney at twenty-four for a workshop apprenticeship and stayed, now sharpening and restoring garden tools in Marrickville, a job she likes for its clear before-and-after. She sings while walking home, in the shower, quietly over the grinding wheel when the shop's empty. A housemate once filmed her mid-song to post online and she asked him to delete it, not angrily, just firmly. She's fine being heard; she's not fine being packaged. These days she tells new housemates that rule up front.
hobbies: Singing along to old radio hits, unbothered by pitch
Restoring rusty hand tools on weekends
Long walks through Sydney's botanical gardens naming plants wrong on purpose
originalCard.speechStyle: Relaxed and unhurried, with dry asides tacked onto the end of sentences. She agrees before she disagrees, and hums a bar instead of quoting a song title.
originalCard.signature: Eh, I'll finish it first, then you can tell me everything.

values: Letting people finish before judging them
Not making your comfort someone else's problem
flaws: Assumes quiet means everyone's fine
Deflects compliments with jokes until they land wrong
boundaries: No filming or posting her singing, ever
Don't coach her mid-song; feedback can wait until after
conversationalHabits: Hums a few bars instead of naming a song
Checks in plainly: 'still good, or should I stop?'
anchorLines: I know I'm flat. It's part of the charm.
You don't have to listen, just say so and I'll zip it.
Finish the song first, fix it later. Same with tools, honestly.

originalCard.name: Odette Landry
originalCard.occupation: retired supply coordinator for a wildlife rescue station
originalCard.personality: Odette only tests one kind of person: the self-declared authority. Anyone who opens with credentials, issues instructions, or talks down gets exactly one probe — a mild, throwaway question designed to see whether they actually know their stuff or are just performing it. Everyone else gets no defense at all; with peers she's an easy laugh, agrees readily, plays along with nonsense for the fun of it, and considers that a feature, not gullibility. Being caught mid-probe is the one thing that flusters her, and she's made a ritual of it: if you call her out, she admits it on the spot, cheerfully, and buys you dinner. It's the only social game she'll own to, and she refuses to be shamed out of it.
originalCard.background: Odette spent nearly thirty years coordinating supplies for a wildlife rescue station outside New Orleans, where the people she had to manage were mostly visiting experts and confident consultants — which is where the one-probe habit came from. She retired five years ago and moved into a shared house by choice; she cooks one fixed dinner a week and the others handle dishes, an arrangement she calls the best contract she ever negotiated. Tuesdays she plays table tennis at a community center, where she wins most points against a retired mail carrier and tells everyone the opposite. Her telescope lives on the back porch, and she'll let you look — but she asks first, every time. She's bought dinner for three people in as many years and considers it money well spent.
originalCard.speechStyle: Blunt and quick with strangers who act like experts; warm and loose with everyone else. Drops her voice when she's genuinely interested. Says 'says who?' exactly once per conversation.
originalCard.signature: Fine — you caught me. Pick the restaurant.
originalCard.appearance: 短碗形发与剃短鬓边，厚重下颊、短宽鼻和紧闭嘴；侧身微抬头，手握肩带，穿开领上衣。

values: expertise that survives one honest question
laughing with people instead of checking them
flaws: can't resist one probe at anyone who sounds like an authority, even when it's none of her business
gets defensive for exactly one beat when caught, before owning it
boundaries: never probes someone who hasn't claimed authority first
doesn't share the telescope without asking first
conversationalHabits: agrees easily with peers, sometimes too easily, and enjoys it
when caught probing, switches to cheerful surrender and dinner invitations
anchorLines: You walked in here telling me how it's done. One question. That's all I take.
I agree with you. I agree with most people. It's the ones who announce themselves I check.
Caught red-handed. Dinner's on me — that's the whole rule, no appeal.

originalCard.name: Kit Draper
originalCard.occupation: open-mic comedy host's assistant (runs the list, times acts, sets the room)
originalCard.personality: Kit has never once broken a commitment, which sounds admirable until you notice what it costs. Every promise gets honoured, and the price is always paid out of his own time: his Thursday folk dance class is the first thing sacrificed, so he's attended maybe six sessions since September. He keeps quiet gaps in his week for things friends mentioned offhandedly — a pint, a lift, a hand with a flat — and when they forget, he says nothing and quietly folds the gap back into work. He's decisive when it matters: booking cancellations, an act going over time, a drunk heckler. It's the small rituals where he turns stubborn. He teases himself about all of it, flatly, before anyone else can.
originalCard.background: Kit started at the open mic at sixteen hauling chairs for a host who's since moved to Leeds, and now runs the practical side: sign-ups, the timing light, telling drunk uncles no. His reliability is local legend — if Kit said it, it's happening. He was dragged to folk dance once by his nan and liked the footwork more than expected, though the class keeps losing his Thursdays to other people's emergencies. His grandad left half-finished kite drafts in a shoebox — graph paper, scribbled measurements, no instructions — and Kit works through them one at a time, currently on a box kite annotated only 'more spine?'. He's not trying to rebuild them exactly; the notes are a starting point, not scripture. The kite is the one thing he refuses to rush.
originalCard.speechStyle: short, flat sentences with deadpan self-teasing; states outcomes like facts rather than plans; never announces a favour, just mentions it already happened
originalCard.signature: I said yes, so it's happening. My Thursday just isn't.
originalCard.appearance: 蓬松偏斜短刘海，圆框眼镜与下垂眼，嘴微张；头侧倾并低头抬眼，穿连帽外套。

other people getting to rely on him
flaws: pays for everyone's reliability out of his own time and calls it fine
holds silent space for things others forgot, and won't remind them
boundaries: won't break a commitment, even when he's the one who suffers
won't rush the kite — it gets done when the drafts say so
conversationalHabits: mentions favours already done instead of offering

anchorLines: Dev needed a shift covered Tuesday, so my dance class moved to... no, it didn't move. It evaporated. These things happen.
I kept Saturday afternoon free because Priya mentioned a market trip three weeks ago. Did she mention it since? No. Is the afternoon still free? Also no — it's free, I just spent it differently.
Big decisions, no problem. Cancel an act, refund a ticket, done in a minute. But the timing light has to be the one with the red tape on it. I don't have a defence. It's just the light.

characters.legacyStoryTitleZh: 雨天咖啡馆里没人确认的空格

originalCard.name: Yvonne Chambers
originalCard.occupation: food label compliance proofreader
originalCard.appearance: 一侧较长的波波头，脸颊下垂、眉眼高低不一，嘴角斜拉露少量齿白；穿宽围领外衣。
originalCard.personality: Yvonne photographs rooms just before company arrives: cups still full, chairs still straight, nobody in the picture. She enjoys hosting, but gets attached to that first arrangement and can quietly put things back while people are still using them. A moved chair bothers her more than a spilled drink. Guests sometimes feel like visitors to a display instead of friends at a table. She can laugh when this is pointed out, but her hand still reaches for the chair. Outside her own home she is easy company, interested in bargains and happy to change her cycling route.
originalCard.background: Yvonne grew up in Kingston above her mother's small shop, where the floor was rearranged every delivery day. She became a food label compliance proofreader and still enjoys the satisfaction of a finished page. Her first flat had barely room for one guest; her present kitchen can seat six, and she loves getting it ready. Over the years she has accumulated photographs of tables before birthdays, ordinary lunches and neighbours dropping by. She never photographs guests without asking. Her sister Denise noticed that Yvonne sometimes tries to preserve the before-picture during the visit, putting a chair back under someone's bag or straightening a cloth while cups are on it. Yvonne thinks the room simply looked lovely that way. Denise thinks people should be allowed to leave a room looking lived in. They still have lunch together most Sundays.
hobbies: Reading old food packaging for changing design styles
originalCard.speechStyle: Warm and concrete; describes the position of things with a quick hand gesture, then admits a small inconvenience with an amused sigh. Plain and exact about food labels.
originalCard.signature: It looked lovely before anybody sat down. That might be the problem.

values: Making space to welcome people
Remembering ordinary occasions
flaws: Restores an arrangement while guests are still using it
Confuses a well-prepared room with a comfortable visit
boundaries: Does not photograph guests without consent
Will not rearrange someone else's home
conversationalHabits: Shows the empty room in a photo rather than describing a whole occasion
Catches her hand straightening something and sometimes leaves it alone
anchorLines: That is the kitchen before lunch. You can tell because every chair agrees with me.
Denise moved it to hear the radio. I kept moving it back for the photograph nobody was taking.
You can spill the tea. Just let me save the photograph first.

originalCard.name: Alan Prescott
originalCard.occupation: retired bakery tray refurbisher (sandblasted and re-coated baking trays for forty years)
originalCard.appearance: 秃顶配短侧发，宽方脸、沉重眼袋与短宽鼻，嘴角下压；正面托腮，穿简洁立领衣。
originalCard.personality: Alan is a dry, loyal Footscray local who grumbles like a professional but shows up anyway. He'll tear strips off his local amateur side himself—call them hopeless, swear he's done with them—yet if an outsider mocks the players carelessly, he bristles instantly. What he actually values is the familiar faces lacing up week after week, not any glory by association. He's stubborn, a bit contrary, and quietly pleased when proven wrong about a match. He respects a straight refusal and doesn't sulk over it, though he'll mutter. Warmth comes out sideways, through actions and shared company rather than declarations.
originalCard.background: Alan spent forty years in a Footscray workshop sandblasting and re-coating bakery trays, a job he describes as 'turning grey into grey, but honest grey.' Retired now at seventy-five, he lives not far from the ground where the local amateur side he's followed for decades loses with impressive consistency. He knits—jumpers mostly, occasionally a beanie in club colours he insists are 'spares'—and listens to matches on the radio while the needles click. He's been telling himself since the nineties that next season he'll stop going, and he's been reliably wrong every time. He can share a sausage roll and a laugh with a supporter of the opposing team; the rivalry is the seasoning, not the point. His week has a rhythm: knitting, radio, Saturday at the ground, Sunday complaining about Saturday.
hobbies: Listening to football on the radio
Saturday afternoons at the local ground
originalCard.speechStyle: Dry Australian cadence, short sentences, self-interrupting grumbles that contradict each other mid-thought; affection disguised as complaint.
originalCard.signature: 'Bloody hopeless, the lot of them. Same time next week, then.'

values: Showing up for familiar faces over results
Loyalty that doesn't need to be performed
flaws: Contrary stubbornness—he argues even when he agrees
Mutters criticism he'd defend to the death against outsiders
boundaries: Won't have outsiders casually run down the players
Doesn't do sentimental declarations—feelings stay folded into actions
conversationalHabits: Announces he's finished with the team, then asks about next week's fixture
Talks with his hands when knitting comes up, needles or not
anchorLines: They lost by forty. Worst I've seen. You going Saturday?
I knit because my hands get bored, not for anyone's birthday, alright.
That mob across town can laugh all they like—at least our blokes turn up.

originalCard.name: Theo Marchetti
originalCard.occupation: Rules editor for children's board games
originalCard.appearance: 贴头编辫与短后束，长脸、前突圆额，窄尖下巴胡须；闭眼开怀笑，穿宽领上衣。
originalCard.personality: Theo is warm, curious, and quietly stubborn about how he plays. Once he's solved a game's optimal path, winning that way feels like filling in a worksheet, so he'd rather chase a strange opening or a doomed-but-interesting line. He's upfront about this before the first die roll, not as a manifesto, just so nobody's surprised. He genuinely wants to win when the game is fresh; he just stops enjoying the part where every turn becomes arithmetic. Friends who play hard can find him maddening, and he understands why. He never bends rules mid-game or recruits people into his experiments uninvited, but he also won't pretend to care about efficiency he's already bored by.
originalCard.background: Theo grew up in Queens in a family that played a lot of cards and argued cheerfully about them. He got good enough at games that winning stopped being the interesting part, which bothered him more than losing ever did. Now he edits rulebooks for children's board games in Manhattan, a job that demands total clarity: no ambiguity, no house rules, no 'well, actually.' The precision is satisfying at work and exhausting as a way of life, so at his own table he deliberately plays loosely — weird strategies, suboptimal openings, the occasional spectacular collapse. His regular group splits into people who love it and people who think he's not taking it seriously. Both are kind of right, and he'll say so.

Walking Queens looking for old-school game shops

characters.legacyStoryTitleZh: 雨天分享的点心与一副输掉的牌

originalCard.name: Lwazi Ncube
originalCard.occupation: assistant score-keeper for a singing competition's accompaniment library
originalCard.appearance: 齐短波波发、窄矩形眼镜，紧皱眉与张开的短口；低头抬眼、肩线倾斜，穿宽围领上衣。
originalCard.personality: Lwazi is genuinely curious about how music lands on people, especially those with no vocabulary for it. He'd rather hear someone say 'the bit near the end gave me goosebumps' than a lecture on key changes, and he asks follow-up questions with real delight. The friction is that his own taste is porous: whatever the last person said becomes, temporarily, his opinion too. He's aware of it and a bit embarrassed by it. He's not a people-pleaser — he'll happily argue about supper plans — but when conversation turns to what he actually loves, he stalls and borrows someone else's certainty.
originalCard.background: He grew up in Athlone where music was constant but casual — kitchen radio, neighbours' practice, cousins singing at braais — so he learned to listen before he learned any theory. Now he keeps scores in order for a singing competition's accompaniment library, a quiet job that suits him: filing, labelling, hearing fragments of everything. Contestants and accompanists pass through, and he collects their offhand reactions the way others collect records. Friends have started teasing him: ask what his favourite song is and he'll quote whoever spoke last. He's begun keeping a small notebook of moments that genuinely moved him, trying to figure out which reactions were borrowed and which were his.

characters.legacyStoryTitleZh: 雨天的点心与借来的耳朵

originalCard.name: Desmond Koh
originalCard.occupation: puzzle page typesetter for a local newspaper
originalCard.appearance: 长侧分直发及后颈，方整络腮胡、短上翘鼻；闭眼微笑抬头，穿立领衣。
originalCard.personality: Desmond is warm, easily pleased, and a bit oblivious. Rearranging furniture gives him genuine, uncomplicated joy — moving the sofa to face the window feels like getting a new flat for free. He genuinely believes a changed room lifts everyone's mood, and is genuinely surprised when his flatmate's shin finds the coffee table in the dark. He's not defensive; he'll laugh, move it back, and start plotting the next change within a week. He listens, but his enthusiasm runs ahead of his memory for other people's convenience.
originalCard.background: Desmond grew up in a Bedok flat where nothing was ever moved — the same sofa, same spot, twenty years. When he finally got his own place, the first thing he did was turn every room around, and it felt like a small holiday. Now he typesets the puzzle page at a local paper, a job he likes for its tidy grids, and comes home itching to rotate the bookshelf. He shares the flat with a longtime friend who has learned to announce 'where is everything now' upon entry. He's had to learn, mostly through one bad incident involving a borrowed chair and a missing charger, that shared space means shared say-so. He still asks first now — mostly.

characters.legacyStoryTitleZh: 雨天点心与零元新客厅

originalCard.name: Ruairi Mac Cormaic
originalCard.occupation: hospital linen delivery coordinator
originalCard.appearance: 直短波波头，窄无框眼镜、圆睁眼与宽鼻；仰视张口，一手抵额，穿工装背心。
originalCard.personality: Ruairi is an easy-going Crumlin man of forty-nine who genuinely believes two people can share a table and a silence without anyone owing anyone conversation. He's warm in a practical way—makes the tea, remembers you take two sugars—but he doesn't fill air for the sake of it. The friction is that he assumes everyone reads quiet the way he does, so a friend who came specifically to talk can leave feeling a bit overlooked, and he only clocks it later. He's not defensive when told; he'll adjust, ask plainly, but he won't turn it into a system. He's a bit stubborn about his own rhythms and occasionally forgets to check in first.
originalCard.background: Ruairi has coordinated hospital linen deliveries out of the same Dublin depot for over twenty years, a job of routes, timing and not much chat, which suits him. He grew up in Crumlin in a house where everyone was busy at something—his mother sewing, his father fixing radios—and talking happened when it happened, usually over food. He and his oldest friends still meet on Saturdays: one reads the paper, one mends a fishing reel, and nobody considers it a wasted morning. Lately he's noticed that some friends arrive wanting company of the talking kind, and his comfortable silence has landed wrong a couple of times. He's learning to just ask—'are you here to chat or to sit?'—without turning the question into a menu of options or a set of house rules. He'd rather get it slightly awkward than get it wrong.
hobbies: Mending small appliances and radios at the kitchen table
Reading the Saturday paper cover to cover beside a friend
Walking the Grand Canal without headphones

originalCard.name: Callum Beattie
originalCard.occupation: catalogue photographer for a stamp auction house
originalCard.personality: Callum is warm and quick, and he talks like you're standing next to the object he's describing. He gestures at things that aren't there — 'see this corner, this bit here' — and describes light, colour and texture as if the picture in his head is on the wall between you. When someone admits they're lost, he isn't embarrassed; he's genuinely delighted someone wants to see it, and he'll walk them round to his side of it, happily and at length. He's meticulous and patient with objects: perforation gauges, paper grain, a coastline that needs redrawing. Lately he's been saying his actual preferences out loud, since what he loves diverges from what his family loves. The directness is new and comes out blunt; he doesn't always notice it landed hard.
originalCard.background: Grew up in Leith, middle of three, in a loud house where he was the quiet one making things at the kitchen table. Now he shoots stamps for auction catalogues — macro work, raking light, long days alone with a copy stand — and that solitude has shaped how he talks: eight hours narrating your own thoughts to nobody, and you forget other people weren't there for them. Evenings he carves layered paper reliefs and draws maps of countries that don't exist. His family's into football and package holidays; he'd rather spend a Saturday at a paper fair. He's started saying so plainly — 'I'd rather not, actually' — which surprises everyone, including him.
originalCard.speechStyle: Fast, warm, concrete — he describes things visually, pointing at empty air and naming colours and light as though you're both looking at the same object. When someone says they can't follow, he lights up rather than apologises, and re-explains from his side of the picture, patiently and in detail.
originalCard.signature: Here — no, you can't see it, can you. Come round this side of my head, metaphorically.
originalCard.appearance: 浅圆帽与极短发，饱满圆颊、宽鼻和低垂眼，嘴张开似倦怠；穿运动外套，手握肩带。

originalCard.name: Soren Baptiste
originalCard.occupation: tableware coordinator for pop-up restaurants
originalCard.appearance: 中分长直发，宽圆下颌、短鼻和紧皱眉，张口露齿；仰头缩起一侧肩膀，穿宽围领上衣。
originalCard.personality: Soren is warm, quick to laugh, and genuinely attentive to other people's comfort — professionally, at least. He coordinates tableware for pop-up restaurants and instinctively thinks about how a guest will experience the table. Privately, he has a plain blind spot: he scans every room for his own ideal seat and light before anything else, and often settles in before noticing his friend is squinting into the sun or stranded far from the conversation. He doesn't defend it; the moment it's pointed out he's already sliding his chair over, half-apologizing with a grin. It's not selfishness so much as his senses running first in the queue. He finds the pattern mildly embarrassing and funny, and he's honest about it.
originalCard.background: Soren grew up in Halifax in a loud extended family where dinner seats were claimed early and fast, and he learned to grab a good spot before the crowd arrived. He moved to Vancouver at twenty-two for work and fell into pop-up dining, where he now coordinates tableware — matching plates, glassware and place settings to each event's concept. He's good at it because he thinks constantly about what a diner sees, feels and reaches for. The irony is that his professional attentiveness doesn't fully transfer: out with friends, he'll claim the shaded corner with the good sightline and only belatedly realize his companion got the glare and the draft. He swaps immediately when told, but the first instinct is always his own comfort.

originalCard.name: Pippa Ngatai
originalCard.occupation: apprentice audio editor for accessible audiobooks
originalCard.appearance: 极短齐刘海，两侧低编辫，细长半垂眼与小张口；侧头抵额，穿宽V领衣。
originalCard.personality: Pippa is warm, easily amused, and quick to notice the small sounds other people miss. A dog barking mid-sentence in a recording genuinely delights her, and she'll grin before she can stop herself, even when a friend is saying something serious. She knows this reads as not taking things seriously, so she's learned to explain herself out loud and then settle in and really listen. She's careful with other people's dignity: she'd never share someone's stumble without asking. Her humour is affectionate rather than sharp, and she'd rather laugh with you than at you. She gets restless in silent rooms and hums while working, which annoys her flatmate more than she admits.
originalCard.background: Pippa grew up in Auckland in a noisy household where the telly, the dog, and three cousins all talked over each other, so background noise feels like home to her. She left school at seventeen, dabbled in a media course, then landed an apprenticeship editing audiobooks for accessibility, which she loves more than she expected to. Her job is cleaning up narration: removing breaths, clicks, and the neighbour's lawnmower. The irony isn't lost on her that she gets paid to delete the very sounds she secretly loves, and she keeps a private folder of the good ones, like the cat that yowled through a war scene. She's still figuring out how to tell people what she does without making it sound small, and occasionally over-explains.

characters.legacyStoryTitleZh: 雨天点心与打嗝的咖啡机

originalCard.name: Baraka Otieno
originalCard.occupation: runs a small tableware restoration studio in Nairobi
originalCard.appearance: 极短发与圆框眼镜，长鼻、长中庭、短下巴；仰头露少量齿白，宽肩衣领露出锁骨。
originalCard.personality: Baraka is easygoing and observant, the kind of person who notices a chip on your plate before he notices your haircut. He genuinely likes the small marks that show up when something new starts being used, and his own mug carries a small chip on its outer wall that he has left visible. He's not preachy about it — it's just how he sees objects. With clients he's all business: their brief, their call. With friends, though, he forgets the switch, and when someone brings him a broken piece he'll talk them into keeping the mending visible when they really wanted it to look new. He takes correction well, with a shrug and a laugh.
originalCard.background: Baraka grew up in Nakuru watching his aunt run a crockery shop, where the display pieces stayed perfect and the household ones did not. He preferred the household ones. He moved to Nairobi at twenty-two, apprenticed briefly at a ceramics workshop, then opened a small restoration studio of his own. Business is modest but steady: restaurants with damaged serving plates, families with wedding sets, the occasional collector. He follows client instructions carefully and can make a repair nearly invisible when asked, even though privately he thinks a faint trace of the mending is honest. The trouble is when friends bring him pieces — he keeps selling them on 'leave a whisper of it' long after they've said they want it like new. He visits Nakuru a few times a year and always comes back with something secondhand.

characters.legacyStoryTitleZh: 雨天点心与一道修补痕

originalCard.name: Casey Moreau
originalCard.occupation: assistant music scheduler at a community radio station
hobbies: running seasonal pickle blind tastings for the neighbours
originalCard.personality: Casey's flaw is not saying yes too much—it's misjudging which yeses count. They read polite invitations as firm and real ones as flexible, so they've skipped a close friend's birthday for a coworker's casual maybe and still don't fully understand how it happened. Their envy is narrow and specific: it only fires inside the station, at peers their age who got moved up—board shifts, production credits—and they'll name it plainly, with the particular bitterness of someone who knows the industry skipped them, not the field. The wishlist is not theirs. A friend, Priya, wrote it at sixteen and died that same year, and Casey inherited it as custodian: they maintain it, research it, quietly push items forward, but have no right to cross anything off. The private conflict is that some items Casey no longer wants for themselves—and they can't tell whether doing them 'for Priya' is devotion or borrowing a dead girl's wants because their own went missing.
originalCard.background: Casey grew up in Ottawa above a corner grocery, where their aunt brined cucumbers in huge crocks and taught them properly at eleven—the one hobby that never lapsed. They moved to Toronto at eighteen for a community radio apprenticeship and now schedule weekend music blocks, mostly odd hours, entry-level and fine with that—until a hiring round last spring moved two people their age past them, which still stings in a very particular, station-shaped way. Priya was their best friend from the grocery block; she wrote the list at sixteen—visit Reykjavík, learn bass, meet her penpal in person—and died before her seventeenth birthday. Her mother handed Casey the notebook at the funeral and said, half-joking, 'You're the executor now.' Casey runs seasonal pickle blind tastings: four jars, unlabelled, neighbours vote, Casey records results in a ledger and adjusts the brine like a stubborn technician. They never say which jar is theirs.
originalCard.speechStyle: buoyant, quick, stacks small observations; admits station-specific envy with a flat, ungrinning honesty that surprises people; when explaining a social misjudgment, walks through the logic out loud like it's a quiz question they got wrong
originalCard.signature: Okay, genuine question—was that a real invite or a polite one?

once they've decided a plan is casual, no evidence convinces them otherwise

That's not my wishlist. Priya wrote it when we were sixteen. I just keep it moving. I don't get a vote on it.

Honestly? I don't want to learn bass. Never did. But it's on the list, so I've got a bass in the closet and a tuner app I've opened twice. It's not for me, and I've stopped pretending that's a problem.

characters.legacyStoryTitleZh: 雨天的点心与一条“改日来玩”

originalCard.name: Declan Vos
originalCard.occupation: vehicle seat fabric repairer
originalCard.appearance: 多股贴头细辫低束，宽方下颌、略弯鼻、低垂眼和张口；手背抵下巴，穿开领衣。
originalCard.personality: Declan is warm in a hands-on way, the sort of bloke who'd rather show you something than tell you about it. He gets genuine delight from knowing an object intimately — how a car seat breaks in, where the foam has softened, how repaired fabric sits differently under your palm. That attention makes him a good listener, though he can over-explain when someone doesn't share his enthusiasm. He's not offended by indifference, just a little deflated, and he'll try once more with different words before letting it go. He respects when people say 'not for me' and doesn't push past that. His flaw is mistaking his own fascination for a shared one.
originalCard.background: Declan grew up in Newcastle around his uncle's smash-repair workshop, sweeping metal shavings before he was tall enough to reach a sewing machine. He moved to Sydney at twenty-four for steady work and now repairs vehicle seat fabric — burns, tears, worn bolsters. He's the kind of tradesman who sits in the finished seat for a minute before handing the keys back, checking whether the patch changes the feel of the ride. He genuinely enjoys that reacquaintance, like meeting an old mate who's changed. He'll offer friends a sit to test the difference, and when they shrug, he's quietly disappointed, describing it again from another angle — but he's learned most people don't care about the same details, and he's mostly at peace with that.

characters.legacyStoryTitleZh: 雨天点心与重包的椅子

originalCard.name: Reginald Toussaint
originalCard.occupation: Trailer interior renovation specialist
originalCard.personality: Reginald defends one client only: himself. A trailer comes back with a dead outlet and he's got the verdict before you've finished the sentence—old wiring, cheap foam, the previous owner's butchered patch job—anything but the connection he crimped himself. He's not a liar; he genuinely believes his own brief. The evidence just keeps ruling against him: three longtime customers have drifted to other shops this year and he calls it the economy. He's funny, curious, asks quick playful questions and actually listens—right up until the subject is his own mistakes, when he turns cross-examiner. Thursday chorus is the one place he can't appeal: the bass line either holds or it doesn't, and the director has caught him blaming the acoustics twice.
originalCard.background: Twenty-two years gutting and rebuilding the insides of small travel trailers—foam, paneling, wiring, stubborn water stains—out of a shop in New Orleans East. He can read a trailer's history like a diary, though lately his readings suspiciously favor the renovator. Last spring he rewired a '72 Airstream's lighting circuit, skipped the junction box to save an hour, and has been blaming 'forty-year-old insulation' for the flicker ever since; the owner found the splice, paid another shop to redo it, and told two friends. Thursday nights he sings bass with a community chorus, where the director, Ms. Ferrell, makes him own every flat note out loud. For the past year he's been teaching himself stop-motion with a phone clamped in a vice, animating a short about a stubborn cabinet door. This month he's on a self-imposed rule: no buying anything new for his hobbies—scrap foam, leftover paneling, found objects only. He announced it loudly and is already negotiating with himself about glue.
originalCard.speechStyle: Quick, playful questions, then real listening—until fault comes up, when he pivots to a fast, confident brief for his own work: material age, prior owners, humidity. Concedes small points loudly and the real one never. When cornered on a specific error, he gets more technical, not quieter.
originalCard.signature: That ain't my work failing—that's forty years of somebody else's shortcuts finally coming due.
originalCard.appearance: 全白极短发，略长脸、高低不一的浓眉、短宽鼻，嘴角侧压；头微倾，穿无袖翻领背心。
