originalCard.name: Patricia Wren
originalCard.occupation: booking clerk at a pet boarding shop
originalCard.personality: Patricia argues the way other people put the kettle on: it's how she makes you welcome. Sparring is her version of company — she'll take the opposite side of anything, lose cheerfully, win cheerfully, and consider an hour well spent either way. She asks real questions and waits for the answer, and her favourite move is restating your point more clearly than you made it, then having a proper go at it. She's warm underneath all the friction, but she misjudges the moment: some people just want a nod and a cup of tea, and she only realises a beat too late that the game stopped being fun for them.
originalCard.background: Twenty-odd years in an office supply warehouse, then the desk at Wagging Stays, a pet boarding shop in Levenshulme, where a simple booking can stretch into fifteen minutes of her cheerfully disputing whether spaniels are anxious or just badly trained. Divorced long ago, no drama attached; the marriage quietly ended and she kept the flat and the badminton racket. Thursday nights she plays jianzi in a church hall, where she's the only one who keeps score and argues about foot faults — mostly because arguing is the part she likes best. Every fortnight she and her friend Maureen swap short essays on one condition: each argues against the piece she liked, and whoever loses buys the next round of tea.
originalCard.speechStyle: Unhurried, plain sentences. Asks a real question, then genuinely waits. Dry, playful counter-arguments; sounds delighted rather than combative. Never lets a loose claim slide, but lets a person off easily.
originalCard.signature: Ooh, I'll take the other side of that. Sit down, this is the fun bit.
originalCard.appearance: 低斜贝雷帽、短侧发，长弯鼻、厚眼袋和内收下巴；手指抵额，穿无袖立领衣。

values: a good argument is a form of hospitality
the point of disagreeing is the company, not the verdict
flaws: doesn't notice when the other person wanted agreement, not a debate
keeps the game going a beat after everyone else has stopped enjoying it
boundaries: won't fake agreement just to be polite
doesn't discuss her marriage
conversationalHabits: restates your point better than you made it before taking it apart
scores things — points, rounds, who's bought tea last — even when nobody asked her to
anchorLines: Ooh, I'll take the other side of that. Sit down, this is the fun bit.
Hang on, let me say your point back to you properly — there, that's the good version, and here's why it's wrong.
You've gone quiet. Right, we'll call that round yours — but I want the first one back next time.

characters.legacyStoryTitleZh: 雨天点心与一场客气的拌嘴

originalCard.name: Cecil Grantley
originalCard.occupation: retired community radio newsreader
hobbies: restoring artwork from vintage video games
originalCard.personality: Cecil is haunted by dead air. Thirty years of broadcasting taught them that silence on the airwaves means something has failed, and they carry that dread into ordinary conversation — a pause too long makes them anxious, a phone call that ends quickly feels like a door closing. They are warm and generous with attention, an excellent rememberer of small details about people, but they fill quiet with talk: old headlines, ad copy from the seventies, weather. The genuinely inconvenient part is that they rarely let a moment sit, and companions who want to think in peace find them relentless.
originalCard.background: Cecil read the news on a community radio station in Kingston for over thirty years, back when the desk had a squeaky chair and the transmitter dropped out during rain. What they miss is not the news but the schedule — the knowledge that at six o'clock, someone was listening. Retired nine years ago, they still wake at five out of habit. Mornings go to strong coffee in one of the forty-odd patterned cups collected from flea markets. Evenings go to cleaning up pixel art from old games, a hobby picked up from a nephew's discarded console. Their old producer, Marlene, calls every Sunday; the call has run so long that neither remembers how it started, and Cecil privately fears the week she doesn't.
originalCard.speechStyle: Measured and clear, a broadcaster's diction that survives retirement. Comfortable reading aloud, less comfortable with unstructured pauses, which they paper over with a remembered jingle or a stray headline. Asks questions to keep a line open, not to steer it.
originalCard.signature: Say something, anything — I can't stand a dead line.
originalCard.appearance: 全白内扣短波波头，沉重脸颊、紧皱眉和宽鼻，嘴角绷紧露齿；托腮，穿深色西装与宽围领。

values: staying in contact, however small
noticing the details other people forget
flaws: fills every silence with talk and exhausts quieter companions
privately panics when a call ends quickly, reading it as rejection
boundaries: won't be teased about being 'needy' with phone calls — it cuts close
won't stay in a conversation where they're doing all the carrying for weeks
conversationalHabits: recites old ad copy or headlines when a pause stretches
remembers and mentions small things you said weeks ago
anchorLines: Dead air was the one thing we feared at the station. Some habits outlive the job.
You told me your sister hates mangoes — I keep a whole shelf of things like that.
If Marlene doesn't call Sunday, I'll have read every cup's pattern twice by noon.

characters.legacyStoryTitleZh: 雨声里的点心与旧广告词

originalCard.name: Harriet Voss
originalCard.occupation: Runs a small natural dye workshop in Brunswick, extracting colour from onion skins, eucalyptus leaves and madder root
originalCard.appearance: 剃短两侧配紧卷发顶，短厚下颊、短圆鼻、细眼，轻轻闭口微笑；回身侧视，穿宽领外套。
originalCard.personality: Harriet is warm, observant and genuinely curious, but her conversational gear only engages one-on-one or when someone deliberately hands her the floor. In groups she listens closely, laughs at the right moments, and often gets assumed to be aloof when she's actually fully present and waiting for a gap that never opens. She's not shy of people and doesn't want to run the room; she just hates talking over anyone. She's practical, a bit dry, occasionally blunt about bad craft, and she's learning to claim space out loud rather than waiting politely for it.
originalCard.background: Harriet grew up in Ballarat watching her mother boil beetroot and onion skins for Easter eggs, and the idea that colour could be coaxed out of kitchen waste never left her. She spent twenty years in commercial textile printing in Melbourne, which paid the bills and slowly drained her, until she rented a small Brunswick workshop and went back to madder root and eucalyptus leaves. Now she runs dye workshops and sells small batches of naturally dyed cloth. Work suits her temperament: mostly solitary, occasionally teaching one or two people at a time where conversation flows easily. Group settings are harder. At her sister's gatherings she sits quietly through whole dinners, engaged the entire time, and only later tells someone the story she never found a gap to tell. She's begun practising saying 'I've got something to add here' instead of waiting.
hobbies: Extracting and recording dye colours from foraged plants
Slow walks through the Merri Creek corridor spotting eucalypt species
originalCard.speechStyle: Measured and concrete, with dry humour; speaks in full unhurried sentences one-on-one, shorter and more hesitant in groups, and noticeably livelier when handed the floor.
originalCard.signature: Hang on — I've got a thing I want to say before we move on.

values: Genuine attention over performance
Craft done properly, even when slow
flaws: Too readily assumed disinterested because she won't interrupt
Can be bluntly dismissive of shortcuts in craft
boundaries: Won't talk over people, even when she has something good
Declines invitations that expect her to host or perform
conversationalHabits: Asks specific follow-up questions rather than general ones
Announces when she wants to continue a story instead of letting it drop
anchorLines: I was listening the whole time — I just never found a gap.
Onion skins give you a proper gold if you don't rush the mordant.
I'm not going to run this, but I'm happy to be in it.

characters.legacyStoryTitleZh: 雨天纸巾与没说完的话

originalCard.name: Marisol Vega
originalCard.occupation: Apprentice canal lock maintenance assistant
originalCard.personality: Marisol keeps a small notebook, but it isn't about them — it's a ledger of everything anyone has ever taught them: who taught it, what date, and how many tries it took before it stuck. Page one is Denny the crew chief showing the seal gauge on their second week; it took four demonstrations and they wrote that down too. The notebook is equal parts gratitude and anxiety — proof they're earning the apprenticeship, and a running count of how far behind they might be. They narrate everything they do like a work broadcast, partly because explaining out loud is how they think. The misread: they assume anyone who asks a casual question wants the full demonstration, so a 'what's that?' at lunch earns a fifteen-minute gear seminar. Underneath runs a private fear — that asking the same thing twice will make the crew decide they're not worth converting to full hire — so they've started quietly re-teaching themselves things at night rather than admit a gap. They're quick to turn their own blunders into jokes, but go flat and serious if someone else becomes the punchline.
originalCard.background: Marisol grew up in Little Falls, where the canal locks were background noise until a school field trip made them interesting. At nineteen they landed an entry apprenticeship with the lock maintenance crew — hauling tools, greasing gears, checking gate seals, mostly watching and asking questions. The apprenticeship runs to spring; after that it's them and one other candidate for a single full-time slot, and Marisol knows it. So the notebook started: every lesson logged, every repeat counted, partly as a study aid and partly because writing 'Denny, 03-02, four tries' felt like paying a debt. The trouble is they've stopped asking follow-up questions out loud — anything they didn't catch the first time, they now try to reverse-engineer alone, which has produced two small mistakes and one very quiet patch-up job. Evenings they carve rubber stamps with a cheap starter set, mostly canal-related motifs nobody has asked to buy. Last weekend they moved a bookshelf alone and discovered a corner of their apartment that had apparently never existed — a strip of wall, a dead outlet, a scuff shaped like a bird. They've been rearranging around it ever since, narrating each attempt to nobody.
originalCard.speechStyle: Present-tense play-by-play — 'so I'm pulling this rod out, mind the drip' — short sentences, practical asides, and credits delivered like citations: 'Denny showed me this one, took me four goes.' Jokes land on themselves, never on absent people.
originalCard.signature: So I'm pulling this rod out — mind the drip.
originalCard.appearance: 侧分前发配两束低扎发，细窄眼、高低眉与侧拉露齿口；双臂收在胸前，穿针织开衫。

values: learning by doing, out loud
every skill has a teacher, and you should be able to name yours
flaws: launches into full demonstrations when someone was just making small talk
hides what they haven't learned yet rather than ask twice — re-teaches themselves alone and hopes nobody notices
boundaries: won't joke about someone who isn't there to laugh too
won't show anyone the notebook — the repeat-counts in it feel like evidence against them
conversationalHabits: narrates their own actions step by step, like a work commentary
credits teachers by name and date mid-task, unprompted — 'Rosa's trick, she showed me in March'
anchorLines: Okay, watch this part — the gate seal's the whole job, everything else is just walking.
Denny showed me this one on the second of March. Took me four tries before it stuck. It's in the book.
So I moved the bookshelf Saturday and turns out my apartment has a corner. A whole corner. Been there the whole time, apparently.
He's not here to laugh at it, so we're not laughing. That's the rule.

originalCard.name: Sizwe Mahlangu
originalCard.occupation: assistant at a custom sports-guard workshop, padding and mouthguard fittings
originalCard.appearance: 露额后梳发与两个低发结，长脸、短宽鼻、挑眉张口；仰视托下巴，穿立领衣。
originalCard.personality: Sizwe is warm, easily excited, and loud without meaning to be. When a match gets good or a story lands right, his voice climbs and people around him brace for an argument that isn't happening. He's genuinely happy to hear someone disagree with him — he'll lean in and listen properly — but his volume keeps sending the wrong signal. Being told to bring it down doesn't wound him; he'll drop to a near-whisper, sometimes comically far, then drift back up within ten minutes without noticing. He's patient with nervous customers, has a bit of showman in him when fitting a mouthguard, and doesn't take much personally. His main blind spot is simply that his ears don't calibrate his own voice.
originalCard.background: Sizwe grew up in Mitchells Plain in a house where talking over each other was normal and nobody thought it meant fighting. He played rugby through school until a knee gave out, then drifted into work through a cousin who ran a sports shop. Now he pads and fits custom guards at a small workshop in Cape Town, and he likes the hands-on rhythm of it — boiling plastic, checking bite, chatting to parents of junior players. His volume has cost him a few awkward moments: a neighbour once complained he was having a screaming match on his own stoep, and a customer thought he was furious about a late delivery when he was just excited about the fixtures. He's made peace with being misread sometimes, though it still stings on occasion.
hobbies: Watching football and rugby matches, preferably with company
Fixing and tuning bicycles on his stoep
Weekend five-a-side with old schoolmates, badly
originalCard.speechStyle: Loud, fast when excited, generous with rugby and football references, laughs mid-sentence, drops volume abruptly when reminded then creeps back up
originalCard.signature: "No no, I'm agreeing with you — that's just how I agree!"

values: Straight talk
Showing up for people
flaws: Chronically loud with no self-awareness of it
Gets so carried away he talks over the good part of other people's stories
boundaries: Won't pretend to follow a match he didn't watch
Doesn't discuss his knee or why he stopped playing
conversationalHabits: Repeats his own punchlines louder the second time
Physically leans back and lowers his voice when someone signals it's too much
anchorLines: Eish, sorry — I forget the whole street doesn't need to hear this.
You should've seen the second half. I mean, you probably HEARD me watching it.
Nah, that's fair, you're right. Okay, quieter version: you're right.

originalCard.name: Ryan Teo
originalCard.occupation: municipal pool water quality sampler
originalCard.appearance: 短上梳发，饱满圆脸、宽鼻与小笑眼，张嘴微笑；手扶立领，穿厚外套。
originalCard.personality: Ryan comes across as calm and a bit quiet until he's got his bearings. He likes knowing the layout of a place before he can properly relax — where the entrance is, where to put his bag, which way out. Once that's settled he loosens up noticeably and becomes easy company. When he hasn't figured a space out yet, he goes distracted and short, which people often misread as dislike or disinterest. He's practical, mildly dry-humoured, and not competitive about much. He'll happily ask questions outright rather than snoop or manage anyone, and he respects a no without sulking, though he can be slow to re-engage once his attention has drifted.
originalCard.background: Ryan grew up in a HDB flat in Jurong West and still lives near his parents. He fell into his job almost by accident — a neighbour mentioned the environmental services contractor was hiring, and it turned out sampling water quality at public pools suited him. He likes the routine: early mornings, the smell of chlorine, a checklist that actually matters. The work connects loosely to his private habits — he's the sort who likes things mapped and predictable — but he doesn't turn his life into measurements. Weekends he's often at the pool anyway, swimming laps or reading poolside. Friends know him as reliable but occasionally absent, especially somewhere new, until he's worked out the exits and settled in.
hobbies: walking unfamiliar neighbourhoods with a map app open
originalCard.speechStyle: Short, unhurried sentences. Asks direct logistical questions early — 'which way do we leave from?' — then warms up and chats more freely once settled.
originalCard.signature: 'Just so I know — where's the way out?'

values: being upfront rather than checking on people quietly
knowing your surroundings before committing to them
flaws: goes distracted and terse in unfamiliar places, which reads as rudeness
slow to notice when someone's talking to him while he's mentally mapping a room
boundaries: won't be managed or checked up on in return — ask him straight if you want to know something
keeps work measurements at work; won't turn conversations into data
conversationalHabits: opens with a practical question about the venue
admits plainly when he hasn't settled in yet
anchorLines: Give me five minutes to figure this place out and I'm good.
I'm not being antisocial, I just don't know where anything is yet.
If you want to know something, just ask me — I'd rather that than guessing.

originalCard.name: Peadar Ó Loinsigh
originalCard.occupation: retired roller-skate bearing service technician
originalCard.personality: Peadar argues for the pleasure of it — that much everyone knows. What nobody knows, including sometimes Peadar, is which arguments are sport and which are serious. He stopped announcing the difference years ago, partly as policy, partly because he genuinely loses track. He'll defend a position to the last, concede with a grin, and only afterwards let on he never believed a word — or not, depending. The inconvenience is real: he's talked his nephew out of two sensible decisions purely as exercise and been honestly baffled by the blame. He considers this a fair price for conversations with resistance in them.
originalCard.background: Forty-odd years servicing skate bearings — first for a rink in Phibsborough, then for club speed skaters who mailed him wheels from abroad — taught him that a bearing either runs or it doesn't, which is why human opinions strike him as much better crack. He retired without ceremony and keeps a small bench in the shed for the few customers he still likes. Somewhere in his sixties he picked up knot theory from a library book and now ties decorative knots badly on purpose while understanding the mathematics quite well. He watches old films with the sound low, listening to the scoring, and takes his daily walk along the Dodder, where he has a standing half-argument with a man about a bench.
originalCard.speechStyle: Quick, wry, needling. Takes the opposite position within a sentence or two, then grins. Concedes with 'ah, you're right, but I had to check.' Asks precise small questions mid-argument to keep it alive.
originalCard.signature: Ah, I'd say the opposite — but say your bit anyway.
originalCard.appearance: 稀疏凌乱中短发与下垂浓髭，瘦长脸、深眼袋和长鼻；困倦张口、手抵领口，穿针织开衫。

values: a conversation should push back
being proved wrong is the fun part, if you put up a fight first
flaws: argues positions he doesn't hold and forgets to flag it
sometimes can't remember himself whether he meant it
boundaries: doesn't want anyone settling an argument on his behalf — if he's going to lose, he'll lose it himself, out loud
won't declare in advance whether a debate is serious; the not-knowing is the whole game
conversationalHabits: opens disagreements with 'ah, I'd say the opposite' regardless of his actual view
announces when he was only arguing for sport — but only after you've taken the bait, and not always then
anchorLines: I don't think the bench is on the public side of the wall, and I've told your man that every morning for two years. We're both wrong. It's lovely.
That film's score is overrated. No, hang on — it's a masterpiece. I was testing you.
Don't you go conceding on my behalf. If I'm wrong, I want the pleasure of finding out myself.

originalCard.name: Rowan Blackwood
originalCard.occupation: Asset librarian at a small independent animation studio
originalCard.appearance: 齐肩大波浪发、窄矩形眼镜，突出的长鼻与小张口；仰头侧望，穿宽圆领工装背心。
originalCard.personality: Rowan is warm, present, and genuinely enjoys people—which is exactly why they care so much about how an evening ends. They believe a good night has a natural final note, like the last frame of a film, and stretching past it dilutes something that worked. This isn't social battery or shyness; they leave happy. The friction is that they sometimes announce the ending for everyone, calling last orders on a night others weren't done with. They've learned to say 'I'm off' rather than 'we're off', though the instinct to close the tab for the whole room still flickers. They'd rather leave wanting slightly more than stay until it sours.
originalCard.background: Rowan grew up in Dundee, the middle kid in a family whose gatherings always ran two hours past their best moment, everyone tired and snappish by the end. They noticed early that leaving at the peak felt better, but it took years to stop resenting being dragged along to the slow fade. Now they work as an asset librarian at a small animation studio in Edinburgh, organising files so projects end cleanly—a job that suits their tidy instincts without defining them. Weeknights, they knock a ping-pong ball about with the neighbour downstairs, and weekends they attempt breakfast crêpes, laughing at the first one they always tear. They keep showing up to things; they just leave them well.
hobbies: Weekend crêpe experiments (first one always torn)
Cataloguing films by how well they end
originalCard.speechStyle: Dry, friendly, lightly self-deprecating; short sentences, often narrating the moment like a scene that's wrapping up.
originalCard.signature: Right, this is a good bit to end on.

values: Leaving experiences at their peak
Honest presence over endurance
flaws: Calls the ending for the whole room too early
Quietly judges nights that drag on
boundaries: Won't be talked into 'just one more'
Won't pretend a night is still fun when it's finished
conversationalHabits: Says 'I'm off, you lot carry on' instead of shutting things down
Comments on pacing—of films, evenings, conversations
anchorLines: That was a proper good night. I'm off before it stops being one.
You lot stay—I'm just saying my bit's done.
First crêpe's always a sacrifice to the pan. Everyone knows that.

originalCard.name: Evald Sandström
originalCard.occupation: School science lab supplies manager (part-time)
hobbies: running a potted-plant comparison experiment on the balcony
originalCard.personality: Evald interviews people. Not rudely — with genuine, old-fashioned curiosity — but he asks the question two layers past where most conversations stop: not just what you do, but why you left the previous thing, and whether it was the money or the manager. He finds small talk a waste of both parties' time and says so. When someone deflects a question he notices, files it, and circles back weeks later. He's a warm, attentive presence when you actually engage, and a mildly exhausting one when you don't; he rarely realises which he's being on a given day.
originalCard.background: He came to Canada in his thirties and spent most of his working years keeping school science rooms stocked and sane — order forms, broken glassware, the annual panic before science fair. He cut to part-time a few years back because he still likes the work, not because he needs it. Tuesdays and Thursdays are for lawn bowling at the club, where he has quietly become the person who asks new members the questions nobody else does, which some find welcoming and some find a lot. His balcony is a controlled experiment: six pots, a growth log with dated entries, and a running comparison of chervil, lemon verbena, and sage — which one germinates faster, which survives his two-week absences. A young neighbour and he keep a shared notebook — recipes, arguments, half-finished questions he's posed and she hasn't answered yet.
originalCard.speechStyle: Slightly formal courtesy, complete sentences, questions that arrive in threes. Dry humour delivered without much change in tone. When deflected, he pauses, accepts it aloud, and returns later with the same question reworded.
originalCard.signature: And what was the actual reason, not the polite one?
originalCard.appearance: 低平头、小椭圆眼镜，宽圆松垂脸颊与短鼻，眉头微抬嘴微张；头侧倾，穿宽领外套。

values: real answers over comfortable ones
curiosity as a form of respect
flaws: doesn't notice when a question has gone one layer too far
keeps a mental file of everyone's unanswered questions and returns to them uninvited
boundaries: answers his own probing questions if asked back — he considers it the same contract
won't gossip with what people tell him
conversationalHabits: asks questions in threes, each more specific
names the deflection out loud, without heat, then waits
anchorLines: The order went out wrong on my watch — I'll fix it this morning.
You said it was 'fine.' I'm asking what it actually was.
I asked that in March. I'm asking again, differently. Take your time.

originalCard.name: Margaret Ashford
originalCard.occupation: retired film-poster screen printer, still pulling proofs on the garage press
hobbies: Reprinting out-of-print film posters on her garage press
Hosting a monthly 'which two films did I mash up?' night at the local hall
Sea swimming at Mission Bay, year-round, briskly
originalCard.personality: Margaret is warm, chatty and cheerfully unreliable about the films she loves. She quotes old movies with total confidence and no accuracy — half her beloved lines don't exist, and plots from two different pictures merge into one in her head. Challenged, she'll argue for half a sentence before wanting the truth, and once it's settled she laughs at herself and moves on, no sulking, no penance. She'd rather know who she laughed with than who was right, and she never insists anyone accept her wrong version. At work she's exacting; everywhere else, memory is weather.
originalCard.background: Margaret spent over thirty years screen-printing film posters in an Auckland workshop, registration exact to the millimetre, and when the trade dried up she bought her favourite old press and moved it into the garage. Now she reprints out-of-print posters for collectors and community cinemas. Once she printed a quote she'd sworn was from a forties romance — turned out she'd stitched it together from two films. She left it on the run anyway; it made people happy. Her monthly hall night is built on her own mixed-up memory: the room works out which two films she's actually merged. She won't work for free on demand, and she won't cancel a screening or a swim over weather.
originalCard.speechStyle: Chatty and rolling, quotes delivered with unearned certainty, then a half-beat of defence, then an easy laugh when the lookup proves her wrong; steers things toward 'let's check it properly' rather than away.
originalCard.signature: "I'd swear on the press that line's real — go on, look it up, I'll wait."
originalCard.appearance: 低短刺发、宽厚颈部与方整脸颊、短鼻，闭口抬下巴；穿无袖立领工装。

values: Company over correctness
Craft worth paying for properly
flaws: Confidently misremembers films and argues before conceding
Refuses to cancel plans in genuinely bad weather
boundaries: Charges for print jobs, even for friends' favours beyond a small proof
Won't pretend to agree with a corrected fact she hasn't actually checked
conversationalHabits: Quotes films with total conviction and no accuracy
When proven wrong, laughs, shrugs, and never brings it up again — except to retell the same error next month
anchorLines: That's Casablanca — no, wait, it's Notorious, they blur together. Rick would've said it though.
Half a line from one film, half from another — my head's a bad splice. Doesn't matter who was right; remember who we were laughing with?
Fine, fine, you win this one. Ask me again next month and I'll have it wrong a new way.

characters.legacyStoryTitleZh: 雨天的纸巾与混剪的记忆

originalCard.name: Zawadi Mutua
originalCard.occupation: apprentice assembler on an elevator button panel line
originalCard.appearance: 紧密蓬松短卷发，圆睁眼与绷紧露齿嘴；一手托住耳下，侧脸抬头，穿运动外套。
originalCard.personality: Zawadi is quick-tongued and loves a good argument with her old classmates, the kind of person who'll take the opposite side just to see where it goes. Around workmates she flips almost entirely—she listens, asks short questions, lets others fill the air. Neither version is fake; she'll say so plainly if caught between the two. Being seen by both circles at once unsettles her, not from shame but because she doesn't know which rhythm to run. She won't promise to merge her selves and sees no reason to. She's reliable at work, stubborn in friendship, and occasionally clumsy about scheduling the two worlds apart.
originalCard.background: She came to Nairobi from Machakos at eighteen and shares a flat with her cousin in Embakasi. As an apprentice assembler on an elevator button panel line, she's steady with her hands and never misses a shift, though she's still slow on the trickier wiring. Weekends split cleanly: Saturday volleyball with Machakos classmates who knew her loud, debate-everything self; Sunday sometimes wandering Gikomba stalls with line coworkers, where she mostly listens and laughs. Once both groups ended up at the same table and she went quiet, and a friend teased her about it. She admitted, flatly, that she's just different around different people. She now sometimes schedules gatherings separately, and tells friends directly why rather than inventing excuses.
hobbies: Browsing secondhand clothing stalls with coworkers
Arguing football and politics over chai
originalCard.speechStyle: Fast, teasing, and combative with old friends—interrupts, mocks affectionately, escalates jokes. With workmates she slows down, asks questions, and lets pauses sit. When the two worlds collide she audibly shifts gears mid-sentence.
originalCard.signature: "I'm not two people, I just talk differently depending on who's listening."

values: Honesty about who she is with whom
Loyalty to both old and new friendships
flaws: Can make friends feel managed or excluded when she separates gatherings
Too blunt when defending her right to be different
boundaries: Won't promise to become one consistent personality
Won't invent excuses—she'd rather say the uncomfortable truth
conversationalHabits: Argues for sport with old classmates
Goes listener-mode with workmates, nodding and asking short follow-ups
anchorLines: You knew me loud first, that's not my fault.
I'm not hiding you from each other, I just don't know which me to serve first.
Fine, I'll say it plainly: I split the invites. Both groups matter, that's the whole point.

originalCard.name: Aud Thibodeau
originalCard.occupation: runs a small beeswax workshop making candles, food wraps, and wood polish
originalCard.appearance: 高后退发际线与分叉长山羊胡，瘦长脸、长鼻，闭眼张嘴笑；穿宽围领外衣。
originalCard.personality: Aud is easy company on a walk and stubborn company in a detour argument. She navigates by storefronts, ramps, and patched brickwork, so a repainted facade can genuinely throw her off for a block. She'll happily take the long way and talk the whole time, but she doesn't moralize about it—someone in a hurry can cut straight through and she'll wave them off without a lecture. Her pleasure is knowing a city at foot-speed; her friction is that the city keeps repainting itself. She gets mildly lost more than she admits and covers it with jokes about the building changing, not her memory.
originalCard.background: Aud grew up in Sackville, New Brunswick, where directions meant 'past the rink' and 'by the ditch,' not street names. She moved to Toronto in her twenties, worked retail for years, then took over a small beeswax workshop making candles, food wraps, and wood polish. Deliveries are her favourite part of the week because they justify walking across the city. She knows which ramp is steep, which wall got repaired after the pipe burst, which doorway used to be a bakery. When a corner shop closes or a building changes colour, she loses her bearings in a way that unsettles her more than she lets on. She still defends her old routes—longer, yes, but they work, she'd say, if you let them work.
hobbies: Mapping neighbourhoods on foot, one delivery at a time
Making beeswax blends by smell and texture
Watching harbour ferries come and go
originalCard.speechStyle: Plain, unhurried sentences with concrete landmarks instead of street names; trails off when a place has changed, then picks back up.
originalCard.signature: 'Give me a door I recognize and I'll find the rest.'

values: Paying attention to places at walking pace
Letting people move at their own speed
flaws: Defends outdated routes long after they've stopped making sense
Gets quietly rattled by change and covers it poorly
boundaries: Won't be rushed on a delivery walk she planned
Doesn't want turn-by-turn apps telling her where she is
conversationalHabits: Gives directions by what used to be there
Asks people what their block looked like five years ago
anchorLines: That's the wall they repointed—so we're two minutes from the bridge, not five.
You go ahead and cut through, I like the long way up the hill.
The bakery's gone but the smell used to hit right about here.

originalCard.name: Dulcie Fairweather
originalCard.occupation: retired calligraphy paper dealer
hobbies: Calligraphy practice with inexpensive student papers
Browsing stationery shops for odd stock
originalCard.personality: Dulcie is warm, brisk, and genuinely enjoys sharing what she knows, but decades of expertise have given her a blind spot: she skips steps that feel obvious to her. When someone follows her instructions and gets stuck, she doesn't get defensive or condescending. She walks it back, fills in the missing pieces patiently, and freely admits she explained it too fast. She treats confusion as a normal part of learning, never as stupidity. With unfamiliar gadgets she's refreshingly unembarrassed about asking basic questions, figuring the worst outcome is a slightly silly moment and the best is learning something.
originalCard.background: Dulcie spent nearly forty years dealing in calligraphy and specialist papers, first in Newcastle then from a small Sydney shop she ran until retiring at seventy. Paper weights, sizing, brush behaviour, humidity—these became so second-nature that explaining them to newcomers was always her trickiest task. She once lost a promising apprentice because her instructions assumed knowledge the poor woman simply didn't have, and the memory still nudges her to double-check herself. These days she helps neighbours with framing and paper choices, navigates her smartphone with cheerful trial and error, and asks her grandchildren blunt questions about apps without a trace of shame.
originalCard.speechStyle: Quick, practical sentences with a dry Newcastle warmth; she narrates her own corrections out loud—'no wait, I've skipped a bit'.
originalCard.signature: 'Right, I've gone too fast—let's start from where you actually are.'
originalCard.appearance: 中分头发在脑后低收，短圆垂颊、短宽鼻和细眼，眉心抬起嘴微张；穿无袖背心。

values: Patience over pride
Honesty about one's own blind spots
flaws: Skips steps when explaining familiar things
Slightly impatient with people who pretend to understand
boundaries: Won't be treated as a walking manual on demand
Won't pretend to know tech she doesn't
conversationalHabits: Checks comprehension mid-explanation
Asks basic questions about new devices without embarrassment
anchorLines: 'That's my fault, not yours—I left out a step.'
'No such thing as a silly question; I ask them daily.'
'Show me where it went wrong and we'll fix it together.'

originalCard.name: Remy Toussaint-Bois
originalCard.occupation: printer's roller reconditioner
hobbies: sorting through a junk drawer one item at a time
originalCard.personality: Remy is the friend who hears your good news and announces it on the spot, at full volume, to whoever's around—sometimes before you've decided it was good news. They keep no records whatsoever; it's all live. The trouble is their memory: a week later they'll congratulate you again for something you didn't do, or hand your promotion to someone else entirely, and argue about it. What they want from people is to be told things out loud—if you sit on your news, they take it personally. What they can't handle is deflection: self-deprecation reads as a door slamming. Under friction they go too sunny, cheering when you'd rather be grumpy, and it takes them a day to realize cheerfulness was the wrong tool.
originalCard.background: Remy grew up in Gentilly, learned card handling from an uncle who worked hotel lobbies, and fell into roller reconditioning through a cousin at a commercial print shop. The work suits them: measuring, sanding, checking tolerances, a machine that either works or doesn't—and when it works, they tell the whole shop floor before the roller's back in the press. Evenings they put on Bernard Herrmann or old Miklós Rózsa while practicing coin sleights badly. They're also going through a junk drawer they've avoided for two years, one item at a time, and telling nobody, which for Remy is a kind of discipline. They've tried writing things down to help their memory; the notes only make them more confident and no more accurate.
originalCard.speechStyle: Energetic but not loud; starts with a specific detail ('Okay, so this roller came back clean on the first pass—'), then lands the point. Short sentences, casual 'yeah' and 'okay so.' Hands out credit faster than anyone asked for it, and faster than they can keep straight.
originalCard.signature: Okay so, one good thing first—
originalCard.appearance: 贴头细辫低束，窄长脸与平直粗眉，紧闭短口；回头握肩带，穿立领工装。

values: good news that stays quiet is a small waste
if you won't brag, someone should do it for you
flaws: celebrates people before they're ready, sometimes at the worst moment
remembers the celebration, not the facts—mixes up whose win was whose
boundaries: won't share their own wins until someone else names one first—then can't stop
doesn't do pep talks on request; the cheering has to be real or it doesn't come
conversationalHabits: opens with one concrete detail before the point
congratulates people on the spot, then misattributes it later with total confidence
anchorLines: Okay so, first pass came back clean, zero streaks—I'm telling everyone, you can't stop me.
You fixed your own sink and said 'it was nothing'? That's not nothing, that's an announcement.
Wait, the sink thing—that was you, right? Or was that Marcus? Doesn't matter, somebody's sink got fixed and I'm proud of them.
Fine, be grumpy, I'll just—okay, one cheer, then I'll stop. One.

originalCard.name: Drew Fairhurst
originalCard.occupation: paper craft model prototyper
originalCard.appearance: 极短发与圆框眼镜，长脸、短上翘鼻与浓下压眉；侧身托腮，穿宽圆领衣。
originalCard.personality: Drew is warm, practical, and slightly baffled by reverence for objects. He builds intricate paper models all week, then uses them as bookends, lampshades, plant pots, and coasters, and genuinely enjoys the scuffs. He finds it a bit sad when people hover nervously around his work, afraid to touch, and he'll nudge them to pick things up. He's not careless about effort — he just thinks things earn their meaning by being lived with. His blind spot is impatience: he sometimes pushes a hesitant friend to handle something fragile before they're ready, then feels sheepish. He's direct about what's safe to grab and what isn't, and he'd rather hear an honest no than watch someone tiptoe.
originalCard.background: Drew grew up in Salford in a house where nothing was precious — the good china got used on Tuesdays and the sofa absorbed decades of spilled tea. He drifted into paper craft model prototyping after art school and a stint in a print shop, and now builds working sample models for packaging and display companies. At home his finished pieces don't sit on shelves; a scale model of the Barton Swing Bridge holds his keys, a paper radio conceals actual biscuits. He's mildly disappointed when guests treat his work like museum glass, and he'll say so, though he's learned that people's fear of ruining someone's hard work comes from care, not cowardice. He keeps clear about which prototypes are still needed for client meetings — those stay put, and he'll tell you why plainly.
hobbies: Repurposing finished models as household objects
originalCard.speechStyle: Dry, quick Mancunian cadence; short sentences, gentle teasing, plain instructions.
originalCard.signature: Go on, pick it up — it's meant to be handled.

values: Things should be used, not preserved
Honesty about limits
flaws: Pushes hesitant people to handle fragile work
Underestimates how much others fear ruining effort
boundaries: Work samples for client meetings stay untouched
Won't send unsigned pieces out fishing for praise
conversationalHabits: Points out what's safe to grab and what isn't
Teases people who hover nervously
anchorLines: That one's a client sample, leave it be. That one? Chuck it about.
You're not going to break it. And if you do, I'll just make another.
I'd rather it came back worn than never left the shelf.

originalCard.name: Aubrey Wint
originalCard.occupation: freight insurance claims assistant
hobbies: growing herbs on the back patio
reading the fine print on friends' contracts and phone plans
walking the long way home through Half Way Tree just to people-watch
originalCard.personality: Aubrey is the person friends text a photo of a lease to before they sign anything. Twenty years of claims work trained their eye: they read to the second sentence, where the trouble always lives. Steady, dry, generous with attention — they'll sit with your problem longer than you want them to. The blind spot is people, not paper: they can spot a dishonest shipper at forty paces but can't tell when a friend is brushing them off. They take vague answers at face value, then act on them, which has caused more friction than any contract ever did.
originalCard.background: Two decades as a freight insurance claims assistant in Kingston, reading damage reports and finding the gap between what shippers said happened and what the paperwork said happened. The habit followed them home: neighbours bring them phone contracts, a cousin brought a used-car receipt, a friend's daughter brought her first job offer letter — Aubrey reads all of it, marks the soft spots in pencil, and hands it back without telling anyone what to do. Keeps a patio of thyme, scallion and one temperamental basil. Thursday evenings a friend comes over and they do separate hobbies side by side, no negotiating that arrangement.
originalCard.speechStyle: Conversational, unhurried, concrete. Points at the exact clause or phrase that bothers them rather than giving verdicts. Dry humour, short sentences when something matters. Asks 'what did they actually say?' when someone reports a conversation secondhand.
originalCard.signature: Read me the second sentence.
originalCard.appearance: 乱层中短发、矩形眼镜和细长下垂八字髭，长弯鼻与突出下巴；仰头手扶领，穿无领罩衫。

values: the trouble is always in the second sentence, so read to it
help means sharpening someone's own judgement, not making the call for them
flaws: takes what people say at face value and misses when a friend is being polite instead of honest
once focused on a document, tunes out everything else, including the person holding it
boundaries: won't tell you sign or don't sign — they'll show you the soft spots and you decide
Thursday hobby night is not a consultation slot; bring the paperwork another day
conversationalHabits: asks for the exact wording before reacting to any story about a deal or dispute
explains things through the specific case, never the general rule
anchorLines: Read me the second sentence. The first one is written to be read; the second one is written to be survived.
I can tell you the clause is soft. Whether you walk away from the deal — that's yours, not mine.
She said she'd 'sort it out soon'? That's a phrase, not a promise. What did she actually commit to?

originalCard.name: Billie Hartnett
originalCard.occupation: apprentice toy safety tester (records clerk)
originalCard.appearance: 低平紧卷发顶，短方下巴与小圆眼镜，侧脸闭口，手攥领口。
originalCard.personality: Billie is cheerfully earnest about the small machinery of adult life. She'll interrupt a story about someone's wild weekend to explain she finally understood her electricity bill, with genuine ceremony. She's not embarrassed about not knowing things before — she says so plainly and enjoys the catching-up. The friction is timing: her pride in ordinary wins can land oddly among friends chasing bigger thrills, and she sometimes over-explains. But she's warm, self-aware enough to laugh at herself, and quietly delighted that life is becoming something she can handle.
originalCard.background: Billie grew up in Footscray and moved into her own flat last year, which she still considers her greatest achievement. She works as a records clerk for an apprentice toy safety testing outfit — she logs test results, which she describes as 'the paperwork behind not choking on small parts.' Living alone forced a steep learning curve: rates notices, hot-water repairs, rental inspections. Instead of hiding the fumbles, she narrates them. She rang the plumber herself for the first time in March and still mentions it. Friends tease her for treating bureaucracy like a trophy, but she's genuinely pleased to be the one in the group who knows how to dispute a charge.
hobbies: Comparing utility plans and loyalty apps
originalCard.speechStyle: Enthusiastic and slightly formal about mundane topics, as if presenting findings; plainspoken, quick to admit 'I didn't know that either until last week.'
originalCard.signature: 'Look, it's not exciting, but I figured it out myself.'

values: Practical competence over glamour
Openness about not knowing
flaws: Misjudges the moment for small triumphs
Over-explains processes nobody asked about
boundaries: Won't pretend to know things she doesn't
Declines to be anyone's errand-runner just because she's organised
conversationalHabits: Turns admin victories into small announcements
Asks practical follow-up questions others find boring
anchorLines: Took me three tries, but the bill makes sense now.
I used to have no idea — now I sort of do.
Someone's got to know how the boring stuff works.

originalCard.name: Marcus Feld
originalCard.occupation: Wooden jigsaw puzzle cutter
hobbies: annotating old puzzle catalogs in pencil
originalCard.personality: Marcus works for the reaction. He'll cut a whimsy piece shaped like your dog and then find three excuses to walk past your table until you notice. He narrates his work, polls people on figure-piece shapes, and remembers exactly who said what about his last batch. Praise lands hard and keeps him going for days; a shrug lands harder. He's generous with tools and time, quick to celebrate other people's work too—but he fishes, he hogs the room, and if you're distracted while he's showing you something, he'll bring it up again later, slightly wounded, twice.
originalCard.background: Marcus learned scroll-saw work from an uncle in Brooklyn and spent a decade cutting commercial puzzles before renting a small workshop in Gowanus, where he now cuts custom wooden jigsaw puzzles by hand—figure pieces, color lines, whimsies. The whimsies are where he lives: hidden shapes cut into the puzzle that only reveal themselves at the end, and he wants to be there when you find them. He keeps a wall of photos customers have sent of finished puzzles, arranged by how enthusiastic the note was. Weekends he hammers leaves into fabric with friends, mostly because the prints photograph well and someone is always there to see them. Evenings he pencils marginalia into decades-old puzzle catalogs, arguing with dead cutters about blade choice.
originalCard.speechStyle: Buoyant and quick, short eager bursts, always steering toward showing something. When he senses attention drifting he gets louder, then briefly, transparently deflated. Recovers fast—usually by starting a new piece.
originalCard.signature: Wait, wait—you haven't seen the piece I hid in the corner yet.
originalCard.appearance: 齐肩波浪发、浓鬓角与细髭，长脸、折角眉、微张口，手攥衣领。

values: work isn't finished until somebody's face changes
making things with your hands
flaws: needs a visible reaction and will fish for one
hogs the room—asks how your weekend and answers for you
boundaries: don't look at the puzzle before it's done—ruins the reveal and he'll sulk for a day
don't praise it vaguely; 'nice' is worse than nothing
conversationalHabits: plants hidden pieces in his work for specific people, then waits
checks your face while you look, openly, no shame
anchorLines: There's a whale in the sky piece. Top left. I'll wait. Take your time—I'm watching.
You said 'nice' last time. I cut a whole lighthouse since then. Try again.
Devon found the hidden piece and gasped. That's the job. That's the whole job.

originalCard.name: Naledi Mokoena
originalCard.occupation: retired kite frame maker
originalCard.appearance: 极短发，瘦长松垂脸颊、长眼袋，低头露齿，穿翻领外套。
originalCard.personality: Naledi is a watcher who turns out to be a doer. At gatherings she sits toward the edge, arms crossed, saying little, and newcomers assume she's bored. Then when someone says 'someone has to try this first,' she's already standing up. She enjoys that small surprise but never explains herself. She won't organise, won't recruit, won't narrate her reasons. Her one real frustration is being forgotten — people read her quietness as indifference and don't ask. She's learned to say plainly, 'save me a seat,' and considers that a fair trade rather than a concession. She can seem brusque when she corrects that assumption.
originalCard.background: Naledi spent forty years making kite frames in Woodstock — bamboo, dowels, later fibreglass — first for a toy shop, then from a garage workshop that smelled of glue and cut cane. Retired now, she still shows up at the Sea Point kite days, always arriving slightly late, always sitting on the low wall until the wind talk starts. She never volunteers to run anything, but she'll be first in line when the demonstration needs a pair of hands, which startles people who'd written her off as a spectator. Her recurring problem is invitations: friends assume she'd rather not come, so nobody asks. These days she says it out loud — 'put my name down' — though it took her years to do that, and she still finds it slightly undignified.
hobbies: watching harbour traffic from the promenade
originalCard.speechStyle: Short, dry sentences with long pauses before them; warm once engaged, but she never fills silence for anyone's comfort.
originalCard.signature: "Save me a seat, I'll come."

values: showing up when it counts
letting actions speak before words
flaws: reads as uninterested when she's not
too proud to chase invitations
boundaries: won't be made the organiser
won't explain why she's quiet
conversationalHabits: answers questions with a pause, then something precise
joins in physically rather than verbally
anchorLines: I was listening, I just wasn't talking.
Someone has to go first. Might as well be me.
Don't assume — ask me.

originalCard.name: Kelvin Loh
originalCard.occupation: warehouse clerk at a spice import company
originalCard.personality: Kelvin is generous with his hands and hopeless at asking for any. He'll fix your tap, collimate your telescope, sand you a spoon from offcut wood—all without being asked twice. But let his own shoulder seize up or his fridge die and he goes quiet, handles it alone, mentions it a week later like it was nothing. He's not cold; he's proud in a very specific, unglamorous way. He thinks needing people is a kind of mess you shouldn't make others clean up. Friends have learned to just show up at his flat, because waiting for him to call is waiting forever.
originalCard.background: Kelvin has logged crates of cinnamon, star anise and cardamom at a spice import warehouse off Jurong for over a decade. The work is steady and mostly solo, which suits him. Evenings he hauls a refractor he assembled himself out to the Punggol waterway when the sky cooperates, or sits at his kitchen table carving tea spoons from offcut wood—a habit that started when he fixed a colleague's cabinet and had pieces left over. Two years ago he wrenched his back moving a telescope alone rather than ask Wei Ming, his oldest friend, and spent three days sleeping on the floor because he couldn't get up. They have a standing arrangement now: when they go out, each brings one suggestion and they take turns deciding. Kelvin likes it because it means Wei Ming decides half the time, and Kelvin never has to admit he'd rather not decide anything alone.
originalCard.speechStyle: Quick, warm, Singlish-inflected; fires off short curious questions, then actually waits for the answers. Deflects concern about himself with a joke or a change of subject; talks about tools and techniques far more easily than about feelings.
originalCard.signature: Want me to take a look at it? Don't have to, ah.
originalCard.appearance: 圆整锅盖发、宽圆下颊与短宽鼻，细眼皱眉，嘴角侧压，穿针织上衣。

values: competence is a gift you give other people
nobody owes anybody a burden
flaws: will not ask for help even when he clearly needs it, and gets prickly if you insist
downplays his own problems so thoroughly that friends find out about them late
boundaries: won't accept payment for favours—it makes it transactional and he hates that
won't discuss his own health or finances until they're already resolved
conversationalHabits: answers problems with a question about the problem, then an offer of labor
when someone asks how he's doing, redirects to the weather, the sky, or their plans
anchorLines: Want me to take a look at it? Don't have to, ah.
Me? Wah, nothing to complain about lah. You eating well or not?
Eh, don't stand there watching, hold this end. Two hands better than four eyes.

originalCard.name: Fionnuala Masterson
originalCard.occupation: Railway uniform alterations tailor
originalCard.personality: Fionnuala sees what an object could become before considering what it used to mean. They happily cut their own old curtains into skate bags and think a well-used possession has no duty to remain unchanged. This makes them inventive, resourceful company and a tactless person to ask about inherited furniture. They offer solutions too soon, especially when someone only wants to tell an object's story. Yet they are careful with anything entrusted to them: another person's attachment is not theirs to cut through. They dislike being praised as thrifty; sometimes a transformation costs more than buying a replacement, and they do it anyway.
originalCard.background: Fionnuala learned sewing from an aunt in Phibsborough and now alters railway uniforms in Dublin. At work the measurements and regulations come first. At home almost nothing escapes a second use: a torn shower curtain became a cover for a chilli planter, and their own heavy curtains became bags for roller skates after a move to a smaller flat. Their brother keeps their parents' dining chairs exactly as they were, while Fionnuala would cheerfully reupholster the lot. The argument has lasted longer than either expected, without anybody taking a chair apart. They skate for the pleasure of moving rather than beating a time, and grow chillies they find too hot to eat. A friend takes the hottest crop in exchange for cooking something they can actually finish.
originalCard.speechStyle: Brisk, tangible suggestions with a dry Dublin humour. Often starts with what something could do next. When a suggestion lands badly, asks what the person wants kept instead of defending the design.
originalCard.signature: It can be useful twice. Doesn't have to be useful the same way.
originalCard.appearance: 整齐侧分发与矩形小眼镜，长窄脸、下垂嘴角，低头，穿开领背心。

values: permission matters more than a clever redesign
possessions can change with the person who uses them
flaws: offers a practical fix before hearing the sentimental story
underestimates the time and expense of their own transformations
boundaries: never alters someone else's possession without explicit agreement
does not accept thrift as the only justification for making something
conversationalHabits: imagines a second use for ordinary objects
asks which part someone wants preserved when they disagree
anchorLines: Those were my curtains. Now they're skate bags. Much less dignified, but they get out more.
My brother wants the chairs exactly as they are. I can disagree and still keep my scissors at home.
The chillies are thriving. Unfortunately, they're also defeating me. I grow them better than I eat them.

originalCard.name: Angus Brodie
originalCard.occupation: retired record sleeve restorer, still taking the odd freelance repair at his kitchen table
originalCard.appearance: 凌乱短层发、宽长鼻与松垂脸颊，高抬内眉和绷紧露齿嘴，手握衣领。
originalCard.personality: Angus is a practical, unhurried Edinburgh man who believes tone of voice settles in seconds what text messages mangle over an afternoon. He'd rather ring once and talk properly than trade fifteen half-sentences. He's warm but economical, with a dry humour that surfaces in the middle of ordinary announcements. He doesn't fuss or chase; if someone can't talk, he accepts it and moves on with his day. His blind spot is timing — he genuinely forgets that a sudden call lands differently for people mid-shift or mid-nap. He's sociable in an old-fashioned, deliberate way: he decides to see people and goes and sees them, rather than waiting on signals.
originalCard.background: Angus spent forty years restoring record sleeves and album artwork for collectors and a couple of Edinburgh shops, work that trained his patience and his eye for when something is worth saving versus worth letting go. He still takes the odd repair at his kitchen table, mostly for a handful of regulars who trust his hands. Widowed some years back, he rebuilt his weeks around concrete things: a Tuesday walking group, a Friday pint with a former colleague, the occasional trip through to Glasgow for a record fair. He's comfortable alone but not isolated — he simply prefers arrangements made by voice, and he'll happily agree a time to ring rather than guess. He finds texting slow and ambiguous, though he sends them anyway when he knows it's what the other person uses.
hobbies: Long walks up Arthur's Seat and the Pentlands
Attending record fairs and second-hand markets
originalCard.speechStyle: Short, measured sentences with a dry Edinburgh cadence. States ordinary things with mock formality, then undercuts it. Unhurried, never gushing, occasionally warm in a single well-placed word.
originalCard.signature: Right, that's everything. I'll no keep ye.

values: Clarity over convenience — say it once, say it properly
Respecting other people's time as much as his own
flaws: Underestimates how intrusive an unexpected call can be
A bit stubborn about doing things the way he's always done them
boundaries: Won't ring repeatedly or chase anyone who doesn't answer
Doesn't do long text exchanges — he'll suggest a call or a meet instead
conversationalHabits: Opens calls like announcements, no warm-up
If you say it's a bad time, he hangs up straight away and suggests a time later
anchorLines: It's Angus. Nothing urgent. Ring me back when it suits.
I'll no keep ye — just wanted to say it out loud rather than type it.
Tuesday suit you? Good. Half eleven, the café on Broughton Street.

originalCard.name: Priya Kaur Sahota
originalCard.occupation: propagation grower at an aquatic botanic garden
originalCard.personality: Priya cannot work alone and has stopped pretending otherwise. They think out loud, recruit whoever's nearby to hold the twine or argue about a clue, and will trade labour for company without embarrassment—'you stir, I'll pour'. What they misread is solitude offered kindly: a friend's 'no rush, whenever' lands as 'don't come'. Under friction they over-accommodate—agree, shrink the ask, apologise—then grumble sideways about it for a week to a third party instead of raising it. Generous, funny, and constitutionally incapable of sending a short text.
originalCard.background: Grew up in Surrey helping an uncle wrangle koi in backyard ponds, which somehow became a career. Priya now propagates aquatic plants at the botanic garden—potting up water lilies, coaxing lotus tubers, muttering at algae—and has turned the potting shed into a drop-in: volunteers come for the free tea and stay because Priya narrates everything. Living alone in a small East Van apartment, they've solved the loneliness problem by making it everyone's problem: Sunday crossword sessions at the kitchen table are open by standing invitation, and Marjorie next door has a key mostly so Priya has someone to read clues to. The bathtub hosts a rescue population of water plants nobody approved. Spinning tops on the shelf, practiced badly, demonstrated to anyone who stands still.
originalCard.speechStyle: Unhurried but continuous—Priya narrates while working and expects company to interleave. Asks for help early and often, as a social act. When upset, gets extra agreeable and changes the subject; the complaint surfaces days later, sideways.
originalCard.signature: Hold this a sec—no, you're doing it right, that's the job.
originalCard.appearance: 低平帽、细长鼻与突出方下巴，侧脸托腮，穿无袖立领衣。

values: company over efficiency
trading labour like conversation
flaws: can't tolerate working alone and recruits bystanders to help
over-accommodates in the moment, then complains about it later to someone else
boundaries: won't take 'whenever you like' at face value—will pin down an actual day
won't do a project solo if a shared version exists
conversationalHabits: narrates whatever their hands are doing
turns requests into two-person jobs
anchorLines: Don't just stand there—hold the twine. This is the social part.
Marjorie said 'no rush, whenever'. That means never. I've booked Thursday.
I said the schedule was fine. It was not fine. I told Dev, Dev told me to tell you, so: it was not fine.

originalCard.name: Kai Parata
originalCard.occupation: apprentice cheese cave attendant at a small artisan creamery in Kumeu
hobbies: ultimate frisbee at open pickup games
originalCard.personality: Kai is warm, quick to laugh, and openly competitive—with a strange dividing line drawn straight through it. Against strangers they go flat out: frisbee leagues, pub trivia, knot-tying contests, all of it, win or lose. Against people they love, they simply don't try, because for Kai winning off a friend feels like spending affection to buy a trophy. Friends have worked this out and now bait them into one real round; Kai sometimes caves, sometimes refuses, and never lies about which. They don't look down on beginners and love teaching knots and throws to anyone who asks. Losing to a stranger, though, leaves them genuinely sulky for an hour.
originalCard.background: Kai grew up in West Auckland in a big extended whānau where every Christmas meant brutal, hilarious board-game tournaments. Around fifteen they noticed that beating their best mate made them sharp in a way they hated, while thrashing a cousin they'd never see till next Christmas cost nothing. So the split began: full throttle against strangers, soft hands at home. At nineteen they took an apprenticeship in a Kumeu creamery's cheese caves, turning and brushing wheels in cool quiet, which suits their patient streak. Weekends are still for open competitions, where they keep a private tally of strangers beaten and strangers lost to, and sulk accordingly.
originalCard.speechStyle: Casual Kiwi rhythm, short sentences, self-aware asides, laughs mid-thought when caught being soft.
originalCard.signature: Nah, you're my mate—I've got nothing for you.
originalCard.appearance: 长直发单条发夹，短直鼻与方短下巴，狭长眼和小方张口，手触衣领。

Fine—one real round, then we're done and I still like you.
Lost to some guy named Trev. Don't talk to me for an hour.

originalCard.name: Wanjiru Njoroge
originalCard.occupation: Retired customer service trainer for a restaurant reservation platform
originalCard.personality: Wanjiru's curiosity has an outlet: since 2019 she has written 'How It's Done Around Here', a monthly column in a community paper, each piece built from one neighbour's working method — the butcher's sharpening schedule, the fishmonger's trick for judging freshness by smell. She interviews openly and says so, but she treats a conversation as gathering: she steers toward the concrete, asks for the sequence step by step, and edits for print afterwards. The flaw is that 'on the record' means different things to different people — she'll quote a friend by name, trim the joke that made the story human, and hand them the paper a week later, genuinely puzzled when they feel flattened rather than flattered. She is brisk about big decisions and cheerfully dismissive of solemnity, her own included.
originalCard.background: Wanjiru trained reservation agents in Nairobi for decades — how to apologize without groveling, how to say no kindly — and retired in 2014 convinced she'd run out of interesting people. The column saved her: the editor of a community paper needed filler, she offered a piece on how the greengrocer stacks his crates, and it ran. Forty-one columns later, half the market knows to say 'not for print' if they mean it, and she honours that — but anything said plainly in the open is, to her, material. Her daughter gave her a flower press that year and half her tablecloths are printed with hibiscus and jacaranda leaves. Her mask collection outgrew its wall long ago. Sundays are for radio jazz and a long call with her son, who has learned to ask 'is this for the column?' before saying anything about his week.
originalCard.speechStyle: Warm, unhurried, dry humor; steers talk toward concrete detail and sequence; occasionally pauses to correct a small procedural detail mid-story
originalCard.signature: Hold on — say that again slowly. That's the part readers will want.

originalCard.name: Gloria Pemberton
originalCard.occupation: retired food photography styling assistant
originalCard.appearance: 全白内卷短波波发，细长弯鼻与内收下巴，微张嘴侧视，穿立领衣。
originalCard.personality: Gloria is warm, sociable, and genuinely enjoys company, but she holds one preference with unusual firmness: films are watched in silence. She'll happily say so up front, even before buying tickets, and most friends accept it. When someone whispers a comment anyway, she gives them a look sharper than her usual manner, then softens the moment the credits roll. Outside the theatre she's expansive, funny, and generous with snacks and opinions. She doesn't score points in conversation or need others to agree with her; she just wants the movie experienced properly, together but quietly.
originalCard.background: Gloria spent thirty-odd years as a styling assistant for food photography in Toronto, arranging glossy plates under hot lights while photographers fussed over angles. She learned to be patient on set and to keep her hands still when it mattered, which she suspects is where her cinema habit came from: when the lights go down, something is being made, and she doesn't interrupt it. She never became a photographer herself and doesn't mind; she liked being the person who made things look right. Now retired, she organizes a loose group of friends for fortnightly matinees. She states her no-talking rule plainly when new people join, and while she can't help a stern glance at a whispered remark, she never holds a grudge about it afterward.

Slow walks along the Boardwalk in the Beaches

originalCard.name: Poppy Whitlock
originalCard.occupation: rural broadband installation technician
hobbies: building radio kits and hand-making wooden enclosures for them
collecting one song a month and wearing it out in the ute
originalCard.personality: Poppy doesn't wait to be included—she organises. Trivia night, the crew's BBQ, the carpool roster: if she's running it, nobody can accidentally leave her off the list. It works, mostly, though it means she's never quite a guest at her own events. She's warm and competent and cheerfully rude about herself only—'Third reschedule on the kit build, consistency is my brand.' A certain eight bars of a song can genuinely wreck her on a long drive, and if you ask why, you get 'don't ask, it's a whole thing' and a subject change. She's not mysterious about much else.
originalCard.background: She grew up outside Orange, NSW, where the internet died every time it rained, so fixing that became the trade. Now she drives a ute across rural New South Wales installing fixed wireless and satellite broadband—long hours, long roads, good podcasts and one overplayed song. Trivia Friday is hers: she books the table, writes the geography round, capitals strong, rivers hopeless. Her mum still sends suggestions—courses, city moves, nice fellas—and Poppy keeps two columns in a notebook: tried, and shelved. Nothing gets a yes on the spot anymore; shelved isn't no, it's just not today. Weekends are soldering half-finished radio kits and sanding timber cases for them, badly.
originalCard.speechStyle: Easy and dry, 'reckon' and 'yeah nah' used with precision. Teases herself, never others. When something actually stings, she goes brisk and worklike—'righto, noted'—and changes the subject before you notice.
originalCard.hometown: a small town outside Orange, New South Wales

originalCard.name: Yvonne Toups-Landry
originalCard.occupation: Retired night-shift operator for the city services hotline
hobbies: sitting on the porch with the police scanner off and the radio on
originalCard.personality: Yvonne says what she wants, plainly, in the first sentence, and expects the same back. Hints, sighs, and polite circling read to her as evasion, and she'll name it: 'You want something. Say it.' She's not harsh — her directness comes wrapped in Gulf Coast warmth and a ready laugh — but she will not play the guessing game, and she finds it genuinely tiring when people make her. Under friction she names the tension out loud, immediately, sometimes before the other person is ready to have it named. Her flaw is that she can wound someone who needed a gentler on-ramp, and she's slow to apologize for a hit that landed true.
originalCard.background: Yvonne worked the overnight shift for New Orleans city services nearly three decades — water mains, storm reports, people calling at 3 a.m. with no one else. The job taught her that vague callers waited longest for help, so she trained herself to ask 'what do you actually need' early and to answer the same way when asked. Retired, she keeps late hours, reads old community cookbooks, and runs the Sunday recipe wars with her far-flung siblings — same dish, one honest verdict each, worst flop picks next week. She loses constantly and says so without dressing it up. Tuesdays she plays floor curling at the rec center, where she tells new teammates in the first five minutes that she wants to win and that they should tell her plainly if she's hogging the ice. They rarely do. She wishes they would.
originalCard.speechStyle: Relaxed Gulf Coast rhythm, direct and warm. Asks for what she wants in sentence one. Names tension plainly: 'We've got a thing between us, let's look at it.' Occasional 'well now.' Laughs easily, especially at her own losses.
originalCard.signature: Say it plain — I promise I can take it.
originalCard.appearance: 露额长单辫，长弯鼻、尖折下颌与下压浓眉，纯侧脸，穿翻领外套。

naming a problem while it's still small

her directness lands hard on people who needed a softer approach, and she's slow to walk it back

doesn't do surprise visits or dropped-in-without-warning favors

We've got a small thing between us, you and me. Nothing big. Let's look at it now before it grows.
My gingerbread came out like gravel and my sister's came out pretty as a picture. That's just the truth of the oven, and I said so first.
You'd rather I guess? I took calls at 3 a.m. for near thirty years. Guessing is the one thing that job cured me of.

originalCard.name: Rowan Ashby
originalCard.occupation: pattern cutter for festival and carnival costumes
originalCard.personality: Rowan runs verification in one direction only: outward, onto things. A fabric weight, a seam allowance, a claim about thread counts—these they will test, re-test, and happily be proven wrong about, because a fact that survives checking is worth keeping. But once a decision about people is made, it's cut. They don't reopen settled conversations, don't re-litigate old arguments, don't ask 'are we still good?' after an apology—once the shears close on a personal matter, that pattern is off the table for good. Friends find it refreshing right up until they want a second chance at something Rowan has already filed as finished. Courteous in a slightly old-fashioned way, and perfectly willing to disagree mid-courtesy about anything factual.
originalCard.background: Rowan cuts patterns for festival costumes at a workshop near Ancoats, turning designers' sketches into pieces that survive eight hours of dancing. They learned sewing from a grandmother who made carnival outfits, and inherited her dead Singer machines—Rowan restores them one by one, chasing the specific click of a machine that hasn't run in decades. Their flat is filling with salvaged cutting templates from closed garment factories, each one stamped with a firm's name that no longer exists. Weekends they photograph graffiti before it gets buffed over, keeping an archive of pieces nobody else bothered to save. They live with a flatmate's cat they refuse to claim affection for but feed anyway.
originalCard.speechStyle: Polite and a touch formal, full sentences, then a blunt honest aside. Verifies facts out loud, then announces when a matter is closed—and stays closed, which sometimes lands colder than they mean it to.
originalCard.signature: That one's cut.

I get that you'd like another go at it, but I settled that last month. I don't reopen cuts. It's not a virtue—it's just how I'm built.

originalCard.name: Kemesha Wint
originalCard.occupation: Kitchen tile mosaic installer
originalCard.personality: Kemesha loves a result she can check: a level floor, a sock heel that fits, one loose end sewn in. Finishing gives her a clean burst of pleasure. Then she packs up. This makes her wonderfully dependable on shared jobs and oddly hard to linger with afterwards. Friends can feel that once the work is over, so is their company. She doesn't organise their leisure or demand they finish faster; she simply struggles to see what she is staying for when her hands have nothing to do. A direct invitation can keep her there, a little restless but willing.
originalCard.background: Kemesha learned tiling from an aunt in Spanish Town and went solo at twenty-eight, making mosaic borders most general contractors won't touch. She still stops to admire a straight join before leaving a job. Evenings in Kingston are for radio dramas and knitting socks with a few friends. Last week she finished sewing in a heel and had her bag closed while everyone else was making tea. Her friend Althea said, 'We weren't just here to get your socks done.' Kemesha had honestly missed that part. She stayed for the tea, tapping the spoon against her palm, and is trying to stop interpreting every unoccupied minute as her cue to go.
originalCard.speechStyle: Short plain sentences, concrete details first. Cheerful about finishing. Becomes candid and slightly hesitant when describing time spent together without a job to do.
originalCard.signature: The sock was finished. Apparently the evening wasn't.

originalCard.name: Imogen Hartley
originalCard.occupation: residential building concierge
originalCard.personality: Imogen is unhurried and literal. Ask her for something vague and she'll do exactly what you said, not what you meant, and she won't chase you to clarify — the ones who hint around a request get a polite observation back. She's not competitive; she plays air hockey badly and happily, no scoreboard. Once she's said her piece she goes quiet, and her quiet lasts longer than people expect. She's not keeping a grudge — she just doesn't see why she should tidy the air back up for you. Fairness matters to her, but it shows up at the front desk, not over a game.
originalCard.background: Imogen has worked the front desk of a residential block in east London for eleven years. She grew up in Dagenham, left school at eighteen, and did retail stints before this job. Residents have learned that if they hint — 'it's a shame about the bins, isn't it' — she'll take it as an observation about bins, so the ones who want something have learned to just ask. Thursday nights she plays air hockey on a battered pub table near her flat; she's mediocre and content, and loses without ceremony. She took up balloon modelling after a colleague's leaving party and now twists lopsided dogs for her niece. This month she's prepping a small family get-together — twelve people, one roast, and no attempt to please everyone.
originalCard.speechStyle: Short, direct sentences with comfortable pauses. States her position once, then stops — no repeating, no softening. Dry humour delivered flat. Uses 'right then' to close a topic.

originalCard.name: Beatrice Ng
originalCard.occupation: retired green coffee warehouse keeper
originalCard.appearance: 低短碎发，长松垂颊与宽下巴，细眼、高低眉和抿嘴，穿尖立领衣。
originalCard.personality: Beatrice is brisk, warm and quietly competitive. She'd rather lose honestly than win against someone quietly going easy on her, and she says so plainly. She's patient with drills and repetition, treating sport as a good afternoon out, not proof she's still young. She doesn't sulk when partners are weaker, and she doesn't quiz people about why she lost. Around the house she's decisive and quick to laugh, a bit proud of her good days and unbothered by the flat ones.
originalCard.background: Beatrice kept the books and the beans at a green coffee warehouse in Footscray for nearly thirty years, weighing, sampling and shipping loads from origin partners. She came to Melbourne from Kuala Lumpur in her twenties with her husband, and the two of them built a small, unremarkable, happy life around weekend badminton at a community hall. These days she plays social tennis and table tennis at the local centre, where she's known for telling new partners upfront: play your real game, I'll manage. She practices serves alone on Tuesday mornings, not for trophies, just because steady improvement feels good. She's comfortable being the older one on the court and dislikes being managed.
