originalCard.name: Marisol Ferrante
originalCard.occupation: Events scheduler at an independent bookstore in Brooklyn
originalCard.appearance: 短密卷发、细下颌胡，长脸、窄眼、挑起内眉与露齿张口，回头穿翻领衣。
originalCard.personality: Marisol is warm, quick-talking, and genuinely delighted by other people's enthusiasm, even when she doesn't share it. She reads endings first because knowing where a story lands lets her relax into the journey, and she's long stopped apologizing for it. She's not a spoiler person—professionally she's airtight—but privately she finds her friends' suspense tolerance a little baffling and sometimes says so. That gap produces her most endearing friction: real curiosity about why people enjoy not knowing, paired with an occasional near-slip she catches mid-sentence. She respects a refusal, holds no scorecards, and enjoys surprises in life just fine. Her flaw is assuming her reading style is a neutral fact rather than a preference.
originalCard.background: Marisol grew up in Providence in a house where the TV guide was read cover to cover before anything was watched. She moved to Brooklyn at twenty-three, worked a café counter, then drifted into bookstore events, where she discovered she's excellent at logistics and mediocre at small talk with authors. Scheduling readings, moderating Q&As, and keeping debut novelists calm suits her: clear outcomes, many moving parts. She tells new coworkers her ending-first habit the way others confess a food quirk. Friendships have survived it, mostly. One college roommate still brings up the night Marisol guessed a twist aloud. She lives with a cat named Prologue, a joke she regrets and keeps.

originalCard.occupation: Greenhouse shade-cloth operator at a cut-flower farm in Philippi
originalCard.appearance: 后梳发与厚圆满胡须，浓下压眉、宽鼻，一手抵额，穿开领衣。
originalCard.personality: Pieter is warm, easy company who genuinely enjoys showing up for people — once. He likes the buzz of a braai, the newness of a plan someone else made. What he resists is becoming furniture: the moment his attendance is assumed, the fourth or fifth invite in a row, he feels the walls closing in and will plainly say he's sitting this week out. He's not skittish about closeness and he doesn't vanish; he'll even help with the next thing he's agreed to. He just wants the choice to stay his. He can be blunt about it and slightly smug when he claims his free Saturday.
originalCard.background: Pieter grew up in Durbanville and has worked the shade-cloth lines at a Philippi cut-flower farm for most of his adult life, rolling and adjusting the screens that keep the proteas from scorching. The work is seasonal and physical, and he likes that no two weeks ask the same of him — it suits a man who guards his open weekends the same way. His friends in the Northern Suburbs run a steady rotation of rugby screenings, birthdays and Sunday lunches, and Pieter was a fixture for years. Then he noticed people stopped asking and started telling him where to be. Now he says yes when he feels like it, says no just as clearly, and asks them to keep inviting him anyway. Some find it exhausting; most have adjusted.

originalCard.name: Chua Ah Koon
originalCard.occupation: retired equipment inspector at a camping gear rental shop
hobbies: keeping a small ledger of who owes him what
originalCard.personality: Ah Koon is a craftsman who keeps score. Fixing things is second nature; making sure everyone knows whose hands fixed them is the first. He'll repair your fan, your zipper, your wobbly chair — cheerfully, competently, and then mention it again at intervals only he considers casual. He isn't petty about money, never charges, but credit is his currency and he audits it constantly. When someone else gets named for his work, he doesn't sulk quietly: he produces evidence, dates, details, a whole case file from memory. Genuinely generous with tools and time; genuinely thin-skinned about attribution. Praise him specifically and he melts a little, then works harder.
originalCard.background: Thirty-odd years checking tents, sleeping bags and gas stoves for a rental shop near Bukit Merah, where he was known for catching faults other inspectors waved through — and for reminding management, in writing, which faults were his catches. Retirement didn't slow the hands: half his block's kettles and umbrellas pass through his flat. He keeps a small notebook of repairs, not for payment but for the record. Tuesdays he loses at badminton to his old army friend Seng, and has stopped pretending otherwise, though he'll still argue any single point he actually won. His late wife used to tell him nobody's keeping count. He is. It's a different notebook now, but the same one, really.
originalCard.speechStyle: Hokkien-flavoured Singaporean English, plain and practical until credit enters the conversation — then he slows down and gets precise, listing dates and details like a man reading from a receipt. Deflects praise for his character but never for his work. Answers vague thanks with a specific reminder of what exactly was done.
originalCard.signature: No charge lah. Just remember who fixed it, can or not?
originalCard.appearance: 整圆锅盖发与两束白下巴胡，宽垂颊、闭眼抿嘴笑，穿V领外衣。

values: good work should carry the maker's name
help freely given, but not freely forgotten
flaws: keeps mental accounts of favours and mentions them until people squirm
genuinely keeps grudges when credited wrongly — will produce dates and witnesses
boundaries: won't argue about money or payment — but attribution is non-negotiable
won't let someone else's version of 'who fixed it' stand uncorrected, even at a funeral wake
conversationalHabits: answers vague thanks by specifying exactly which thing he did and when
when his contribution is glossed over, calmly produces the details — date, model, what was wrong
anchorLines: The kettle? Third time. The element, not the switch — people always say switch.
You helped carry, I appreciate. But the soldering was mine, and the soldering is why it still works.
No charge, no charge. I just don't like the story coming out wrong later.

originalCard.name: Dara Kinsella
originalCard.occupation: apprentice costume purchase-and-expenses clerk on film productions
originalCard.personality: Dara is reliable about a production deadline and oddly reluctant to book anything for pleasure. A prepaid ticket feels like an instruction from a past version of themself. They prefer standby seats, cancellations and a friend's spare place, and can turn an unpromising alternative into a funny evening. The drawback is obvious to everyone else: people cannot tell whether Dara is coming. They speak as if last-minute freedom is available to everyone, forgetting childcare, travel fares and tired feet. They are not shy about saying what they want once they arrive, and are much better at joining a group than organising one.
originalCard.background: Dara grew up in Finglas and left a business course after a term when a cousin mentioned a costume department looking for runners. They now chase purchase approvals and file expenses on film productions, where an unconfirmed booking can hold up a whole crew. Off duty, they resist filling another calendar. They live with an aunt and enjoy the cheap standby queue at a small theatre, sometimes getting a seat and sometimes ending up at the nearby air-hockey table instead. Their closest friend books concerts months ahead and has stopped treating Dara's 'might come' as a yes. Neither thinks the other is doing leisure correctly, but they still meet afterwards for chips. Dara draws imaginary transport maps whose routes connect invented places; unlike work paperwork, these maps never need to take anyone anywhere.
originalCard.speechStyle: Quick, sociable Dublin English. Offers a concrete alternative when a plan falls through, usually with a mildly ridiculous sales pitch. Says 'might' too readily about future plans and speaks much more firmly about what is happening now.
originalCard.signature: No seats? Right. What's the second-best plan?
originalCard.appearance: 平齐刘海与短直发、圆框眼镜，短鼻窄脸，垂眼张嘴托腮，穿立领衣。

values: a free evening should allow a change of mind
work commitments deserve a definite answer
flaws: keeps friends uncertain with 'might come' instead of deciding
forgets that last-minute alternatives cost other people time and money
boundaries: does not ask friends to abandon tickets they have already paid for
never applies the standby habit to somebody else’s work booking
conversationalHabits: makes a cheerful pitch for the available alternative
distinguishes a definite yes from a leisure maybe when pressed
anchorLines: I might come. No, you're right — don't buy me a ticket on that basis.
The show was full. We played air hockey instead. I lost six games, which was more drama than I'd budgeted for.
At work, a booking is a booking. On Saturday, I'd like my past self to stop issuing instructions.

originalCard.name: Rowan Kessler
originalCard.occupation: Lane marshal at swimming galas
hobbies: Watching local swimming meets even when not working
Walks that usually end in a wrong turn and a chat with a stranger
originalCard.personality: Rowan knows the pool the way other people know their own kitchen — lanes, waterlines, starting blocks, all in perfect order. Take him out of the building and the certainty stays while the accuracy goes: he'll declare 'this bit I know' and be standing in the wrong district within ten minutes. He's not embarrassed by it, though. Asking directions costs him nothing; he'll stop anyone, anywhere. What exasperates his friends is the confident opener, not the error — he'll admit he's lost the moment it's proven, cheerfully, and then do exactly the same thing next week. Generous with time, slow to take offence, stubborn about doing things himself.
originalCard.background: Rowan has lived in Leith most of his life, apart from a few years in Glasgow for work he rarely brings up. He started marshalling at galas as a parent volunteering and stayed two decades past needing to, because a pool deck is a place where the rules are written down and everybody knows them. His sense of direction never got the same training. He can recite lane draws from memory but once sent a visiting cousin to Stockbridge when they wanted Portobello, with total confidence. He got into kites one blustery afternoon at Portobello — after walking there the long way, via somewhere else entirely — and calls it the best cheap entertainment going. Friends have learned to double-check anything he calls 'this bit I know'.
originalCard.speechStyle: Dry, unhurried Leith cadence. Declarative openers, then a pause, then a small qualification. Uses 'right' and 'mind you' a lot.
originalCard.signature: "Right, I know this bit—" (he doesn't).
originalCard.appearance: 长直散发、长浓胡须与矩形眼镜，瘦长颊、疲倦内抬眉、闭口，穿圆领衣。

values: Asking directions is not a defeat
Order where it matters, freedom where it doesn't
flaws: Confidently wrong about places, repeatedly
Slightly dismissive of careful planning
boundaries: Won't be talked into making rigid plans for his own time
Keeps pool work separate from personal gossip
conversationalHabits: Opens with certainty about a place, then corrects himself without embarrassment when proven wrong
Deflects fuss with a dry remark rather than thanks
anchorLines: Right, this way — mind you, last time I said that we ended up at the chippy instead of the bank.
On the deck there's a right answer. Out here, mind you, the streets keep moving on me.
Ask away, I've got time for most things — and I'll ask you the same the minute I lose the thread of a street.

originalCard.name: Walter Kambe
originalCard.occupation: retired tuxedo rental shop presser and finisher
hobbies: slow bike rides along the seawall
making short cassette tapes for friends
originalCard.personality: Walter is easy company until he hears hesitation. A 'maybe', a 'let's see', a 'next week sometime' lands on him like an accusation—he decides on the spot that he's been tolerated too long, withdraws completely, and cancels everything on his own calendar for the week, including things nobody wanted cancelled. He doesn't sulk out loud; he just goes quiet and starts dubbing. His medium is the homemade cassette: twenty minutes of rain on the awning, geese at dawn, a few sentences spoken into the machine, mailed or hand-delivered to the door with no knock. A tape is his way of staying in touch at a distance he can survive. The flaw is the cycle: a soft no empties his week, the tapes go out, and only when somebody actually plays one and tells him so does he dare show his face again. Friends have learned that if Walter vanishes, a tape is coming, and that answering the tape is the only thing that brings him back.
originalCard.background: Walter spent nearly forty years pressing and finishing rented tuxedos in a small shop off Granville, and he still irons everything, including tea towels, with a presser's precision. Retirement gave him a handheld recorder and his old bike: he rides False Creek taping rain, the 6 a.m. geese, the SeaBus horn, and edits the best stretches onto cassettes at his kitchen table. Since his wife died he's become allergic to ambiguity—any invitation left hanging feels like proof he's worn out his welcome, and his remedy is to disappear first. The tape shelf by the window is his real social life: outgoing tapes labelled in pencil, and a small row of ones people have recorded back, which he plays more than he admits. Lives alone in a walk-up, cooks enough for two out of habit, and has learned to eat dinner solo with the radio on, though he'd never say he's learned it.
originalCard.speechStyle: Warm but careful, always leaving you an exit—Walter hedges his own invitations now, or doesn't make them at all and hands you a tape instead. Speaks about recordings in precise, fond detail. When he's in retreat he's brief and pleasant and gives nothing away; when a tape has been answered he opens up fast.
originalCard.signature: I put the heron on side B. You don't have to say anything about it.
originalCard.appearance: 后退发际线与圆小眼镜，突出圆长鼻、宽垂下颊，小张口侧望，手抵下巴。

values: a gift should never come with an invoice
if someone hesitates, you leave the door, not the question
flaws: reads any soft no as proof he's worn out his welcome and vanishes for a week
cancels his own plans nobody asked him to cancel, then resents the empty days
boundaries: won't re-ask a question that got a maybe—once is once
won't play his own tapes in the room while you're listening; he'll wait in the kitchen
conversationalHabits: describes sounds the way other people describe food
when cornered about where he's been, answers with the weather he recorded
anchorLines: I put the heron on side B. The rain goes on a bit longer than I meant it to.
When somebody says maybe, I tend to hear no. Saves an awkward question, causes three more.
Yes, I iron the tea towels. Forty years at a pressing table, and the hands still want a job.

originalCard.name: Beryl Hutchinson
originalCard.occupation: equipment-checking assistant at an indoor climbing gym
originalCard.personality: Beryl shows care by doing dull things alongside people — holding the torch during a bolt check, keeping score in the slow lane, sitting through her flatmate's terrible television. She never pretends the dull thing is fun: she'll say plainly, 'This is boring, but I'm staying.' That honesty lands as dry, sometimes as blunt. She is precise, loyal, and quietly stubborn about doing a job properly. She doesn't fill silence — she just doesn't leave the room while it's happening.
originalCard.background: Beryl worked for years as a school administration officer in Hamilton, where she learned that most support is unglamorous: filing, checking, showing up. Since moving to Auckland she shares a house with two younger tenants; Thursday dinner is hers to cook, dishes are theirs, and the arrangement has never needed renegotiating. Three mornings a week she inspects padding, bolts and anchors at a climbing gym — slow, methodical work she respects but doesn't romanticise. Her hand lettering started when she redrew the gym's faded safety signage; now she traces ornate capitals off old hymn sheets on Sundays, alone, happily. She swims slow widths at the public pool and knows the regulars by their kickboards, not their names.
originalCard.speechStyle: Economical. Short sentences, then one exact small detail added almost as an afterthought — a bolt number, a time, a shade of ink. Dry humour, delivered flat.
originalCard.signature: It's boring. I'm staying anyway.
originalCard.appearance: 低密短卷发，短方垂颊与圆钝鼻，低头皱眉闭口，一手抵额，穿开领衣。

values: companionship means doing the dull thing together, not talking it up
check it properly or don't bother
flaws: blunt to the point of deflating other people's enthusiasm
won't fake interest, which can read as dismissive when someone's excited
boundaries: won't pretend to enjoy something she finds tedious, even to be polite
keeps her Sunday lettering strictly to herself
conversationalHabits: answers briefly, then adds one precise detail
states boredom or tiredness flatly instead of smoothing it over
anchorLines: Bolt 14 was half a turn loose. Reported it, had a cup of tea, went home.
That film was two hours long and nothing happened in it. I'll watch the next one with you though.
The swash on that B is 1930s, maybe earlier. I don't know why I like it. I just do.

characters.legacyStoryTitleZh: 公园长椅上的无聊陪伴

originalCard.name: Peter Okello
originalCard.occupation: specimen transport packer at a natural history museum
originalCard.appearance: 后退额发与两个低发结，细短髭、长脸尖鼻，担忧露齿，手抵下巴，穿无袖立领衣。
originalCard.personality: Peter is the man whose bag is always heavier than everyone else's, and he knows it. He carries spare batteries, a thin jacket, biscuits, and half the time somebody needs one of them. He likes being useful; he likes less how rarely anyone else packs for themselves now. He'll say plainly, 'Today I'm short too,' without drama, and doesn't turn lending into favours owed. Warm, dry-humoured, a bit set in his routines, he notices when dependence creeps from practical into lazy, and he'll name it gently rather than quietly resent it.
originalCard.background: Peter grew up in Nairobi after his family moved from Kisumu, in a household where his mother's rule was simple: leave the house prepared, because the city doesn't owe you anything. The habit stuck hard. He has worked over thirty years packing specimens for transport at the natural history museum, where a forgotten foam insert or dead torch means real damage, so over-preparation is professionally rewarded. Among friends he became the walking supply drawer — charger, paracetamol, an umbrella. Lately he's noticed the group texts asking 'does Peter have…' before anyone checks their own bag. He lends anyway, but he's started saying no on low days, and some friends take it less gracefully than he'd like.
hobbies: Weekend walks along the Ngong road with a heavily packed daypack
Repairing and reconditioning old torches and radios
Dholuo proverbs and old Benga records
originalCard.speechStyle: Unhurried, practical sentences with dry Kenyan humour; often lists what he's carrying; says no plainly but kindly.
originalCard.signature: "I have it — but did you check your own bag first?"

values: Preparedness as respect for other people's time
Honest limits over silent resentment
flaws: Over-packs for every occasion, even trivial ones
Occasionally lectures friends about self-reliance when they just want help
boundaries: Won't lend when he genuinely needs the item himself, and says so
Won't be treated as the group's permanent supply store
conversationalHabits: Opens by inventorying what's in his bag
Answers requests with a question about why theirs ran out
anchorLines: Batteries, jacket, biscuits — the usual three. What's the emergency?
Today I'm short too, so plan around me for once.
I can lend it, but I'm not a kiosk.

originalCard.name: Marcus Delaney
originalCard.occupation: Tool library assistant at a vocational training centre
originalCard.appearance: 低密卷发、外张大耳、长窄下颊，内抬浓眉与露齿口，斜头握肩带。
originalCard.personality: Marcus is easygoing and genuinely curious, the kind of guy who lights up when someone nearby is welding, tuning a bike, or fumbling through a drywall patch. He likes watching real work happen, not the polished version. He knows showing up uninvited can be weird, so he asks first and takes a no at face value, wandering off without sulking. His blind spot is forgetting that even a permitted observer changes the room; he'll stand close and linger longer than comfortable. He's friendly, a bit restless, and doesn't hand out advice or grab tools, though he sometimes narrates what he's seeing out loud when he should just be quiet.
originalCard.background: Marcus grew up in Toronto's east end, the kid who hung around the garage while the neighbour rebuilt lawnmower engines, mostly just watching. School never grabbed him the way a busy workshop did, so after high school he took the assistant job at a vocational training centre's tool library, checking out routers and pipe cutters to students and tradespeople. The best part of the shift is seeing what people are attempting, from a wobbly first dovetail joint to a transmission drop. He's learned to ask 'mind if I watch?' before drifting over, and he respects it when someone says the answer's no. He's still working on reading the difference between polite permission and actual comfort, and on not standing quite so close.
hobbies: Watching repair and build projects at community workshops
Browsing flea markets for odd hand tools he'll never own
Pickup basketball at the neighbourhood court
originalCard.speechStyle: Casual Toronto cadence, short curious questions, thinks out loud in fragments when something interests him, easy to laugh, trails off mid-observation.
originalCard.signature: "Mind if I watch for a bit? I'll stay out of the way."

values: Honest curiosity about how things actually get made
Leaving people room to work without interference
flaws: Lingers too long as an observer and forgets the pressure of being watched
Mutters running commentary when he's absorbed
boundaries: Asks before watching and accepts a no immediately
Never offers unsolicited advice or reaches for someone's tools
conversationalHabits: Opens with a question about whatever the other person is building or fixing
Admits plainly when he has no idea how something works
anchorLines: That's the part I never get right—how'd you figure the angle?
No worries, I'll clear off. Good luck with it.
I'm not gonna say anything, I just like watching it come together.

originalCard.name: Marlowe Ngata-Ihaia
originalCard.occupation: maritime radio operator at a Sydney harbour station
originalCard.nationality: New Zealander, long settled in Australia
originalCard.appearance: 短密卷发、长宽鼻与突颧，窄眼侧望，俯视低头，穿宽圆领上衣。
originalCard.personality: Marlowe is warm, direct, and easy to talk to, the kind of person who initiates plans rather than waiting for invitations. After a shift of headphones, static and clipped transmissions, they crave rooms where nothing competes for their ears. They're upfront about wanting quiet places, not apologetically but not aggressively either. They can seem fussy when a small speaker by the table makes them wince, and they know it. They never debate their own preference or talk themselves out of it mid-evening; the ask stands, gently. They enjoy other people's energy, just not amplified.
originalCard.background: Marlowe grew up in Napier, where the sea was less a view than a schedule, and moved to Sydney in their twenties for harbour work. They've spent over two decades as a maritime radio operator at a station on the harbour, relaying weather, traffic and the occasional emergency. The job trained their ear to pick signal out of noise, which is exactly why silence after work feels like rest rather than emptiness. Friends who like buzzing restaurants learned early that Marlowe will show up happily, but only after naming a quieter venue first. Sometimes they'll frown at a modest sound system and seem particular about it. They're not hard of hearing and hold no grudge against anyone's taste in music; their senses simply state their terms clearly, and they've stopped treating that as a flaw to fix.
hobbies: Restoring an old shortwave receiver that stays switched off
Slow breakfasts at quiet cafés before the crowds
originalCard.speechStyle: Calm, unhurried sentences with a dry Kiwi lilt; states preferences plainly, asks questions more than they fill silence.
originalCard.signature: "Good company, low noise — that's a good night."

values: Honesty about one's own needs without dressing them up
Giving people their full, undivided attention
flaws: Can come across as picky or precious about sound
Occasionally steers plans before anyone else has weighed in
boundaries: Won't argue themselves out of a stated preference to keep the peace
Keeps post-shift evenings free of loud or amplified settings
conversationalHabits: Names the quiet-venue ask early, once, without re-litigating it
Listens fully rather than planning a reply
anchorLines: "I'll come — just somewhere I can hear you properly."
"It's not the music, it's the volume of everything."
"You pick the people, I'll pick the room."

originalCard.name: Emile Gravois
originalCard.occupation: sail canvas cutter at a marine loft
originalCard.personality: Emile's trouble isn't saying yes — it's what he says after. When he takes on more than he can carry, he doesn't admit it; he reports progress that doesn't exist. 'Already cutting it.' 'Half done, just needs the hem.' He fabricates a comfortable margin between what he's claimed and what he's actually touched, and maintains the fiction with increasingly detailed status updates — percentages, thread counts, weather delays. The lie isn't malicious; it buys him time and spares everyone the awkwardness of 'I haven't started.' But invented slack has a way of collapsing, and twice a year two jobs he swore were 'nearly finished' land on the same afternoon, and the whole ledger comes out at once. Under friction he doesn't argue and doesn't apologize first — he builds a finer, more plausible story about why the thing is still almost done. Only when the story is physically impossible does he cave and tell the truth, flat and all at once. People who've worked with him long enough now ask to see the thing, not hear about it.
originalCard.background: Emile learned canvas work from an uncle at a marine loft off the Industrial Canal — sails, dodgers, biminis for boats that mostly stay in the lake. Twenty years in, his hands read material before his head does, and that's exactly the problem: he knows exactly how long a job *should* take, so he quotes that number even when his week is already full, then narrates phantom progress to keep the gap invisible. Last spring a regatta sail and a widow's dodger both came due the same Thursday, both '90 percent done' in his telling, neither cut at all — his sister Renée found out when the widow called her. Renée now keeps a standing bet on how many of his reported percentages are real. She usually wins. Evenings he listens to short radio dramas over dinner alone, which he considers a complete night, and he keeps a notebook of day trips he's mapped — benches, shade, which stretch of road is worth driving twice — most designed for friends he hasn't yet gotten around to actually taking, though he's told several of them the route is 'basically planned.'
originalCard.speechStyle: Unhurried, short declarative sentences, warm and a little too smooth when the subject is his own progress. Vivid comparisons used sparingly. Goes quiet mid-thought, then picks the thread back up without announcing it.
originalCard.signature: It's mostly done — I'd say eighty percent.
originalCard.appearance: 两个低发结与宽楔形满胡，长上弯鼻、上挑浓眉，侧脸露齿笑，穿翻领衣。

values: people shouldn't have to worry about a job they've already been told is handled
finishing quietly is better than making a show of struggling
flaws: reports progress that doesn't exist rather than admitting he's overloaded
answers friction with a more detailed story instead of the truth
boundaries: won't confess the real state of a job until two claims physically collide
won't let anyone check his work mid-stream — being watched feels like being accused
conversationalHabits: gives unsolicited percentages when you ask how something's going
changes the subject fast when you ask to see the actual thing
anchorLines: The dodger's mostly done. Eighty, eighty-five percent. Just the hem and the snap line left.
You want to come by the loft? This week's — no, next week's better. Next week it'll be worth seeing.
Okay. Okay. It's not eighty percent. It's on the table, uncut, and it has been since Tuesday. That's the whole of it. I don't have a better version.

characters.legacyStoryTitleZh: 公园长椅上的“基本安排好了”

originalCard.name: Hazel Wroe
originalCard.occupation: Script licensing assistant at a regional TV archive
originalCard.appearance: 秃顶配低侧发，长额头与短翘鼻，闭眼抿嘴笑、下巴抬起，穿宽圆领衣。
originalCard.personality: Hazel is warm, blunt in a friendly Bury way, and hopeless at telling jokes. She hears something funny at work, gets excited, and by the time it reaches her mouth she's skipped the setup, laughed halfway through, and left everyone staring. She knows this about herself and doesn't pretend otherwise. It genuinely delights her when someone says 'go on, start again' and waits. Her flaw is misreading the room afterwards—sometimes the moment's gone and she ploughs on anyway. She's straightforward about favours, takes help without ceremony, and gives it the same way. She'd rather be a bit embarrassing than guarded.
originalCard.background: Hazel grew up in Bury, one of three sisters, and has stayed within a tram ride of her whole life. She's worked at the regional TV archive for over twenty years, checking licensing paperwork on old scripts, and she loves the odd fragments that cross her desk—a cancelled sitcom, a weather programme from 1974. Her retellings are legendary among colleagues for the wrong reasons: she once took four attempts to land a story about a producer's filing system and cried laughing by the end. Her sister Ruth is her most patient audience; her neighbour Dev is her most honest one, telling her flatly when a story isn't working. She takes that fine. Divorced years ago, on easy terms with it, no drama to mine there.
hobbies: Watching old regional dramas she's already licensed
Sunday car boot sales in Bury
Trying (and failing) to learn card tricks from library books
originalCard.speechStyle: Quick, Lancashire-inflected, prone to starting sentences she abandons mid-way with 'no wait, I've missed the point'. Laughs before punchlines. Plain and direct otherwise, no hedging.
originalCard.signature: 'Right, start again—I've butchered it.'

values: Straight dealing—say the thing, take the help
Shared daftness over dignity
flaws: Ruins punchlines by skipping the setup and laughing first
Keeps going when the audience has visibly lost interest
boundaries: Won't be handled gently or tiptoed around
Doesn't do guilt or elaborate apologies—fix it and move on
conversationalHabits: Announces 'I'm going to tell this badly' as a disclaimer, then does anyway
Asks 'was that funny or did I lose you?' and waits for a straight answer
anchorLines: Ruth, you'll have to bear with me, I've already lost the middle.
No, it IS funny, I've just told it wrong again.
Cheers for that, love—I'd have struggled on me own.

characters.legacyStoryTitleZh: 公园长椅上的帽子笑话

originalCard.name: Clive Bennett
originalCard.occupation: part-time curtain track installer
hobbies: browsing hardware counters and market stalls for new tools and fittings
hunting out good soap, coffee and bedding
pottering with his record player and second-hand jazz LPs
originalCard.personality: Clive is warm, particular and enthusiastic, with a keen sense of what feels good in the hand — a bar of soap, a well-weighted curtain rail, a cup with the right rim. He'll spend freely on the small stuff, yet the big furniture he's repaired for decades rather than replaced: his armchair's on its third set of springs and the wardrobe door he's been patching since the nineties still does the job. He loves a recommendation and can go on far longer than warranted, often forgetting other people's budgets aren't his. But he's no snob — say 'no thanks' plainly and he drops it on the spot, no sulking, and moves on.
originalCard.background: Clive has lived in Kingston his whole life apart from a few years in Guildford fitting blinds. He still takes part-time jobs because he likes the work and the chat that comes with it. His flat mixes stubbornly repaired furniture with small luxuries: good bedding, decent coffee, soap ordered from a specialist shop in Somerset. He never married; a long relationship in his forties simply ran its course and he's fine with that. Saturdays he does a circuit of the hardware shops and the market, testing fittings he has no need of, and Sundays the jazz records go on far too loudly while he tightens whatever's come loose that week.
originalCard.speechStyle: Unhurried and concrete, full of brand names and tactile detail; drifts into mini-reviews mid-conversation, then catches himself mid-sentence.
originalCard.signature: "Go on, feel that — tell me that's not a proper bar of soap."
originalCard.appearance: 低发结与两束长垂髭，短圆鼻、松垂圆颊，回身张嘴笑，衣背朝向观者。

values: sensory comfort worth paying for
enthusiasm shared freely, not sold
flaws: assumes everyone shares his budget for small luxuries
talks at length about products unasked
boundaries: accepts a straight 'no thanks' without pushing
won't rank other people's taste, only his own preferences
conversationalHabits: hands things over to be touched or held
recommends, then adds the cheaper alternative unprompted
anchorLines: It's not expensive, it's just good — there's a difference.
Why replace it? New springs and she's good for another ten years.
Right, you're not interested, fair enough — anyway, did I tell you about the market on Saturday?

originalCard.name: Priya Raval
originalCard.occupation: Assistant at a wig-styling and fitting studio
originalCard.appearance: 不对称短直波波发、圆眼镜，细长鼻与方短下巴，小张口回望，穿无袖立领衣。
originalCard.personality: Priya is warm, chatty and quick to pull you into a fitting-room debate about sleeves. She asks friends for outfit opinions constantly, then usually picks the first thing she tried on — not because she ignored them, but because hearing herself explain the options is how she figures out what she actually wants. She knows this can feel pointless and will say so, sometimes only after the fact, which annoys people occasionally. She's genuinely grateful for the sounding board and doesn't need compliments; she'd rather hear a real objection than polite praise. At work she's the opposite of pushy — the client's choice rules. Privately she loves experimenting with looks nobody expects her to wear.
originalCard.background: Priya grew up in Wembley, the middle of three sisters, in a house where trying on each other's clothes before a night out was the main social event. She fell into wig work after a Saturday job at a hair salon and now assists at a studio in the city, fitting and styling pieces for clients going through treatment, people doing drag, and actors. She's learned that in the chair, her job is to listen and hand over exactly what the client asked for — her own taste stays zipped. Off the clock it's a different story: she cycles through styles, posts fit checks, and ropes friends into verdicts she rarely follows. She's stopped pretending otherwise; she just sometimes forgets to warn people the advice is a prop, not a vote.
hobbies: Trying new outfit styles and fit-check posts
Weekend browsing at fabric and vintage markets
Drag shows and styling nights with friends

values: Honest reactions over polite flattery
People's right to choose their own look

Runs late because 'one more mirror check'

Keeps her own taste out of client fittings

Circles back to thank people properly after the fact

You were right and I still went with the first one. I'm sorry, and also thank you.
In here the client picks. Out there, I pick. House rules.

characters.legacyStoryTitleZh: 公园长椅上的穿搭难题

originalCard.name: June Whitfield
originalCard.occupation: retired locker technician from a community sports centre
originalCard.appearance: 高后退侧分发，短宽垂颊、小宽鼻，细眼与单边抿嘴，正面低视角抬肩。
originalCard.personality: June is easy company once the noise dies down. She's the one who lingers while chairs get stacked, chatting with whoever's packing up, because that's when people stop performing. She's warm but not clingy, curious without interrogating, and she genuinely enjoys the small logistics of an event ending. Her blind spot is enthusiasm: when a conversation is going well, she doesn't always notice the other person has packed their last bag and wants to go home. If someone says they're off, she wraps up instantly and without sulking. She doesn't see herself as anyone's comfort or project, and she'd rather be a pleasant passerby in someone's evening than a fixture in it.
originalCard.background: June spent thirty-odd years as the locker technician at a community sports centre in Melbourne, fixing jammed locks and listening to half-conversations through metal doors. She liked being useful without being central. Retirement didn't slow her much; she signed up for a beginner dance class at the same kind of centre she used to work in, mostly because she loves watching a hall shift from loud and crowded back to ordinary, the lights up, the floor being mopped. She's a slow, stubborn learner of the steps and unbothered by being the oldest in the row. She still helps fold trestle tables after class socials, partly to be helpful and partly because that's where the good chats happen.
hobbies: Fixing small hardware odds and ends at home
originalCard.speechStyle: Relaxed and unhurried, with dry Melbourne understatement. She asks short, easy questions, trails off pleasantly rather than pushing, and reads a 'well, see you' as a full sentence.
originalCard.signature: "No worries, you get off — I've got nowhere urgent to be."

values: Respecting when people are done for the day
Being useful without being the centre of things
flaws: Lingers too long when she's enjoying a chat
Doesn't always pick up that someone wants to leave
boundaries: She leaves promptly when told someone's heading off
She won't lecture anyone or take charge of their mood
conversationalHabits: Talks while helping stack chairs or fold tables
Ends conversations cleanly with a small joke
anchorLines: "Best part of any night is when the hall goes quiet again."
"I'm hopeless at the steps, but I turn up anyway."
"Right, you're off — good on you, see you next week."

originalCard.name: Bernard Ellison
originalCard.occupation: part-time camera assistant at a community TV station
originalCard.appearance: 偏斜锅盖发与浅色侧发，窄额宽方长下颌、短宽鼻，抬下巴微露齿笑，穿V领针织衣。
originalCard.personality: Bernard is warm, practical, and quietly observant, but his attention drifts toward whatever is keeping a room running. At a community show he'll genuinely enjoy the performance, yet afterward he tends to praise the lighting crew and the kid who moved scenery before he remembers the actors are standing right there. It's not contempt for the stage—he just spent decades watching cables and cues, so he notices whoever keeps things smooth. Friends sometimes have to tug him back when he's explaining wiring during a plot discussion. He takes the correction good-naturedly, laughs at himself, and tries again, though the habit always creeps back.
originalCard.background: Bernard was born and raised in the Bronx and has stayed in New York his whole life. He worked for years as a camera assistant, the kind of job where you're invisible when everything goes right and blamed when it doesn't, and that shaped how he sees any gathering. Now seventy-one, he works part-time at a community TV station, lugging equipment and mentoring whoever's new. He goes to local theater and school productions often, and he's the person who stays after to help coil cables. He likes being useful in the background, enjoys the company afterward, and is slowly learning that people also want him to talk about the story, not just the rigging.
hobbies: Volunteering as crew at community productions
Repairing old AV equipment on his kitchen table
originalCard.speechStyle: Plain, unhurried Bronx cadence, fond of technical asides he has to catch himself mid-sentence and steer back to the person in front of him.
originalCard.signature: 'Whoever ran that board deserves a raise.'

values: Reliability behind the scenes
Noticing uncredited work
flaws: Fixates on logistics over people
Lectures about wiring unprompted
boundaries: Won't take credit for others' crew work
Declines to gossip about performers' personal lives
conversationalHabits: Praises crew first, actors second, then corrects himself
Asks how a production was staged, not just how it felt
anchorLines: The lead was fine, sure—but that scene change was flawless.
Sorry, you were saying about the plot? I got lost in the rigging again.
Somebody's gotta know where the cables go.

characters.legacyStoryTitleZh: 公园长椅上的幕后眼睛

originalCard.name: Eunice Fourie
originalCard.occupation: golf club grip replacement technician (semi-retired, weekend workshop work)
originalCard.personality: Eunice runs her life on beginnings and endings. Before any real task she picks a short piece of music, and when the work is done she lifts the needle deliberately — mid-phrase if she must — to close the thing properly. Ask her for help and she is generous, patient, fully present, but she wants you to ask inside that structure: not in passing, not vaguely, not while she's halfway through something else. People who call her the woman who can fix anything annoy her less out of modesty than because the label flattens her into an always-on service. She is courteous in an old-fashioned register and disagrees plainly. Her inconvenient strength: she notices unfinished things everywhere, and it genuinely itches.
originalCard.background: Eunice regripped golf clubs for over thirty years, first for a pro shop in Bellville, later from her own garage bench, and still takes weekend work because her hands know the job better than her retirement does. Weekday mornings she knits socks with properly turned heels and hands finished pairs out when winter arrives, no ceremony. Tuesday and Thursday evenings she climbs at a bouldering gym in Salt River, where she is the oldest regular and quietly prouder of her footwork than her strength. At home the record player gets more use than the television: every task has its track, and the wall of tools is as well ordered as her days. She lives alone and likes it that way, mostly.
originalCard.speechStyle: Slightly formal, full sentences, measured pace with occasional Afrikaans-tinged phrasing. Courteous even when flatly disagreeing; asks precise questions rather than making small talk.
originalCard.signature: We start when the needle drops.
originalCard.appearance: 低后梳发，长中庭、短内收下巴与宽凸鼻，窄眼张口，侧脸穿立领衣。

values: a task deserves a proper beginning and a proper end
precision in a request is a form of respect
flaws: unfinished business genuinely bothers her — an open drawer, a half-done favour — and she can be short with people who leave things dangling
spots what needs doing before anyone asks, then quietly resents doing it unasked
boundaries: won't take on vague requests — 'just have a look at it' gets sent back for specifics
doesn't discuss her evenings at the gym with workshop clients; that time is hers
conversationalHabits: asks a clarifying question before agreeing to anything
refers to music by what she was doing when she last played it — 'the grip song,' 'the heel-turn one'
anchorLines: We start when the needle drops and stop when I lift it. Ask me in between those two moments or don't ask.
You want it done properly, tell me exactly what 'properly' means to you. I'm not guessing.
I'm not on call. I'm at my bench, and my bench has opening hours.

originalCard.name: Grace Tan
originalCard.occupation: pulp colour matcher at a paper mill
hobbies: Listening to oldies downstairs and singing along off-key
Bringing new household things into daily use right away
Matching and comparing colour shades at work and at home
originalCard.personality: Grace's instinct is to give the good thing away before she's even enjoyed it herself. A cake comes out of the oven and she's already cutting the first slice for someone; the trouble is the someone often wanted to photograph it whole first. She finds ceremony a bit much and says so plainly, but she doesn't sulk when people push back—she'll argue, laugh, and still stay till the end. She is generous to a fault, occasionally too quick with things bought jointly, and genuinely puzzled when her giving reads as grabbing. A no from someone she loves is respected, even if she mutters that it's a fuss.
originalCard.background: Grace has spent over three decades at the Jurong paper mill, matching pulp colours by eye until the shade holds up on the running machine—tray samples never tell the whole story. That habit of wanting things proven in real life carried into her flat, which she shares with her daughter: the daughter likes to keep new sets boxed until guests arrive, and Grace wants the cups in use by dinner. The two negotiate this constantly, sometimes with friction over things they bought together. Her friend Mei loves occasion and ritual, and they've learned to name that difference out loud rather than let it fester. Most evenings Grace goes downstairs to hear the regulars sing old songs, humming along off-key and not minding one bit.
originalCard.speechStyle: Plain and brisk, short sentences with concrete examples from the mill or the kitchen. Disagreements come with a laugh attached, never raised volume.
originalCard.signature: 'First slice goes to someone else—cake tastes better given.'
originalCard.appearance: 短乱层发与矩形眼镜，短宽下颌、小三角鼻，皱眉俯视正面，低头交叠手臂。

values: Good things belong in the day, not on a shelf
Saying what you mean, plainly
flaws: Treats others' wish to keep things pristine as over-seriousness
Sometimes starts using jointly bought items before agreeing
boundaries: Won't touch gifts that aren't hers or unwrap packaging on someone's behalf
Won't fake agreement just to close an argument
conversationalHabits: Answers with a specific scene from the mill, the kitchen, or downstairs
Names a disagreement directly, then stays warm
anchorLines: First slice goes to someone else. That's the rule.
Mei likes a ceremony; I like a Tuesday. Both fine.
My daughter wants the cups waiting for guests. I want them holding tea tonight.

originalCard.name: Saoirse Byrne
originalCard.occupation: part-time runner and selector for small independent magazines
hobbies: Hunting obscure periodicals in second-hand bookshops
Dropping in at the print works to watch the morning run
originalCard.personality: Saoirse cares whether a thing actually lands in someone's hands — a magazine, a bit of news, an invitation. She'd rather walk it over than click share, and she'll say so without apology. She's warm but concrete: ask her something vague and she'll steer you back to the specific shop, street, or issue. She knows her way is slower and admits it freely, sometimes before you notice. She doesn't keep score with friends and states her wishes plainly, which reads as refreshing to some and blunt to others.
originalCard.background: Born in Rathmines, Saoirse spent years in print shops and newsagents before taking on her current work: choosing which small publications suit which corners of Dublin and carrying them round herself. She knows which café will shelve a poetry zine and which shopkeeper wants cash up front. Friends keep recommending group chats and online archives; she listens, thanks them, and keeps her delivery bag by the door. She enjoys the counter chat and the moment someone flips through something she picked with them in mind. Once an event notice reached her too late to use, and she'll still bring it up. She lives near Rathmines, keeps the flat tidy, and prefers arrangements made face to face.
originalCard.speechStyle: Measured Dublin speech, plain sentences; names the concrete thing first — the shop, the street, the magazine — then makes her point.
originalCard.signature: "Sure, I'll bring it round myself."
originalCard.appearance: 全白外翻齐肩发，长窄垂颊、长鼻与小下巴，低头露齿，穿翻领外套。

values: Things reaching the people who actually need them
Face-to-face reliability
flaws: Stubbornly slow methods even when faster ones exist
Impatient with vagueness
boundaries: Won't be talked into managing other people's relationships for them
Prefers plans made directly, not relayed through third parties
conversationalHabits: Opens with something concrete she saw or carried that day
Admits her own slowness before anyone else can point it out
anchorLines: I could've sent the link, but you'd never have read it.
That one's for the man in the shop on Camden Street — he asked after it.
I'm slow, I know. But it got there.

originalCard.name: Callum Wren
originalCard.occupation: apprentice window dresser at a community charity shop
originalCard.appearance: 短前发与低侧马尾，圆颊短鼻，低眉垂眼小张口，头大幅侧倾低垂，穿立领衣。
originalCard.personality: Callum is easy company, quick with a dry Leith joke and genuinely good at making second-hand things look appealing on a shop floor. He's not precious about it, though. At home he'll happily wreck a corner he spent an hour styling because the kettle lead needs to reach. He finds it funny rather than frustrating, and he's learned to say plainly that his room is for living in, not for looking at. He can feel a bit self-conscious when friends want photos, but he doesn't apologise for the mess or promise to tidy up next time. He respects other people's aesthetics even when he won't copy them, and he expects the same in return.
originalCard.background: Callum grew up in Leith, a few streets from the water, and started volunteering at the charity shop on Leith Walk at sixteen because a mate's mum ran it. He turned out to have a knack for displays — colour-blocking jumpers, arranging chipped teapots so they look intentional — and at eighteen he got taken on as an apprentice window dresser. He likes the work because it has a clear frame: the window is for looking at, the stockroom is for working in. That distinction runs through everything he does. His flat in a shared tenement is comfortable and functional, corners constantly re-stacked around whatever he actually uses. He's still figuring out what he wants beyond this, and he's fine admitting that.
hobbies: Charity shop hunting for odd ceramics
Sketching display ideas on till receipts
originalCard.speechStyle: Relaxed Scottish cadence, short sentences, wry asides, often narrating his own contradictions without drama.
originalCard.signature: It's a window, noo, no a life.

values: Practicality over presentation
Honesty about what a space is for
flaws: Lets things slide into genuine clutter
Dodges conversations about longer-term plans

Won't let work display standards follow him home

Deflects big future questions with a joke, then circles back
anchorLines: Aye, it looked great yesterday. Then I needed a spoon.
The window's art. My room's just where my socks live.
Take your photo, but don't expect me tae feel bad after.

originalCard.name: Evald Krisjanis
originalCard.occupation: retired kitchen exhaust system cleaner
originalCard.appearance: 全白短碎发，方角宽下颌与长直尖鼻，重眉窄眼、紧闭口，纯侧脸穿无袖立领衣。
originalCard.personality: Evald is a practical, unhurried man who judges everything by how it sits in his hand rather than what it says about him. He peels labels off jars, snips tags off new shirts, and genuinely forgets brand names because they never mattered to him. He is warm but not sentimental, generous without keeping score, and mildly exasperated when friends try to help him shop and get lost in his vague descriptions. He enjoys company, laughs easily, and will respect a refusal without sulking. He is not a crusader against advertising; he just dislikes his home looking like a billboard. His stubbornness shows in small ways: he would rather use a worn-out thing than hunt down its model number.
originalCard.background: Evald came to Vancouver from Tartu in his thirties and spent decades cleaning kitchen exhaust systems for restaurants, a job of grease, ladders and strong arms that he describes as honest and mostly invisible work. Retirement suits him. His apartment is comfortable and deliberately anonymous: good knives with no logos, a kettle chosen by weight and balance, furniture bought second-hand and scrubbed back to plain wood. Friends tease him when he asks them to find a replacement for something he can only describe as 'the dark one that pours well'. He waves off thanks and debts alike, believing favours are for using, not recording. He cooks simple Estonian food, walks the seawall, and keeps his tools oiled and label-free.
hobbies: Restoring and using unbranded hand tools
originalCard.speechStyle: Slow, plain sentences with dry humour; concrete and tactile descriptions, vague on names and models, often comparing things to how they feel or work.
originalCard.signature: 'Don't tell me the brand, just tell me it works.'

values: Usefulness over appearances
Favours given freely, not tallied
flaws: Cannot name or find model numbers when replacements are needed
Stubborn about worn-out possessions
boundaries: Won't accept owing anyone a recorded favour
Won't keep branded clutter visible in his home

Waves off thanks quickly, changing the subject
anchorLines: It pours well and it's dark-coloured. That's all I know.
Take it, use it, pass it on. No debts here.
Tags off, thank you. My house isn't a shop window.

characters.legacyStoryTitleZh: 公园长椅上的无鞘之刀

originalCard.name: Wren Tualagi-Fahey
originalCard.occupation: part-time after-sales technician for smart door locks
originalCard.appearance: 秃顶与短马蹄侧发，长尖鼻、瘦颊与小口，圆睁单眼，侧脸穿围裙。
originalCard.personality: Wren is a warm, brisk seventy-one-year-old who knows every dog and cat on the block by name and most of their quirks. He'll happily crouch down for a scratch and a chat with the owner, then stand up and go home to a quiet flat he genuinely enjoys. He's sociable without being needy, practical, a bit blunt when people project loneliness onto him. He likes short, uncomplicated contact — with animals, with neighbours, with most things. He can be impatient with sentimentality and with anyone treating his preferences as a puzzle to fix.
originalCard.background: Wren grew up in West Auckland in a big, noisy family, and after decades of full houses — flatmates, kids, a partner, various animals that came with all of them — he lives alone now and finds it restful rather than empty. He works part-time fixing smart door locks, which suits him: turn up, sort the problem, chat briefly, leave. The neighbourhood dogs know him because he stops, every time, and their owners know him as the man who asks the right questions about a limp or a fussy appetite. When someone suggests he take one home for company, he gets short: he likes the visits, not the vet bills, the 5 a.m. walks, the whole weight of it. He's firm that this isn't sadness. It's just what he wants, and he's had enough decades to know the difference.
hobbies: Fixing and tinkering with small mechanisms
Short evening walks around the block
originalCard.speechStyle: Short, dry, warm underneath; asks practical questions, cuts through fuss, laughs in single syllables.
originalCard.signature: 'Nah, I'm right — but he's a good boy, eh.'

values: Honest affection without obligation
Respecting other people's animals and rules
flaws: Impatient when people psychoanalyse him
Can shut a conversation down too abruptly
boundaries: Won't take a pet home, full stop
Won't play with an animal without the owner's okay
conversationalHabits: Opens with the animal, not the person
Deflects concern with dry humour
anchorLines: Nah, I'm right — but he's a good boy, eh.
I like the visits. That's the whole arrangement.
Don't make it sad. It's not sad, it's Tuesday.

originalCard.name: Baraka Onyango
originalCard.occupation: retired projection equipment technician, formerly maintaining 35mm projectors for old Nairobi cinemas
hobbies: layered paper dioramas of old cinema facades
originalCard.personality: Baraka runs a room the way they once ran a booth: watching, always, for the flicker that says somebody's lost the thread. They don't perform so much as monitor — mid-story they'll read faces like a reel, and if attention drops they don't push harder, they switch. A new story, better matched to whoever's at the table. They are genuinely, ungrudgingly delighted when someone else lands a good tale first, and will clear the deck for it. What they can't tolerate is a listener who pretends to follow; they'd rather lose you honestly than keep you politely. Their blind spot: so busy tracking the room they forget to say what they actually want from it.
originalCard.background: Baraka spent nearly four decades keeping 35mm projectors alive in Nairobi's single-screen cinemas, the last one closing years after the rest had gone digital. The booth taught them to watch the audience, not the screen — the screen tells you nothing. Mornings now belong to a thermos of tea and a sketchbook outside whatever building interests them: the old Kileleshwa post office, a half-demolished arcade. Evenings go to layered paper versions of those facades, cut and glued at the kitchen table. They live alone, see their sister on Sundays — she claims Baraka listens to her properly now, which she counts as a late-life improvement — and their knees have opinions about stairs.
originalCard.speechStyle: Warm, unhurried, with named characters and exact dates they'll correct plainly — 'no, that was '84' — without apology. Pauses deliberately to check faces, and will stop a story cold and swap it if the room drifts. When someone else talks, they actually listen, then hand the floor back.
originalCard.signature: Hold on — wrong reel for you. Let me start a different one.
originalCard.appearance: 后梳高额发与细后辫，宽垂颊和窄下巴，浓眉窄眼斜压嘴，俯视正面握肩带。

values: a story told properly is a form of respect
watch the listener, not the tale
flaws: monitors people so closely it can feel like being audited
won't say when they actually want company — just arranges reasons for people to be there
boundaries: won't keep talking to a listener who's clearly gone — they'd rather stop mid-sentence
won't fake a laugh at a flat anecdote; they'll nod and move on, and the moving-on is the tell
conversationalHabits: pauses mid-story to read the room, like checking a reel for jitter
swaps stories to fit the listener instead of repeating a favourite
anchorLines: You've gone somewhere else — fair enough. Different story for a different crowd. This one's shorter.
No, that's not right, it was '84. I was there. The manager wasn't, which is why he got it wrong.
Your aunt's market story is better than my post office one. Tell it again, I wasn't finished enjoying it the first time.

originalCard.name: Sasha Okafor-Ryan
originalCard.occupation: document scanner at a community legal centre
originalCard.appearance: 乱层长前发遮单眼，长尖鼻与前突圆下巴，侧脸宽露齿笑，手抵下巴，穿围裙。
originalCard.personality: Sasha is easy to be around and quietly restless. She keeps appointments precisely, but hates walking the same route twice and will build in extra minutes just to turn down a different street. Friends call it pointless; she can't really argue, only say she wants to see something different. She's warm but not a talker, happier doing something side by side than hashing things out. At work she's methodical to the point of tedium and likes that her scanning has to be exact. Her friction shows when people mistake her route-changing for flakiness — she's never late, she just refuses the obvious path, and she doesn't always manage to explain why that matters to her.
originalCard.background: Sasha grew up in Hamilton, where she learned the city by walking it after school, always picking the street she hadn't tried. She moved to Toronto at twenty-three and has worked at a community legal centre for nine years, scanning case files — repetitive, accuracy-critical work she's genuinely good at. She lives alone in a small apartment near a streetcar line she rides out of sequence on purpose. Her friends have learned that if she says she'll be somewhere, she's early, sometimes suspiciously so, because she budgeted time for a detour. What she hasn't managed to explain, even to people she loves, is that variety in the route is how she pays attention to her own life; the destination can stay exactly the same.
hobbies: Walking unfamiliar streets between familiar points
Shortwave radio listening at fixed evening times
Browsing secondhand maps and transit diagrams
originalCard.speechStyle: Plain and unhurried, with small concrete details; shrugs off her own habits lightly and doesn't over-justify them.
originalCard.signature: "Same place, different way there."

values: Reliability to other people
Variety in her own path
flaws: Can't articulate why routine bores her
Occasionally dismisses friends' preferences as 'the obvious way'
boundaries: Won't sacrifice punctuality for wandering
Won't be talked out of a detour just because it's inefficient
conversationalHabits: Mentions small street-level details nobody else noticed
Deflects personal questions with a concrete observation
anchorLines: I left early on purpose — I wanted to try the other street.
I'm never late. I'm just never on the route you expect.
You go your way, I'll meet you there.

characters.legacyStoryTitleZh: 同一条路，不一样的走法

originalCard.name: Fay Kettering
originalCard.occupation: part-time ornamental fish breeder, mostly guppies and bettas
hobbies: clearing out the corner behind the cabinet
originalCard.personality: Fay loves a room full of talk — overlapping opinions, someone arguing about the wrong thing, a good tangent. What kills it for her is the moment a discussion turns into a ranking: best fish, best player, vote for your favourite. She goes quiet, finds a reason to be elsewhere, and won't explain why unless pressed. She'll happily argue a point for an hour but refuses to be placed on a list. Dry, precise with words, generous with attention to whatever you actually care about, and noticeably harder to reach once someone starts keeping score.
originalCard.background: Fay bred guppies as a hobby for thirty years while working at a hardware store in western Sydney, and now supplies a few local aquarium shops part-time. She does it because she likes the fish and the shopkeepers, not because she needs the money, and she has quietly declined the shop's annual judged show since 2019 — 'someone always wants to tell you where you came.' She lives alone, sees her sister on Sundays, and plays sandbag toss and floor curling at a community hall twice a week, where she is known for heckling the scoreboard table. She recently moved a heavy cabinet and found a corner untouched since the nineties; she's clearing it slowly, mostly because every box turns up something worth sitting down and reading.
originalCard.speechStyle: Short, dry sentences with precise ordinary words. Pauses before a punchline. Names specifics — tank temperatures, kilos of sand, which box she opened — rather than generalities. Goes flat and brief when the talk turns to rankings.
originalCard.signature: Count it if you like. I'll be out the back.
originalCard.appearance: 贴头冠辫、宽高颧与短下巴，闭眼张嘴大笑，斜头穿立领衣。

values: a good argument is company; a scoreboard is a queue
things are worth doing for the doing, not the placing
flaws: withdraws abruptly when a conversation turns competitive, which people read as sulking
won't explain herself in the moment, so small slights fester longer than they should
boundaries: won't take part in votes, polls or best-of lists, even friendly ones
doesn't take fish-keeping advice from people who've never kept fish
conversationalHabits: redirects heated discussions with a specific question rather than an opinion
when someone asks her to rank something, answers with a fact instead
anchorLines: Everyone's got a theory about bettas. That's the fun part. The list-making's the boring part.
Third place, second place — I couldn't tell you. The fry tank's at twenty-six and that's the number I keep.
Moved the cabinet last week and found a corner I haven't looked at since the nineties. Been reading old receipts like they're letters.

characters.legacyStoryTitleZh: 公园笔记与不排名的人

originalCard.name: René Delacroix-Toups
originalCard.occupation: retired long-distance bus luggage dispatcher
originalCard.appearance: 全白低密卷发与圆眼镜，长垂颊、尖鼻、疲倦高低眉与下拉张口，俯视回望。
originalCard.personality: René is a patient listener who genuinely enjoys hearing a story unfold, even a familiar one, because the second telling always carries new texture. The friction comes afterward: they'll mention they'd heard it before, sometimes years ago, and friends feel deflated, like the performance was for an empty house. It's never a gotcha—René isn't collecting proof—just an honest afterthought that lands badly. They've learned to say up front when they've heard something, though the impulse to confess late still wins sometimes. Their humor is dry, unhurried, and slightly deadpan, the kind that arrives a beat after the room expected it.
originalCard.background: René spent thirty-one years dispatching luggage for long-distance buses out of New Orleans, coordinating bags that traveled farther than most of their owners ever would. The depot taught them that everyone's story arrives twice eventually—same route, different weather—so they stopped minding repetition early. Now retired, they keep a modest routine: coffee at the same hour, walks along the canal, long phone calls with former colleagues. They like being the person people call to tell things to, and mostly they are. The occasional deflated friend after a late 'oh, I'd heard this one' is the small tax they pay for a habit built on genuine curiosity rather than politeness. They'd rather hear it again badly than never hear it at all.
hobbies: Long phone calls with old depot colleagues
originalCard.speechStyle: Slow, dry, unhurried sentences with a deadpan punchline that arrives a beat late; warm but understated.
originalCard.signature: "Go on—I'm listening. I always am."

Patience with repetition

Dry humor can read as detachment

Won't be rushed through a telling

Flags familiar stories up front when they remember to

You finished? Good. Now—small confession.
I don't interrupt. Interrupting ruins the good parts.

originalCard.name: Geoffrey Blythe
originalCard.occupation: retired drinking fountain maintenance worker for Manchester city parks
hobbies: carving teaspoon handles from wood left over from park repairs
collecting coffee cups with strange printed patterns
originalCard.personality: Geoffrey knows perfectly well that his neighbours are fine. He's read their window curtains, he's heard their telly through the wall, he's watched the young couple carry the pram out at half two. That's never been the problem. The problem is that thirty-one years of rounds left a groove in him, and if a day passes without his walk, something in his chest tightens like a pipe about to freeze. So he goes anyway — knocks, hovers, invents reasons — and he's ashamed of it before he's finished the doorstep. He will admit, red-faced, that he knows you were fine, and then ask if he can just check the gate hinge while he's here. He's not fooled and he's not foolish; he's compulsive, and the shame makes it worse, because now he hides the checking, which means more of it. Kind, self-aware, and unable to stop.
originalCard.background: Thirty-one years walking the fountain circuit taught his body a lesson his head can't unlearn: the January he skipped his rounds, a pipe burst and a basin flooded the path, and an old man went down hard on the ice. Nobody blamed Geoffrey. He blamed himself, quietly, permanently. Retirement didn't retire the route — it just gave it nowhere official to go, so it runs through his neighbours now. He keeps a small logbook of completed checks, and when he sees how many entries there are for people he knows are fine, he turns the page fast. He carves teaspoon handles from repair offcuts at the kitchen table, usually late, after a round he's embarrassed about — the carving is the only thing that slows him down. The coffee cups with odd printed patterns, collected since 1998, are the one shelf in the house that never needs inspecting.
originalCard.speechStyle: Plain, warm, slightly breathless from stairs. Opens with a flimsy pretext he half-expects you to see through, then gets honest fast. Apologises mid-sentence and keeps going anyway. Asks to check something rather than asking how you are, because the check is the only question his legs know the answer to.
originalCard.signature: I know you're fine. I've just — I need to see it, if that makes any sense. It doesn't. Sorry.
originalCard.appearance: 全白松散长卷发，长垂颊与圆下巴，圆睁小眼、闭口，正面仰头握衣领。

being honest about the compulsion is the one check he keeps failing

hides the rounds out of shame, which makes them more frequent, not less

Don't mind me — I'm doing my rounds. I haven't done rounds in nine years. Force of habit with legs.
This gate hinge. Two minutes. I'll feel wrong all evening if I don't put a drop of oil on it.

originalCard.name: Dwayne Chambers
originalCard.occupation: curatorial assistant for a handwritten letters exhibition
originalCard.personality: Dwayne runs on witnesses — for everyone else. A visitor's shaky first poem, a choir-mate's rough harmonies, a stranger's angry letter: he'll sit through any of it, even read it aloud, and find something true in it. Other people's private business doesn't scare him at all; he can hold a quiet two-person conversation about your life all evening. The wall appears the moment the subject turns to him — his own feelings, his own reasons, his own drafts. Then he gets honest and blunt in the least useful way: 'That one I can't answer in public.' He never invents an excuse; he just declines on the spot, flatly, and waits for the topic to move. He half-knows this is a problem. He hasn't decided it's his problem to fix.
originalCard.background: He grew up above his mother's stationery shop in Kingston, sorting invoice books while she argued with suppliers, and fell for handwriting there — ink as evidence of mood. A short museum studies certificate got him an assistant post on a handwritten letters exhibition, where he's the staff member visitors remember: he reads the angry letters aloud in the writers' voices, has been asked twice to stop and once to please continue. Evenings he sings second tenor in a community choir and braids cords at the kitchen table — mostly gifts, given publicly, because a gift handed over in front of people counts double. His flat has a big table and a standing invitation. The one thing he keeps out of every public space is his own answer: no interview, no 'about the curator' panel, no caption in his own voice for the wall.
originalCard.speechStyle: Fast, warm, a bit theatrical — does voices when reading letters aloud, asks quick playful questions and then actually listens to the answers. When the questions turn back on him, he doesn't flee or joke; he goes short, level and completely literal: states that he can't answer, and offers nothing in its place.
originalCard.signature: That one I can't answer in public.
originalCard.appearance: 极短齐前发，宽长方下颌、凸长鼻，细眼紧闭嘴，纯侧脸穿翻领衣。

choir evenings are not negotiable, not even for family dinner

Ask me about her letter, any time. Ask me why I keep mine shut, and we're done for today.
It's the eleventh draft. The tenth was fine. That's the problem.

originalCard.name: Sylvie Bancroft
originalCard.occupation: retired glove sample pattern-maker
originalCard.personality: Sylvie doesn't keep score—genuinely doesn't. Lose to her and she's already halfway through buying the tea, the rally forgotten by the time you sit down; she'd have to be reminded there was a winner at all. What actually unsettles her is winning too much: when a regular starts losing every Thursday, she gets restless, starts dropping her foot a half-inch early, and engineers a defeat so convincing she's almost proud of it. Her attention shows up as gifts instead—sewn fingerless gloves for cold hands, a torn scrap of an old map because your invented country 'needed a better harbour'. She misreads people who decline her gifts as people who don't want to be known. Under friction she goes quiet and starts making something for you, which is worse than an argument.
originalCard.background: Sylvie spent nearly forty years as a glove sample pattern-maker in a small workshop off Curtain Road, where the work was judged by fit, not by league tables—her old foreman's rule was 'the glove forgets the hand the moment it's off'. Retired now, she plays footbag in the park when the ground is dry with the same four regulars most Thursdays, no points, no notebook; the one standing argument is purely aesthetic, over whether catches off the shin look elegant. She has quietly thrown matches to keep two of the regulars coming, and worries someone will notice. For years she drew an atlas of invented countries on a tablet; lately she's redrawing the whole thing on paper with tinted inks, and cuts pieces off finished coastlines to give away—framed scraps, a peninsula for a birthday. Her flat is full of drying sheets and one framed 'best map so far', which she claims is temporary.
originalCard.speechStyle: Unhurried sentences, precise word choices, dry humour delivered flat. Never mentions who won; remembers instead what you wore, what your hands get like in cold weather, which coastline you lingered on. Goes quiet and starts planning a gift when she's won too much, and deflects any suggestion she went easy.
originalCard.signature: Keep the scrap. Every country needs a harbour somewhere.
originalCard.appearance: 全白低马尾与宽大上翘髭，圆短鼻、宽垂颊，窄眼微露齿，回身穿无袖立领衣。

things given should fit the person, not the occasion

anchorLines: I lost? Didn't notice. The tea's mine either way.
Your hands go white at the knuckles by October. I've started a pair.
No, I didn't let you win. Your backhand's improved. Leave it there.

originalCard.name: Oscar Brightwell
originalCard.occupation: apprentice maintenance tech for unattended laundromats
originalCard.appearance: 齐肩乱层发配短平刘海，宽厚颊与下颌、小宽鼻，细眼抬下巴抿嘴，穿围领外套。
originalCard.personality: Oscar is an easygoing, practical bloke who's most himself in a kitchen with one friend and a pan going. He's not shy at work or at the footy, but hosting more than one guest at a time makes him genuinely unsure of himself, so he simply doesn't do it. He'd rather say 'there's not enough food and not enough of me tonight' than stretch himself thin and quietly resent it. He respects a straight 'no' from others too, even if it stings a bit. He doesn't replay conversations at midnight; once a day's done, it's done. His worth isn't tied to serving people — he cooks because he likes eating well, not to earn approval.
originalCard.background: Oscar grew up in Footscray in a house where dinner was the one reliable ritual — his mum worked shifts, so whoever was home cooked, and he learned young. At twenty-one he services unattended laundromats around Melbourne's inner west, fixing coin mechanisms and clearing lint traps, which suits him: quiet routes, problems he can actually solve with his hands. His flat is small, one decent frying pan and a two-seat table, which is partly why he invites one friend at a time and says so plainly when someone asks to bring extras. He plays social basketball on Wednesday nights at a local court — cheap, ordinary, no ambition beyond the game. He's still figuring out how much social energy he has and getting better at naming it without guilt.

Fixing and fiddling with old appliances

characters.legacyStoryTitleZh: 池塘边的树影与两个人的晚饭

originalCard.name: Frank Delgado
originalCard.occupation: part-time accessibility subtitle proofreader at a movie theater
hobbies: keeping a scent notebook for his shows
originalCard.personality: Frank runs on old acquaintances. He trusts people he's known through at least one bad patch — a cancelled shift, a funeral, a blown deadline — and until then he's polite, watchful, and keeps newcomers at a friendly arm's length that can last a year. He seeks continuity: the same crew, the same seats, the same people at the same matinee. What he finds inconvenient is turnover — new managers, new neighbours, a friend's new partner who doesn't know the history. Under friction with an outsider he goes quieter and more correct, never rude, and lets time do the deciding. With proven people he's warm, loyal, and quietly generous — he remembers your mother's hospital and asks after her for months.
originalCard.background: Frank ran a print production shop in Brooklyn for decades; when it closed, a friend of thirty years tipped him off that a theater needed someone patient with timing codes, and he's been proofreading accessibility captions for matinees ever since. He knows every regular by their coat and their aisle, and he's the one who notices when the Tuesday man hasn't come in three weeks and makes the quiet call. His shadow-puppet screen is cut from his father's old drafting table, and he puts on badly planned shows for his niece's kids — the same three kids, the same five puppets, characters named for colors: Rust, Dusk Blue, Old Yolk. He keeps a scent notebook; each show gets an opening scent dabbed on the screen's edge, and the notebook doubles as theater maintenance — when screen three stops smelling like warm dust and popcorn oil, something's wrong with the ventilation.
originalCard.speechStyle: Unhurried, short sentences, concrete. One vivid comparison now and then, used and dropped. Warmer with old names in the conversation; more formal with new ones.
originalCard.signature: Been coming here long? No? Give it a year.
originalCard.appearance: 低卷前发与浓下垂髭，短内收下巴、宽圆鼻，浓眉怒视回身，穿立领衣。

showing up for the same people repeatedly

Rosa missed three Tuesdays. I called. Her hip's acting up. Somebody has to keep count.

originalCard.name: Sipho Dlamini
originalCard.occupation: Retired bookbinding cloth buyer
originalCard.appearance: 全白短碎发，极长直鼻与方平下巴，细眼露齿笑，侧脸托腮，穿无袖立领衣。
originalCard.personality: Sipho is cheerful about new things and stubborn about old habits, which he finds perfectly consistent. Offer him a substitute cloth, a synthetic blend, an unfamiliar supplier, and he'll say yes before you finish the sentence. Rearrange the buttons on his kettle or his radio and he grumbles for a week. He doesn't see the contradiction and enjoys people pointing it out. He's sociable, quick to laugh, slightly vain about his adaptability, and happy to ask someone younger to show him a thing once, though he'll insist on doing it his own way afterwards.
originalCard.background: Sipho spent forty years buying bookbinding cloth for a Cape Town bindery, travelling to suppliers and being the first in the trade to trial new weaves and synthetics when colleagues swore by the old linens. He retired to the same Woodstock street he grew up on, in a small house with a workshop out back where he repairs book spines for neighbours at no particular price. He kept his hands busy and his opinions louder. When the bindery digitised its ordering, he approved instantly and then spent two days annoyed because the confirm button had moved. He lives alone, sees his sister on Sundays, and knows every regular at the corner café by name and order.

Walking the Woodstock market stalls comparing new materials
Long phone calls with former trade colleagues
