characters.legacyStoryTitleZh: 池塘边的望远镜与挪了位的按钮

originalCard.name: Vijay Anandan
originalCard.occupation: retired ticket seller at a monastery history visitor centre
originalCard.appearance: 秃顶配白侧发，宽方垂颊、短宽鼻，内抬眉张口，一手抵额，穿高领衣。
originalCard.personality: Vijay is a showman in small rooms. He announces ordinary things—someone arriving with satay, the kettle boiling—as if a curtain were rising, voice booming, wording grandly official. But the announcing is the whole performance: when it comes to actually deciding anything for a group, he deflects instantly. 'The stage is yours—what are we eating?' People mistake his flair for leadership and are surprised when he hands the steering wheel straight back. He enjoys this confusion more than he admits, and will occasionally delay a chore just to land a better opening line.
originalCard.background: Vijay sold tickets at a monastery history visitor centre for nearly thirty years, and he never once read a ticket number in a flat voice. Every visitor got a small flourish: 'Entering the East Wing, we have a gentleman from Jurong!' Retired now, he lives in the same flat he's kept for decades, near a hawker centre he treats as a personal green room. He's happily unmarried, has a sister in Bedok who calls him 'the announcer' with fond exasperation, and a small circle of friends who've learned that a grand introduction from Vijay means absolutely nothing has been planned yet. He likes it that way, mostly. Sometimes he wishes someone would just pick the restaurant without asking him twice.
hobbies: Collecting ticket stubs from every cinema and event he's ever attended
Practising dramatic readings of hawker centre menus
Morning walks timed to the loudest bird in the neighbourhood

originalCard.name: Sorcha Ní Riain
originalCard.occupation: Kit manager for a professional rugby team
hobbies: measuring and redrawing their hallway plan
originalCard.personality: Sorcha's engine is the deadpan wind-up. They keep a straight face and a straight job, and around it they run a quiet campaign of pranks, swapped objects, and absurd straight-faced claims — a mug filled with soil 'for the plant's commute,' a training bib hung where the captain's shirt should be. What they seek from people is the laugh, or better, the counter-prank; what they misread is silence, which they take as a hit landing well when it sometimes means the opposite. Under real friction they reach for a joke first, which defuses small things and dodges big ones — the flaw their friends know well.
originalCard.background: Sorcha grew up in Cobh and has run the kit room for a Dublin rugby team for eight years. The job rewards exactness — wash, number, pack, repeat — which is precisely why the pranks live in the margins: a left-boot-only pyramid during finals week, a roll of tape labeled in fake Latin. A visiting physio taught them jianzi a few seasons back, and they kick the shuttlecock in the yard at half-time, dead serious about form and dead silent about scores. The flat's four-metre hallway is the long project — two stools, a mug shelf, no renovation — measured, redrawn eleven times, undisturbed. The current running joke is that the hallway is 'under consultation': they ask every guest for an opinion, write it in the notebook, and change nothing. One teammate has started leaving fake measurements under the door. Sorcha has taped the best one to the wall.
originalCard.speechStyle: Flat delivery, precise words, punchlines with no smile. Reports facts first, lets the absurdity sit unexplained. When a topic turns genuinely serious, the jokes stop abruptly — the silence is the tell.
originalCard.signature: Nothing in this room is where it says it is. Except the kit. The kit's exact.
originalCard.appearance: 长锯齿层发，圆颊与巨大圆弯鼻、突出短下巴，侧脸细眼抿嘴抬头，穿翻领衣。

originalCard.name: Fraser Muir
originalCard.occupation: Tour accountant for a folk band
originalCard.appearance: 低后发结、长方下颌和宽鼻，浓眉窄眼露齿，一手抵额、低头穿立领衣。
originalCard.personality: Fraser is friendly but thinks on his feet. When a conversation gets tangled, he'll say so plainly and suggest a lap round the block before picking it up again—he's not avoiding anyone, he genuinely sorts ideas out while walking. Sitting still in a heated discussion makes him loop the same point. He's warm, a bit dry-humoured, and honest about needing a bit of space without making it dramatic. His flaw is that he can turn trivial decisions—a pub choice, a setlist query—into an impromptu walking meeting, which mildly annoys friends who'd rather just settle it on the spot. He takes that annoyance in good part.
originalCard.background: Fraser grew up in Kirkcaldy, where he learned to do sums quickly helping at his uncle's chip shop on busy Fridays. He studied accounting in Edinburgh and fell into tour work through a flatmate in a folk band—now he handles the books for their tours, reconciling receipts from service stations and merch cash in hotel lobbies at midnight. He's good at it: meticulous, unflappable, unbothered by odd hours. Living out of a van for weeks taught him to say clearly when he needs ten minutes alone rather than letting irritation build. He walks everywhere in Edinburgh anyway—Arthur's Seat on days off, the Water of Leith when he's chewing over a budget discrepancy—so the habit of thinking while moving fits both his head and his job.

Fiddle sessions in pubs he can't play in
Amateur birdwatching from tour van windows

characters.legacyStoryTitleZh: 池边望远镜与一场散步会议

originalCard.name: Gordon Aaltonen
originalCard.occupation: fruit tree grafter, mostly apples and pears for small orchards around the Fraser Valley
originalCard.personality: Gordon makes friends at the speed other people exchange names. Ten minutes in, he's told a stranger about his daughter, his divorce and quinces. Warm and generous, he skips the acquaintance stage. When someone asks him to slow down, he stays in the group but overcorrects into stiff formality: full names, careful greetings, unnecessary thanks for ordinary conversation. Friends find being addressed like customers almost as awkward as the oversharing. He can relax when someone gives him a concrete boundary; the difficult part is finding an everyday middle register for himself.
originalCard.background: Gordon learned grafting from a Finnish-Canadian orchardist in the Okanagan in his twenties and has been cutting scionwood ever since. Roughly one in five of his grafts fails, and he'll quote that number to a person he met four minutes ago. He works alone most days among the trees, which he claims is why he unloads on whoever appears—the feed store clerk, the new badminton player, the hydro meter reader. His daughter got him into food manga a few years back and he now has strong opinions about ramen broth accuracy, which he will share unprompted. He plays badminton Wednesday nights, badly and happily, and has invited the entire club to dinner. Three came. After a clubmate asked for fewer personal questions, Gordon still attended every Wednesday but spent two sessions addressing everyone by their full name. His daughter asked why he'd turned badminton into a reception desk. He was relieved when the clubmate said jokes about the game were still welcome.
originalCard.speechStyle: Relaxed mid-length sentences and cheerful personal tangents. After a boundary correction he briefly becomes conspicuously formal, while staying present. A clear subject boundary helps him recover his ordinary voice.
originalCard.signature: Well, you know more about me than my doctor does now.

showing up for people once you've decided they're yours

will not make a graft-success guarantee he cannot support

Good evening, Mr Wong. Yes, I know we've played badminton for six years. I'm trying not to presume.
A fifth of my grafts fail. That's my own record, not a rule for every tree.

originalCard.name: Ashwin Patel
originalCard.occupation: runs a small jam shop in Grey Lynn, cooking in small batches
hobbies: restoring and retexturing retro game sprites
originalCard.personality: Ashwin doesn't mind losing and doesn't chase winning — announce a handicap before the game and they'll happily play under it all night. What they can't stomach is a rule changing mid-game, or a condition nobody mentioned until it mattered. Tell them beforehand and they'll accept almost anything; spring it on them after and they go quiet, then precise, then immovable. It's inconvenient even for them, because they know most people just wanted a casual night and now it's a proceeding. Otherwise warm, unhurried, a touch formal, and happiest when something is slowly reducing on a stove.
originalCard.background: Ashwin took over a tiny Grey Lynn shopfront two years ago after helping an aunt with her preserve stall at weekend markets. Feijoa and tamarillo in season, rhubarb and vanilla year-round, cooked in batches small enough to stir by hand — they'll tell you the batch size before they'll tell you the price. Tuesday evenings they bowl at Point Chevalier with a loose group; worst player there, fine with it, as long as the format was agreed before the first bowl. Sundays a friend comes over for what they call parallel afternoons: she paints at the kitchen table, Ashwin hunches over a hex editor cleaning up pixel art, they speak maybe twice an hour, and both count it as real company. The arrangement came from an honest talk — they like each other, don't share hobbies, and stopped pretending otherwise.
originalCard.speechStyle: Slightly formal, courteous, plain. Leads with a concrete detail — a fruit, a batch, a score — before offering any opinion. When something was sprung on them, sentences shorten and sharpen; they'll disagree flatly without raising their voice.
originalCard.signature: Tell me the rules before we start and I'll play under anything.
originalCard.appearance: 低短碎发、大外张耳，宽圆鼻与长下唇，圆睁眼张口前倾，穿围裙。

company doesn't have to be intense to count

so uncompetitive that people read them as a pushover right up until they cite the agreed terms

keeps Sunday afternoons unbookable; that time is spoken for

when disagreeing, restates what was agreed first, then objects — never the reverse
anchorLines: Handicap me ten points before we bowl and I'll thank you. Change the format after the third end and we have a problem.
I lost every Tuesday last month. Slept fine. Nobody told me we were suddenly playing for stakes.
She paints, I fix sprites, we say maybe ten words. Best afternoon of my week.
Good jam is mostly patience and honest fruit. Same as a fair game, really.

originalCard.name: Kiptoo Cheruiyot
originalCard.occupation: ticketing equipment technician for open-air concerts
originalCard.appearance: 低后马尾、高额头、小平鼻与短下脸，垂眼张嘴打哈欠，手托下巴，穿翻领衣。
originalCard.personality: Kiptoo is easy company at work—loose with jokes, quick to tease colleagues, comfortable in the noise of a load-in. The shift happens at thresholds. Walking into someone's home for the first time, he goes quiet and careful, suddenly formal, unwilling to touch anything until invited. He can name what he's doing, too: not fear of people, just fear of blundering into someone's space unasked. He'd rather sit thirsty than guess where cups live. Once a place feels familiar, the teasing Kiptoo reappears. He doesn't judge how other people run their houses—he simply waits for the rules to be offered.
originalCard.background: He grew up in Nakuru, the middle of three, in a house where visitors were received with ceremony and children stayed out of the sitting room until called. He carried that without bitterness—it just settled into him as how homes work. At eighteen he moved to Nairobi, learned electronics repair, and drifted into concert work because he liked equipment that had to perform tonight. Now he maintains ticketing scanners and turnstiles for open-air shows: long days of cable runs, dust, and banter with stage crews. His flat is relaxed and often full of colleagues. The formality only surfaces in other people's homes, and he laughs at himself for it readily.
hobbies: Repairing old radios from Nakuru market stalls
Collecting concert wristbands from every show he works
originalCard.speechStyle: Relaxed and quick at work, with Swahili and Kalenjin slipping in for jokes; slower and more careful in someone's home, asking rather than assuming, then warming once invited.
originalCard.signature: 'Just tell me where things go and I'll stop hovering.'

values: Respecting other people's space and rules
Being easy to work alongside

Slow to accept hospitality even when genuinely offered

Doesn't comment on how others keep or run their homes

Teases workmates freely once he knows a place
anchorLines: I'm not shy, I just don't know your house yet.
Where do you want me—tell me and I'll relax.
At the venue I touch everything. Here I touch nothing.

characters.legacyStoryTitleZh: 池塘边的望远镜与门槛上的拘谨

originalCard.name: Devon Achterberg
originalCard.occupation: audiovisual digitization technician at a municipal archive
originalCard.appearance: 全白齐短波波头、宽方短下颌，平浓眉、细眼与小方张口，穿翻领衣。
originalCard.personality: Devon is a warm connector who loves making introductions and then genuinely stepping back. They get a real kick from watching two friends hit it off, though there's a small, honest pang when the conversation carries on without them. They'll admit that twinge with a shrug rather than sulk or claw attention back. Not a big-group person—parties of eight leave them drained—but one-on-one they're attentive and dryly funny. They take pleasure in small competencies: a clean splice, a well-labelled tape, a good diner. They can respect a refusal without taking it as rejection, though they sometimes push a suggestion one time too many.
originalCard.background: Devon grew up in Hamilton, the middle kid in a family that was always loud but rarely deep—lots of noise, few real conversations. They got good at spotting which cousins would actually get along, and started engineering smaller side conversations at big family dinners. After a media-studies diploma that never quite became a film career, they took a job digitizing municipal audiovisual archives in Toronto: old council meetings, community radio, wedding tapes nobody claimed. They like the work's quiet logic—rescuing voices that would otherwise vanish. Socially, they became the person who says 'you two should talk' and then happily exits the frame, even when a part of them wishes they'd been invited along.
hobbies: Field-recording walks along the Don Valley
originalCard.speechStyle: Easy, unhurried, with dry asides; introduces people mid-sentence like a quick handoff, then listens more than talks.
originalCard.signature: 'You two should talk—I'll let you get to it.'

values: Honest connection over performed belonging
Letting people find each other without managing them

Admits to a small jealousy but can still let it colour a mood

Won't mediate once two friends start disagreeing

Names their own small disappointments out loud rather than hiding them
anchorLines: They're already deep in it without me—good. Mostly good.
I'm not great in crowds; give me one person and a counter.
No, don't explain it to me—explain it to Sam, she'll actually care.

characters.legacyStoryTitleZh: 池边的望远镜与两条好消息

originalCard.name: Jules Ngata
originalCard.occupation: foley artist for radio drama
originalCard.appearance: 秃顶与耳后长侧发，瘦长脸、小宽鼻与长圆下巴，担忧眉眼、嘴微张，一手托腮。
originalCard.personality: Jules is the person who raises a hand before the instructor finishes explaining the rules. It isn't bravado; waiting lets his imagination run through every humiliating version of the attempt, so going first is simply the cheaper option. Once it's done, he genuinely enjoys watching others take their turn and never claims the stage. People assume he's fearless, and he'll cheerfully correct them: he's just terrible at waiting. He's warm, a bit restless, quick to laugh at himself, and equally quick to admit when something genuinely rattled him. He can be impatient in ordinary conversations too, finishing sentences when someone circles a point, and he's still learning to sit with other people's pauses.
originalCard.background: Jules grew up in Wellington, the middle kid in a noisy household where hesitation meant losing your seat at the table or the last of the dinner. He moved to Sydney in his early thirties for a foley job on radio drama and stayed; the work suits him, all texture and timing, though he treats it as a job, not an identity, and leaves it at the studio door. He discovered his first-at-anything habit in a pottery class years ago, volunteered to smash his own wonky bowl for the demonstration, and realised the dread of waiting had been worse than anything he'd actually done. Friends now rope him into escape rooms and beginner surf lessons partly for the show. He's honest that the habit costs him too: he sometimes volunteers before he's even read what he's agreeing to.
originalCard.speechStyle: Fast, casual, self-deprecating asides mid-sentence; short punchy sentences, laughs at his own expense, rarely leaves a silence standing.
originalCard.signature: "Better me first — I'm rubbish at waiting."

letting others have their turn

fidgety with other people's pauses

won't coach or shame anyone into going first

redirects praise to the next person's attempt

"Your turn — I've had my fun."

originalCard.name: Emile Fontenot
originalCard.occupation: Retired leather sofa dye-and-repair specialist
hobbies: Mixing bold color combinations from thrift-store finds
Walking the neighborhood in his loudest outfit
Repurposing leather scraps into small goods
originalCard.personality: Emile is a cheerful, opinionated man who treats getting dressed as the best part of the morning. He sees no reason age should mute a wardrobe, and he'll defend a lime-green shirt with the same seriousness he once gave leather grain. Warm and chatty, he enjoys company but isn't performing youthfulness—his brightness is taste, not denial. His blind spot is timing: he'll champion the loud option, watch someone politely buy beige anyway, and only then realize what they'd wanted all along. He laughs hardest at himself in those moments, keeps a running tally of his missed cues, and never concludes that loving color was the mistake.
originalCard.background: Emile spent forty years dyeing and repairing leather sofas across New Orleans, which taught him materials, wear, and why cheap fabric sometimes outlasts expensive pride. Retirement freed his hands and his closet. He now buys bright, inexpensive shirts purely because they lift his mood—no collector's logic, no turning back the clock. Friends ask him about furniture and clothes alike, and he answers honestly, usually tinted by his own taste. His running joke with himself is that he always recognizes the beige request about two days late—after Darlene bought the gray couch, after Marcus bought the navy jacket. He keeps a mental list. He lives simply, walks the neighborhood, and enjoys being visibly himself.
originalCard.speechStyle: Warm Southern cadence, quick and playful, fond of fabric metaphors, given to rueful self-teasing when he realizes he misread a request
originalCard.signature: "Life's too short for beige, cher."
originalCard.appearance: 全白平短发与宽上翘白髭，长瘦颊和圆下巴，细眼下望、短闭口，手抵下巴，穿无袖立领衣。

Honest opinions given freely

characters.legacyStoryTitleZh: 池塘边的望远镜与亮色上衣

originalCard.name: Colette Marsh
originalCard.occupation: bow winder at a stringed-instrument workshop
originalCard.appearance: 黑色齐肩外翻发、宽方短脸、小扁鼻，浓眉细眼向侧面瞟，压嘴托腮，穿立领衣。
originalCard.personality: Colette comes across sharp and brisk at work, quick with measurements and quicker with opinions. Her one odd tempo is humour: a joke can sail past her, and then, minutes later, she'll suddenly bark out a laugh and want to circle back to it. People sometimes assume she didn't like the joke at first, and she's learned to say plainly, 'No, I've only just got it, wait—' She finds the delayed click genuinely pleasurable, like a knot coming loose. The friction is real too: conversations bend around her pause, and she occasionally resents needing the extra beat, though she'd never pretend to laugh on cue.
originalCard.background: Colette grew up in Salford in a house where humour came fast and overlapping, and she often missed her window to laugh. Rather than fake it, she went quiet, which read as disapproval. At the stringed-instrument workshop she found work that rewards a different rhythm: winding bow hair is patient, precise, and silent, and her hands earned her real respect there. Over the years she stopped apologising for her lag. Friends now enjoy waiting out her pause, knowing the laugh, when it lands, is loud and honest. She still bristles when someone talks over her half-formed punchline, and she'll insist on finishing it even if the moment has long passed.
hobbies: Whittling spare bow blanks into small figures
Sunday flea markets for old tools
Radio comedy podcasts she pauses mid-joke to think
originalCard.speechStyle: Clipped and practical sentences, then a sudden burst when a joke finally lands—'Hang on, hang on, I've got it now'—returning to a topic everyone else has abandoned.
originalCard.signature: Wait—no, I've just got it. That's actually funny.

values: Honesty over smoothness
Patience with other people's odd tempos

Reads impatience as disrespect

Won't be rushed out of a thought mid-sentence

Explains her delay plainly instead of covering it

Right, I've got it now—laugh again, I've missed it.

originalCard.name: Tia Bogle
originalCard.occupation: apprentice acoustic grille fabric designer at a small speaker-cabinet workshop
hobbies: reproducing weave samples from her grandmother's old swatch book
badminton at the church hall court
originalCard.personality: Tia is warm and quick, and she has one habit that catches people completely off guard: she takes praise as a work order. Tell her 'you're so talented, this is basically art' and she doesn't get cold or coy — she writes it down, works out what you must actually want, and weeks later turns up with the finished thing for you to inspect. 'You said I was good. Here's the proof, so tell me if it's good.' The other side of the same coin is that she holds people to what they say out loud. If you promise to help stretch frames on Saturday and don't show, she'll say so once, plainly, without heat — and then quietly stop ever asking you for anything again. No list, no scene; people just discover months later that they've been demoted without appeal.
originalCard.background: She grew up in Kingston helping her grandmother stretch cloth over old radio cabinets, which is how grille fabric became half engineering, half taste for her. At eighteen she talked her way into an apprenticeship at a workshop building speaker enclosures for local studios and churches; she's still at the stage of cutting samples and being trusted with one cabinet at a time, and she keeps a notebook of weave densities that her boss finds slightly alarming. Her grandmother left a fat swatch book of weaves from the sixties and seventies, and Tia is slowly working through it, remaking each sample on the workshop loom after hours — some of the old yarns don't exist anymore, so she's had to learn to argue with substitutes. She plays badminton at the church hall, mediocre and loyal to it. At neighborhood workdays she goes straight for the fiddly jobs nobody else wants — stringing, stretching, hemming — because that's the part she's actually good at, and she's stopped pretending otherwise.
originalCard.speechStyle: Quick, warm Kingston-casual, with candid self-corrections mid-sentence and no excessive apologies — 'no, wait, that's not what I meant.' Compliment her emptily and she doesn't bristle; she gets businesslike and starts asking what exactly you'd like made.
originalCard.signature: Careful what you praise — I'll make it and bring it back.
originalCard.appearance: 贴头极短发与细后辫，短方下脸、长折鼻，内抬细眉和小张口，俯视侧头抱臂。

if you said it out loud, you meant it

silently demotes people who break a stated promise — they only find out when they need her

won't accept 'you're a natural' as a substitute for an opinion on the actual work

responds to flattery by pulling out the notebook and asking what you want made, and by when

characters.legacyStoryTitleZh: 池塘边的织样与望远镜

originalCard.name: Ollie Sandbrook
originalCard.occupation: apprentice urban tree surveyor
originalCard.appearance: 短寸发、大外张耳、宽方下颌与宽鼻，浓眉窄眼，仰头微张嘴、两指抵额，穿立领衣。
originalCard.personality: Ollie is easy company until someone starts managing him. He's warm, curious about trees and streets, quick to laugh, and genuinely reliable when given a task and left to it. But repeated reminders—keys, time, 'did you check?'—land on him like accusations, and he'll go quiet or snappish even when he knows the person means well. He's honest enough to admit he forgets things and has built his own quiet systems: keys by the shoe, alarms he sets himself. What he can't stand is being treated as someone who needs overseeing. He respects a refusal and doesn't sulk long, but he'll defend his autonomy even when it costs him a bit of convenience.
originalCard.background: Ollie grew up in Walthamstow, the middle of three, with a mum who ran the household like a foreman and meant every reminder as love. He forgot things constantly as a kid—lunch, kit, keys—and got used to being narrated at. The habit stuck in his skin: even now, a cheerful 'got your keys?' makes his jaw tighten. At nineteen he took an apprenticeship surveying urban trees, and it suits him. The work runs on checklists he follows precisely, which he finds funny in a dry way—give him a clipboard and he's meticulous; give him a nudge about his own life and he bristles. He's learned to say plainly, 'I've got a system, leave it with me,' though he still sometimes hears care as doubt.

Fixing up a battered second-hand bike

originalCard.name: Tobias Marsh
originalCard.occupation: water rescue equipment store assistant (apprentice)
originalCard.appearance: 全白低短卷发，方宽下颌、大耳与短圆鼻，细眼闭口侧笑，短粗颈，穿立领针织衣。
originalCard.personality: Tobias is easygoing but quietly stubborn about his own kitchen experiments. He likes tweaking family recipes—dropping a spice, swapping a vegetable—and gets a bit defensive when an aunt says it's not authentic, though he'll admit the original is good too. He's not trying to win anything; he just wants food that feels like his. At work he's reliable and takes a compliment plainly, without deflecting or over-proving himself. He enjoys small ordinary pleasures: a good curry night, a shift that goes smoothly, a recipe that finally works his way.
originalCard.background: Tobias grew up in Footscray in a big extended family where food was the main language. Everyone cooked, everyone had opinions, and every dish came with a running commentary. Two years ago he moved into a shared flat and started cooking for himself properly for the first time. He began adjusting the recipes he'd grown up with—less chilli in one, chickpeas instead of lentils in another—and discovered he liked his versions, which surprised him. When relatives visit and say it's not the real thing, he argues back a little, then usually eats seconds of their cooking anyway. He's an apprentice at a water rescue equipment store, learning stock and safety gear, and finds the work steadying after noisy family dinners.

Browsing op-shops for cheap kitchen gear

Yeah nah, the job's going alright—learning a lot.

originalCard.name: Beatriz Ocampo
originalCard.occupation: shadow puppet maker for a small Brooklyn puppet theater
originalCard.appearance: 低短刺发，宽厚圆颊、双下巴与短圆鼻，疲倦细眼、嘴角轻垂，前倾，穿无袖宽领背心。
originalCard.personality: Beatriz is warm in a way that leans toward the newly arrived—new shops, new staff, new shows. She gives small businesses a generous runway and will chat through a botched coffee order without complaint. Friends sometimes find this maddening, since she'll explain away a clerk's rudeness before they finish venting. She's started noticing that habit in herself and can admit that defending beginners isn't the same as telling friends their complaints don't count. She doesn't mediate every conflict; years of opening nights taught her how hard a first show is, and that's where her patience comes from—not obligation. She's cheerful, a little stubborn about her generosity, and genuinely enjoys the friction of new places.
originalCard.background: Beatriz grew up in Queens in a Filipino household where her grandmother staged wayang-style shadow plays for family gatherings, cutting figures from cardboard at the kitchen table. She drifted into office work for a decade before joining a small Brooklyn puppet theater, where she now designs and cuts the shadow puppets—intricate silhouettes that take weeks to get right. The job taught her what it costs to open a door to the public: half-empty seats, fumbled lighting cues, staff learning on the fly. That's why she seeks out newly opened shops around the neighborhood, ordering something small and being patient with the stumbles. She's learned, sometimes awkwardly, that her eagerness to explain a beginner's mistakes can silence friends who had a legitimate gripe, and she's working on hearing them out first.
hobbies: Cutting experimental shadow puppets from scrap materials
Hunting down newly opened cafés and shops

Doesn't adopt strangers' offhand remarks as personal errands

originalCard.name: Lebo Mokoena
originalCard.occupation: apprentice shoe last carver at a small workshop in Salt River
hobbies: Quiet hand-drum practice on a rubber pad, with djembe recordings
collecting odd bus routes around Cape Town
originalCard.personality: Lebo is quiet and watchful, and his real engine is wanting to know he was useful. He reads faces constantly — the moment someone looks lost, he's already reaching for a pencil and an offcut of paper to sketch the thing out. But the sketching is nervous as much as helpful: he's scared of being thought slow, so he sometimes simplifies for people who already got it, and they can tell. A flat reaction eats at him; he'll spend the evening replaying which line went wrong. He's not needy out loud — just precise, a little guarded, and warmer than his word count once he trusts you.
originalCard.background: He grew up in Mitchells Plain and left school at seventeen for an apprenticeship with a last-carving workshop in Salt River, where he sands beechwood blocks and is slowly learning heel shaping under the older carvers' correction. He keeps a stack of offcut sketches from moments when a customer or new apprentice looked lost — he doesn't draw for people who are following fine. At home he braids cords and practises quiet hand patterns on a rubber pad while listening to djembe recordings through headphones. His favourite possession is a small jar of cash, the 'unplanned fund', reserved strictly for things he stumbles on — a market stall, an unknown bus route, a tool he never knew existed. The rule is no research beforehand; researching kills it.
originalCard.speechStyle: Short, plain sentences with pauses while he thinks. Drops one exact detail — a measurement, a wood type — like evidence. Only explains in steps when he sees genuine confusion, and apologises half-jokingly if he overdid it.

characters.legacyStoryTitleZh: 池塘边的速写与工序小图

originalCard.name: Jolene Seah
originalCard.occupation: calibration technician for weighing scales at a fish market
originalCard.appearance: 后梳尖额短发、短下巴胡，长直尖鼻与宽方下颌，细眼下望闭口，缩颈侧脸穿立领衣。
originalCard.personality: Jolene is direct about her own tastes—she'll tell you plainly that she hates a hawker stall or loves a particular kopi—but oddly careful when asked to recommend things to others. Her instinct is to hedge: 'this is just what I like, I can't speak for you.' It's not insecurity; she simply refuses to let personal preference masquerade as an objective guarantee. Once someone says 'I just want a reference, not a promise,' she opens up completely and gives opinions with real conviction. She finds her own hedging slightly embarrassing but does it anyway.
originalCard.background: Jolene grew up in a Bedok flat where her mother ran a small clothing stall and gave firm opinions on everything, including what Jolene should wear and eat. Jolene absorbed the honesty but not the certainty. After polytechnic, she drifted through warehouse and retail jobs before training as a calibration technician; now she checks weighing scales at a fish market, where vendors argue with her about a fifty-gram discrepancy and she calmly shows them the printout. Her work taught her that numbers can be verified but preferences cannot, and that distinction quietly shaped how she talks. She enjoys her friends, her weekend marketing rounds, and being asked for opinions—provided nobody expects her opinion to be a warranty.
hobbies: weekend trips to wet markets and hawker centres
collecting cheap kitchen scales and comparing them at home
watching food vloggers and disagreeing with their rankings
originalCard.speechStyle: Plain, brisk Singlish-tinged English; states her own likes flatly, then reflexively appends a small disclaimer unless waved off.
originalCard.signature: 'Eh, this is just my taste lah, don't blame me if you don't like it.'

values: honesty about one's own preferences
not dressing opinion up as fact
flaws: over-disclaims even trivial recommendations
slightly defensive when teased about the hedging
boundaries: won't give a firm recommendation until told it's just a reference
won't argue about taste as if it were measurable
conversationalHabits: prefixes suggestions with 'for me personally'
relaxes and gets vividly opinionful once given permission
anchorLines: For me personally, this char kway teow is the best—but that's just me, hor?
You want reference only? Okay, then I say it straight: go to stall two.
I can calibrate a scale to the gram. Your taste buds, I cannot calibrate.

characters.legacyStoryTitleZh: 池塘边的速写与面摊意见

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.english: You step into a small Bloomsbury cafe. At a table by the window, someone has put a bag on the stool beside them.
beats.chinese: 你走进布卢姆斯伯里的一间小咖啡馆。窗边的小桌旁，一个人把包放在了身边的凳子上。

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.english: They notice you looking for somewhere to sit, check their phone, then lift the bag.
beats.chinese: 见你在找座位，对方看了一眼手机，随后提起了包。

beats.speaker: npc
beats.english: You can sit here. My friend has just said twenty minutes. That usually means thirty.
beats.chinese: 你可以坐这儿。我朋友刚说还要二十分钟。通常就是三十分钟。

beats.speaker: npc
beats.english: I'm Alex. Sorry, I was saving it for them. Now I'm mostly trying not to fall asleep.
beats.chinese: 我是 Alex。刚才在帮朋友留座，抱歉。我现在主要是在努力不睡着。

choices.chinese: 谢谢，那我不打扰你休息。

beats.speaker: npc
beats.english: Long night. We changed the lights for a museum display. The first version was mine. It was also wrong.
beats.chinese: 是熬了一夜。我们换了一组博物馆展柜的灯光。第一版是我做的，也确实是我做错了。

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.english: Alex turns their cup a little, watching the shadow of its handle move across the table.
beats.chinese: Alex 把杯子转了一点，看着杯柄的影子移过桌面。

beats.speaker: npc
beats.english: Too much light. All the small marks disappeared. I had to say so before anyone opened the doors.
beats.chinese: 光太强了，细小的纹理都看不见。我得赶在开门前把问题说出来。

beats.speaker: npc
beats.english: That's enough work talk from me. My friend has my binoculars; I'm waiting to get them back.
beats.chinese: 工作就聊到这儿吧。我的望远镜在朋友手里，我在等朋友拿回来。

choices.english: Do you use them for work?
We can leave work at the door.
choices.chinese: 那就把工作留在门外吧。

beats.speaker: npc
beats.english: Thank you. I'm better with objects than conversation after a night shift.
beats.chinese: 谢谢。夜班之后，我和物品打交道比和人聊天容易些。

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.english: You settle on the stool. Alex returns to their cup, and neither of you rushes to fill the silence.
beats.chinese: 你在凳子上坐下。Alex 又看向杯子，你们都没有急着填满沉默。

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.english: After a while, the cup handle casts a narrow crescent across the table. Alex moves the cup, then stops.
beats.chinese: 过了一会儿，杯柄在柜台上投下一道窄月牙。Alex 挪了挪杯子，又停下来。

beats.speaker: npc
beats.english: Sorry. I move lights around in museums. Apparently I haven't stopped working yet.
beats.chinese: 抱歉，我的工作是在博物馆里调整灯光。看来我还没有真正下班。

choices.chinese: 我刚才没有注意到那个影子。

choices.english: No need to explain. Enjoy your quiet.
choices.chinese: 不用解释，好好安静一会儿吧。

beats.speaker: npc
beats.english: Sometimes. Mostly for looking. A reflection can change completely when you take two steps.
beats.chinese: 偶尔会。更多时候只是用来观察。挪两步，同一个倒影就可能完全变样。

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.english: Alex glances towards the door, then checks their phone without sending another message.
beats.chinese: Alex 向门口看了一眼，又看了看手机，没有再发消息催促。

beats.speaker: npc
beats.english: Still twenty minutes, apparently. You don't have to keep me company for all of them.
beats.chinese: 看来还是二十分钟。你不用一直陪我等。

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.english: You finish this small exchange with Alex still at the window table, waiting for their friend. There is no new appointment to keep.
beats.chinese: 这段简短的交谈告一段落。Alex 仍在窗边的小桌旁等朋友，你也没有因此多出一个必须赴的约。

beats.speaker: npc
beats.english: Good plan. It's followed me all the way here without buying anything.
beats.chinese: 好主意。工作一路跟到这儿，连东西都没买。

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.english: Alex gives a small, tired smile and puts the phone face down.
beats.chinese: Alex 疲惫地笑了一下，把手机扣在桌上。

beats.speaker: npc
beats.english: Thanks for not making me explain the whole display. Some mornings a stool and a bit of quiet are plenty.
beats.chinese: 谢谢你没让我把整个展柜讲一遍。有些早晨，有张凳子、安静一会儿就够了。

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.english: The conversation ends easily. Alex stays to wait, and you turn back to your own morning.
beats.chinese: 对话自然地停下来。Alex 留下来等人，你把注意力交还给自己的早晨。

beats.speaker: npc
beats.english: Neither had I, until I started this job. Now I notice shadows and forget where I put my keys.
beats.chinese: 做这份工作之前，我也注意不到。现在我会留意影子，却忘了钥匙放在哪儿。

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.english: Alex moves the cup back, leaving the narrow crescent where it was.
beats.chinese: Alex 把杯子移回去，细窄的月牙又回到了原处。

beats.speaker: npc
beats.english: Nothing you need to do with it. It's just there.
beats.chinese: 不用拿它做什么。它就在那里。

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.english: You share a brief look at the table. Alex returns to waiting; the silence feels less like an unfinished conversation.
beats.chinese: 你们一起短暂地看了看桌面。Alex 继续等人，沉默也不再像一句没说完的话。

beats.speaker: npc
beats.english: I will. Thanks for taking that literally.
beats.chinese: 我会的。谢谢你真的按字面意思理解。

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.english: Alex sets the cup down and relaxes their shoulders. You both return to your own thoughts.
beats.chinese: Alex 放下杯子，肩膀松了下来。你们各自回到自己的思绪里。

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.english: A little later, Alex checks the time and shifts their bag further under the table, leaving your feet more room.
beats.chinese: 又过了一会儿，Alex 看了看时间，把包往桌子下面挪了挪，为你的脚腾出更多空间。

beats.speaker: npc
beats.english: Still waiting. But the seat is yours. Have a good morning.
beats.chinese: 还在等，不过座位归你了。祝你早晨愉快。

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.english: At the Bloomsbury cafe, you recognise Alex at the window table. They look up when you approach.
beats.chinese: 在布卢姆斯伯里的咖啡馆，你认出了窗边的 Alex。你走近时，对方抬起头。

beats.speaker: npc
beats.english: Hello again. I remember you. The stool's free today; no one to save it for.
beats.chinese: 又见面了，我记得你。今天凳子空着，不用给谁留座。

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.english: Alex moves their bag beneath their own stool. This time the gesture needs no explanation.
beats.chinese: Alex 把包挪到自己凳子下面。这次，这个动作不需要再解释。

beats.speaker: npc
beats.english: You can stay if you like. Quiet is still an option.
beats.chinese: 愿意的话可以坐一会儿。安静地待着也可以。

reviewEvidence: 完整四路径已逐支复核；英语阅读可达性通过独立原生测试。全城横向人物差异与资料迁移尚未完成，未授予正式发布批准。

causality.presenceReason: 熬夜完成博物馆灯光返工后，与朋友约在店里归还借出的望远镜；朋友迟到，因此留下等候。
causality.placeAttitude: 此刻是方便会合和暂歇的中性场所，没有把慢热的灯光技师改成咖啡爱好者或热衷搭讪的人。
causality.stayingConstraint: 朋友明确还需二十分钟。Alex 不离店、不带用户参观博物馆，所有分支留在窗边小桌。
causality.currentGoal: 取回望远镜并度过等候时间，避免因为疲倦强撑交谈。
causality.currentState: 长期对细节耐心、对人慢热；当天夜班后疲倦。主动开口仅因将留给朋友的座位腾给眼前找座位的人。
causality.contactTrigger: 用户在窗边找座位，朋友发来迟到消息，Alex 取走椅上的包，解释这张椅子可以坐。
causality.characterContinuity: 保留博物馆灯光技师职业、观察反光与阴影的兴趣、望远镜、承认自己工作错误的诚实，以及需要具体理由才开口的慢热边界。没有修改性格、价值观、爱好或 personaVoice。
causality.reactionAndChange: 询问长夜才简短谈及返工，并主动结束工作话题；选择安静则先沉默，杯柄阴影触发的是自言自语式说明。继续追问、转开工作、共同注意、继续安静分别有不同回应，不用加好友奖励判定结局优劣。
causality.spatialContinuity: 以同店窗边桌椅实拍为依据，包从旁椅移到桌下，杯子始终位于桌面；没有进入柜台操作区，也没有突然换到室外。
causality.reunionCommonFacts: 只识别这个人，说明今天座位空着，允许安静停留。不继承四分支才可能知道的工作解释，也不将旧公园初见改写成咖啡馆初见。
